data.title: Brown Butter-Chocolate Soufflé
data.source: Claire Ptak, Bon Appétit
data.description: A shared chocolate soufflé with a browned-butter crust and a soft, airy center, served straight from the oven.
data.prepTime: About 35 min, including overlapping butter chilling

scaling.reason: This batch fits one 1 1/2-quart soufflé dish. Changing the batter depth or vessel changes the rise and baking time; keep this batch and dish size together.

ingredients: --- Separate for the base and meringue ---
2 tbsp granulated sugar, approximate coating amount; tap out excess
7 oz (200 g) bittersweet chocolate, 65–70% cacao, chopped
--- Meringue, with the reserved egg whites ---

learning.focus: Lighten a chocolate base with meringue while preserving an evenly distributed egg-white foam
learning.outcome: A risen, lightly crusted top over a moist chocolate center, without large white pockets or a dense unmixed bottom.
before: Use a straight-sided 1 1/2-quart soufflé dish and leave room above it in the oven. A shallow baking dish or individual ramekins need different timing. Have plates and serving cream ready before the soufflé finishes baking.

Use room-temperature eggs and a clean, grease-free bowl for the whites. Keep yolk out of the whites when separating. If the eggs are still refrigerator-cold, allow extra preparation time rather than leaving them out for hours.

The 200 g sugar belongs entirely in the meringue. The roughly 2 tbsp coating sugar is additional, and some will be tapped out. All the browned butter coats the dish; none is mixed into the chocolate base.
Use the listed Morton kosher salt or the specific Diamond Crystal alternative below. Different crystal densities need different spoon measures; do not substitute the larger volume of fine salt.

checkpoints.cue: The milk solids are brown and smell toasted; after chilling, the butter is opaque and brushable.
checkpoints.why: Browning gives the coating its flavor. A spreadable coating stays on the sides instead of pooling at the bottom.

checkpoints.cue: The meringue is smooth and glossy, with peaks that hold their shape but bend at the tips.
checkpoints.why: A moist foam blends into the dense chocolate base more readily than dry clumps, so less folding is needed.

checkpoints.cue: The batter is light and mostly uniform, with no large white pockets or heavy chocolate layer at the bottom.
checkpoints.why: The first addition loosens the base; subsequent folds distribute the remaining foam without beating out its air.

checkpoints.cue: The top has risen and formed a light crust; the center moves gently rather than sloshing, and reaches at least 160°F / 71°C.
checkpoints.why: Texture cues show how the soufflé is setting, while a temperature check verifies the egg-dish cooking endpoint.

troubleshooting.problem: The butter smells bitter or has black specks
troubleshooting.cause: The milk solids scorched, especially if the butter stayed in the hot skillet.
troubleshooting.fix: Start the butter coating again. Burnt flavor cannot be removed by mixing it into the dish.

troubleshooting.problem: The meringue is clumpy and dull
troubleshooting.cause: The whites were beaten beyond the moist medium-peak stage.
troubleshooting.fix: For a dependable rise, remake the meringue with fresh whites and its measured sugar and cream of tartar. Do not beat the clumps into the chocolate base.

troubleshooting.problem: The soufflé is dense or has a heavy layer at the bottom
troubleshooting.cause: The base was not lightened first, the mixture was not reached at the bottom, or prolonged mixing deflated the foam.
troubleshooting.fix: Bake the mixed batter promptly; lost air cannot be restored by whipping it again. Next time stir in the first quarter of meringue completely, then sweep the spatula along the bottom with each fold.

troubleshooting.problem: The soufflé sinks after it leaves the oven
troubleshooting.cause: Some settling is normal as the hot foam cools; a liquid center can also mean insufficient baking.
troubleshooting.fix: Serve immediately. If the center is still fluid or below 160°F / 71°C, return it to the oven until cooked, accepting that its original height may not return.

substitutions.alternative: 1 1/2 tsp Diamond Crystal kosher salt for this whole batch
substitutions.effect: These are the two density-specific alternatives for this formula. Use one, not both; do not substitute fine salt by either spoon measure without a supported conversion.

substitutions.alternative: Omit it
substitutions.effect: The chocolate and browned-butter flavors remain; no replacement liquid is needed for this optional ingredient.

substitutions.alternative: Another plain chocolate within the specified 65–70% cacao range
substitutions.effect: Flavor varies, but keep the 200 g amount. Milk chocolate and unsweetened chocolate change both sweetness and the balance of the base.

learning.timing: Allow about 75 minutes from ready, room-temperature ingredients: about 35 minutes of preparation, including egg separation and the 20-minute butter chill overlapped with making the base and whipping the whites, followed by 35–40 minutes baking. Start the whites about halfway through the butter's chill so they are ready shortly before folding. A hand mixer, cold eggs, slower butter chilling or a slow-preheating oven may add time. Bake the finished batter promptly and serve straight away; there is no resting stage.
learning.storage: Best immediately; the airy texture does not keep. Refrigerate leftover portions in shallow containers within 2 hours, or 1 hour above 90°F / 32°C, and keep at 40°F / 4°C or below for up to 3–4 days. Reheat individual portions to 165°F / 74°C; expect a denser, pudding-like texture rather than a restored rise.

sources.title: Claire Ptak / Bon Appétit — Brown Butter Chocolate Soufflé, corrected February 2025
Lauren Weisenthal / Serious Eats — Chocolate soufflé and staged folding
Culinary Institute of America — Egg Cookery, soufflé folding and immediate service
Exploratorium — Egg proteins, foams and heating
FDA — Egg dishes, cooking temperature and leftover storage

components.name: Separate for the base and meringue

ingredients.name: granulated sugar
ingredients.preparation: approximate coating amount; tap out excess

components.name: Meringue, with the reserved egg whites

steps.title: Separate the eggs and heat the oven
steps.text: Separate {{ingredients}}, reserving all the whites in a clean, grease-free mixer bowl and all the yolks in a second bowl. Keep any yolk out of the whites. Set an oven rack in the middle and heat the oven to 375°F / 190°C. Have the remaining ingredients measured and plates ready before you begin mixing.

steps.title: Brown and cool the butter
steps.text: Melt {{ingredients}} in a small skillet over medium heat, swirling until the milk solids turn brown and smell nutty, about 4 minutes. Transfer immediately to a small heatproof bowl. Refrigerate for about 20 minutes, stirring halfway through, until opaque but soft enough to brush. Prepare the chocolate base while it chills.

steps.title: Make the ganache
steps.text: Use {{ingredients}} for the ganache. Put the chopped chocolate in a large heatproof bowl with room for folding later. Heat the cream in a small saucepan until steaming, about 2 minutes, then pour it over the chocolate. Stir occasionally for about 5 minutes, until smooth and slightly cooled.

steps.title: Finish the chocolate base
steps.text: Whisk {{ingredients}} into the ganache. Whisk in all the reserved yolks just until smooth; the base should be warm, not steaming hot.

steps.title: Whip the whites
steps.text: When the butter has chilled for about 10 minutes, add the meringue’s {{ingredients}} to the reserved whites. Beat at medium-high speed until glossy medium peaks form, about 8–10 minutes. Lift the whisk to check: the peaks should hold but their tips should bend. Stop before the whites turn dry or clumpy.

steps.title: Coat the dish
steps.text: Brush the bottom and sides of the 1 1/2-quart soufflé dish generously with all the cooled, browned {{name:coating.butter}}, including the browned solids, right up to the rim. Add the coating’s {{ingredients}}, turn the dish to distribute it, and tap out the excess. Refrigerate the coated dish while you fold the batter. If using a stand mixer, you can coat the dish as the whites finish whipping, watching their texture.

steps.title: Lighten, then fold
steps.text: Stir about one quarter of the meringue into the chocolate base until fully blended. Add the remaining meringue in three batches. For each, sweep a flexible spatula down through the middle and along the bottom, then lift the batter over itself as you turn the bowl. Stop once the batter is mostly uniform with no large white pockets; a few fine streaks are preferable to prolonged mixing. Scrape into the prepared dish and bake promptly.

body:
## Chef's Note

Brown butter gives this French-style chocolate soufflé a toasted crust around its soft center. Beaten egg whites supply the bubbles that expand in the oven while the egg proteins set around them. Loosen the chocolate with a little meringue before folding in the rest, and bring the dish to the table as soon as it is baked.

## Directions

1. **Separate the eggs and heat the oven:** Separate large eggs, reserving all the whites in a clean, grease-free mixer bowl and all the yolks in a second bowl. Keep any yolk out of the whites. Set an oven rack in the middle and heat the oven to 375°F / 190°C. Have the remaining ingredients measured and plates ready before you begin mixing.
2. **Brown and cool the butter:** Melt unsalted butter in a small skillet over medium heat, swirling until the milk solids turn brown and smell nutty, about 4 minutes. Transfer immediately to a small heatproof bowl. Refrigerate for about 20 minutes, stirring halfway through, until opaque but soft enough to brush. Prepare the chocolate base while it chills.
3. **Make the ganache:** Use bittersweet chocolate, 65–70% cacao and heavy cream for the ganache. Put the chopped chocolate in a large heatproof bowl with room for folding later. Heat the cream in a small saucepan until steaming, about 2 minutes, then pour it over the chocolate. Stir occasionally for about 5 minutes, until smooth and slightly cooled.
4. **Finish the chocolate base:** Whisk Dutch-process cocoa powder, dark rum (if using), Morton kosher salt, and hot water into the ganache. Whisk in all the reserved yolks just until smooth; the base should be warm, not steaming hot.
5. **Whip the whites:** When the butter has chilled for about 10 minutes, add the meringue’s granulated sugar and cream of tartar to the reserved whites. Beat at medium-high speed until glossy medium peaks form, about 8–10 minutes. Lift the whisk to check: the peaks should hold but their tips should bend. Stop before the whites turn dry or clumpy.
6. **Coat the dish:** Brush the bottom and sides of the 1 1/2-quart soufflé dish generously with all the cooled, browned unsalted butter, including the browned solids, right up to the rim. Add the coating’s granulated sugar, turn the dish to distribute it, and tap out the excess. Refrigerate the coated dish while you fold the batter. If using a stand mixer, you can coat the dish as the whites finish whipping, watching their texture.
7. **Lighten, then fold:** Stir about one quarter of the meringue into the chocolate base until fully blended. Add the remaining meringue in three batches. For each, sweep a flexible spatula down through the middle and along the bottom, then lift the batter over itself as you turn the bowl. Stop once the batter is mostly uniform with no large white pockets; a few fine streaks are preferable to prolonged mixing. Scrape into the prepared dish and bake promptly.
8. **Bake:** Bake at 375°F / 190°C for about 35–40 minutes. Look for a risen top with a slightly darker, just-set surface and a gentle wobble in the center. Check near the end of baking that the center reaches at least 160°F / 71°C, without touching the dish with the probe. A liquid center needs more time; the clock and surface color alone do not establish doneness.
9. **Serve immediately:** Finish with powdered sugar and heavy cream: dust the top with the sugar, then spoon into dessert portions and pass the extra cream for drizzling. Reach through the airy top to the soft center. Some settling as you serve is normal.

data.title: Brownie Oatmeal
ingredients: 1/4 cup Milk of choice (Almond or Oat preferred)

body:
## Chef's Note

Blending oats directly with wet ingredients creates a smooth, cake-like texture that mimics an actual brownie. Natural acids in the banana react with baking soda to provide rise and texture. Finishing with flaky sea salt cuts through the sweetness and enhances the chocolate flavor.

## Directions

1.  **Prep:** Preheat oven to 350°F. Lightly grease a small oven-safe ramekin or baking dish.
2.  **Blend:** Add oats, banana, egg, milk, cocoa powder, baking soda, and salt to a blender. Blend on high until completely smooth.
3.  **Topping:** Pour the batter into the prepared dish. Sprinkle chocolate chips on top.
4.  **Bake:** Bake for 15-18 minutes until the center is set but still slightly soft (like a fudgy brownie).
5.  **Finish:** Sprinkle with a pinch of flaky sea salt and serve warm.

data.title: Brownie Protein Balls
ingredients: 2 tbsp Ground Flaxseed or Chia Seeds
1-2 tbsp Water or Almond Milk (if needed)

body:
## Chef's Note

These no-bake bites prep in bulk for lunchboxes, pre-workout snacks, or yogurt toppings. Different protein powders absorb liquid at varying rates, so add milk one teaspoon at a time until dough reaches fresh brownie consistency. Chilling sets the almond butter's healthy fats so balls hold their shape.

## Directions

1.  **The Base:** In a medium bowl, combine almond butter, protein powder, almond flour, cocoa powder, maple syrup, and sea salt.
2.  **Hydrate:** Mix with a spatula until a thick dough forms. If it is too crumbly to hold a shape, add 1 tbsp of water or milk. If it's still too dry, add another tbsp.
3.  **Texture:** Fold in the flaxseed (or chia) and the mini chocolate chips.
4.  **Roll:** Scoop out 1-tbsp portions and roll between your palms into balls.
5.  **Set:** Place on a plate and chill in the refrigerator for at least 20 minutes before eating.
6.  **Store:** Keep in an airtight container in the fridge for up to a week.

data.title: Cooked-Chicken Taco Bar
ingredients: 600 g fully cooked chicken, bones and skin removed, shredded into bite-size pieces
1/4 cup (60 ml) low-sodium chicken broth, plus up to 1/4 cup (60 ml) only if needed
1 tbsp fresh lime juice, added gradually to taste
1/2 tsp fine salt, only if needed
18 small soft corn or flour tortillas, about 5–6 inches across, total across both types
2 avocados, about 300 g edible flesh, sliced just before serving
1 tbsp fresh lime juice, for the avocado
1/2 cup (120 g) Mexican crema or sour cream
60 g cotija or queso fresco, crumbled, optional
data.description: A measured six-person taco setup using already cooked chicken, warm tortillas, cabbage and fresh toppings, with a cooked-pork variation.

learning.focus: Reheat an existing protein without drying it out, then assemble for contrast
learning.outcome: Hot, moist chicken in flexible tortillas with crisp cabbage, fresh radish and small amounts of creamy or sharp toppings.
before: The thirty-five-minute plan starts with fully cooked chicken. It does not include roasting a bird or cooking carnitas from raw.
Use 600 g cooked meat in total, even if offering both the chicken and cooked-pork variation. Two complete protein batches would double the planned filling.

checkpoints.cue: Chicken steams gently under the lid with a little moisture at the bottom of the pan.
checkpoints.why: A small broth addition and cover limit drying while heat moves through the cooked shreds.

checkpoints.cue: Several portions of reheated chicken reach 165°F / 74°C without a long hard boil.
checkpoints.why: Warm to the touch is not a reliable leftover reheating endpoint. Prolonged simmering can toughen already cooked meat.

checkpoints.cue: Each tortilla can fold around about one-eighteenth of the filling plus a little vegetable and sauce.
checkpoints.why: Measured total quantities prevent a taco bar from becoming several full meals piled into one shell.

troubleshooting.problem: Chicken is dry despite sauce at the table
troubleshooting.cause: It reheated uncovered or simmered far beyond the endpoint.
troubleshooting.fix: Add broth a tablespoon at a time while reheating under the lid. Sauce can moisten the bite but cannot reverse severe overcooking.

troubleshooting.problem: The bar gets cold before everyone eats
troubleshooting.cause: A large serving bowl sat out while tortillas and toppings were still being prepared.
troubleshooting.fix: Prepare cold components first and heat tortillas at the end. Put out a small amount of meat and replenish promptly; for an extended buffet keep hot food at 140°F / 60°C or above.

substitutions.alternative: 600 g fully cooked carnitas or other pulled pork
substitutions.effect: Use the same total cooked weight. Start with 1 tsp oil instead of 1 tbsp and omit cumin if already well seasoned. Reheat with broth as needed to 165°F / 74°C; taste before lime or salt. This is a moist reheat, not a promise of crisp carnitas edges.

learning.timing: About thirty-five minutes using cooked, refrigerator-cold chicken: twenty minutes for toppings and measuring, then about fifteen for reheating and batch tortilla warming. Starting with raw meat requires a separate cooking recipe and its full time.
learning.storage: Refrigerate in shallow containers within 2 hours (1 hour above 90°F / 32°C), at 40°F / 4°C or below. Use within 3–4 days; reheat leftovers to 165°F / 74°C. If using existing leftovers, plan within their original 3–4-day refrigerated storage window; making tacos does not give older ingredients a fresh week. Store toppings separately and freeze suitable meat portions promptly if they will not be used in time.

body:
## Chef's Note

This is a practical use for cooked chicken, with the raw-meat cooking already done. It is distinct from [Weeknight Ground-Turkey Tacos](/mise/recipes/tacos), which begin with raw ground meat. Keep the toppings measured and let each diner choose a few: cabbage supplies crunch, avocado and crema supply richness, and salsa or lime can supply sharpness. Every taco need not contain every topping.

## Directions

1. **Prepare the cold components first:** Shred cabbage, slice radishes, dice onion and chop cilantro. Portion crema, salsa, optional cheese and hot sauce. Slice the optional jalapeño and cut the serving lime. Keep perishables chilled until the bar is ready; leave the avocado whole for now.
2. **Start the filling:** Heat oil in a 12-inch skillet over medium. Stir cumin for 15–20 seconds, then immediately add the initial measured broth and cooked chicken. Toss, cover and heat gently, stirring every couple of minutes. Add extra broth a tablespoon at a time only if the pan is drying.
3. **Verify and season:** After roughly 6–10 minutes, check several portions with a thermometer; continue until the reheated chicken reaches 165°F / 74°C throughout. Remove the lid briefly if liquid pools. Taste before adding any measured lime or salt, since cooked chicken and broth may already be seasoned. Cover off heat for the brief tortilla warming period.
4. **Warm tortillas and finish avocado:** Warm tortillas in a dry skillet over medium-high, about 10–30 seconds per side until hot and flexible, wrapping each batch in a clean towel. Alternatively, microwave stacks of four to six between damp paper towels for 30–45 seconds, adding short bursts if needed. Slice avocado and gently toss with its separately measured lime juice. This helps limit browning but does not preserve it indefinitely.
5. **Set the bar and serve promptly:** Set out hot filling, warm tortillas and the chilled toppings. Offer three small tacos per person, about 33 g cooked chicken per tortilla before toppings. A thin layer of cabbage and a small spoonful of sauce are enough to start. Taste a bite before adding lime or hot sauce.
6. **Manage any longer serving period:** Replenish small dishes rather than leaving all the food out at once. For an extended buffet, keep cooked meat at 140°F / 60°C or above and cold toppings at 40°F / 4°C or below. Refrigerate unheld perishables within 2 hours, or 1 hour above 90°F / 32°C.

data.title: Buttered Egg Noodles
ingredients: 1 tsp Kosher Salt (plus more for pasta water)

body:
## Chef's Note

Buttered egg noodles are the ultimate comfort base -- the kind of thing your grandmother made without a recipe. Wide egg noodles have a tender, slightly chewy texture that cradles butter and sauce better than any Italian pasta. The secret is tossing the hot noodles with butter and a splash of starchy pasta water, which emulsifies into a silky coating rather than a greasy puddle. This is meant to be a supporting player: simple, satisfying, and ready in the time it takes to boil water.

## Directions

1.  **Boil:** Bring a large pot of generously salted water to a rolling boil. The water should taste like the sea. Add egg noodles and cook according to package directions until al dente, usually 7-8 minutes.

2.  **Reserve Water:** Before draining, scoop out 1/4 cup of the starchy pasta water and set aside.

3.  **Drain and Toss:** Drain the noodles and return them to the pot over low heat. Add butter in pieces, reserved pasta water, salt, and pepper. Toss vigorously for 30-60 seconds until the butter melts and emulsifies with the starchy water into a glossy coating on every noodle.

4.  **Serve:** Transfer to a warm serving bowl, scatter with parsley if using, and serve immediately alongside braises, stews, or saucy mains.

data.title: Buttermilk Cornflake Baked Chicken
ingredients: 3 lbs (1360 g) bone-in, skin-on chicken pieces: 2 breast halves, 2 thighs, 2 drumsticks and 2 wings; back excluded
75 g peeled yellow onion, thinly sliced
12 g fine salt, for the marinade
150 g plain cornflakes, weighed before crushing into small crumbs
data.description: Bone-in chicken in a tangy buttermilk marinade, baked with a cornflake, Parmesan and thyme coating. Allow at least three hours for marinating.

learning.focus: Match a crisp crumb coating with separately checked chicken pieces
learning.outcome: A golden, attached cornflake crust and chicken that reaches at least 165°F / 74°C in every piece, without holding finished breasts in the oven for the legs.
before: Buy an unseasoned cut-up broiler, with no added salt solution. The listed weight is the eight cooking pieces, excluding the back and giblets. Four portions means sharing the meat; a wing is not a main portion. If buying a whole bird, allow extra shopping weight for the unused back.

Use an 18-by-13-inch rimmed sheet pan with an oven-safe rack, not a cooling rack with an unknown heat rating. The pieces must fit without touching, with roughly an inch between them. Use a second pan and rack if the breasts are too broad or the batch is increased; rack footprint matters more than the printed pan size.

Cornflakes are weighed before crushing so cereal volume and crumb volume cannot be confused. Make small irregular crumbs, not powder. Check the label if avoiding gluten; many cornflakes contain barley malt.

checkpoints.cue: Small crumbs are lightly moistened with oil, with no large flakes or wet oily clumps.
checkpoints.why: Small crumbs attach more evenly; distributing oil before breading avoids brushing the fragile coating off afterward.

checkpoints.cue: Chicken has a thin film of buttermilk, without streams of marinade or attached onion slices, and crumbs cling when lightly pressed.
checkpoints.why: Excess liquid and bulky aromatics create gaps and a heavy wet layer under the coating. Drying the marinated chicken completely would remove its binder.

checkpoints.cue: Crust is golden and the thermometer reads at least 165°F / 74°C in the thickest meat of each piece, away from bone.
checkpoints.why: Brown crumbs cannot reveal whether the center is cooked. Breast halves, wings and legs can finish at different times.

troubleshooting.problem: Coating falls off or is wet underneath
troubleshooting.cause: Too much clinging marinade, large flakes, pieces touching or repeated handling.
troubleshooting.fix: Let excess marinade drain and press on small crumbs before baking. Leave the chicken skin-side up without turning. Once baked, a detached coating cannot be reliably glued back on; serve the chicken with the coating that remains.

troubleshooting.problem: Crumbs darken before the chicken is cooked
troubleshooting.cause: A hot oven spot, oversized chicken pieces or too much exposed Parmesan is browning faster than the center heats.
troubleshooting.fix: Loosely shield the darkening piece with foil and continue until its center reaches 165°F / 74°C. If several pieces darken, lower the oven to 375°F / 190°C and allow more time. Burned crumbs cannot be restored, and foil may soften the coating.

troubleshooting.problem: Breasts are dry although the legs are tender
troubleshooting.cause: All pieces were left in the oven until the slowest one finished.
troubleshooting.fix: Begin individual checks early and remove each breast at 165°F / 74°C. Legs may be cooked further for your preferred texture. Further resting or marinating cannot reverse overcooking.

substitutions.alternative: 1 1/2 cups plain unsweetened regular yogurt mixed with 1/2 cup water
substitutions.effect: A similar tangy coating, with a different flavor and thickness. Use regular yogurt rather than thick Greek yogurt and drain well before breading. Yogurt thickness varies, so let excess coating drip away before adding crumbs.

substitutions.alternative: 150 g certified gluten-free plain cornflakes
substitutions.effect: Preserves the cereal coating while avoiding barley malt; verify the hot sauce and other packaged ingredients too. Flake size and sugar content may change browning speed.

substitutions.alternative: 1360 g bone-in, skin-on thighs of similar size
substitutions.effect: More even portioning and checking, with all dark meat. Piece count depends on size; retain the spacing and thermometer endpoint instead of assuming the same baking time. Boneless breasts need a separate, shorter cooking schedule.

learning.timing: Allow four hours twenty-five minutes from the start: about ten minutes to assemble the marinade, at least three hours refrigerated, fifteen minutes to preheat and coat, up to fifty-five minutes baking and five minutes resting. Marinate for three to twelve hours; a longer soak adds directly to elapsed time. With the marinade already complete, allow about seventy-five minutes. Begin checking at thirty minutes; many pieces take thirty-five to fifty-five minutes, and large breast halves or two pans can take longer. Scaling ingredients does not scale oven capacity or multiply the timer.
learning.storage: Marinate covered at 40°F / 4°C or below for three to twelve hours, within the chicken's original one-to-two-day refrigerated storage window; marinating does not restart that clock. Discard raw-contact marinade, aromatics and unused breading. Refrigerate cooked leftovers in shallow containers within two hours, or one hour above 90°F / 32°C, and use within three to four days. Reheat on a rack in a 350°F / 175°C oven until every piece reaches 165°F / 74°C; begin checking around twenty minutes and allow longer for large pieces. The crust softens in storage and may not recover its original crispness; a microwave softens it further.

body:
## Chef's Note

This Southern-inspired home-style chicken keeps the buttermilk soak and bakes a cornflake-and-Parmesan coating instead of deep-frying. Cultured buttermilk supplies tang and a wet layer for the crumbs to grip; the rack raises the chicken above its drippings. Aim for a crisp crumb coating, and do not expect the covered skin beneath it to resemble bare roast-chicken skin.

## Directions

1. **Marinate ahead:** Whisk buttermilk, hot sauce, lemon juice and the twelve grams salt in a food-safe container; add onion, smashed garlic and thyme sprigs. Add the chicken without rinsing it. Use a snug covered container or a food-safe resealable bag set in a dish to keep the marinade against the pieces. Refrigerate at 40°F / 4°C or below for three to twelve hours, turning the closed bag or pieces once if needed for coverage. Wash hands and clean raw-contact surfaces.
2. **Set up the oven:** Near the end of the soak, heat the oven to 400°F / 205°C with a shelf in the center. Line an 18-by-13-inch rimmed sheet pan with foil and place an oven-safe rack on top. Brush the rack with one teaspoon of the measured oil. Check the usable rack area before coating; have a second pan and oven-safe rack ready if all pieces cannot fit with the stated gaps. If using two pans, place shelves in the upper and lower thirds and plan to swap their positions halfway through baking.
3. **Prepare the crumbs:** Crush the weighed cornflakes in a bag with a rolling pin until mostly small crumbs, with some texture remaining. Mix in the remaining five teaspoons oil, rubbing lightly to distribute it, then add Parmesan, chopped thyme and pepper. Put half in a shallow dish and keep the other half in a clean bowl to add as needed. The marinade, cereal and cheese supply salt; do not automatically salt the coating as well.
4. **Coat and arrange:** Lift chicken from the marinade and remove clinging onion, garlic and thyme stems. Let excess buttermilk drip away, leaving a thin film. Press each piece into the crumb mixture on all sides, adding reserved crumbs to the dish as needed. Press on one thin, even coat and leave excess crumbs in the dish; do not heap them on just to use them up. Place skin-side up on the rack with roughly an inch between pieces. Use a second pan if they would touch. Discard remaining raw-contact marinade, aromatics and crumbs; wash hands and utensils before handling side dishes or cooked food.
5. **Bake and check each piece:** Bake without turning the chicken. After thirty minutes, check the breasts, wings and legs individually with a thermometer in the thickest meat, avoiding bone; check more than one spot in large breast halves. Continue baking and recheck as needed until every piece reaches at least 165°F / 74°C, commonly thirty-five to fifty-five minutes total. Remove finished pieces to a clean rack over a plate while the others continue. Thighs and drumsticks can stay longer if you prefer softer dark meat, but do not keep finished breasts in the oven for them. If the crust darkens too quickly, loosely shield that piece with foil. With two pans, swap their shelf positions and rotate front to back around halfway, allowing additional time if needed.
6. **Rest and portion:** Let the final pieces rest for five minutes, uncovered so steam can escape. Divide the meat among four diners, sharing breast meat and distributing thighs, drumsticks and wings by appetite; two pieces are not automatically equal portions. Serve the chicken beside the vegetables and mash rather than burying its crust under them. Mixed pieces may finish twenty minutes or more apart; a clean uncovered rack protects the crust but does not keep them hot indefinitely. Have the sides ready near the chicken finish. For closer finish times, use similarly sized bone-in thighs as described in the substitution.

body:
## Chef's Note

Buttermilk's acidity reacts with baking soda for extra lift and tang. Rest the batter for 10-15 minutes before cooking so flour fully absorbs the liquid - this produces waffles that are crispy outside and airy inside. The batter should become slightly bubbly during the rest.

## Directions

1.  **Dry Mix:** In a large bowl, whisk together flour, sugar, baking powder, baking soda, and salt.
2.  **Wet Mix:** In a separate bowl, whisk the buttermilk and melted butter. Whisk in the eggs until just combined.
3.  **Combine:** Pour the wet ingredients into the dry. Whisk until **just combined** - a few small lumps are essential for a light texture. Fold in the vanilla.
4.  **The Rest:** Let the batter rest at room temperature for 10-15 minutes. It should become slightly bubbly.
5.  **Cook:** Preheat your waffle iron and grease lightly. Pour about 1/3 to 1/2 cup of batter (depending on your iron size).
6.  **Finish:** Cook until the steam stops rising from the iron and the waffles are deep golden brown.
7.  **Serve:** Serve immediately with salted butter, maple syrup, and fresh berries.

data.title: Butternut Squash Fettuccine Alfredo
ingredients: 1/2 cup Low-sodium Chicken Broth (or Veggie Broth)

body:
## Chef's Note

This modern variation on Roman fettuccine Alfredo adds roasted butternut squash to the traditional butter-and-Parmesan sauce. Roasting the squash at 425°F until deeply caramelized concentrates its natural sugars and prevents a watery sauce - boiling produces inferior results. The original 1908 dish created by Alfredo di Lelio used only butter and cheese; American versions added cream in the 1960s.

## Directions

1.  **Roast:** Preheat oven to 425°F. Toss squash cubes and garlic with olive oil, salt, and pepper. Spread on a baking sheet and roast for 25-30 minutes cook until caramelized and golden brown and caramelized.
2.  **The Emulsion:** Let squash cool for 10 minutes. Transfer to a blender. Add heavy cream, broth, Parmesan, and nutmeg. Blend on high until completely smooth and velvety.
3.  **Pasta:** Boil fettuccine in salted water until **al dente**. **Reserve 1/2 cup of pasta water**, then drain.
4.  **Combine:** Return pasta to the pot. Pour the butternut sauce over the noodles and toss vigorously.
5.  **Adjust:** If the sauce is too thick, add reserved pasta water one tablespoon at a time until it reaches a glossy, coating consistency.
6.  **Serve:** Garnish with fresh parsley and extra Parmesan.

data.title: Cantonese Steamed Fish
ingredients: 1 lb Whole Fish or Fillet (Tilapia, Flounder, or Sole)
3 Green Onions, thinly sliced (white and green separated)

body:
## Chef's Note

Cantonese steamed fish is a classic from Guangdong province, prized for its delicate simplicity. The fish is steamed with ginger to infuse flavor, then the real magic happens: smoking-hot oil is poured over raw scallions and cilantro on top of the fish. This flash-cooks the herbs and releases their aromatics directly into the fish. Light soy sauce with a touch of sugar balances the seasoning perfectly.

## Directions

1.  **Steam:** Place the fish on a heat-proof plate. Scatter half the ginger on top. Steam over boiling water for 8-10 minutes until the fish flakes easily.
2.  **Drain:** Carefully pour off any excess liquid from the plate (this liquid can be "fishy").
3.  **Layer:** Arrange the remaining ginger, scallion greens, and cilantro in a pile on top of the cooked fish.
4.  **The Sauce:** Whisk the soy sauce and sugar. Pour it around the base of the fish.
5.  **The Sizzle:** In a small saucepan, heat the oil until it is literally smoking.
6.  **Finish:** Carefully pour the hot oil directly over the herbs and ginger. It should sizzle loudly. Serve immediately.

data.title: Cantonese Shrimp and Pork Wontons
data.totalTime: 60–90 min (planning estimate; wrapping and batches vary)
ingredients: 1 lb Ground Pork (20% fat is ideal)
1/2 lb Shrimp, peeled and deveined (half finely chopped, half kept in chunks)
1/2 cup Water Chestnuts, finely minced (See Chef’s Note for substitution)
Thin square wonton wrappers, as needed for all the filling (package counts vary; have extra available), or [Homemade Wrappers](/mise/recipes/fresh-wonton-wrappers)
Hot broth or dipping sauce, for serving (optional)

body:
## Chef's Note

These wontons pair a springy pork filling with distinct pieces of shrimp and the crunch of water chestnuts. Stir the cold, seasoned meat until it becomes sticky and holds together, then fold in the chunky ingredients so they keep their texture. Finely minced celery or Fuji apple can replace the water chestnuts; celery adds a fresh herbal note, while apple makes the filling a little sweeter.

Plan on 60–90 minutes for mixing, wrapping, and cooking the batch, depending on your wrapping speed and pot capacity. Wrapper size and filling scoops determine the final count. Use the filling across six portions, and have extra wrappers available rather than relying on an unspecified package size.

## Directions

Work with small batches: keep unused filling and waiting uncooked wontons refrigerated throughout mixing, wrapping, and cooking. Use clean utensils for serving.

1.  **The Paste:** In a large bowl, combine the pork, the **finely chopped** half of the shrimp, ginger, garlic, soy sauce, Shaoxing wine, sesame oil, sugar, white pepper, salt, and egg.
2.  **The Texture:** Stir the mixture **vigorously in one direction** for 3-5 minutes until it becomes pale, sticky, and forms a cohesive paste. Do not skip this!
3.  **Add Texture:** Fold in the water chestnuts (or celery), green onions, and the remaining **shrimp chunks**.
4.  **The Test:** Cook a small flattened portion of filling in a small nonstick skillet until the center reaches 165°F / 74°C. Taste only after it is fully cooked, then adjust the remaining filling with a clean utensil if needed.

data.title: Shumai
ingredients: 1/2 lb Shrimp, peeled and deveined (finely chopped)
2/3 cup Dried Shiitake Mushrooms, soaked and minced
1/4 cup Finely diced carrots or Goji berries

body:
## Chef's Note

Shumai (also spelled siu mai) are open-topped Cantonese dumplings, a dim sum staple from Guangdong province. The distinctive bouncy texture comes from stirring the pork and shrimp mixture vigorously in one direction for several minutes until it becomes sticky - this develops the protein and gives it that characteristic snap. Dried shiitake mushrooms are essential for their concentrated umami flavor. The yellow egg wrappers and the small diced carrot or goji berry garnish on top are traditional touches.

## Directions

1.  **The Paste:** In a large bowl, combine pork, chopped shrimp, cornstarch, wine, and seasonings. Stir **vigorously in one direction** until the meat is pale and very sticky.
2.  **Add Texture:** Fold in the mushrooms and water chestnuts.
3.  **Shape:** Place a wrapper in your palm. Scoop 1.5 tbsp of filling. Squeeze the wrapper around the meat to form a "cup" with the meat exposed at the top. Flatten the base so it stands up.
4.  **Garnish:** Press a tiny amount of diced carrot into the center of each top.
5.  **Steam:** Place in a bamboo steamer lined with parchment. Steam over boiling water for 8-10 minutes until the internal temp is 165°F.
6.  **Serve:** Serve immediately with hot chili oil.

data.title: Cantonese Wonton Broth
ingredients: 1 tbsp Dried Shrimp (The traditional source of 'ocean' umami)
2 stalks Green Onion, cut into 3-inch lengths
1 tsp Fish Sauce (Fallback if dried shrimp is unavailable)
Salt and white pepper to taste

body:
## Chef's Note

Authentic Cantonese wonton broth from Hong Kong should have a subtle seafood note to complement the shrimp in the wontons. Dried shrimp steeped with ginger creates this delicate oceanic flavor. The broth should be crystal clear and golden, not cloudy. Always boil wontons in a separate pot of plain water so the starch doesn't cloud your carefully made broth.

## Directions

1.  **Infuse:** In a large pot, combine the chicken broth, smashed ginger, green onion pieces, and dried shrimp.
2.  **Simmer:** Bring to a gentle boil, then reduce heat and simmer for 20 minutes.
3.  **Strain:** Pour the broth through a fine-mesh strainer to remove the solids. The liquid should be perfectly clear.
4.  **Season:** Stir in the light soy sauce and fish sauce. Add salt and a pinch of white pepper to taste.
5.  **Serve:** Keep hot while you boil the wontons in a **separate** pot of plain water. This ensures your broth stays clear and doesn't get thickened by the starch on the wonton skins.

data.title: Caramelized Black Pepper Chicken
ingredients: 1.5 lbs (680 g) boneless skinless chicken thighs, cut into 1-inch pieces
1/2 cup (100 g) packed dark brown sugar
1/4 cup (60 ml) water, plus more as needed
data.description: Peppery chicken thighs in a concentrated brown-sugar and fish-sauce glaze. Learn when to stop reducing a sauce and how to balance it with the rest of the meal.
data.source: Adapted from Charles Phan’s caramelized black pepper chicken, demonstrated with Food52

learning.focus: Reduce a glaze without scorching it
learning.outcome: Tender chicken coated in a flowing sweet-salty glaze, with distinct pepper aroma and no burnt bitterness.
before: Measure the sauce before heating the pan; sugar-rich reductions can change quickly.
This is an intensely seasoned main. Cook plain rice and a vegetable alongside it; their time is additional.

checkpoints.cue: Chicken has golden patches, while the center is still unfinished.
checkpoints.why: Searing builds flavor; it is not the final cooking endpoint. Batches give moisture room to evaporate.

checkpoints.cue: The glaze runs from the spoon in a thick stream, rather than sticking like candy.
checkpoints.why: Evaporation concentrates both sugar and fish-sauce salt. Brown sugar already contains molasses, so darkness alone is not a useful endpoint.

checkpoints.cue: Several larger chicken pieces reach 165°F / 74°C in the center.
checkpoints.why: A browned exterior and hot sauce do not prove the chicken center is cooked.

troubleshooting.cause: Too much water evaporated; fish-sauce brands also vary in saltiness.
troubleshooting.fix: Stir in water a tablespoon at a time until the sauce flows. Serve with plain rice and use only enough glaze to coat each portion.

troubleshooting.cause: Sugar or the aromatics scorched against a hot dry pan.
troubleshooting.fix: Burnt flavor cannot be reliably diluted away. Transfer unburnt chicken away from the residue and remake the sauce over gentler heat.

substitutions.alternative: Omit for less heat
substitutions.effect: Black pepper still makes the dish peppery. Use 1 tsp pepper initially if cooking for heat-sensitive eaters.

learning.timing: 40 minutes allows preparation, two searing batches, and gentle finishing. Rice and sides are separate tasks.
learning.storage: Refrigerate in shallow containers within 2 hours (1 hour above 90°F / 32°C), at 40°F / 4°C or below. Use within 3–4 days; reheat leftovers to 165°F / 74°C. Add a little water when reheating the glaze.

body:
## Chef's Note

This brown-sugar shortcut takes its flavor direction from Charles Phan's caramelized black pepper chicken. The sugar, fish sauce, vinegar, and pepper are intentionally assertive, so plain rice is part of the meal's balance. The method reduces a sauce; you do not need to take dry sugar to a dark caramel or burn the chicken to obtain its color.

## Directions

1. **Prepare:** Pat chicken dry. Mix brown sugar, fish sauce, water, vinegar, ginger, garlic, pepper, and optional chiles in a bowl. Set a separate clean plate aside for the finished chicken.
2. **Brown in batches:** Heat half the oil in a 12-inch skillet over medium-high heat. Add half the chicken in a single layer and cook about 2–3 minutes per side, until golden in patches. Transfer to a temporary plate. Repeat with the remaining oil and chicken. The chicken is not fully cooked yet; keep its plate and juices away from ready-to-eat food.
3. **Soften the shallot:** Reduce heat to medium. Add shallot to the skillet and cook about 3 minutes, stirring, until softened. Add a tablespoon of water if the pan is dry or the browned residue is darkening too quickly.
4. **Start the glaze:** Stir in the prepared sauce, scraping up golden residue. Bring to a gentle simmer and cook 2–4 minutes, stirring, until the sugar dissolves and the sauce begins to coat a spoon. Lower the heat if it thickens rapidly.
5. **Finish the chicken:** Return chicken and any accumulated juices to the sauce. Simmer gently, turning the pieces, for about 3–6 minutes, until several larger pieces measure 165°F / 74°C at the center. Add water as needed to keep the sauce fluid while the chicken finishes.
6. **Serve:** Taste the sauce with a bite of plain rice if serving it. Loosen with water if too concentrated. Fold in cilantro and serve the chicken and a restrained spoonful of glaze with rice and vegetables.

export.ingredients:
1.5 lbs (680 g) boneless skinless chicken thighs, cut into 1-inch pieces
1 tbsp neutral oil, divided
1/2 cup (100 g) packed dark brown sugar
1/4 cup (60 ml) fish sauce
1/4 cup (60 ml) water, plus more as needed
3 tbsp unseasoned rice vinegar
1 tbsp grated fresh ginger
2 cloves garlic, minced
2 tsp coarsely ground black pepper
1–2 fresh Thai chiles, halved, optional
1 large shallot, thinly sliced
2 tbsp chopped cilantro
export.directions:
1. Prepare: Pat chicken dry. Mix brown sugar, fish sauce, water, vinegar, ginger, garlic, pepper, and optional chiles in a bowl. Set a separate clean plate aside for the finished chicken.
2. Brown in batches: Heat half the oil in a 12-inch skillet over medium-high heat. Add half the chicken in a single layer and cook about 2–3 minutes per side, until golden in patches. Transfer to a temporary plate. Repeat with the remaining oil and chicken. The chicken is not fully cooked yet; keep its plate and juices away from ready-to-eat food.
3. Soften the shallot: Reduce heat to medium. Add shallot to the skillet and cook about 3 minutes, stirring, until softened. Add a tablespoon of water if the pan is dry or the browned residue is darkening too quickly.
4. Start the glaze: Stir in the prepared sauce, scraping up golden residue. Bring to a gentle simmer and cook 2–4 minutes, stirring, until the sugar dissolves and the sauce begins to coat a spoon. Lower the heat if it thickens rapidly.
5. Finish the chicken: Return chicken and any accumulated juices to the sauce. Simmer gently, turning the pieces, for about 3–6 minutes, until several larger pieces measure 165°F / 74°C at the center. Add water as needed to keep the sauce fluid while the chicken finishes.
6. Serve: Taste the sauce with a bite of plain rice if serving it. Loosen with water if too concentrated. Fold in cilantro and serve the chicken and a restrained spoonful of glaze with rice and vegetables.

export.notes:
Chef's Note

This brown-sugar shortcut takes its flavor direction from Charles Phan's caramelized black pepper chicken. The sugar, fish sauce, vinegar, and pepper are intentionally assertive, so plain rice is part of the meal's balance. The method reduces a sauce; you do not need to take dry sugar to a dark caramel or burn the chicken to obtain its color.

data.title: Carnitas Bowl
ingredients: 3 lbs Pork Shoulder, cut into 2-inch chunks
2 ears Corn, charred and cut off cob

body:
## Chef's Note

True carnitas from Michoacán are braised low and slow, then crisped to create edges that shatter against tender, pull-apart meat. This technique packs pork tightly in a dish so it braises in its own rendered fat - no vat of lard required. The double-broil finish is non-negotiable: broil, stir, broil again. For a faster weeknight version using ground pork, see [Chipotle Pork Bowls](/mise/recipes/chipotle-pork-and-sweet-corn-tamale-bowls).

## Directions

1.  **Season:** Salt the pork chunks generously. Let sit 30 minutes (or overnight in fridge).
2.  **Arrange:** Preheat oven to 275°F. Pack pork tightly in a 9x13 baking dish. Squeeze orange quarters over meat and nestle them in. Add onion, garlic, bay leaves, and cinnamon. Drizzle oil over top.
3.  **Braise:** Cover tightly with foil. Bake 3-3.5 hours until fork-tender.
4.  **Strain:** Remove aromatics and discard. Drain pork, reserving liquid. Skim fat from liquid and add it back to the meat.
5.  **Shred:** Pull pork into large chunks with two forks. Season with salt.
6.  **Crisp:** Spread on a sheet pan. Broil 6 minutes until edges crisp. Stir. Broil 6 more minutes.
7.  **Elote Sauce:** Mix mayo, sour cream, half the cotija, and chile powder.
8.  **Assemble:** Rice in bowls. Top with carnitas, black beans, charred corn dressed with elote sauce, pickled onions, cabbage, avocado, pepitas, remaining cotija, cilantro, and lime.

data.title: Cauliflower Alfredo
ingredients: 1 cup Milk of choice (or Chicken Broth for dairy-free)
1/2 cup Parmesan Cheese or Nutritional Yeast

body:
## Chef's Note

Cauliflower replaces some of the cream in traditional alfredo, cutting richness while adding body - the natural starches thicken the sauce. It's a smart weeknight shortcut that tastes more like creamy comfort than a vegetable swap. Blend the cooked cauliflower until completely smooth before adding cheese, or the sauce will be gritty.

For the dairy-free option, use dairy-free milk or broth, olive oil, and nutritional yeast together.

## Directions

1.  **Boil:** In a pot, combine cauliflower and milk/broth. Bring to a boil, cover, and simmer for 12-15 minutes until very soft.
2.  **Infuse:** In a small pan, sauté the garlic in the chosen butter or olive oil for 1 minute until fragrant.
3.  **Blend:** Transfer the hot cauliflower and its cooking liquid to a blender. Add the garlic and its cooking fat, the chosen Parmesan or nutritional yeast, salt, and nutmeg.
4.  **Emulsify:** Blend on high for 1 minute until completely smooth and velvety.
5.  **Serve:** Toss immediately with your favorite pasta or use as a base for roasted veg.

data.title: Cauliflower Rice
ingredients: 1 large head Cauliflower (about 2 lbs), cut into florets
2 tbsp Olive Oil or Avocado Oil
2 tbsp Fresh Herbs such as parsley, cilantro, or chives (optional)

body:
## Chef's Note

Cauliflower rice is a clever low-carb swap, but it needs proper technique to avoid the two common failures: mushy texture and raw cauliflower taste. The solution is high heat and short cooking time - you want to evaporate moisture quickly while keeping some bite. Don't overcrowd the pan or the cauliflower will steam instead of sauté. Work in batches if needed.

## Directions

1. **The Rice:** Working in batches, pulse cauliflower florets in a food processor until they resemble rice grains. Don't over-process - you want texture, not mush.

2. **The Sauté:** Heat oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat. Add cauliflower rice in an even layer (work in batches to avoid crowding). Cook undisturbed for 2 minutes, then stir.

3. **The Season:** Continue cooking, stirring occasionally, for 3-4 more minutes until lightly golden and tender-crisp. Add garlic in the last 30-45 seconds if using, until fragrant.

4. **The Finish:** Remove from heat, season with salt and pepper, and toss with fresh herbs if desired. Serve immediately.

data.title: Chana Begoon
ingredients: 1 lb Chinese Eggplant, cut into 1-inch cubes
2 cans (15 oz) Chickpeas, rinsed and drained
Neutral Oil, as needed for roasting and sautéing
Water, as needed to loosen the gravy

body:
## Chef's Note

This Indian chickpea and eggplant curry keeps the eggplant from turning mushy by roasting it separately at 425°F until browned and tender, then folding it into the gravy at the end. Chinese eggplant works especially well because it's less watery than globe eggplant. Lemon juice stirred in at the finish brightens the spiced tomato gravy.

## Directions

1.  **Roast Eggplant:** Preheat oven to 425°F. Toss eggplant cubes with enough oil to lightly coat their surfaces and salt to taste. Roast on a sheet pan for 15-20 minutes until golden and tender. Set aside.
2.  **The Gravy:** In a large skillet over medium heat, heat enough oil to coat the bottom in a thin film. Add the onion and sauté until deep golden brown (10 mins). Add ginger and garlic; sauté for 2 minutes.
3.  **Bloom:** Add all dry spices and sauté in the oil for 1 minute to bloom. Add the crushed tomatoes and simmer for 10 minutes until the tomatoes thicken into a gravy; add a splash of water if the spices begin to catch.
4.  **Chickpeas:** Stir in the chickpeas and a splash of water. Simmer for 5 minutes.
5.  **Fold:** Gently fold the roasted eggplant into the gravy. Let it sit for 2 minutes to absorb the spices (do not over-stir).
6.  **Finish:** Stir in cilantro and lemon juice a little at a time, tasting between additions. Adjust salt before serving.

ingredients: 2 (15 oz) cans chickpeas, drained and rinsed; about 250 g drained chickpeas per can
250 g yellow onion, peeled and finely diced
1 tbsp finely grated fresh ginger, peeled

1/4 tsp fine salt, reserved for finishing; use only as needed

2 tbsp chopped fresh cilantro, for finishing

1 tbsp additional fresh lemon juice, only if replacing the amchur
data.description: Tender chickpeas in a concentrated onion-and-tomato masala, with whole cumin, coriander, green chile and the fruity tang of dried mango.

learning.focus: Build a fragrant masala before adjusting the curry's body and acidity
learning.outcome: The chickpeas crush easily, the sauce clings without forming a dry paste, and the tangy finish leaves the cumin and coriander clear.
before: Drain and rinse the canned chickpeas. Taste one: it should already be tender enough to crush easily. Firm chickpeas need separate simmering in fresh water before entering this tomato sauce; allow extra time. The can weight includes packing liquid.

Use a wide 4-quart pot, about 9–10 inches across, with a lid. For half a batch use a 2-quart pot; for a quarter use a 1-quart pot. Larger amounts need a wider, larger pot with stirring room or separate pots. Keep the onion dice small and use the scaled water reserves; cooking times do not simply multiply or halve.

Measure the ground spices before heating the oil. Keep half the garam masala separate for finishing. Have the tomatoes open and ready to stop the brief dry spice stage. Two serranos give noticeable heat; use the milder option if needed.

checkpoints.cue: Cumin sizzles and smells fragrant, with slightly deeper color but no black seeds.
checkpoints.why: Small seeds can scorch quickly; the onion cools the oil as soon as it is added.

checkpoints.cue: Onion is soft and evenly golden, with no crunchy white pieces or black edges.
checkpoints.why: The onion needs time to soften before tomatoes and water turn this into a wet simmer.

checkpoints.cue: The tomato masala is thick and moist, and a spoon leaves a brief trail across the base.
checkpoints.why: Reducing the tomato liquid concentrates the base; visible pools of oil are not required.

checkpoints.cue: Mashed chickpeas blend into the sauce while most beans remain whole.
checkpoints.why: Crushing a portion supplies body without pureeing the whole curry.

troubleshooting.problem: Curry has a watery ring around the beans
troubleshooting.cause: The tomato base retained excess liquid or the pot lost little steam.
troubleshooting.fix: Simmer uncovered for a few extra minutes, stirring the bottom. Mash a little more of the cooked chickpeas if needed, then stop while the sauce is still spoonable.

troubleshooting.problem: Curry is dry or catches on the bottom
troubleshooting.cause: The pan is wide, the heat is high or too much liquid evaporated.
troubleshooting.fix: Lower the heat and add the reserved hot water a tablespoon at a time, within the listed reserve. If the bottom has burned, transfer the unburned upper curry without scraping the base; lemon will not remove a scorched taste.

troubleshooting.cause: The tomatoes were sharp or too much finishing lemon was added at once.
troubleshooting.fix: Stop adding lemon. More salt does not remove acid. Serve with plain rice or bread; a small spoonful of plain yogurt is an optional accompaniment but adds dairy. Next time taste after the amchur before adding the measured lemon.

substitutions.alternative: For each can, about 250 g fully cooked and drained chickpeas prepared ahead from dried beans
substitutions.effect: This replaces the edible cooked beans, not their dry weight. Soaking and boiling are separate work; the beans should already crush easily before adding them.

substitutions.alternative: Omit it and use the listed additional lemon juice at the finish
substitutions.effect: Lemon gives fresh acidity without dried mango's fruity flavor. Combine both listed lemon portions and add gradually after the simmer; do not fry the juice with the spices.

substitutions.ingredient: Serranos and Kashmiri red chile powder
substitutions.alternative: Omit the serranos and replace the ground chile with the same amount of sweet paprika
substitutions.effect: Makes a milder curry while retaining its cumin, coriander, turmeric and garam masala. Do not substitute an equal amount of cayenne, which can be much hotter.

substitutions.alternative: The same amount of neutral oil
substitutions.effect: Keeps the curry vegan and dairy-free, with less buttery aroma; choose accompaniments accordingly.

learning.timing: Allow about 70–80 minutes with tender canned chickpeas: 20 minutes to drain, chop and measure, 12–15 minutes for the onion, a brief aromatic stage, 8–10 minutes for tomatoes, heating to a simmer, 20 minutes covered, and a short uncovered finish. Hands-on work is about 35–40 minutes. Firmer beans or a slow tomato reduction extend the time. Rice, bread and dal are separate recipes.
learning.storage: Divide into shallow containers and refrigerate within 2 hours, or 1 hour above 90°F / 32°C, at 40°F / 4°C or below. Use within 3–4 days or freeze for up to three months for best quality. Thaw in the refrigerator. Reheat with a little water, stirring until the curry reaches 165°F / 74°C throughout. Keep extra cilantro separate.

body:
## Chef's Note

Chana masala brings chickpeas together with an onion-and-tomato gravy and aromatic spices. Here, whole cumin gives small bursts of flavor, while amchur adds fruity acidity. Brown the onion gently, reduce the tomatoes, then mash a few chickpeas into the sauce so it coats the rest without becoming soupy.

## Directions

1. **Prepare:** Drain and rinse the chickpeas and check that one crushes easily. Finely dice the onion, mince the garlic, grate the ginger and slit the serranos. Measure the spices and separate the garam masala into two equal portions. Keep the initial cooking water and the correction reserve separate.
2. **Start with cumin:** Heat the oil or ghee in the wide pot over medium heat. Add cumin seeds and stir for about **20–30 seconds**, until sizzling and fragrant. As soon as they darken slightly, add the onion; do not wait for black seeds or smoke.
3. **Soften and brown the onion:** Cook for about **12–15 minutes**, stirring regularly, until soft and evenly golden. Lower the heat if edges brown before the centers soften. If it begins sticking, use a small splash from the hot-water reserve and scrape up the golden residue. Stir in garlic, ginger and serranos for about **1 minute**.
4. **Concentrate the masala:** Lower the heat. Stir in coriander, turmeric, amchur, ground red chile and **half the garam masala** for about **15–20 seconds**. Immediately add all the crushed tomatoes and their juice. Return to medium heat and cook uncovered for **8–10 minutes**, stirring frequently, until thick and aromatic. A spoon should leave a brief trail through the moist base; do not keep frying just to force out a pool of oil.
5. **Simmer and thicken:** Add chickpeas, the initial fine salt and all the measured cooking water. Bring to a gentle simmer, allowing a few minutes to heat through, then cover and cook over medium-low for **20 minutes**, stirring once or twice. Uncover and mash about **one-quarter of the chickpeas** against the pan with the spoon. Stir them through and simmer uncovered for **3–5 minutes**, until the sauce clings but still moves around the beans. Use the remaining hot-water reserve only if needed to keep it spoonable.
6. **Balance and serve:** Stir in the remaining garam masala and simmer for **1 minute**, then turn off the heat. Taste before adding lemon. Add the measured lemon juice gradually; if replacing amchur, combine both listed lemon portions and use only as much as needed. Add the reserved salt after tasting a chickpea with its sauce. Remove the serranos or tell diners they are present, then fold in cilantro. Divide into portions of roughly **1 1/4 cups each**, with plain basmati or warm naan.

export.name: Chana Masala
export.ingredients:
2 (15 oz) cans chickpeas, drained and rinsed; about 250 g drained chickpeas per can
250 g yellow onion, peeled and finely diced
4 cloves garlic, finely minced
1 tbsp finely grated fresh ginger, peeled
2 green serrano chiles, slit lengthwise but left attached at the stem
1 (14 oz / 400 g) can crushed tomatoes, with all their juice
3 tbsp neutral oil or ghee
1 tsp cumin seeds
1 tbsp ground coriander
2 tsp garam masala, a salt-free ground spice blend, divided
1 tsp ground turmeric
1 tsp amchur (dried green mango powder)
1/2 tsp Kashmiri red chile powder, pure ground chile rather than a salted seasoning blend
3/4 tsp fine salt, for the chickpea simmer
1/4 tsp fine salt, reserved for finishing; use only as needed
1 cup (240 ml) water, for the chickpea simmer
1/2 cup (120 ml) hot water, reserved only if the pan or curry becomes too dry
2 tbsp chopped fresh cilantro, for finishing
1 tbsp fresh lemon juice, added gradually to taste
1 tbsp additional fresh lemon juice, only if replacing the amchur

data.title: Char Siu (Chinese BBQ Pork)
ingredients: 3 lbs (1.36 kg) boneless pork shoulder, cut into strips about 2 inches thick
1 tsp beet juice, optional for color
1 cup water, for the roasting pan, plus more as needed
data.description: Cantonese-style roast pork with a glossy sweet-savory glaze. Learn to manage sugar, meat temperature, and clean basting.

learning.focus: Build a glaze without burning it
learning.outcome: Sliced pork with a lacquered red-brown surface, lightly charred edges, and a measured safe center temperature.
before: Cut the pork shoulder into uniform strips and marinate at least 8 hours in the refrigerator.
Reserve clean glaze before any marinade touches raw meat. Use separate clean utensils for finishing and serving.

checkpoints.cue: A separate covered container holds marinade that has never touched raw pork.
checkpoints.why: Reserving after coating raw meat would contaminate the finishing glaze.

checkpoints.cue: The center reaches at least 145°F / 63°C before removal; the surface is deep red-brown.
checkpoints.why: Glaze color reflects sugar browning, not the temperature inside the pork.

checkpoints.cue: Glaze bubbles and deepens in color, without widespread blackening.
checkpoints.why: Sugar-rich coatings can progress from caramelized to burnt quickly under a broiler.

troubleshooting.cause: Sugar is exposed to too much direct heat.
troubleshooting.fix: Move the pan lower, reduce oven heat, and loosely shield dark areas with foil while the pork finishes.

troubleshooting.cause: Shoulder contains connective tissue and strip size or cooking time varied.
troubleshooting.fix: Slice thinly across the grain. For future batches use consistent 2-inch strips; this sliced roast should not be judged by pulled-pork tenderness.

substitutions.alternative: Pork tenderloin
substitutions.effect: A leaner, faster-cooking variation requiring a separate temperature-led cook time. Do not use the shoulder schedule unchanged.

learning.timing: 9 hours 30 minutes includes an 8-hour minimum marinade, 20 minutes preparation, about 1 hour cooking, and a 10-minute rest. Overnight marinating extends elapsed time.
learning.storage: Refrigerate in shallow containers within 2 hours (1 hour above 90°F / 32°C), at 40°F / 4°C or below. Use within 3–4 days and reheat leftovers to 165°F / 74°C. Slice only what you need; reheat covered with a splash of water to limit drying.

body:
## Chef's Note

Char siu is a Cantonese roast pork preparation known for its sweet-savory lacquer and charred edges. This home-oven version suspends strips above a little water to keep drippings from scorching; the water does not guarantee juicy meat. Uniform strips, careful glazing, and temperature checks are the useful controls.

## Directions

1. **Mix and reserve:** Whisk hoisin, honey, soy sauces, wine, sugar, five-spice, garlic, pepper, and optional beet juice. Before touching raw pork, place 3 tbsp in a separate covered container and refrigerate for glazing. Coat pork strips with the remaining marinade and refrigerate, covered, at least 8 hours or overnight.
2. **Prepare the oven:** Heat to 425°F / 220°C. Line a rimmed roasting pan with foil and set a rack inside. Add 1 cup water beneath the rack, without touching the meat. Set pork strips on the rack with space between them. Discard raw-contact marinade.
3. **Start roasting:** Roast 15 minutes, then turn the strips and reduce oven to 375°F / 190°C. Continue 20 minutes. Check the pan occasionally and carefully add hot water if the bottom is drying out.
4. **Glaze and measure:** Brush with the reserved clean glaze. Roast another 10–20 minutes, turning and glazing once more, until the thickest part of each strip reaches at least 145°F / 63°C. Times vary with thickness. Do not use raw marinade or pan drippings as an uncooked finishing sauce.
5. **Char briefly:** If the glaze needs more color, broil briefly, checking every 30 seconds and turning as needed, usually 1–3 minutes total. Skip this if the glaze is already dark. Avoid blackening the entire surface.
6. **Rest and slice:** Rest for 10 minutes before slicing; whole pork cuts require at least a 3-minute rest after reaching 145°F / 63°C. Slice thinly across the grain and serve with rice and greens.

data.title: Charred Asparagus with Parmesan
ingredients: 1 lb Asparagus, woody ends snapped off
2 cloves Garlic, finely grated on a Microplane

body:
## Chef's Note

The broiler is the most underused tool for vegetables. It delivers restaurant-quality char in a fraction of the time that roasting takes, and asparagus is the ideal candidate because the spears lie flat and cook in minutes. The key is positioning the oven rack 4-6 inches from the element and watching constantly -- the line between perfectly blistered and burnt is about 60 seconds. Grating garlic on a Microplane creates a paste that melts into the oil, distributing flavor evenly without any raw garlic chunks.

## Directions

1.  **Preheat:** Set oven broiler to high. Position an oven rack 4-6 inches from the heating element. Line a baking sheet with foil.
2.  **Prep:** Snap the woody ends off each asparagus spear by bending from the bottom -- they break naturally at the right point. Choose medium-thick spears; pencil-thin ones burn too quickly under a broiler.
3.  **Season:** Toss asparagus on the sheet with olive oil, grated garlic, salt, and pepper. Spread in a single layer.
4.  **Broil:** Place under the broiler for 4-6 minutes, shaking the pan once halfway through. Watch carefully -- the tips should be charred and blistered, and the stems should be tender-crisp with bright green color.

data.title: Charred Broccoli with Garlic
ingredients: 450 g broccoli florets, with any thick attached stems sliced about 1/4 inch thick
1/4 cup (60 ml) water, divided, plus a small splash if needed
1 tbsp fresh lemon juice, added gradually to taste
data.description: Skillet-browned broccoli with a tender stem, gently warmed garlic, and a little soy and lemon at the finish.

learning.focus: Treat surface browning and stem tenderness as separate jobs
learning.outcome: Broccoli with browned patches and tender stems that retain a little bite, finished with fragrant garlic and light acidity.
before: Dry washed broccoli before searing. Keep florets about 1 1/2–2 inches wide and slice thick stems so they cook at a similar rate.
A short covered water addition follows browning; the goal is a tender stem as well as colored florets.

checkpoints.cue: Cut faces have brown patches without an acrid burned smell.
checkpoints.why: Dry surfaces and pan contact favor browning. Making the oil smoke or turning the whole floret black is unnecessary.

checkpoints.cue: A knife enters the thickest stem with a little resistance, and cooking water has evaporated.
checkpoints.why: Steam reaches the interior after the surface has browned; a rigid stem needs more covered time, not more scorching.

checkpoints.cue: Garlic smells fragrant and remains pale gold when the broccoli returns.
checkpoints.why: Thin garlic slices burn quickly in the heat used to sear vegetables. Lower heat before adding them.

troubleshooting.problem: Florets burn while stems stay hard
troubleshooting.cause: The pieces were uneven or the pan stayed too hot without the covered stage.
troubleshooting.fix: Lower heat, add a tablespoon of water, cover briefly and check a stem again. Remove any bitter blackened fragments.

troubleshooting.cause: It entered the pan wet or the skillet was crowded.
troubleshooting.fix: Uncover and let water evaporate, then allow short undisturbed contact. Next time dry well and keep the two batches.

troubleshooting.cause: All juice was added without tasting or the lemon was particularly sharp.
troubleshooting.fix: Begin with half the measured juice and add more only after tasting. An oversoured batch needs more unseasoned vegetables to dilute it.

substitutions.alternative: 1 tsp gluten-free tamari
substitutions.effect: Preserves a fermented savory note; check its label and taste because salinity varies.

learning.timing: About 25 minutes includes trimming/drying, two small batches with brief steaming, and a short garlic finish.
learning.storage: Refrigerate in shallow containers within 2 hours (1 hour above 90°F / 32°C), at 40°F / 4°C or below. Use within 3–4 days; reheat leftovers to 165°F / 74°C. Best freshly cooked. Reheated broccoli softens and loses the dry surface contrast.

body:
## Chef's Note

A browned floret can still have a hard stem. Sear first for flavor, then add a measured splash of water and cover briefly for tenderness. Evaporate the water before finishing. Garlic goes in at lower heat so it can become fragrant without burning. This soy-and-lemon home side is distinct from the site's oven-roasted Parmesan broccoli.

## Directions

1. **Prepare:** Wash and dry broccoli thoroughly. Cut florets about 1 1/2–2 inches wide and slice thick attached stems about 1/4 inch thick. Divide into two batches. Slice garlic and measure water and seasonings.
2. **Brown the first batch:** Heat 1 tbsp oil in a 12-inch lidded skillet over medium-high heat until shimmering. Add half the broccoli in a loose layer with cut faces against the pan where possible. Leave about 2 minutes, then turn and cook another 1–2 minutes until several surfaces brown.
3. **Tenderize and dry:** Lower heat to medium, carefully add 2 tbsp water and cover for about 1–2 minutes. Check a thick stem with a knife; it should yield with a little resistance. Add a small splash of water and cover a little longer only if still hard. Uncover and let residual water evaporate, then transfer broccoli to a bowl.
4. **Repeat:** Cook the remaining broccoli with the other tablespoon oil and the remaining 2 tbsp measured water, following steps 2–3. Transfer to the bowl.
5. **Finish gently:** Lower heat to medium-low. Stir garlic and optional pepper flakes in the oil film remaining in the skillet for about 30 seconds, just until fragrant and pale gold. Return all broccoli, add soy sauce, and fold briefly to warm and coat. Turn off heat and add half the lemon juice. Taste, adding the rest only if wanted. Divide into four side portions and serve promptly.

data.title: Charred Guacamole with Pomegranate
ingredients: 1 tsp Cumin Seeds, toasted and ground (or 1 tsp ground cumin, toasted in dry pan)

body:
## Chef's Note

Broiling the jalapeños and tomatoes transforms familiar guacamole into something with smoky depth and caramelized sweetness. The charred vegetables add complexity that raw versions can't match - their sugars concentrate and their skins develop bitter-sweet char. Two upgrades make this version exceptional: toasting the cumin first (30 seconds in a dry pan until fragrant) blooms its essential oils, and adding olive oil to the mash creates silkiness that carries the smoke flavor across your palate. Pomegranate seeds contribute jewel-like color, tart juice bursts, and unexpected crunch.

## Directions

1. **The Toast:** If using whole cumin seeds, toast in a dry skillet over medium heat for 30 seconds until fragrant. Grind in a mortar or spice grinder. (If using ground cumin, toast it in a dry pan for 20 seconds.)

2. **The Char:** Position oven rack 6 inches from broiler. Place jalapeño and tomato halves cut-side down on a foil-lined sheet pan. Broil for **5-7 minutes** until skins are blistered and blackened in spots. Let cool slightly. Peel off and discard the blackened tomato skins (they can be bitter). Chop the flesh and jalapeños finely.

3. **The Mash:** Scoop avocado flesh into a large bowl. Add lime juice and zest immediately and toss to coat. Add olive oil. Mash with a fork to desired consistency - slightly chunky is ideal for texture.

4. **The Fold:** Add the chopped charred vegetables, red onion, garlic, cilantro, toasted cumin, and salt. Fold gently until just combined. Taste and adjust salt and lime.

5. **The Finish:** Transfer to serving bowl. Drizzle with a little more olive oil. Scatter pomegranate seeds over top. Finish with a pinch of flaky salt.

6. **Serve:** Serve immediately with quality tortilla chips. If making ahead, press plastic wrap directly onto the surface and refrigerate up to 2 hours.

data.title: Cheese Fondue
ingredients: 1 cup Dry White Wine (Sauvignon Blanc or Riesling)

body:
## Chef's Note

Cheese fondue is a fragile **Emulsion**. If the heat is too high, the cheese will "break" into a stringy ball and a pool of oil. The secret is the **Cornstarch and Acid**: the cornstarch coats the cheese proteins, while the acid in the wine and lemon juice prevents the proteins from clumping together. Always add the cheese in small handfuls, waiting for each to melt before adding the next.

## Directions

1.  **Rub:** Rub the inside of a heavy pot (ceramic or cast iron) with the garlic halves. Discard the garlic.
2.  **Coat:** In a bowl, toss the shredded cheeses with the cornstarch until evenly coated.
3.  **Simmer:** Add the wine and lemon juice to the pot. Bring to a very gentle simmer over medium-low heat.
4.  **Whisk:** Add one handful of cheese. Whisk constantly in a **Figure-8 motion** until melted. Repeat until all cheese is incorporated and the sauce is smooth.
5.  **Finish:** Stir in the Kirsch, nutmeg, and dry mustard.
6.  **Serve:** Keep warm over a low flame. Serve with crusty bread, green apples, and blanched broccoli.

6. Serve: Keep warm over a low flame. Serve with crusty bread, green apples, and blanched broccoli.
export.notes:
Chef's Note

Cheese fondue is a fragile Emulsion. If the heat is too high, the cheese will "break" into a stringy ball and a pool of oil. The secret is the Cornstarch and Acid: the cornstarch coats the cheese proteins, while the acid in the wine and lemon juice prevents the proteins from clumping together. Always add the cheese in small handfuls, waiting for each to melt before adding the next.

Mise recipe: https://jordansilton.com/mise/recipes/cheese-fondue/

## Chef's Note

Shabbat brisket is the Friday ritual that defines Jewish home cooking - it goes into the oven before sundown and emerges fall-apart tender hours later. The slow braise at low temperature (275-300°F) breaks down collagen without drying the meat. Slice against the grain and spoon the braising liquid over each portion to keep it moist.

## Directions

1.  **Season:** Season the brisket generously with salt and pepper on both sides. Place fat-side up in a heavy foil pan or Dutch oven.
2.  **Vegetables:** Scatter the onions and carrots over and around the meat.
3.  **Sauce:** In a bowl, whisk all sauce ingredients together. Pour over the entire brisket, ensuring it is fully covered. Add 1 cup of water around the edges.
4.  **Bake:** Cover tightly with foil. Bake at 350°F for 1.5 to 2 hours until tender.
5.  **The Chill:** Remove from oven. Let cool, then refrigerate the entire pan **overnight**.
6.  **Slice:** Remove the cold meat from the sauce. Slice very thin **against the grain**.
7.  **Finish:** Return the slices to the sauce. Re-bake, covered, at 325°F for 30-45 minutes until hot and the sauce is bubbling.

data.title: Chewy Chocolate Meringues
ingredients: 1 cup Egg Whites, room temperature (about 6-7 large eggs)

body:
## Chef's Note

The secret to a meringue that is "Chewy" rather than just "Crispy" is the **Sugar Dissolution**. By gently heating the egg whites and sugar before whipping, you ensure the sugar crystals are fully dissolved into the protein structure. This results in a silky, stable foam that bakes into a cookie with a "shattering" shell and a marshmallow-like fudgy center.

## Directions

1.  **Prep:** Preheat oven to 250°F. Line two baking sheets with parchment paper.
2.  **Dissolve:** In a heat-proof bowl set over a pot of simmering water (double boiler), combine egg whites, sugar, and salt. Whisk gently until the sugar is dissolved and the mixture feels smooth (not gritty) between your fingers.
3.  **Whip:** Transfer to a stand mixer. Add cream of tartar. Whip on high speed for 8-10 minutes until the whites are stiff, glossy, and the bowl feels cool to the touch.
4.  **Fold:** Gently fold in the chocolate chips by hand.
5.  **Portion:** Use a large spoon or cookie scoop to place clouds of batter onto the sheets. They will not spread, so you can place them 1 inch apart.
6.  **Bake:** Bake for 45-50 minutes. The cookies are done when the outside is firm but the center still feels slightly soft.
7.  **Cool:** Let cool completely on the baking sheet to allow the shell to set.
