data.title: Chicken & Spinach Pasta with Lemon
ingredients: 12 oz (340 g) dried penne or rigatoni
1 lb (450 g) boneless skinless chicken breast, cut into 1-inch pieces
10 oz (280 g) baby spinach, washed and thoroughly drained
1/4 tsp fine salt, for the chicken
1/4 tsp black pepper, plus more to taste
1 1/2 tsp fine salt, for 3 quarts pasta water
1 cup (240 ml) reserved pasta water, added as needed
data.description: Chicken, spinach, and short pasta in a light lemon-Parmesan sauce. Use pasta water and a gentle cheese finish to make the sauce cling.

learning.focus: Finish a light sauce with water and movement
learning.outcome: Pasta coated in a thin, glossy sauce, spinach just wilted, and tender chicken pieces without a puddle of lemon juice.
before: Wash and drain spinach, grate cheese, and zest the lemon before juicing it.
Use a deep 12-inch skillet to accommodate the spinach in several additions.

checkpoints.cue: Several larger chicken pieces read 165°F / 74°C in the center.
checkpoints.why: Small pieces still need a measured endpoint; outside color is not sufficient.

checkpoints.cue: Spinach is wilted and there is a shallow film of liquid, not a soup, under the pasta.
checkpoints.why: Spinach releases water while pasta absorbs liquid; add reserved water according to the pan rather than all at once.

checkpoints.cue: Active bubbling has stopped before the cheese goes in.
checkpoints.why: Gentle heat and available water help disperse the cheese instead of setting it into clumps.

troubleshooting.cause: The full lemon was juiced into the sauce without tasting; lemon size and acidity vary.
troubleshooting.fix: Start with 1 tbsp juice and add more only after tossing. If already too sharp, dilute with a little pasta water and reassess with a complete bite.

troubleshooting.problem: Pasta is dry and cheese clumps
troubleshooting.cause: Too little water or too much heat during the cheese finish.
troubleshooting.fix: Remove from heat, add warm pasta water by the tablespoon, and toss. Hard cheese clumps may remain; use a cooler pan next time.

substitutions.alternative: 120 ml low-sodium chicken broth
substitutions.effect: Less acidity and wine aroma; finish with lemon to taste.

substitutions.alternative: Gluten-free pasta of the same dry weight
substitutions.effect: Follow its own cooking time and toss gently; starch release and resistance to breaking differ.

learning.timing: 40 minutes includes heating pasta water and cooking chicken alongside the pasta. Extra portions may need a second pan or additional batches.
learning.storage: Refrigerate in shallow containers within 2 hours (1 hour above 90°F / 32°C), at 40°F / 4°C or below. Use within 3–4 days; reheat leftovers to 165°F / 74°C. Reheat gently with water; spinach softens and the fresh lemon aroma fades.

body:
## Chef's Note

Spinach, pasta, and cheese all change the water balance of the pan. Start with a little reserved cooking water, let the spinach wilt, then decide whether more is needed. Lemon zest contributes aroma without much acidity; juice is added at the end so you can control the tartness.

## Directions

1. **Boil the pasta:** Bring 3 quarts water and the pasta-water salt to a boil. Add pasta and stir. Cook until about 1 minute short of the package's suggested time, tasting for a slightly firm center. Reserve 1 cup cooking water before draining.
2. **Cook chicken alongside:** Pat chicken dry and season with its measured salt and pepper. Heat 1 tbsp oil in a deep 12-inch skillet over medium-high. Cook in a single layer, turning occasionally, for about 6–9 minutes, until golden in patches and several larger pieces measure 165°F / 74°C. Work in batches if needed. Transfer to a clean plate.
3. **Build the sauce:** Reduce heat to medium and add the remaining oil. Stir in garlic for about 30 seconds, until fragrant but not brown. Add wine and scrape up golden residue. Simmer 2–4 minutes, until reduced by roughly half.
4. **Finish the pasta:** Add drained pasta and 1/3 cup reserved water to the skillet. Toss over medium-low heat for 1–2 minutes, until the pasta is just tender. Add a splash of water if it sticks.
5. **Wilt the greens:** Add spinach in two or three batches, tossing each until it begins to wilt. Return cooked chicken and its juices. Toss just until the chicken is hot and the spinach is fully wilted, about 2–3 minutes. Keep a little liquid in the pan; add reserved water only as needed.
6. **Add cheese and lemon:** Remove the skillet from heat and wait until active bubbling stops. Add Parmesan in two additions while tossing. Add the zest and the lower end of the listed lemon-juice range. Taste a complete bite, then add more juice, pepper, or a pinch of salt if needed. Loosen with water by the tablespoon and serve promptly.

data.title: Chicken and White Bean Enchiladas
ingredients: 15 oz can Navy or Cannellini Beans, rinsed
12 oz Tomatillo Salsa or Enchilada Sauce
1/2 cup Light Sour Cream or Greek Yogurt

body:
## Chef's Note

Enchiladas Suizas (Swiss-style enchiladas) originated in Mexico City in the 1950s at Sanborns restaurant, named for their creamy, dairy-rich green tomatillo sauce. This version adds white beans to the chicken filling for extra protein and fiber. Blending green chiles and cilantro directly into sour cream creates a lighter, tangy version of the traditional cream-based sauce.

## Directions

1.  **The Filling:** In a bowl, toss the shredded chicken, beans, cumin, and 1/4 cup of the green sauce.
2.  **The Sauce:** In a blender, combine the enchilada sauce, diced green chiles, cilantro, and sour cream. Pulse until smooth and creamy.
3.  **Assemble:** Spread 1/2 cup of sauce on the bottom of a 9x13 dish. Fill each tortilla with the chicken/bean mixture, roll tightly, and place seam-side down.
4.  **Bake:** Pour the remaining sauce over the top. Cover with cheese.
5.  **Crisp:** Bake at 375°F for 20-25 minutes until the sauce is bubbling and the cheese is golden.
6.  **Finish:** Top with fresh cilantro and [quick Pickled Red Onions](/mise/recipes/pickled-red-onions).

3. Assemble: Spread 1/2 cup of sauce on the bottom of a 9x13 dish. Fill each tortilla with the chicken/bean mixture, roll tightly, and place seam-side down.
4. Bake: Pour the remaining sauce over the top. Cover with cheese.
5. Crisp: Bake at 375°F for 20-25 minutes until the sauce is bubbling and the cheese is golden.
6. Finish: Top with fresh cilantro and quick Pickled Red Onions (https://jordansilton.com/mise/recipes/pickled-red-onions).

This version adds white beans to the chicken filling for extra protein and fiber. Blending green chiles and cilantro directly into sour cream creates a lighter, tangy version of the traditional cream-based sauce.

data.title: Chicken and Wild Rice Soup
ingredients: 1 cup (160 g) uncooked wild rice; check the package for processing and cook time
4 cups (960 ml) water, for cooking rice, plus more as needed
8 cups (1.9 liters) low-sodium chicken broth, plus up to 2 cups to adjust consistency
2 lbs (900 g) boneless skinless chicken thighs, cut into 1-inch pieces
1/4 tsp fine salt, plus more to taste
data.description: A brothy chicken soup with nutty wild rice, tender vegetables, and fresh herbs. Cook the grain separately so its timing does not dictate the chicken’s texture.

learning.focus: Give grains and chicken separate endpoints
learning.outcome: Chewy-tender wild rice, soft but intact vegetables, and moist chicken in a clear, lightly seasoned broth.
before: Wild-rice processing affects its cooking time. Read the label before planning; quick-cook grain can finish much earlier than dark-finished wild rice.
Use a saucepan for the rice and a soup pot of at least 6 quarts. For make-ahead meals, keep cooked rice separate until serving.

checkpoints.cue: Many grains have opened and the center is tender with a pleasant chew, not a hard core.
checkpoints.why: The grain’s processing and age change how fast it takes up water; a universal 45-minute promise is unreliable.

checkpoints.cue: Broth moves gently, with occasional small bubbles, and larger chicken pieces reach 165°F / 74°C.
checkpoints.why: A gentle simmer cooks the chicken without the agitation and rapid tightening associated with a hard boil.

troubleshooting.problem: Rice is hard but the soup is ready
troubleshooting.cause: This batch of grain needs longer than expected.
troubleshooting.fix: Keep cooking the rice in its own saucepan, adding hot water if needed. Hold the soup hot briefly; add the rice only when tender.

troubleshooting.cause: Rice continues absorbing broth during storage.
troubleshooting.fix: Add broth or water when reheating. Next time store the rice separately and combine portions as needed.

substitutions.alternative: Boneless skinless chicken breast in 1-inch pieces
substitutions.effect: A leaner, less forgiving texture. Begin checking sooner and stop cooking when pieces reach 165°F / 74°C.

substitutions.alternative: Unseasoned wild-and-brown-rice blend, same dry weight
substitutions.effect: Different texture and yield. Cook separately according to the package, then add as much cooked grain as suits the soup.

learning.timing: Allow about 85 minutes including preparation for a slower-cooking wild rice; soup preparation overlaps the grain simmer. Quick-cook or hand-parched grain may finish sooner. A particularly slow batch may extend the total.
learning.storage: Refrigerate in shallow containers within 2 hours (1 hour above 90°F / 32°C), at 40°F / 4°C or below. Use within 3–4 days; reheat leftovers to 165°F / 74°C. Rice and soup can be stored separately to preserve the broth; reheat both thoroughly.

body:
## Chef's Note

Wild rice is the seed of an aquatic grass. Its processing changes how quickly it cooks, so a dark-finished grain and a quick-cook product should not share a rigid timer. Cooking it separately also lets you keep this soup brothy and finish the chicken on its own schedule.

## Directions

1. **Cook the grain:** Rinse the wild rice. Combine with the measured rice-cooking water in a saucepan and bring to a boil. Reduce to a gentle simmer, cover, and cook according to the package range, checking early for quick-cook grain. Add hot water if the pan dries before the rice is tender. When many grains open and have a tender, chewy center, drain any excess water.
2. **Soften vegetables:** While the rice simmers, heat oil in a 6-quart pot over medium heat. Add onion, carrots, and celery. Cook 8–10 minutes, stirring, until the onion is softened. Add garlic and cook about 30 seconds, until fragrant.
3. **Build the broth:** Add the initial measured chicken broth, thyme, salt, and pepper. Bring to a gentle simmer. Cook about 8–10 minutes, until carrots are approaching tenderness; they will cook further with the chicken.
4. **Poach the chicken:** Add chicken and return gently to a simmer. Cook about 12–18 minutes, stirring occasionally, until several larger pieces reach 165°F / 74°C and the vegetables are tender. Avoid a rolling boil.
5. **Combine:** Stir in the tender, drained rice and heat through. Add extra broth as needed to keep the soup spoonable and brothy. If the rice is not yet ready, keep the soup gently hot while it finishes; do not keep boiling the chicken.
6. **Finish:** Add parsley and the lower end of the listed lemon-juice range. Taste the broth with some chicken and rice, then add more lemon, salt, or pepper as needed. Ladle into eight bowls. For planned leftovers, keep the remaining rice and soup separate before chilling promptly.

data.title: Chicken, Apple, and Butternut Stew
ingredients: 2 lbs (900 g) boneless skinless chicken thighs, cut into 1-inch pieces
1/2 tsp fine salt, divided, plus more to taste
1 cup (130 g) parsnip, peeled and cut into 1/2-inch pieces
1 1/2 cups (360 ml) unsweetened apple cider (cloudy apple juice, not vinegar or hard cider)
1 1/2 cups (360 ml) low-sodium chicken stock, plus more as needed
3 cups (420 g) butternut squash, peeled, seeded, and cut into 3/4-inch cubes
2 cups (250 g) Granny Smith apple, cored and cut into 3/4-inch cubes
1–2 tsp apple cider vinegar, optional, to finish
data.description: Chicken thighs simmered with squash, parsnip, cider, and sage, with tart apple added late. Learn to stagger ingredients so each finishes at the right texture.

learning.focus: Stagger ingredients by how fast they soften
learning.outcome: Tender chicken and squash with apple pieces that are warm and just tender, in a lightly thickened cider sauce.
before: Cut squash and apple into even 3/4-inch cubes; parsnip takes longer to soften, so cut it smaller.
Use unsweetened apple cider or cloudy apple juice. Apple cider vinegar is a different ingredient and is used only by the teaspoon at the end.

checkpoints.cue: Flour coats the vegetables without dry pockets before liquid is added.
checkpoints.why: Dispersing flour through the cooking fat helps prevent lumps; the starch thickens as the sauce heats.

checkpoints.cue: A knife enters squash easily but the cubes still hold their edges; chicken reaches 165°F / 74°C.
checkpoints.why: Vegetable tenderness and chicken temperature are separate checks. Keep the simmer gentle so cubes do not break apart.

checkpoints.cue: Apple is hot and just tender with a little bite.
checkpoints.why: Apple added late avoids the long cooking that would turn it into sauce.

troubleshooting.cause: Cider and squash are naturally sweet; cider brands differ.
troubleshooting.fix: Finish with optional cider vinegar a teaspoon at a time, tasting after each. Pair with green vegetables rather than another sweet starch.

troubleshooting.problem: Sauce thickens before the squash is tender
troubleshooting.cause: The pot evaporated more liquid than expected.
troubleshooting.fix: Add stock a little at a time, cover partially, and continue a gentle simmer. Do not use high heat to rush the vegetables.

substitutions.alternative: Unsweetened cloudy apple juice
substitutions.effect: Choose a product without added sugar; taste the final sauce before adding vinegar.

substitutions.alternative: Another firm tart cooking apple
substitutions.effect: Soft varieties may collapse sooner; check frequently after adding.

learning.timing: 80 minutes allows 25 minutes preparation and about 55 minutes for batch browning, vegetables, and simmering. Precut squash can shorten preparation.
learning.storage: Refrigerate in shallow containers within 2 hours (1 hour above 90°F / 32°C), at 40°F / 4°C or below. Use within 3–4 days; reheat leftovers to 165°F / 74°C. Apple and squash soften further on reheating; warm gently and stir sparingly.

body:
## Chef's Note

This stew depends on contrast: savory chicken, sweet squash and cider, aromatic sage, and tart apple. The ingredients do not soften at the same speed. Smaller parsnip pieces get a head start; squash simmers with the chicken; apple goes in only near the end.

## Directions

1. **Brown chicken in batches:** Pat chicken dry and season with half the salt and the pepper. Heat 1 tbsp oil in a Dutch oven over medium-high. Brown half the chicken for about 3 minutes per side, then transfer to a temporary plate. Repeat with remaining oil and chicken. It need not be cooked through yet.
2. **Soften the base:** Reduce heat to medium. Add onion, parsnip, and remaining salt. Cook about 7–9 minutes, stirring, until onion is softened and lightly golden. Add a small splash of stock if the browned residue threatens to scorch. Add sage and ginger and stir for 30 seconds.
3. **Disperse the flour:** Sprinkle flour over the vegetables and stir for 1 minute. Gradually stir in cider, scraping up golden residue and smoothing out flour pockets. Add stock and bring to a simmer.
4. **Simmer chicken and squash:** Return chicken and its accumulated juices. Add squash. Keep at a gentle simmer, partially covered, for about 18–25 minutes, stirring occasionally. Continue until squash and parsnip are tender and several larger chicken pieces reach 165°F / 74°C. Add stock if the sauce becomes too thick before the vegetables soften.
5. **Add apple late:** Fold in the apple and simmer 5–8 minutes, until hot and just tender but still holding its shape. Stir gently so the squash stays intact.
6. **Balance and serve:** Taste a spoonful containing sauce and vegetables. Add optional cider vinegar 1 tsp at a time if the stew needs more tartness, and adjust salt or pepper. Serve in six bowls with a green vegetable or salad.

data.title: Hyderabadi-style Chicken Biryani
ingredients: 2.5 lbs (1.13 kg) boneless skinless chicken thighs, cut into pieces about 2 inches across and no more than 1 inch thick
2 tbsp ginger-garlic paste (or 1 tbsp each finely grated ginger and garlic)
1 1/2 tsp fine salt, for the chicken
1/2 cup loosely packed chopped cilantro, divided
1/2 cup loosely packed chopped mint, divided
2 1/2 cups (500 g) aged basmati rice, not parboiled or quick-cooking
10 cups (2.4 liters) water, for boiling the rice
1 tbsp fine salt, for the rice water
3 large yellow onions (about 600 g trimmed total), sliced evenly about 1/8 inch thick
1 cup (240 ml) neutral oil, for frying onions
2 tbsp of the drained onion frying oil, reserved for layering
1 tsp food-grade rose water or kewra water, optional (not concentrated essence or essential oil)
1/4 cup (60 ml) hot water, only if needed during cooking
data.description: Marinated chicken and partially cooked basmati finish together in a covered pot. Learn to coordinate rice hydration, gentle heat, and a verified chicken endpoint.

learning.focus: Finish chicken and rice together under controlled steam
learning.outcome: Fully cooked, tender chicken beneath separate, fragrant rice grains, with golden onions and no hard rice core.
before: Marinate chicken in the refrigerator for 4–24 hours. Use a wide, heavy 5–6 quart pot, about 10–11 inches across, with a tight lid.
Use aged regular basmati for this method. Sella/parboiled and quick-cooking rice have different hydration and cooking behavior.
The listed time includes a 4-hour marinade and 15-minute final rest. Side dishes are prepared separately.

checkpoints.cue: Onions are evenly golden brown when lifted out, before they turn dark brown.
checkpoints.why: They continue darkening briefly in hot oil after removal. Burned onions make the entire pot bitter.

checkpoints.cue: A tasted rice grain is soft outside with a distinct firm core.
checkpoints.why: Partially hydrated grains need remaining capacity to take up liquid and finish under steam. Fully cooked rice can become mushy in the second cooking stage.

checkpoints.cue: A gentle simmer is audible and light steam escapes at the lid edge.
checkpoints.why: The pot needs enough heat to generate steam throughout. A burner at its lowest setting may be too weak; vigorous heat can scorch the bottom.

checkpoints.cue: Several of the largest chicken pieces and the rice reach 165°F / 74°C, and rice has no chalky core.
checkpoints.why: A sealed lid and a timer cannot verify raw chicken is cooked. The rice shares the pot with raw poultry juices, so check it as well.

troubleshooting.cause: The burner was too low, chicken pieces too thick, or the cold pot needed longer to heat.
troubleshooting.fix: Re-cover and maintain a gentle simmer. Check again in 10 minutes. Add a little hot water only if the rice is drying; keep cooking until both rice and poultry reach the endpoint.

troubleshooting.problem: Rice is still firm but the bottom is drying
troubleshooting.cause: The lid leaked steam or the rice was drained too early.
troubleshooting.fix: Sprinkle 2 tbsp hot water over the rice, seal again, and cook gently for 5–10 minutes. Repeat with the remaining measured water if needed and recheck chicken temperature.

troubleshooting.cause: Heat is too concentrated or liquid has evaporated before the center is cooked.
troubleshooting.fix: Lower the heat immediately. Transfer the unburned upper portion to another heavy pot without scraping up the burnt layer, add a little hot water, cover, and finish to the same temperature and texture endpoints.

substitutions.alternative: 200 g full-fat Greek yogurt mixed with 40 ml water
substitutions.effect: Restores a looser marinade; yogurt thickness still varies, so watch rice moisture during the final cooking.

substitutions.alternative: 1 1/2 tsp sweet paprika plus 1/2 tsp cayenne
substitutions.effect: A different chile flavor and potentially more heat. Start with less cayenne for a mild version.

substitutions.alternative: Omit it
substitutions.effect: The saffron, herbs, and whole spices still provide fragrance. Concentrated essence is not an equal-volume substitute.

learning.timing: About 6 1/2 hours with a 4-hour marinade, including 45 minutes preparation, about 90 minutes cooking across onions/rice/dum, and 15 minutes rest. Overnight marinating extends elapsed time. Pot, burner, and rice variation may extend the final cook.
learning.storage: Refrigerate in shallow containers within 2 hours (1 hour above 90°F / 32°C), at 40°F / 4°C or below. Use within 3–4 days; reheat leftovers to 165°F / 74°C. Divide the deep pot into shallow containers promptly; do not leave the entire pot out to cool. Reheat portions covered with a small splash of water, verifying both chicken and rice reach 165°F / 74°C.

body:
## Chef's Note

This Hyderabadi-style biryani uses the kacchi approach: raw marinated chicken is layered beneath partially cooked rice, then both finish in a covered pot. The central problem is coordination. The rice must retain enough firmness to finish with the chicken, and the burner must sustain steam without scorching the bottom. Aromas and elapsed time help you follow the process; a thermometer and a tasted grain establish the final endpoints.

## Directions

1. **Marinate 4–24 hours:** Mix yogurt, ginger-garlic paste, Kashmiri chile powder, turmeric, garam masala, ground cumin, ground coriander, the chicken salt, lemon juice, half the cilantro, and half the mint. Coat the chicken, cover, and refrigerate at 40°F / 4°C or below. Do not leave raw chicken out while preparing the other components.
2. **Fry onions:** Heat the neutral oil in a wide skillet over medium heat. Fry onions in two batches, stirring frequently, until evenly golden brown, about 12–18 minutes per batch. Lower heat as they color; lift them out before dark brown. Drain in a metal strainer over a heatproof bowl, then spread on a tray lined with paper towels. Reserve 2 tbsp drained onion oil for the biryani; the remaining frying oil is not poured into the dish.
3. **Prepare rice and saffron:** While the onions cook, rinse basmati in several changes of cool water, soak for 20–30 minutes, and drain. Steep saffron in the warm milk for at least 15 minutes. Bring the measured rice water to a boil in a large pot with its salt, cardamom, cinnamon, cloves, bay leaves, and cumin seeds.
4. **Partially cook rice:** Add the drained soaked rice to the boiling water. Stir once gently and return to a boil. Begin tasting at 3 minutes; drain when the outside is soft but the center is distinctly firm, often about 4–6 minutes depending on the rice. Do not wait until fully tender. Retain the whole spices with the rice, or remove large whole spices now if preferred.
5. **Layer promptly:** Spread the reserved 2 tbsp onion oil over the bottom of the heavy cooking pot. Take chicken from the refrigerator and spread it with all its marinade in an even layer. Scatter one-third of the fried onions over it. Spread the hot, drained rice on top without packing it down. Drizzle with saffron milk, melted ghee, and optional rose or kewra water. Scatter the remaining onions, cilantro, and mint over the top. Cover tightly; use a sheet of foil under the lid if needed for a snug fit.
6. **Cook under steam:** Heat over medium until you hear a gentle simmer and see light steam at the lid edge, about 5–8 minutes. Reduce heat enough to maintain that gentle simmer, rather than automatically using the lowest burner setting. Cook covered for 30 minutes, lowering heat if you smell scorching. Keep the lid closed between checks to retain steam.
7. **Verify before resting:** Open carefully away from your face. Probe several of the largest chicken pieces at the center and near the pot edge, avoiding the pot itself; each must reach 165°F / 74°C. Check the rice temperature in several places also reaches 165°F / 74°C, and taste a grain for tenderness without a chalky core. If either temperature or texture is short, re-cover and cook another 5–10 minutes before checking again. If rice is drying, sprinkle 2 tbsp hot water over it, with up to the remaining 2 tbsp as needed. Do not use resting time as a substitute for these endpoints.
8. **Rest and serve:** Once chicken and rice meet the checks, turn off heat and rest covered for 15 minutes. Lift portions from the bottom with a wide spoon so each serving includes chicken and rice, disturbing the grains as little as possible. Remove any visible whole spices and tell diners that some may remain. Serve with raita or kachumber salad; additional rice is unnecessary.

data.title: Chicken Chile Enchiladas
ingredients: 1 lb Shredded Chicken (Rotisserie or Pressure Cooked)
1 can (15 oz) Red Enchilada Sauce (Hatch or homemade)
Sour Cream, Fresh Cilantro, and Sliced Jalapeños

body:
## Chef's Note

Traditional Mexican enchiladas briefly fry corn tortillas before dipping them in sauce to prevent them from becoming soggy during baking. Searing each tortilla in a little oil for just 5 seconds makes them pliable enough to roll without cracking while creating a protective layer that holds their structure. Red chile enchilada sauce delivers the classic earthy, deeply spiced profile.

## Directions

1.  **Prep:** Preheat oven to 375°F. In a bowl, toss shredded chicken with the green chiles and diced red pepper.
2.  **Coat:** Heat a splash of oil in a small skillet. Flash-fry each tortilla for 5 seconds per side just until pliable.
3.  **Dip & Roll:** Dip a warm tortilla into the red sauce. Place a large scoop of chicken in the center, sprinkle with a little cheese, and roll tightly. Place seam-side down in a baking dish.
4.  **Bake:** Pour the remaining sauce over the top and cover generously with cheese.
5.  **Melt:** Bake for 15-20 minutes until the cheese is bubbly and the edges of the tortillas are slightly crisp.
6.  **Serve:** Top with cold sour cream and cilantro to balance the heat.

data.title: Coq au Vin with Chicken Thighs
ingredients: 2 lbs (900 g) bone-in skin-on chicken thighs
4 oz (113 g) bacon or lardons, diced
1 tbsp neutral oil, only if needed to supplement rendered fat
1/2 tsp fine salt, plus more only if needed
8 oz (225 g) fresh cremini mushrooms, halved or quartered if large
3 medium carrots (about 250 g total), cut into 1-inch pieces
1 cup (240 ml) unsalted chicken stock, plus a little more if needed
2 tbsp (28 g) unsalted butter, cold and cubed
data.description: Bone-in chicken gently braised with red wine, bacon, and mushrooms, with a glossy butter finish.

learning.focus: Brown first, then braise gently
learning.outcome: Tender bone-in thighs with softened skin, distinct mushrooms, and a wine sauce that coats a spoon.
before: Use a wide 5–6 quart Dutch oven that holds the thighs in one snug layer for braising. Sear in batches.
The browned skin softens during covered braising. This dish is about tender meat and sauce, not a crisp roast-chicken skin.

checkpoints.cue: Thigh skin is golden and releases with gentle pressure.
checkpoints.why: Leaving the skin in contact with the pan builds browning and renders fat; tearing it up early can leave it stuck.

checkpoints.cue: Liquid bubbles gently around the edges rather than boiling hard.
checkpoints.why: A controlled simmer lets connective tissue soften without aggressively tightening and drying the muscle.

checkpoints.cue: Thickest meat reaches at least 165°F / 74°C and a fork enters easily near the joint.
checkpoints.why: Safety temperature and braising tenderness answer different questions. Thighs may need more time after reaching the minimum temperature.

checkpoints.cue: Reduced sauce lightly coats a spoon before butter is added.
checkpoints.why: Butter adds gloss and richness, but it cannot turn a large volume of thin broth into a properly reduced sauce.

troubleshooting.cause: Too much bacon and chicken fat was left in the pot.
troubleshooting.fix: Skim surface fat before reducing and before adding the finishing butter.

troubleshooting.problem: Chicken is firm although the temperature is safe
troubleshooting.cause: Connective tissue has not softened enough.
troubleshooting.fix: Continue a gentle covered simmer and check every 10 minutes, adding stock if liquid runs low.

troubleshooting.problem: Sauce tastes harsh or overly concentrated
troubleshooting.cause: The wine is particularly tannic or the sauce reduced too far.
troubleshooting.fix: Loosen with unsalted stock. Use a moderate, dry red wine next time; more salt will not correct excessive tannin.

learning.timing: Allow 2 1/2 hours for preparation, two searing batches, wine reduction, and 45–60 minutes of gentle braising. Very large thighs may need longer.
learning.storage: Refrigerate in shallow containers within 2 hours (1 hour above 90°F / 32°C), at 40°F / 4°C or below. Use within 3–4 days; reheat leftovers to 165°F / 74°C. Refrigerate chicken in the sauce. The chilled fat can be lifted off before reheating; stir gently after heating through.

FoodSafety.gov — Clean, separate, cook, chill
American Chemical Society — Chemistry of grilling
Exploratorium — Meat, collagen, and tenderness

body:
## Chef's Note

This coq au vin uses modern chicken thighs, bacon, and a red-wine braise. Brown the mushrooms separately so they develop color instead of steaming among the carrots and onions. Gentle cooking then softens the chicken; a reduced sauce and an off-heat butter finish supply body and gloss. Wine remains an ingredient after cooking, so this is not an alcohol-free dish.

## Directions

1. **Prepare and render:** Pat chicken dry and season with the measured salt and pepper. Cook bacon in a wide Dutch oven over medium heat for 6–8 minutes, stirring, until it releases fat and begins to crisp. Transfer bacon to a bowl. Leave about 2 tbsp fat in the pot, adding some of the optional neutral oil if there is too little.
2. **Brown mushrooms:** Add mushrooms and cook over medium-high heat for 6–8 minutes, stirring occasionally, until moisture evaporates and golden surfaces develop. Transfer to a separate bowl for the end of the braise.
3. **Brown chicken:** Keep about 2 tbsp fat in the pot. Sear chicken in two batches, skin-side down for 6–8 minutes, then 2 minutes on the other side. Transfer to a plate. Adjust heat if the browned residue darkens too far. Spoon out excess rendered fat, leaving about 2 tbsp.
4. **Cook vegetables:** Lower heat to medium. Add onion and carrots and cook 6–8 minutes, stirring, until onion softens. Add garlic and tomato paste and stir for 1 minute. Scrape away any black burned residue rather than incorporating it into the sauce.
5. **Reduce wine:** Take the pot briefly off the burner to add wine. Return to medium-high heat, scrape up golden browned residue, and simmer uncovered until the wine reduces by roughly half, about 10–15 minutes.
6. **Braise gently:** Return chicken, accumulated plate juices, and bacon. Add stock and thyme. Liquid should come about halfway to two-thirds up the thighs, not cover them; add a little stock only if needed. Bring to a simmer, cover, and lower heat to maintain gentle bubbles. Cook about 45–60 minutes, adding the reserved mushrooms for the last 10 minutes. Check meat away from the bone reaches at least 165°F / 74°C and feels tender near the joint; continue in 10-minute increments if still firm.
7. **Concentrate and finish:** Transfer tender chicken to a clean platter. Remove thyme stems and skim excess surface fat. Simmer the uncovered sauce about 5–10 minutes until it lightly coats a spoon. Turn off heat, let vigorous bubbling stop, and swirl in cold butter. Taste before adding any extra salt.
8. **Serve:** Return chicken to the warm sauce, spoon sauce over it, and finish with parsley. Serve with one starch such as mashed potatoes and a green vegetable.

4. Cook vegetables: Lower heat to medium. Add onion and carrots and cook 6–8 minutes, stirring, until onion softens. Add garlic and tomato paste and stir for 1 minute. Scrape away any black burned residue rather than incorporating it into the sauce.
5. Reduce wine: Take the pot briefly off the burner to add wine. Return to medium-high heat, scrape up golden browned residue, and simmer uncovered until the wine reduces by roughly half, about 10–15 minutes.
6. Braise gently: Return chicken, accumulated plate juices, and bacon. Add stock and thyme. Liquid should come about halfway to two-thirds up the thighs, not cover them; add a little stock only if needed. Bring to a simmer, cover, and lower heat to maintain gentle bubbles. Cook about 45–60 minutes, adding the reserved mushrooms for the last 10 minutes. Check meat away from the bone reaches at least 165°F / 74°C and feels tender near the joint; continue in 10-minute increments if still firm.
7. Concentrate and finish: Transfer tender chicken to a clean platter. Remove thyme stems and skim excess surface fat. Simmer the uncovered sauce about 5–10 minutes until it lightly coats a spoon. Turn off heat, let vigorous bubbling stop, and swirl in cold butter. Taste before adding any extra salt.
8. Serve: Return chicken to the warm sauce, spoon sauce over it, and finish with parsley. Serve with one starch such as mashed potatoes and a green vegetable.

data.title: Chicken Fingers
ingredients: 1 lb Chicken Tenderloins or Breasts cut into strips
2 large eggs, beaten with the separately measured water
1 tbsp water, for beating with the eggs

body:
## Chef's Note

Set up the breading ingredients separately so each piece of chicken gets an even coating. By using **Panko** and Parmesan instead of crackers, we achieve a much lighter, crispier texture that doesn't turn greasy. The secret to the crunch is **High-Heat Roasting** on a wire rack - this allows the hot air to circulate under the chicken, ensuring it is crispy on all sides without needing deep frying.

## Directions

1.  **Prep:** Preheat oven to 425°F. Place a wire cooling rack on top of a large baking sheet. Spray the rack with oil.
2.  **Station:** Set up three shallow bowls:
    - Bowl 1: Flour, salt, and pepper.
    - Bowl 2: Beaten eggs.
    - Bowl 3: Panko, Parmesan, garlic powder, and oregano.
3.  **Bread:** Dip each chicken strip in flour (shake off excess), then egg, then press firmly into the panko mixture until fully coated.
4.  **Roast:** Arrange on the wire rack. Spray the tops of the chicken lightly with oil.
5.  **Crisp:** Bake for 12-15 minutes until golden brown and the internal temp is 165°F. (No need to flip if using a wire rack!).
6.  **Finish:** Serve hot with a squeeze of lemon or your favorite dipping sauce.

data.title: Korean-inspired Chicken Glass-Noodle Salad
ingredients: 10 oz (280 g) dangmyeon (Korean sweet-potato glass noodles)
2 tbsp water, plus more for loosening noodles
1 bell pepper, seeded and thinly sliced
1/2 cup loosely packed cilantro leaves, roughly chopped
data.description: Chewy sweet-potato noodles with savory chicken, crisp pepper, and a sesame-vinegar dressing made separately from the cooking sauce.

learning.focus: Separate the cooking sauce from the noodle dressing
learning.outcome: Springy noodles coated with a light dressing, moist chicken, and vegetables that keep their crunch.
before: Mix the clean dressing before handling raw chicken. Set out a separate serving bowl and utensils.
If using oi muchim, prepare it first or use an already prepared portion; its 30-minute preparation is additional.

checkpoints.cue: Noodles are flexible and chewy with no hard center.
checkpoints.why: Dangmyeon brands differ in thickness; the package and a tasted noodle are more useful than one universal boiling time.

checkpoints.cue: Chicken reaches 165°F / 74°C and is lightly glazed, without a pool of sauce.
checkpoints.why: The thermometer verifies poultry safety; modest evaporation keeps the filling moist without diluting the salad.

checkpoints.cue: Dressing coats the noodles and the strands separate when lifted.
checkpoints.why: Starch-rich noodles firm and stick as they cool. A little water loosens the coating without adding more salt.

troubleshooting.cause: They cooled in a drained heap or absorbed the dressing.
troubleshooting.fix: Separate gently with tongs and add water a tablespoon at a time. Do not keep adding soy sauce.

troubleshooting.cause: The glaze was cooked until the meat became crisp throughout.
troubleshooting.fix: Loosen with a tablespoon of water and stop cooking as soon as the temperature and light-glaze cues are met.

substitutions.alternative: 450 g boneless skinless chicken thighs, sliced 1/4 inch thick
substitutions.effect: Cook in two batches if necessary, then glaze. Check the thickest slices reach 165°F / 74°C; allow extra cooking time.

learning.timing: 35 minutes for the noodle salad alone. Prepare optional oi muchim separately; only 1/2 cup is used here, not its full four-portion batch.
learning.storage: Refrigerate in shallow containers within 2 hours (1 hour above 90°F / 32°C), at 40°F / 4°C or below. Use within 3–4 days; reheat leftovers to 165°F / 74°C. Store the chicken and noodles separately from fresh herbs, pepper, and cucumber when preparing ahead. Reheated noodles have a softer texture.

body:
## Chef's Note

This is a Korean-inspired noodle salad with soy, sesame, ginger, and garlic. The old name, “galbi,” suggested a rib dish that this ground-chicken recipe does not make. A cooked glaze seasons the chicken; a separate clean dressing seasons the noodles. Keeping those jobs separate lets you control moisture and salt without using raw-meat marinade as a finishing sauce.

## Directions

1. **Mix two sauces:** In a large serving bowl, dissolve 1 tbsp brown sugar in the vinegar and 2 tbsp soy sauce, then whisk in the sesame oil. In a small bowl, mix the remaining 2 tbsp soy sauce, remaining 1 tbsp sugar, and 2 tbsp water for the chicken.
2. **Cook the noodles:** Boil dangmyeon according to its package, tasting for a chewy texture without a hard center. Drain, rinse briefly under cool running water, and drain thoroughly. Cut long strands with clean kitchen shears. Toss promptly with the dressing in the serving bowl.
3. **Cook the chicken:** Heat the neutral oil in a wide skillet over medium-high heat. Add chicken and break it into small pieces. Cook about 5–7 minutes, stirring occasionally, until most visible moisture has evaporated and some edges are golden.
4. **Glaze:** Lower heat to medium. Add garlic and ginger and stir for 30 seconds. Add the small bowl of cooking sauce and simmer 2–3 minutes, stirring. Check several thick clusters of chicken reach 165°F / 74°C, keeping the thermometer tip off the pan. Continue cooking if needed. Leave a thin glaze rather than cooking the meat dry.
5. **Toss and finish:** Add the cooked chicken to the noodles. Fold in pepper, cilantro, and sesame seeds. If the noodles stick, loosen with water a tablespoon at a time. Divide among four bowls and top each with 2 tbsp prepared oi muchim if using. Serve promptly, warm or cool.

data.title: Chicken Katsu Curry
ingredients: 30 g all-purpose flour, reserved only for the sauce
2 cups (480 ml) unsalted chicken stock, plus a little water if needed
150 g potato, peeled and cut into 1/2-inch dice
4 boneless skinless chicken breast portions, about 6 oz (170 g) each
60 g all-purpose flour, for coating chicken
500–750 ml neutral frying oil, or enough for 1/2-inch depth in your skillet
data.description: Crisp panko-coated chicken cutlets with a separately simmered vegetable curry sauce, served alongside rice prepared separately.

learning.focus: Finish the sauce first, then protect the cutlet crust
learning.outcome: Golden, crisp chicken with a moist center and a spoonable curry sauce served beside it.
before: The curry and four cutlets take about one hour. Rice is separate; start its soak first if making the linked short-grain rice.
Measure the sauce flour into its own clean container before handling raw chicken. Used breading flour must never be tipped into the sauce.
Use a deep skillet and leave ample space above the oil. Keep water away from the hot oil and use separate clean tools for finished chicken.

checkpoints.cue: Potato and carrot are tender and sauce coats a spoon before frying begins.
checkpoints.why: The sauce can wait gently; fried cutlets lose crispness if they sit while a whole sauce is made.

checkpoints.cue: Chicken has a thin flour film, drained egg coating, and an even layer of panko.
checkpoints.why: Loose excess flour and pooled egg can leave weak spots. There is no useful two-second egg-dip rule.

checkpoints.cue: Oil is around 350°F / 175°C before a batch and remains about 325–350°F / 165–175°C during frying.
checkpoints.why: Adding cold cutlets lowers oil temperature. Adjust heat between batches so breading cooks at a controlled pace.

checkpoints.cue: The thickest center of each cutlet reaches 165°F / 74°C.
checkpoints.why: Golden breadcrumbs can form before the meat is fully cooked. Check from the side into the center.

troubleshooting.problem: Coating browns before the center reaches temperature
troubleshooting.cause: Oil is too hot or the cutlet is thicker than 1/2 inch.
troubleshooting.fix: Transfer to a rack on a tray and finish in a 350°F / 175°C oven until 165°F / 74°C in the center. Reduce oil heat for the next batch.

troubleshooting.cause: Water evaporated or the starch thickened further as the sauce cooled.
troubleshooting.fix: Stir in a small splash of hot water and warm gently until it flows from a spoon.

troubleshooting.cause: Excess flour, wet spots, or rough handling weakened the coating.
troubleshooting.fix: Let excess egg drip off, press panko on gently, and avoid repeatedly moving the cutlet before its first side firms.

substitutions.alternative: 1 tsp sugar mixed with 2 tsp water
substitutions.effect: Adds sweetness without mirin aroma. Add it with the stock so it dissolves through the sauce.

learning.timing: About 60 minutes includes sauce preparation, breading, two frying batches, and a short rack rest. Rice needs its own start time and is not included in the ingredient quantities.
learning.storage: Refrigerate in shallow containers within 2 hours (1 hour above 90°F / 32°C), at 40°F / 4°C or below. Use within 3–4 days; reheat leftovers to 165°F / 74°C. Store cutlets and curry separately. Reheat cutlets on a rack in a 350°F / 175°C oven to 165°F / 74°C; gently reheat sauce to the same endpoint, stirring and adding water as needed. The crust is best freshly fried.

## Chef's Note

Katsu curry depends on contrast: a crisp cutlet, soft vegetables, and a smooth sauce. Cook the sauce first, then fry the chicken close to serving and ladle gravy beside the breading. This sauce uses its own measured flour; the original ingredient list supplied only dredging flour and could not reliably make the promised gravy.

## Directions

1. **Start the sauce:** Melt butter in a saucepan over medium heat. Add onion and cook about 6–8 minutes until soft and lightly golden. Stir in garlic and ginger for 30 seconds. Add the 30 g sauce flour and stir for 2 minutes. Lower the heat, stir in curry powder and tomato paste, and cook about 30 seconds without scorching.
2. **Simmer vegetables:** Gradually whisk in stock, then soy sauce and mirin. Add carrot and potato. Bring to a gentle simmer and cook about 18–22 minutes, stirring the bottom regularly, until both vegetables are tender and sauce coats a spoon. Add peas and simmer 2 minutes more. Add a small splash of water if the sauce is too thick. Cover and take off heat while frying; rewarm before serving.
3. **Prepare cutlets:** While the sauce simmers, put each chicken portion between sheets of food-safe wrap and pound with a meat mallet to an even 1/2-inch thickness. Pat dry and season with the measured salt and pepper. Keep raw chicken and its tools away from the sauce and cooked food.
4. **Bread:** Set out separate shallow dishes of the 60 g coating flour, beaten eggs, and panko. Coat each cutlet lightly in flour and shake off excess. Dip in egg, let excess drip away, then press both sides into panko. Place on a clean tray and refrigerate until the oil is ready. Discard leftover coating ingredients that touched raw chicken.
5. **Heat oil:** Set a wire rack over a rimmed tray. For holding the first batch briefly, heat the oven to 225°F / 110°C. Add oil to a deep skillet to reach about 1/2 inch, keeping the pan less than half full. Heat to about 350°F / 175°C. Use the pan depth as the guide; the required oil volume varies with its shape.
6. **Fry in batches:** Lower in two cutlets without overlapping. Fry about 3–4 minutes per side, adjusting heat to keep oil around 325–350°F / 165–175°C. Check each cutlet from the side for 165°F / 74°C in its thickest center; cook longer if needed. Transfer to the rack and hold the first batch in the low oven while the second fries. Skim loose crumbs and let the oil return to temperature between batches.
7. **Finish and serve:** Rest the last cutlets on the rack for about 3 minutes. Rewarm the sauce, adding a little water if needed. Slice chicken into strips and divide sauce among four plates, pouring it alongside rather than over the whole crust. Serve with rice prepared separately.

data.title: Chicken Lettuce Wraps
ingredients: 1 lb (450 g) ground chicken or ground turkey
1/2 cup sliced scallions, whites and greens separated
2 tbsp water, plus more if needed
1 large head butter lettuce, leaves separated (about 12 usable leaves)
1/2 cup purchased ready-to-eat crispy rice noodles, optional
data.description: A moist hoisin-ginger chicken filling with crisp celery, served in cold, dry lettuce leaves. Learn to reduce a glaze without drying out the meat.

learning.focus: Keep the filling moist and the lettuce crisp
learning.outcome: Small pieces of chicken with a clinging glaze, crunchy celery, and cool leaves that can be folded around the filling.
before: Wash and thoroughly dry the lettuce, then refrigerate it until serving. Wet leaves make slippery wraps.
Hoisin is already sweet and salty; measure the additional soy sauce before adjusting seasoning.

checkpoints.cue: Chicken has some golden edges and celery remains firm.
checkpoints.why: Brief browning adds flavor, but cooking until every piece is crisp would dry this small ground-meat filling.

checkpoints.cue: The glaze clings and the chicken reaches 165°F / 74°C.
checkpoints.why: A bubbling sauce does not establish the center temperature of every poultry cluster.

troubleshooting.cause: The sauce is too watery or the cups are overfilled.
troubleshooting.fix: Reduce the filling briefly in the skillet, checking it stays moist, and use smaller spoonfuls. Double up small lettuce leaves.

troubleshooting.problem: Glaze is sticky or too salty
troubleshooting.cause: Bottled sauces vary, or too much water evaporated.
troubleshooting.fix: Add water one tablespoon at a time. Serve with more plain lettuce or rice; extra vinegar does not remove salt.

substitutions.alternative: 100 g drained, finely diced canned water chestnuts
substitutions.effect: A different, clean crunch. Stir them in with the aromatics; they need only heating, not the celery cooking time.

substitutions.alternative: Ground turkey
substitutions.effect: Use the same 165°F / 74°C endpoint. Very lean turkey dries faster; keep a little loosened sauce around it.

learning.timing: 30 minutes includes washing and drying the leaves. Four light portions make about three wraps each; add plain rice for a fuller dinner.
learning.storage: Refrigerate in shallow containers within 2 hours (1 hour above 90°F / 32°C), at 40°F / 4°C or below. Use within 3–4 days; reheat leftovers to 165°F / 74°C. Store the cooked filling separately. Keep washed, dried lettuce refrigerated and fill it only when serving.

body:
## Chef's Note

These Chinese-American-inspired wraps depend on contrast: warm, savory chicken against cool, crisp lettuce. Celery gives the filling a fresh crunch; water chestnuts are another good option with a different texture. Hoisin provides sweetness and salt, so the sauce needs only a modest amount of additional soy.

## Directions

1. **Prepare leaves and sauce:** Wash and dry the lettuce leaves and chill them. Mix hoisin, soy sauce, vinegar, and water in a small bowl. Separate scallion whites from greens.
2. **Start the chicken:** Heat neutral oil in a wide skillet over medium-high heat. Add chicken and break into small pieces. Cook 5–6 minutes, stirring occasionally, until released liquid mostly evaporates and some edges begin to brown.
3. **Add crunch and aromatics:** Add celery and scallion whites and cook 2 minutes. Lower heat to medium, add ginger and garlic, and stir for 30 seconds, keeping the garlic from scorching.
4. **Glaze and check:** Add the hoisin mixture. Simmer, stirring, for 2–3 minutes until it coats the filling. Check several thick clusters reach 165°F / 74°C, keeping the thermometer tip off the hot pan. Continue cooking if necessary; add a spoonful of water if the glaze becomes sticky.
5. **Finish and serve:** Turn off heat and stir in sesame oil and scallion greens. Transfer to a serving bowl and let stand briefly until no longer fiercely steaming. Spoon small portions into the lettuce at the table, adding ready-to-eat crispy noodles if desired. Keep the rest of the leaves unfilled until needed.

data.title: Chicken Marsala
ingredients: 1.5 lbs (680 g) boneless skinless chicken thighs, opened flat
1/2 cup (60 g) all-purpose flour, for dredging
8 oz (225 g) fresh cremini mushrooms, wiped clean and thickly sliced
3/4 cup (180 ml) unsalted chicken stock, plus more for loosening
2 tbsp (28 g) unsalted butter, cold and cubed
data.description: Golden chicken cutlets in a mushroom and dry Marsala pan sauce, finished gently with butter.

learning.focus: Build a pan sauce in the right order
learning.outcome: Tender chicken, browned mushrooms, and a fluid sauce that lightly coats the meat without separating into oil.
before: Use a wide, heavy skillet and plan for two chicken batches.
Use fresh cremini mushrooms here. Dried porcini are concentrated and require soaking; they are not a weight-for-weight replacement.

checkpoints.cue: Mushroom moisture evaporates and golden patches develop.
checkpoints.why: Crowded, wet mushrooms steam; giving them room and time allows browning before wine is added.

checkpoints.cue: Chicken centers reach 165°F / 74°C before the butter finish.
checkpoints.why: Safety comes before emulsification: the chicken can finish simmering while the sauce still tolerates heat.

checkpoints.cue: Butter disappears into a glossy sauce with no oily puddles.
checkpoints.why: Swirling butter into an aqueous sauce off heat disperses its fat. Hard boiling afterward makes separation more likely.

troubleshooting.problem: Sauce is too thick or salty
troubleshooting.cause: Flour thickened the liquid or too much evaporated; prosciutto also contributes salt.
troubleshooting.fix: Add unsalted stock a tablespoon at a time. Taste before using the reserved salt.

troubleshooting.cause: It was boiled after the butter finish or had too little water remaining.
troubleshooting.fix: Take the pan off heat and swirl in a tablespoon of cool stock. Repeat if needed, without boiling.

substitutions.alternative: 680 g chicken breast cutlets about 1/2 inch thick
substitutions.effect: Lean breasts have less tolerance for overcooking. Begin checking sooner and finish at 165°F / 74°C.

substitutions.alternative: 180 ml additional unsalted stock with 1–2 tsp lemon juice added to taste at the end
substitutions.effect: An alcohol-free mushroom pan sauce with a different flavor; it will lack Marsala’s distinctive wine character.

learning.timing: 50 minutes allows two searing batches and mushroom browning. Prepare one starch separately; its cooking time is not included.
learning.storage: Refrigerate in shallow containers within 2 hours (1 hour above 90°F / 32°C), at 40°F / 4°C or below. Use within 3–4 days; reheat leftovers to 165°F / 74°C. The butter sauce may separate when reheated; loosen with stock and stir gently after reaching the reheating temperature.

body:
## Chef's Note

This version pairs chicken thighs with fresh mushrooms and dry Marsala. A light flour coating helps the chicken brown and gives the sauce some body. Prosciutto is a seasoning here, so the stock is unsalted and final salt comes only after reduction. Cooking with wine does not make a dish reliably alcohol-free; use the stock-and-lemon alternative when needed.

## Directions

1. **Prepare the cutlets:** Open thighs flat, trim loose fat, and gently pound only the thick sections to about 1/2 inch between sheets of plastic wrap. Season with half the measured salt and the pepper. Spread flour in a shallow dish, dredge lightly, and shake off excess. Discard leftover flour after raw chicken contact.
2. **Brown in batches:** Heat 1 tbsp oil in a wide skillet over medium-high heat. Cook half the chicken about 3–4 minutes on the first side and 2–3 minutes on the second, until golden; it can finish cooking later in the sauce. Transfer to a plate. Repeat with the remaining oil and chicken. Reduce heat if the flour browns too quickly; discard any black, burned bits.
3. **Brown mushrooms:** Lower heat to medium. Add prosciutto and stir for 1 minute. Add mushrooms and cook 6–8 minutes, stirring occasionally, until their liquid has evaporated and they begin to brown. If the pan becomes dry and sticks before the mushrooms release moisture, add a tablespoon of stock and scrape gently.
4. **Make the sauce:** Take the pan briefly off the burner to pour in the Marsala. Return to medium heat and scrape up the golden pan residue. Simmer until the wine reduces by about half, roughly 4–6 minutes. Add stock and simmer 2–3 minutes; the sauce should still be pourable.
5. **Finish cooking the chicken:** Return the chicken and its plate juices to the pan. Simmer gently for about 3–5 minutes, turning once, until the thickest parts reach 165°F / 74°C. Continue if needed, adding stock if the sauce gets too thick. Transfer the cooked chicken to a clean serving platter.
6. **Finish with butter:** Turn off heat and let vigorous bubbling subside. Swirl in the cold butter a few pieces at a time. Add parsley, taste, and use the reserved salt only if needed. Spoon sauce and mushrooms over the chicken and serve. Choose mashed potatoes or pasta, with a green vegetable alongside.

Season with half the measured salt and the pepper. Spread flour in a shallow dish, dredge lightly, and shake off excess. Discard leftover flour after raw chicken contact.

Brown in batches: Heat 1 tbsp oil in a wide skillet over medium-high heat. Cook half the chicken about 3–4 minutes on the first side and 2–3 minutes on the second, until golden; it can finish cooking later in the sauce. Transfer to a plate. Repeat with the remaining oil and chicken. Reduce heat if the flour browns too quickly; discard any black, burned bits.

Brown mushrooms: Lower heat to medium. Add prosciutto and stir for 1 minute. Add mushrooms and cook 6–8 minutes, stirring occasionally, until their liquid has evaporated and they begin to brown. Make the sauce: Take the pan briefly off the burner to pour in the Marsala. Return to medium heat and scrape up the golden pan residue. Simmer until the wine reduces by about half, roughly 4–6 minutes. Add stock and simmer 2–3 minutes; the sauce should still be pourable.

Spoon sauce and mushrooms over the chicken and serve. Choose mashed potatoes or pasta, with a green vegetable alongside.

data.title: Chicken Milanese
ingredients: 1.5 lbs (680 g) boneless skinless chicken breasts, for thin cutlets
1 cup (240 ml) neutral oil, approximately, for a 1/8-inch layer in the skillet
1 batch [Everyday Arugula Salad](/mise/recipes/everyday-arugula-salad), using the linked recipe’s original yield; keep undressed until serving
data.description: Thin chicken cutlets with a crisp Parmesan-panko coating, served with freshly dressed arugula and lemon.

learning.focus: Match crust browning to the chicken center
learning.outcome: Evenly thin chicken with a golden, crisp coating and a center that reaches 165°F / 74°C.
before: Set out the ingredients for one whole four-portion arugula salad, including its oil, lemon, cheese, and seasonings. Keep the leaves dry and undressed.
Set a wire rack over a sheet pan. If holding a first batch briefly, heat the oven to 200°F / 95°C.

checkpoints.cue: The cutlets are an even 1/4 inch thick with no thick hump.
checkpoints.why: Uniform thickness allows the center to cook before the crumbs burn.

checkpoints.cue: Oil bubbles steadily around the crumbs; the crust turns golden gradually.
checkpoints.why: Oil that is too hot burns the cheese and crumbs early; weak heat lengthens frying and gives a greasy coating.

checkpoints.cue: The center of each cutlet reaches 165°F / 74°C.
checkpoints.why: A golden exterior does not prove poultry doneness. Inserting the probe from the side keeps the sensing tip in thin meat.

troubleshooting.problem: Crumbs darken before the chicken is ready
troubleshooting.cause: Oil is too hot or the cutlets are uneven.
troubleshooting.fix: Lower the heat. If the crust is already dark, finish on a rack in a 350°F / 175°C oven until the center reaches 165°F / 74°C.

troubleshooting.cause: Steam was trapped underneath or salad dressing soaked it.
troubleshooting.fix: Drain on a rack, avoid stacking, and serve salad beside the cutlet or add it only at the last moment.

substitutions.alternative: 90 g fine dry breadcrumbs
substitutions.effect: A finer, denser crust that may brown faster. Watch the heat closely; do not rely on the same volume measure.

learning.timing: 40 minutes includes two frying batches and a five-minute salad prepared during setup. Allow more time for extra batches or washing a large bunch of greens.
learning.storage: Refrigerate in shallow containers within 2 hours (1 hour above 90°F / 32°C), at 40°F / 4°C or below. Use within 3–4 days; reheat leftovers to 165°F / 74°C. Store chicken separately from salad. The coating softens in storage; reheat on a rack in the oven to the safe endpoint. Dress new greens at serving.

body:
## Chef's Note

This chicken version of a Milanese-style cutlet uses panko and Parmesan for an open, crisp coating. Thin, even meat is essential: the crumbs should turn golden at about the same time the center finishes cooking. The lemon-arugula salad provides acidity and freshness; keep it beside the chicken if you want the crust to stay crisp longer.

## Directions

1. **Prepare chicken and salad:** Slice the breasts horizontally into four cutlets, then pound between sheets of plastic wrap to an even 1/4 inch. Season both sides with the measured salt and pepper. Prepare one four-portion batch of [Everyday Arugula Salad](/mise/recipes/everyday-arugula-salad), keeping its dressing and cheese separate from the dry leaves. Set a rack over a sheet pan. Heat the oven to 200°F / 95°C if holding the first batch briefly.
2. **Set the coating station:** Place flour in one shallow dish, eggs in a second, and panko mixed with Parmesan, oregano, and garlic powder in a third.
3. **Coat:** Dredge each cutlet lightly in flour, dip in egg and let excess drip off, then press into crumbs on both sides. Keep coated cutlets in one layer. Discard coating ingredients left after raw chicken contact and wash hands and utensils.
4. **Heat and fry:** Pour enough neutral oil into a large skillet to reach about 1/8 inch deep; the amount depends on its flat base. Heat over medium to medium-high to about 350°F / 175°C. Lower two cutlets carefully into the oil, away from you. Fry about 2–3 minutes per side, adjusting the heat so the coating turns golden without burning. Do not crowd or stack them.
5. **Check and drain:** Insert a thermometer horizontally from the side of each cutlet; the meat must reach 165°F / 74°C. Continue cooking as needed. Move cooked cutlets to the rack and hold briefly in a 200°F / 95°C oven while frying the next batch. Skim burned crumbs, replenish oil if needed, and let it reheat before adding more chicken.
6. **Serve promptly:** Toss and finish the arugula salad according to its recipe. Divide among four plates with the hot cutlets and lemon wedges. Add salad on top only just before eating, or serve it alongside to preserve the crust.

data.title: Phở Gà (Chicken Pho)
ingredients: 1 chicken (about 3.5 lbs / 1.6 kg each), cut into quarters, giblets removed
2 lbs (900 g) chicken wings or backs
450 g yellow onions, halved with skin on
5 quarts (4.7 liters) water, plus more to adjust the strained broth
1/4 cup (60 ml) fish sauce, added gradually to taste
1 1/2 tsp fine salt, added gradually to taste
1 lb (450 g) dried flat rice noodles (bánh phở)
200 g bean sprouts, optional, cooked thoroughly before serving
1 cup loosely packed Thai basil leaves, optional
3 tbsp hoisin sauce, optional at the table
3 tbsp sriracha, optional at the table
data.description: A gently simmered chicken broth with toasted aromatics, rice noodles, and sliced chicken that is removed early to preserve its texture.

learning.focus: Separate tender serving meat from long-cooked broth
learning.outcome: An aromatic broth with moist sliced chicken, tender noodles, and fresh garnishes added at serving.
before: Use a 12-quart stockpot for the water plus chicken and bones. Do not fill a smaller pot to its rim.
Keep serving meat separate from the bones during the long simmer. Noodles and toppings are prepared near serving.

checkpoints.cue: Onion and ginger have some charred patches and smell sweetly aromatic, without being burned throughout.
checkpoints.why: Surface charring adds roasted aroma; loose blackened skins can make broth gritty or bitter.

checkpoints.cue: Every quarter reaches 165°F / 74°C at its thickest meat, away from bone.
checkpoints.why: Chicken quarters differ in size. The clock alone does not establish doneness, and breast portions may finish sooner than legs.

checkpoints.cue: Strained broth tastes savory and lightly sweet before noodles are added.
checkpoints.why: Evaporation concentrates seasoning, while noodles dilute each bite. Adjust only after the broth volume is settled.

troubleshooting.cause: It stayed in the pot for the full broth simmer.
troubleshooting.fix: Slice thinly and warm briefly in broth. Next time remove each quarter as it reaches temperature, strip the meat, and return only the bones.

troubleshooting.cause: Too much water remains for the amount of chicken used.
troubleshooting.fix: Reduce the strained broth gently before final seasoning. Do not try to replace missing chicken flavor with excessive fish sauce.

troubleshooting.cause: They were cooked or stored in the broth too long.
troubleshooting.fix: Prepare noodles separately in portions and combine only when serving. Follow the package for the noodle width you have.

learning.timing: About 3 1/2 hours includes aromatics, heating the large pot, chicken cooking, approximately two hours further broth simmering, and final bowl assembly.
learning.storage: Refrigerate in shallow containers within 2 hours (1 hour above 90°F / 32°C), at 40°F / 4°C or below. Use within 3–4 days; reheat leftovers to 165°F / 74°C. Store strained broth, meat, and noodles separately. Cool broth in smaller shallow containers or an ice bath before refrigerating promptly; do not leave a large stockpot out to cool. Reheat meat in the broth to 165°F / 74°C.

body:
## Chef's Note

The serving meat and broth have different cooking needs. Remove the chicken quarters when cooked, then let the bones continue simmering for body and flavor. Aromatics vary between phở gà recipes; this version retains a modest amount of star anise, cinnamon, and coriander. Hoisin, chile sauce, and fresh herbs are optional at the table so the broth can be tasted on its own first.

## Directions

1. **Toast aromatics:** Put onion halves and ginger cut-side up on a rimmed sheet pan under the broiler, watching closely and turning as needed, for about 10–15 minutes until softened with charred patches. Cool enough to handle, remove loose blackened onion skin, and scrape off any burned debris. Toast star anise, cinnamon, and coriander in a dry skillet over medium heat for about 1 minute until fragrant.
2. **Start broth:** Put chicken quarters, wings or backs, aromatics, and spices in a 12-quart stockpot with the measured water. Bring just to a boil, skim surface foam, and reduce to a gentle simmer with only occasional bubbles. Do not wash raw chicken in the sink.
3. **Remove serving meat when cooked:** Begin checking quarters after about 30 minutes of simmering. Probe the thickest breast and thigh meat away from bone; remove each quarter only after it reaches 165°F / 74°C. Pieces may need 40 minutes or longer. Transfer to a clean tray and let stand about 10 minutes until safe to handle. Remove meat from bones, put the meat in a shallow covered container, and refrigerate promptly. Return the bones to the stockpot.
4. **Continue the broth:** Simmer bones and aromatics gently for about 2 more hours, skimming occasionally. Add a little water if needed to keep bones submerged. Avoid vigorously stirring the pot.
5. **Strain and balance:** Strain carefully through a fine-mesh sieve into another large pot and discard solids. Skim excess fat, leaving some for flavor. Aim for roughly 3.5–4 liters broth; reduce if weak or add water if overly concentrated. Stir in sugar and start with half the fish sauce and half the salt. Taste and add the remainder gradually only as needed.
6. **Prepare noodles and toppings:** Cook bánh phở according to its package until tender but not falling apart; different widths require different soaking or boiling methods. Drain and divide among six large bowls. Prepare scallion, cilantro, lime, and optional basil, chile, and cooked sprouts.
7. **Warm meat and assemble:** Slice the refrigerated chicken. Add it to simmering broth and heat through to 165°F / 74°C. Distribute meat among the noodle bowls, then ladle in about 500–600 ml broth per bowl. Finish with scallion and cilantro and offer the remaining toppings and sauces at the table. Refrigerate any unused broth promptly.

data.title: Chicken Piccata
ingredients: 1.5 lbs (680 g) boneless skinless chicken breasts, for thin cutlets
1/2 cup (120 ml) unsalted chicken broth, plus more if needed
2 tbsp (28 g) unsalted butter, cold and cubed
2 tbsp brined capers, drained and briefly rinsed
data.description: Thin chicken cutlets with a bright lemon-caper pan sauce. This unfloured version finishes with butter off the heat.

learning.focus: Finish a bright, fluid butter sauce
learning.outcome: Tender cutlets lightly coated in a lemon-caper sauce that is glossy and pourable.
before: Make four cutlets, then pound evenly to 1/4 inch. Plan to cook in two batches.
Use brined capers here. Salt-packed capers need a longer rinse or soak according to their package.

checkpoints.cue: The broth lifts the golden pan residue and remains fluid.
checkpoints.why: There is little liquid to start with. Reducing too far concentrates salt and leaves too little water for a stable butter sauce.

checkpoints.cue: All cutlet centers reach 165°F / 74°C before finishing the sauce.
checkpoints.why: Chicken can finish in the broth if necessary; boiling after butter is added can separate the sauce.

checkpoints.cue: Butter blends into the liquid without a visible layer of oil.
checkpoints.why: Swirling off heat disperses fat into the broth. This unfloured sauce is light and less resistant to hard boiling than a starch-thickened sauce.

troubleshooting.cause: Too little liquid remains or the finished sauce became too hot.
troubleshooting.fix: Take it off heat and swirl in a tablespoon of cool broth. Keep the sauce below a boil after finishing.

troubleshooting.cause: Lemon acidity and caper saltiness vary.
troubleshooting.fix: Loosen with a little unsalted broth and taste with a bite of chicken. Next time hold back some lemon until the final tasting.

learning.timing: 35 minutes includes two batches of thin cutlets. Make any pasta or potatoes separately; their time is not included.
learning.storage: Refrigerate in shallow containers within 2 hours (1 hour above 90°F / 32°C), at 40°F / 4°C or below. Use within 3–4 days; reheat leftovers to 165°F / 74°C. Reheat chicken in the sauce with a splash of broth, then stir gently. The sauce can separate during reheating.

body:
## Chef's Note

Piccata pairs a thin cutlet with lemon, capers, and butter. This version omits a flour coating, leaving a light pan sauce. The goal is a thin, bright coating, not a thick gravy. Save the lemon for the finish and keep enough broth in the pan to carry the butter.

## Directions

1. **Prepare:** Slice the breasts horizontally into four cutlets and pound between sheets of plastic wrap to an even 1/4 inch. Pat dry and season with the measured salt and pepper.
2. **Sear in batches:** Heat 1 tbsp oil in a wide skillet over medium-high heat. Cook half the cutlets about 2–3 minutes per side, until lightly golden. Transfer to a plate and repeat with the remaining oil and chicken. Lower heat if the pan residue darkens too quickly.
3. **Deglaze:** Reduce heat to medium. Stir garlic and capers in the pan for 30 seconds, then add broth. Scrape up golden residue and simmer for about 1 minute. Discard blackened residue rather than incorporating it into the sauce.
4. **Check chicken:** Check each cutlet by inserting a thermometer from its side into the center. If any are below 165°F / 74°C, return them and their plate juices to the broth and simmer gently until they reach that temperature. If all are already cooked, add only their plate juices to the broth and bring it back to a simmer. Transfer cooked chicken to a clean platter. Add a little broth if the pan is becoming dry.
5. **Finish off heat:** Turn off heat and let vigorous bubbling stop. Add lemon juice and swirl in cold butter a few pieces at a time until glossy. Stir in parsley. Taste before adding any additional seasoning, then spoon the sauce over the chicken and serve immediately.

data.title: Chicken Pot Pie
ingredients: 300 g all-purpose flour, plus a little for rolling
225 g cold unsalted butter, cut into 1/2-inch cubes
100–120 ml ice-cold water, added only as needed
450 g cooked boneless chicken, chilled and cut into bite-size pieces (weight after cooking)
1/4 tsp fine salt, plus more only if needed
data.description: A double-crust chicken pie with tender vegetables, a measured milk-and-stock gravy, and cold butter pastry made from scratch.

learning.focus: Keep pastry cold and filling thick enough to support it
learning.outcome: Golden layered pastry surrounding moist chicken and tender vegetables in a gravy that settles after slicing.
before: Start with 450 g already-cooked chicken, weighed after removing skin and bones. Cooking that chicken is a separate preparation; raw chicken cannot be folded into this filling.

Use a deep 9-inch metal pie pan with at least 7 cups (1.65 liters) capacity. A shallow pie plate will not hold this batch. Scaling ingredients requires changing the number or size of pies; baking time does not scale directly.
Allow about three hours for scratch pastry, chilling, filling preparation, assembly, baking, and resting. Filling preparation overlaps the dough chill.

checkpoints.cue: A squeezed handful of dough holds together, with visible flattened butter pieces and no wet paste.
checkpoints.why: Enough water connects the dough; keeping some butter in separate pieces helps produce flaky layers.

checkpoints.cue: Carrot dice are almost tender before the flour goes in.
checkpoints.why: Vegetables surrounded by thick gravy cook less predictably than small pieces softened first in the pan.

checkpoints.cue: Gravy coats a spoon and a stirred track closes slowly.
checkpoints.why: Heating hydrated flour thickens the liquid. Cooling and resting help the filling hold together, but a watery gravy will still make a wet pie.

checkpoints.cue: Pastry is deeply golden and the center of the filling reaches 165°F / 74°C.
checkpoints.why: A browned lid alone does not show whether the cold center has heated through.

troubleshooting.cause: The butter has warmed or the surface is under-floured.
troubleshooting.fix: Slide dough onto a tray and refrigerate until firm. Use only enough rolling flour to prevent sticking.

troubleshooting.problem: Top browns before the center is hot
troubleshooting.cause: The filling started very cold or the oven browns strongly from above.
troubleshooting.fix: Cover the browned areas loosely with foil and continue baking until the center reaches 165°F / 74°C.

troubleshooting.cause: The pan received too little direct heat or the filling was too wet.
troubleshooting.fix: Use the lower oven rack and a preheated metal sheet as directed. Next time verify gravy thickness before chilling; do not fill raw pastry with hot gravy.

substitutions.alternative: Enough ready-made unsweetened pie dough for a deep 9-inch double-crust pie
substitutions.effect: Follow its handling instructions and check that it is large enough for this pan. A shallow frozen shell is not an equivalent container.

learning.timing: About three hours with already-cooked chicken. Make dough first; cook and cool the filling during its one-hour chill. Baking takes about 50–65 minutes and the pie rests 20 minutes before slicing.
learning.storage: Refrigerate in shallow containers within 2 hours (1 hour above 90°F / 32°C), at 40°F / 4°C or below. Use within 3–4 days; reheat leftovers to 165°F / 74°C. Cut remaining pie into portions for prompt cooling. Reheat portions in a 350°F / 175°C oven, loosely covered if needed, until the center reaches 165°F / 74°C. Pastry loses crispness in storage.

body:
## Chef's Note

A pot pie asks the pastry and filling to do different jobs. The filling should already contain tender vegetables and a thickened gravy; the oven then bakes the crust and reheats the center. Keep the filling cool enough that it cannot melt the butter in the raw pastry. This version includes its own savory dough rather than sending you through a dessert recipe.

## Directions

1. **Make pastry:** Mix the 300 g flour and pastry salt in a bowl. Work in cold butter with fingertips or a pastry cutter, leaving a mixture of crumbs and flattened pea-size butter pieces. Toss with 100 ml ice water. Squeeze a handful: if it falls apart, add the remaining water a teaspoon at a time just until it holds. Bring together without kneading smooth. Divide into two discs, one slightly larger for the bottom, wrap, and refrigerate for at least 1 hour. Do not taste raw dough.
2. **Prepare filling ingredients:** While the dough chills, cut carrots and celery into small, even dice. Keep the cooked chicken refrigerated until needed. Measure the filling flour separately from any flour used for pastry or rolling.
3. **Soften vegetables:** Melt filling butter in a large saucepan over medium heat. Add onion, carrots, and celery; cook, stirring, about 10–12 minutes until onion is soft and carrot is almost tender. Lower the heat if vegetables begin to brown rapidly.
4. **Thicken gravy:** Stir in the 45 g flour, garlic powder, celery seed, salt, and pepper. Cook and stir for 1 minute. Gradually stir in broth, then milk, scraping the bottom and dispersing the flour mixture. Bring to a gentle simmer and cook about 3 minutes, stirring, until thick enough to coat a spoon. Fold in chicken and frozen peas. Taste for seasoning, then spread the filling in a shallow heatproof dish to release heat. Refrigerate promptly until cool, about 30–45 minutes in a shallow layer; do not leave it out for the whole dough chill.
5. **Heat oven and roll:** Put a sturdy rimmed metal baking sheet on the lower rack and preheat to 425°F / 220°C. On a lightly floured surface, roll the larger dough disc to about a 13-inch circle, roughly 1/8 inch thick. Ease into a deep 9-inch metal pie pan without stretching. Roll the second disc to about 12 inches. If either becomes soft, refrigerate briefly before continuing.
6. **Fill and seal:** Spoon cool filling into the lined pan, keeping it below the rim. If your pan cannot hold it, bake excess separately in a small ovenproof dish to 165°F / 74°C. Lay on the top crust, trim to about 1/2 inch beyond the rim, fold the edges together, and crimp. Cut four generous vents in the lid. Brush lightly with beaten egg; discard the remainder. Refrigerate the assembled pie for 10 minutes if the pastry has softened.
7. **Bake through:** Place the metal pie pan on the hot baking sheet. Bake 20 minutes at 425°F / 220°C, then reduce to 375°F / 190°C and bake about 30–45 minutes longer. Shield darkening edges with foil as needed. The pastry should be deeply golden and filling should bubble through the vents; also insert a thermometer through a central vent to verify 165°F / 74°C in the middle. Continue baking, loosely covered if necessary, until that endpoint is reached.
8. **Rest and serve:** Rest on a rack for 20 minutes, then cut into eight slices. The gravy will settle but remain soft rather than forming a firm slab. A lightly dressed green salad complements the rich pastry.

On a lightly floured surface, roll the larger dough disc to about a 13-inch circle, roughly 1/8 inch thick. Ease into a deep 9-inch metal pie pan without stretching. Roll the second disc to about 12 inches. If either becomes soft, refrigerate briefly before continuing.

Fill and seal: Spoon cool filling into the lined pan, keeping it below the rim. If your pan cannot hold it, bake excess separately in a small ovenproof dish to 165°F / 74°C. Lay on the top crust, trim to about 1/2 inch beyond the rim, fold the edges together, and crimp. Cut four generous vents in the lid. Brush lightly with beaten egg; discard the remainder. Refrigerate the assembled pie for 10 minutes if the pastry has softened.

Bake through: Place the metal pie pan on the hot baking sheet. Bake 20 minutes at 425°F / 220°C, then reduce to 375°F / 190°C and bake about 30–45 minutes longer. Shield darkening edges with foil as needed. The pastry should be deeply golden and filling should bubble through the vents; also insert a thermometer through a central vent to verify 165°F / 74°C in the middle. Continue baking, loosely covered if necessary, until that endpoint is reached.

Rest and serve: Rest on a rack for 20 minutes, then cut into eight slices. The gravy will settle but remain soft rather than forming a firm slab. A lightly dressed green salad complements the rich pastry.

export.name: Chicken Pot Pie
export.ingredients:

300 g all-purpose flour, plus a little for rolling
225 g cold unsalted butter, cut into 1/2-inch cubes
1/2 tsp fine salt
100–120 ml ice-cold water, added only as needed

450 g cooked boneless chicken, chilled and cut into bite-size pieces (weight after cooking)
100 g carrots, cut into 1/4-inch dice
100 g yellow onion, finely diced
50 g celery, cut into 1/4-inch dice
100 g frozen peas
56 g unsalted butter
45 g all-purpose flour
1 3/4 cups (420 ml) low-sodium chicken broth
2/3 cup (160 ml) whole milk
1/2 tsp garlic powder
1/4 tsp celery seed
1/4 tsp fine salt, plus more only if needed

1. Make pastry: Mix the 300 g flour and pastry salt in a bowl. Work in cold butter with fingertips or a pastry cutter, leaving a mixture of crumbs and flattened pea-size butter pieces.
