data.title: Japanese Cucumber Sunomono
ingredients: 400 g Japanese, Persian, or English cucumber, washed and ends trimmed
1 tsp finely grated fresh ginger, optional
1/4 tsp shichimi togarashi, optional; check the label
data.description: Thin cucumber slices in a light sweet-sour rice-vinegar dressing, finished with toasted sesame.

learning.focus: Control cucumber water before adding the vinegar dressing
learning.outcome: Delicate, lightly crisp cucumber slices with a clear sweet-sour dressing that remains bright at serving.
before: Weigh cucumber rather than substituting two large English cucumbers for four unspecified garden cucumbers. Remove a tough peel or large watery seed core if needed, then weigh the usable portion.
Use unseasoned rice vinegar. Seasoned vinegar already contains sugar and salt and changes this balance.

checkpoints.cue: Cucumber slices bend without becoming limp, and some liquid has drained after 10 minutes.
checkpoints.why: A measured salt rest removes some water before it can dilute the dressing.

checkpoints.cue: No sugar grains remain in the dressing.
checkpoints.why: Undissolved sugar gives uneven sweetness instead of a consistent sweet-sour liquid.

checkpoints.cue: The dressed slices taste lightly sweet and distinctly vinegary after a short chill.
checkpoints.why: Salting and draining reduce immediate dilution, but the salad continues to soften and release water as it stands.

troubleshooting.cause: Cucumber was not drained well or the usable weight was much larger than specified.
troubleshooting.fix: Lift slices from excess pooled liquid, then add a small amount of unseasoned rice vinegar to taste. Next time weigh and drain as directed.

troubleshooting.cause: Seasoned vinegar was used or sugar was measured generously.
troubleshooting.fix: Add unseasoned rice vinegar gradually to rebalance. Check the bottle before making the next batch.

learning.timing: About 25 minutes includes slicing, a 10-minute salt rest with dressing preparation alongside, and a brief 5-minute chill after dressing.
learning.storage: Best on the day it is made. Refrigerate promptly at 40°F / 4°C or below; use within 1–2 days for quality. Keep dressing separate from prepared cucumber for a few hours if assembling later. This quick vinegar dressing is not a shelf-stable pickle.

body:
## Chef's Note

This small side offers acidity and a delicate cucumber texture beside a rich curry or fried cutlet. Salt and drain the slices before dressing, then serve soon. Unlike garlic-led smashed cucumber salad or gochugaru-seasoned oi muchim, this version centers on thin slices, rice vinegar, and a little sweetness. Sesame, optional ginger, and optional shichimi finish the dish.

## Directions

1. **Slice evenly:** Cut cucumber into rounds about 1–2 mm thick with a sharp knife or a mandoline with its hand guard. Halve and remove large seed cores first if necessary. Aim for thin intact slices, not crushed fragments.
2. **Salt and drain:** Toss with the draining salt in a colander over a bowl. Leave for 10 minutes. Gently squeeze small handfuls to remove excess water without crushing, then transfer to a clean bowl. Discard the drained liquid.
3. **Dissolve the dressing:** While the cucumber rests, stir rice vinegar, sugar, and dressing salt until fully dissolved. Stir in optional grated ginger.
4. **Dress briefly:** Toss the drained cucumber with dressing and refrigerate for about 5 minutes. Taste a slice with some dressing; adjust with a little extra vinegar only if needed.
5. **Finish:** Divide among four small side bowls, including a little dressing. Sprinkle with toasted sesame and optional shichimi just before serving. For preparation a few hours ahead, refrigerate cucumber and dressing separately and combine near serving.

## Chef's Note

Reducing soy-mirin-vinegar until it becomes heavy syrup, then brushing it onto trout in multiple layers under the broiler creates a mahogany-colored, crispy glaze that contrasts delicate, flaky meat. Poaching julienned vegetables in dashi for exactly 1 minute keeps them crisp while infusing them with clean, oceanic flavor that balances the rich glaze.

## Directions

1.  **The Glaze:** In a small saucepan, bring soy sauce, mirin, sugar, and vinegar to a boil. Simmer for 10 minutes until reduced by half and thick enough to coat a spoon.
2.  **The Bath:** In a separate pot, bring [Dashi](/mise/recipes/dashi-japanese-sea-stock) to a boil. Add carrots and leeks. Simmer for exactly 1 minute. Remove vegetables with a slotted spoon and set aside. Keep dashi warm.
3.  **Thermal Prep:** Preheat the broiler. Arrange trout fillets, skin-side up, on a sturdy baking sheet.
4.  **The Lacquer:** Broil for 2 minutes until the skin sizzles. Carefully peel off and discard the skin. Brush the meat with the glaze.
5.  **Stage 2:** Broil for 3 minutes, brushing twice more with the lacquer, until the trout is cooked through and the surface is mirror-glossy.
6.  **Assemble:** Mound rice in shallow bowls. Top with the glazed trout, nori, and the poached vegetables.
7.  **Serve:** Carefully pour the hot dashi around the perimeter of the bowl. Serve immediately.

data.title: Japchae (Korean Glass Noodle Stir-Fry)
ingredients: 8 oz Sweet Potato Glass Noodles (dangmyeon), also called Korean glass noodles
8 oz Beef Sirloin or Tenderloin, thinly sliced
2 Medium Carrots, cut into thin matchsticks
1 Medium Zucchini, cut into thin matchsticks
4 oz Mushrooms (shiitake or cremini), thinly sliced
1 cup Fresh Spinach (or 4 oz frozen spinach, thawed and squeezed dry)
2 tsp Gochugaru (Korean red chili flakes, optional)

body:
## Chef's Note

Japchae is Korean mixed stir-fry with sweet potato glass noodles - a dish that shows up at celebrations and fancy dinners because it's elegant and looks harder than it is. The glass noodles (also called dangmyeon) have a silky, slightly gelatinous texture that's completely different from wheat or rice noodles. Korean home cooks marinate the beef separately, cook vegetables individually (so each retains its texture), and then combine everything at the last moment with a simple soy-sesame sauce. This technique keeps everything from turning into mush. It's flexible too - add shrimp, more vegetables, or make it vegetarian by skipping the beef.

## Directions

1. **Cook the Noodles:** Bring a large pot of water to a boil. Add the glass noodles and cook for 4-5 minutes until translucent and tender. Drain in a colander, rinse under cool water, and set aside. The noodles can be tossed with a small drizzle of sesame oil to prevent sticking.

2. **Marinate the Beef:** While the noodles cook, combine the thinly sliced beef with 1 tbsp soy sauce, 1 tsp sesame oil, 1/2 tsp minced garlic, 1/4 tsp black pepper, and 1 tsp cornstarch in a small bowl. This cornstarch coating (velveting) protects the meat from the high heat of the skillet. Let sit for 15 minutes while you prep vegetables.

3. **Cook the Beef:** Heat 1 tbsp vegetable oil in a large skillet over high heat until it shimmers. Add the marinated beef in a single layer and let it sit for 1 minute without stirring to develop color. Stir and cook another 30 seconds until the beef is mostly cooked. Transfer to a plate.

4. **Cook the Vegetables (Separately):** In the same skillet, add a little more oil if needed. Cook the harder vegetables first, one type at a time, for speed and texture control:
   - Carrots: 2-3 minutes, then transfer to a bowl
   - Zucchini: 2-3 minutes, then transfer to the bowl
   - Mushrooms: 2-3 minutes, then transfer to the bowl
   - Onion: 2-3 minutes until softened, then transfer to the bowl
   - Spinach: Cook until wilted (about 1 minute), squeeze out excess moisture, then transfer

5. **Make the Sauce:** In a small bowl, whisk together 2 tbsp soy sauce, 1 tbsp sesame oil, 1 tbsp brown sugar, 1 tbsp rice vinegar, and remaining minced garlic (total 2 tsp). Taste and adjust - it should be balanced between salty, sweet, and tangy.

6. **Combine:** Add the cooked glass noodles and all vegetables back to the large skillet. Return the cooked beef to the pan. Pour the sauce over everything and toss gently but thoroughly for 1-2 minutes until everything is coated and heated through. The heat should be low - you're just combining and warming, not cooking further.

7. **Optional Heat:** If you want spice, add 1-2 tsp gochugaru (Korean red chili flakes) when tossing with the sauce.

8. **Serve:** Transfer to a serving plate or individual bowls. Garnish generously with sesame seeds and a light drizzle of sesame oil. Serve at room temperature or warm.

**Glass Noodle Sourcing:** Also labeled as "Korean sweet potato noodles" or "dangmyeon." They're available at any Asian market and increasingly at regular grocery stores. Do not confuse with rice noodles or tapioca noodles.

**Vegetable Flexibility:** This dish is forgiving. Use whatever vegetables need using: bell peppers, green beans, broccoli, shiitake mushrooms, cabbage. The principle is the same - cook each vegetable separately, then combine.

**Beef Alternative:** Shrimp works beautifully (cook the same way). Or skip the protein entirely for a vegetarian version - the noodles and vegetables are hearty enough.

**Make-Ahead:** Japchae tastes equally good warm or at room temperature and is perfect for meal prep. Store in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Serve cold or reheat gently over low heat.

**Texture Key:** The reason to cook vegetables separately is texture. If you dump everything together and cook it, the vegetables become mushy. Separate cooking preserves the bite of each ingredient.

data.title: Jeri's Lentil Soup
ingredients: 16 oz Dry Green or Brown Lentils, rinsed
1 tbsp Sherry Vinegar or Fresh Lemon Juice
Salt and Black Pepper to taste

body:
## Chef's Note

This traditional recipe was a wedding gift from Pat Miller and Sean Kilpatrick, passed down from Jeri, a Broadway dancer turned nutritionist. Adding sherry vinegar at the end brightens earthy lentils - the acidity wakes up the palate. For creamier texture without dairy, pulse with an immersion blender a few times before serving, releasing lentil starch while keeping the carrot slices intact.

## Directions

1.  **Sauté:** Heat oil in a large skillet. Sauté onions and carrots with the Italian seasoning for 5-8 minutes until translucent.
2.  **The Pot:** Transfer the vegetables to a slow cooker. Add the lentils, crushed tomatoes, and broth.
3.  **Slow Cook:** Cook on **LOW** for 5 hours (or on high for 3 hours) until lentils are tender but not mushy.
4.  **Infuse:** Stir in the white wine and parsley. Cook for another 30 minutes.
5.  **Texture (Optional):** Use an immersion blender to pulse the soup a few times to create a thicker body.
6.  **The Acid Balance:** Stir in the sherry vinegar or lemon juice. Season generously with salt and black pepper.

## Notes

_This recipe was a wedding gift from Pat Miller and Sean Kilpatrick, passed down from Jeri, a Broadway dancer turned nutritionist. It is designed to sustain you through long rehearsals and busy weeks._

data.title: Jerk Pork Shoulder
ingredients: 6 scallions, roughly chopped, white and green parts
1–2 Scotch bonnet or habanero peppers, stemmed; remove seeds and membranes for less heat
2 tbsp fresh thyme leaves or 2 tsp dried thyme
Hot water, only if needed to prevent the braise drying out
data.description: Jerk-seasoned pork shoulder with allspice, thyme, hot chile and citrus, braised until it shreds. A clean, separately refrigerated portion of marinade provides the fresh finish.

scaling.reason: This method is written for one 4 lb shoulder and its pot. A different whole-cut size needs a new vessel and tenderness schedule; make separate batches for more portions.

learning.focus: Keep a clean finishing marinade separate from raw-contact braising marinade
learning.outcome: Shreddable shoulder with warm allspice, chile heat and a fresh aromatic finish.
before: Use one 4 lb shoulder and a heavy pot that holds it with the lid closed and room for the liquids. Keep the meat refrigerated while the oven heats.
Before the marinade touches pork, measure the clean finishing portion into its own covered container. Refrigerate it separately throughout the 8–24-hour marination.
Use gloves if helpful when handling hot peppers, and wash hands and utensils afterward. Habanero changes the chile character; allspice and thyme remain central.

checkpoints.cue: The finishing marinade is in a separate labelled container before any raw pork is handled.
checkpoints.why: Uncooked finishing sauce must not be confused with marinade scraped from raw meat.

checkpoints.cue: The lid is closed, liquid remains in the pot and a fork separates the pork easily at the end.
checkpoints.why: A whole shoulder requires gentle, moist cooking to reach a shreddable texture; time alone is not the endpoint.

checkpoints.cue: Shredded pork is coated with sauce and the clean reserved marinade, without a pool of grease.
checkpoints.why: Skimming and controlling the sauce preserve texture while the clean portion restores fresh aromatics.

troubleshooting.cause: Sugar and marinade solids are scorching before the meat browns.
troubleshooting.fix: Lower the heat and turn the meat. Do not dissolve bitter burned residue into the sauce; transfer to a clean pot if necessary before braising.

troubleshooting.problem: The shoulder is firm when the timer ends
troubleshooting.cause: Its thickness or pot temperature needs a longer braise.
troubleshooting.fix: Check that some braising liquid remains, re-cover and continue until a fork separates the meat easily. Add small amounts of hot water if the pot is drying.

troubleshooting.problem: The finishing marinade touched raw pork
troubleshooting.cause: The clean reserve and scraped marinade were confused.
troubleshooting.fix: Do not add it as an uncooked finish. Omit that finishing portion; all raw-contact marinade used in the recipe must go into the full braise.

substitutions.alternative: Habanero
substitutions.effect: A usable hot-chile option with a different aroma; heat varies by pepper. Neither substitutes for the allspice or thyme.

substitutions.alternative: The listed dried-thyme amount
substitutions.effect: Dried thyme has a more concentrated, less fresh aroma.

substitutions.alternative: Tamari labelled gluten-free when needed
substitutions.effect: Saltiness varies. Check the stock and other ingredients too before treating the meal as gluten-free.

learning.timing: Plan about 13 hours with the minimum 8-hour refrigerated marinade: roughly 30 minutes preparation, up to 4 hours for searing and covered braising, and 20 minutes resting while the sauce reduces. Using the 24-hour marinade adds 16 hours. Thick shoulders can take longer; next-day reheating is a separate stage.
learning.storage: Portion into shallow containers with some sauce and refrigerate promptly, within 2 hours (1 hour above 90°F / 32°C), at 40°F / 4°C or colder. Use within 3–4 days or freeze portions for later. Reheat a portion with its sauce to 165°F / 74°C throughout, stirring or turning to heat evenly. Keep the clean finishing marinade covered and refrigerated until the cooked meat is ready; do not leave it on the counter during marination or braising. For next-day service, reheat the finished pork with its sauce, covered, checking 165°F / 74°C throughout rather than relying on oven time alone.

body:
## Chef's Note

Allspice, thyme, hot chile and citrus season this Jamaican-inspired shoulder. The covered braise gives a shreddable texture, while a small clean reserve of marinade brightens the finish. Reserve that portion before the meat is added, and keep it cold and clearly separate from the marinade that cooks with the pork.

## Directions

1. **Blend and reserve:** Blend all marinade ingredients until mostly smooth. Before handling the pork, measure 1/4 cup into a clean covered container, label it for finishing and refrigerate at 40°F / 4°C or colder.
2. **Marinate:** Score the pork about 1/4 inch deep. Coat it with the remaining marinade, cover and refrigerate for 8–24 hours. Keep the clean finishing portion in its separate container.
3. **Heat the oven:** Heat to 325°F / 165°C. Keep the pork refrigerated until ready to sear; it does not need to reach room temperature.
4. **Sear:** Scrape excess marinade from the pork into a bowl reserved for the braise. Heat the Dutch oven over medium-high heat. Sear the pork, turning to brown its broad surfaces, about 3–4 minutes per side. Lower the heat if the sugary coating starts to blacken.
5. **Braise:** Add the scraped raw-contact marinade, stock and orange juice around the pork. Cover and cook in the oven about 3–3 1/2 hours, until a fork easily separates the meat. Check that liquid remains; add a little hot water if needed. The thickest part must reach at least 145°F / 63°C, but shreddable tenderness requires further cooking. Continue covered if still firm.
6. **Rest and reduce:** Move the pork to a board and rest for 20 minutes. During the rest, skim fat from the braising liquid and simmer it uncovered until glossy but still pourable, about 10 minutes. The rest also exceeds the 3-minute minimum after reaching the pork safety temperature.
7. **Shred and finish:** Shred the meat, discarding large pockets of fat. Toss with the reduced sauce and the clean 1/4 cup marinade reserved before raw contact. Do not use any unbraised scraped marinade here.
8. **Serve or reheat:** Serve in eight portions, or cool promptly for later meals. To reheat, spread pork and sauce in a covered baking dish at 325°F / 165°C until the center reaches 165°F / 74°C. Start checking after 20–25 minutes; a cold, deep dish takes longer.

data.title: Kachumber Salad
ingredients: 300 g cucumber, washed and cut into 1/4-inch dice
250 g firm ripe tomatoes, cut into 1/4-inch dice
2 tbsp fresh lemon juice, plus more only if needed
1/4 tsp chaat masala, optional; check ingredients for dietary needs
data.description: Small-diced cucumber, tomato, and onion with lemon, fresh herbs, and toasted cumin, dressed just before serving.

learning.focus: Choose a consistent cut and dress when the meal is ready
learning.outcome: Fresh, crisp diced vegetables with bright lemon and cumin, lightly moistened rather than sitting in a large puddle.
before: Use firm ripe tomatoes and small even vegetable dice. Remove a very watery seed core if necessary and measure the usable amount.
Chaat masala varies in salt and composition. Taste before adding extra salt; omit it if its ingredients do not suit your dietary needs.

checkpoints.cue: Cumin is fragrant and slightly darker after toasting, then cooled before crushing.
checkpoints.why: The toasted spice gives depth without needing a heavy dressing. Blackened seeds taste bitter.

checkpoints.cue: Cucumber and tomato are similarly sized, with onion cut smaller.
checkpoints.why: An even cut distributes the vegetables in each spoonful; smaller onion pieces avoid a single overpowering raw bite.

checkpoints.cue: Lemon tastes bright and salt is sufficient before any extra seasoning is added.
checkpoints.why: Tomato acidity and optional salty chaat masala vary. More lemon and salt are not automatically improvements.

troubleshooting.cause: It was salted too early or vegetables were unusually watery.
troubleshooting.fix: Lift the vegetables out of excess liquid and retaste. For the next batch, keep the dressing separate until serving.

troubleshooting.cause: The onion is pungent or its dice are large.
troubleshooting.fix: Before mixing, soak diced onion in cold water for 5 minutes and drain thoroughly. This step may soften its bite without requiring more sugar or oil.

learning.timing: About 20 minutes includes cumin toasting/cooling and hand-cut vegetables. Dress just before serving; no long marination is required.
learning.storage: Best freshly dressed. Refrigerate undressed vegetables and dressing separately for a few hours if preparing ahead. Refrigerate leftovers promptly at 40°F / 4°C or below and use within one day for texture; the salad will release liquid.

body:
## Chef's Note

Kachumber provides a fresh chopped-vegetable side with lemon and herbs. Toasted cumin adds aroma; a little olive oil is optional for a rounder dressing. The vegetables should still taste distinct. Dress them when the rest of dinner is ready instead of letting salt draw out their juices for a long period.

## Directions

1. **Toast and cool cumin:** Shake cumin seeds in a small dry skillet over medium-low heat for about 1–2 minutes, until fragrant and a shade darker. Transfer to a plate, cool briefly, and crush with a mortar or the back of a spoon.
2. **Cut vegetables:** Dice cucumber and tomato into roughly 1/4-inch pieces and cut onion more finely. Remove tough cucumber skin or large watery seed cores as needed. Mince optional serrano; omit it for a milder salad. Combine vegetables with cilantro and mint.
3. **Mix dressing:** Stir lemon juice, cooled crushed cumin, measured salt, pepper, optional olive oil, and optional chaat masala together. If not serving yet, refrigerate vegetables and dressing separately.
4. **Dress at serving:** Toss gently with dressing. Taste a spoonful and add a little extra lemon only if the vegetables need more acidity. Divide into six small side portions and serve promptly.

data.title: Kalbi
ingredients: 5 lbs Flanken-style Beef Short Ribs (1/2-inch thick)

body:
## Chef's Note

Kalbi is Korean barbecue short ribs. The secret to tender meat with crisp edges is rubbing the ribs with sake and sugar for 15 minutes before adding the soy sauce. This allows the alcohol and sugar crystals to penetrate the tough flanken-style fibers, ensuring succulent meat. Grill directly over charcoal for exactly 2 minutes per side to develop the smoky lacquered char.

## Directions

1.  **The Prep:** Rinse the ribs in cold water to remove any bone fragments. Pat **bone-dry** with paper towels.
2.  **The Tenderizer:** In a large bowl, toss the ribs with the sake and white sugar. Massage the mixture into the meat and let stand for 15 minutes.
3.  **The Marinade:** In a separate jar, whisk together the soy sauce, brown sugar, sesame oil, garlic, scallions, pepper, and oil until the sugar is dissolved.
4.  **The Soak:** Pour the marinade over the ribs. Ensure every slice is coated. Cover and refrigerate for **at least 8 hours** (overnight is mandatory for the Kitchen Standard).
5.  **Thermal Prep:** Bring the ribs to room temperature for 30 minutes before cooking. Discard the marinade.
6.  **The Sear:** Light a charcoal grill to medium-high heat. Wipe off excess marinade from the ribs to prevent the sugars from burning, then place directly over the coals. Grill for 2-3 minutes per side until seared and charred.
7.  **Finish:** Move to the cooler side of the grill for 5 minutes until the fat is rendered and "Snappy."
8.  **Serve:** Use kitchen shears to cut the ribs into bite-sized pieces.

Let the cooked ribs rest for 5 minutes before cutting and serving.

7 cloves Garlic, minced
1/4 tsp Black Pepper
2 tbsp Vegetable Oil
export.directions:
1. The Prep: Rinse the ribs in cold water to remove any bone fragments. Pat bone-dry with paper towels.
2. The Tenderizer: In a large bowl, toss the ribs with the sake and white sugar. Massage the mixture into the meat and let stand for 15 minutes.
3. The Marinade: In a separate jar, whisk together the soy sauce, brown sugar, sesame oil, garlic, scallions, pepper, and oil until the sugar is dissolved.
4. The Soak: Pour the marinade over the ribs. Ensure every slice is coated. Cover and refrigerate for at least 8 hours (overnight is mandatory for the Kitchen Standard).
5. Thermal Prep: Bring the ribs to room temperature for 30 minutes before cooking. Discard the marinade.
6. The Sear: Light a charcoal grill to medium-high heat. Wipe off excess marinade from the ribs to prevent the sugars from burning, then place directly over the coals. Grill for 2-3 minutes per side until seared and charred.
7. Finish: Move to the cooler side of the grill for 5 minutes until the fat is rendered and "Snappy."
8. Serve: Use kitchen shears to cut the ribs into bite-sized pieces.

Let the cooked ribs rest for 5 minutes before cutting and serving.
export.notes:
Chef's Note

Kalbi is Korean barbecue short ribs. The secret to tender meat with crisp edges is rubbing the ribs with sake and sugar for 15 minutes before adding the soy sauce. This allows the alcohol and sugar crystals to penetrate the tough flanken-style fibers, ensuring succulent meat. Grill directly over charcoal for exactly 2 minutes per side to develop the smoky lacquered char.

data.title: Kale Caesar with Crispy Chickpeas
ingredients: 1 large bunch Lacinato (Dino) Kale, stems removed and shredded
1 can (15 oz) Chickpeas, drained and patted very dry
1 tsp White Miso or Soy Sauce
1/4 tsp Anchovy Paste (optional, for traditional Caesar depth)
1/3 cup Shaved or Grated Parmesan Cheese

body:
## Chef's Note

This Caesar replaces the traditional breadcrumbs and anchovies with crispy roasted chickpeas that add both crunch and plant-based protein. The massage is critical - working salt and a bit of oil into the shredded kale breaks down the tough fibers, transforming them into something tender and sweet. The dressing uses miso or soy sauce for umami depth instead of relying solely on anchovies, making it equally satisfying. This salad is substantial enough to be a meal on its own.

## Directions

1. **Roast the Chickpeas:** Preheat oven to 425°F. Pat the drained chickpeas very dry with a clean kitchen towel - any moisture will prevent them from crisping. Toss with 1 tbsp olive oil, salt, paprika, garlic powder, and pepper on a sheet pan. Spread in a single layer and roast for 20-25 minutes, shaking the pan halfway through, until golden and crispy. Set aside to cool - they will continue to crisp as they cool.

2. **Massage the Kale:** Place the shredded kale in a large bowl. Drizzle with 1 tsp olive oil and a pinch of salt. Using your hands, massage the leaves vigorously for 2 minutes until they turn dark green and soften significantly. This breaks down the cell walls and makes the kale tender.

3. **Make the Dressing:** In a blender or small food processor, combine the 1/4 cup olive oil, grated garlic, lemon juice, Dijon mustard, miso (or soy sauce), anchovy paste if using, water, salt, and pepper. Blend until completely smooth. The dressing should have the consistency of heavy cream. Adjust water if needed.

4. **Toss:** Pour the dressing over the massaged kale and toss well to ensure every leaf is evenly coated.

5. **Assemble:** Top with the crispy roasted chickpeas, shaved Parmesan, and a light dusting of lemon zest.

6. **Rest:** Let the salad sit for 5 minutes before serving. Unlike delicate greens, kale actually improves as it absorbs the dressing - it doesn't wilt.

7. **Make-Ahead:** The crispy chickpeas can be made up to 2 days ahead and stored in an airtight container. The dressing keeps refrigerated for up to 3 days. Massage the kale and dress it just before serving for the best texture.

data.title: Kale Salad with Mango, Avocado and Feta
ingredients: 1 bunch curly kale, tough ribs removed, leaves washed, dried and finely chopped
1 large ripe but firm mango, peeled, pitted and cubed
1 large ripe avocado, peeled, pitted and diced
1/2 cup toasted hulled pumpkin seeds or sunflower seeds
2 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil, for softening kale
3 tbsp + 1 tsp extra-virgin olive oil, for dressing
Salt and black pepper, to taste
data.source: Adapted from What A Girl Eats, Kale Salad with Mango, Avocado and Feta
data.description: Chopped kale with mango, avocado, feta and toasted seeds in an orange, honey and olive-oil dressing.

learning.focus: Soften sturdy kale while preserving ripe fruit pieces
learning.outcome: Supple chopped leaves with a light orange coating, distinct mango and avocado cubes and crisp seeds.
before: Wash kale, remove tough ribs and dry before chopping. Bunch size varies, so judge dressing coverage on the prepared leaves rather than forcing every drop into the bowl.
Use ripe but firm mango and avocado so cubes survive folding. Toast seeds ahead and cool fully, or use ready-toasted seeds. Toasting raw seeds adds time beyond this no-cook preparation.
All the oil for rubbing and dressing comes from the listed oil amounts; do not add another unmeasured massage pour. A wide bowl allows gentle lifting; larger batches may need separate bowls.

checkpoints.cue: Kale shreds feel more flexible after a short rub and have a thin sheen.
checkpoints.why: Removing tough ribs and cutting finely matter more than crushing the leaves until wet.

checkpoints.cue: A dressed leaf tastes balanced alongside mango and feta.
checkpoints.why: Orange sweetness and feta salt vary; assess the combined salad before adding extra seasoning.

checkpoints.cue: Avocado cubes remain intact and seeds stay crisp.
checkpoints.why: Late, gentle folding protects ripe avocado and limits moisture on toasted seeds.

troubleshooting.cause: A small kale bunch received the entire dressing or produce was not dried.
troubleshooting.fix: Lift out of any pool and reserve extra dressing. Next time add it in stages and dry leaves and fruit first.

troubleshooting.cause: Thick ribs remained or leaves were chopped too coarsely.
troubleshooting.fix: Remove rib pieces and cut large leaves smaller. A longer vigorous massage will not make thick ribs pleasant.

substitutions.alternative: The same volume of toasted hulled sunflower seeds
substitutions.effect: A smaller, more delicate crunch with a different nutty flavor.

substitutions.alternative: The same crumbled volume of vegetarian-rennet feta-style cheese
substitutions.effect: Supports a vegetarian version; check saltiness with the orange dressing.

learning.timing: About 25 minutes includes washing and drying kale, preparing mango and avocado, zesting and juicing the orange, mixing dressing and assembly. Already toasted seeds assumed; large bunches or extra portions take longer.
learning.storage: Keep prepared greens and dressing separately refrigerated at 40°F / 4°C or below until serving. Refrigerate perishables within 2 hours, or 1 hour above 90°F / 32°C. Use dressed leftovers by the next day for quality; leaves wilt and crisp toppings soften. Keep any dry seeds separate until serving. Do not freeze the assembled salad.

body:
## Chef's Note

Kale provides a sturdy base for ripe mango, creamy avocado and salty feta. Rub the chopped leaves briefly with part of the measured oil, then add orange dressing gradually. Fold in avocado last and scatter seeds at serving for contrast. Adapted from [What A Girl Eats’ Kale Salad with Mango, Avocado and Feta](https://whatagirleats.com/kale-salad-mango-avocado-feta/).

## Directions

1. **Prepare kale:** Remove tough ribs, wash leaves, dry thoroughly and chop finely. Put in a wide bowl and add the oil labeled for softening kale with a small pinch of salt. Rub gently for about 1–2 minutes until darker and more flexible, stopping before the leaves become wet and limp.

2. **Prepare fruit and dressing:** Peel, pit and cube mango. Finely dice onion and crumble feta. Zest and juice the orange; whisk its juice and zest with the oil labeled for dressing, garlic, Dijon and honey. Taste and add salt and pepper as needed.

3. **Combine gradually:** Toss kale with about half the dressing, then gently fold in mango, onion and feta. Taste a leaf with fruit and cheese. Add more dressing only if needed for a light coating and reserve the rest.

4. **Finish:** Dice avocado just before serving and fold it in gently. Scatter with toasted seeds, divide among side plates and serve promptly.

data.title: Katharine Hepburn’s Brownies
ingredients: 1 cup Walnuts or Pecans, coarsely chopped

body:
## Chef's Note

This is the classic Katharine Hepburn brownie recipe. The secret to its fudgy texture is the ultra-low flour ratio: using only 1/4 cup of flour ensures the structure remains gooey and fudge-like rather than cakey. We melt the cocoa directly into the hot butter to bloom the chocolate flavor instantly. Large nut pieces provide a necessary crunch to contrast the decadent fudge. Do not over-bake; pull them when they still look slightly underdone.

## Directions

1.  **The Bloom:** Preheat oven to 325°F. Grease an 8x8-inch square pan. In a medium saucepan, melt the butter over low heat. Whisk in the cocoa powder until smooth and glossy. Remove from heat and let cool for 5 minutes.
2.  **Emulsify:** Whisk the eggs into the cocoa-butter mixture one at a time. Stir in the vanilla and salt.
3.  **The Fold:** In a separate bowl, whisk the sugar and flour. Add the dry mix and the nuts to the saucepan. Stir with a spatula until **just combined**.
4.  **Bake:** Pour the batter into the prepared pan. Bake for 30-35 minutes. **The Kitchen Standard Test:** The center should still have a slight jiggle and a toothpick should come out with moist crumbs.
5.  **Cool:** Let cool completely in the pan before slicing. These brownies are elite when refrigerated and eaten cold.

data.title: Keto Egg Muffins
ingredients: 5 oz Spanish Chorizo or Salami, finely diced

body:
## Chef's Note

These are ideal for high-protein, low-carb meal prep. The secret to avoiding the rubbery sponginess of many egg muffins is placing the raw chorizo at the bottom of the tin so it renders its spicy fat directly into the egg, creating a crispy finish on the bottom. Whisking the oily pesto directly into the eggs ensures every bite has savory depth that cuts through the richness of the yolk.

## Directions

1.  **Prep:** Preheat oven to 350°F. Generously grease a 12-cup muffin tin with butter (do not use paper liners, as the eggs will stick).
2.  **The Base:** Divide the diced chorizo and scallions evenly among the 12 muffin cups.
3.  **Aeration:** In a large bowl, whisk the eggs with the pesto, salt, and pepper until very frothy and well-integrated.
4.  **Fold:** Stir in 3/4 of the shredded cheese.
5.  **Fill:** Pour the egg mixture into the muffin cups, filling each about 3/4 full. Sprinkle the remaining cheese over the tops for a golden "Bounce."
6.  **Bake:** Bake for 15-20 minutes until the centers are set and the tops are slightly golden.
7.  **Serve:** Let cool for 5 minutes before popping them out with a knife.

parsed.directionsText:
1. Prep: Preheat oven to 350°F. Generously grease a 12-cup muffin tin with butter (do not use paper liners, as the eggs will stick).
2. The Base: Divide the diced chorizo and scallions evenly among the 12 muffin cups.
3. Aeration: In a large bowl, whisk the eggs with the pesto, salt, and pepper until very frothy and well-integrated.
4. Fold: Stir in 3/4 of the shredded cheese.
5. Fill: Pour the egg mixture into the muffin cups, filling each about 3/4 full. Sprinkle the remaining cheese over the tops for a golden "Bounce."
6. Bake: Bake for 15-20 minutes until the centers are set and the tops are slightly golden.
7. Serve: Let cool for 5 minutes before popping them out with a knife.

data.title: Key Lime Pie Ice Cream
ingredients: 1 can (14 oz) Fat-free Sweetened Condensed Milk
1/2 cup Fresh Key Lime Juice (Nellie & Joe’s is the Kitchen Standard)

body:
## Chef's Note

This frozen dessert mimics the exact flavor profile of our [Key Lime Pie](/mise/recipes/key-lime-pie). The secret to a smooth, professional churn is the condensed milk: the sugar and fats act as a powerful stabilizer, preventing the formation of large ice crystals and ensuring a silky texture. We use a two-part graham cracker approach - stir half into the churn and reserve the other half for topping just before serving. This ensures you have both soft, cake-like bits and shatteringly crisp pieces.

## Directions

1.  **The Base:** In a large bowl, whisk together the condensed milk, key lime juice, 2% milk, cream, and salt until perfectly smooth.
2.  **The Churn:** Pour the mixture into your ice cream maker. Churn according to the manufacturer's instructions (usually 20-25 minutes).
3.  **The Crunch:** During the last 2 minutes of churning, add 1/3 cup of the coarsely crushed graham crackers.
4.  **The Finish:** Transfer the soft-serve consistency ice cream to a chilled, freezer-safe container. Cover and freeze for **at least 4 hours** (ideally overnight) to firm up.
5.  **Serve:** Scoop into bowls. Top with the remaining reserved graham cracker crumbs and a fresh lime wedge for the mandatory **Acid Balance**.

data.title: Key Lime Pie
ingredients: 1/2 cup + 2 tbsp Fresh Key Lime Juice

body:
## Chef's Note

This is classic Key lime pie for the holiday table. The key to its texture is whisking the egg yolks into the condensed milk before adding the lime juice. Lime juice thickens the filling, but acidity does not replace cooking the eggs. Bake until the filling reaches its measured endpoint, then chill to firm the texture. Using a high ratio of butter in the crust creates a shatteringly crisp base that stands up to the creamy filling. Chilling for the full 8 hours is mandatory for the acidity to mellow.

## Directions

1.  **The Crust:** Preheat oven to 350°F. Stir together crumbs, sugar, and melted butter until it looks like wet sand. Press firmly into the bottom and up the sides of a 9-inch glass pie plate. Bake for 10 minutes. Let cool.
2.  **The Emulsion:** In a large bowl, whisk the condensed milk and egg yolks until pale and thick.
3.  **The Bind:** Slowly whisk in the key lime juice - the mixture will noticeably thicken.
4.  **Bake:** Pour the filling into the cooled crust. Begin checking after 15 minutes and continue until the center reaches 160°F / 71°C, with set edges and a slight central wobble.
5.  **The Finish:** Cool completely on a rack, then refrigerate for **at least 8 hours** (mandatory).
6.  **The Crown:** Just before serving, whip the heavy cream and powdered sugar until stiff peaks form.
7.  **Serve:** Mound the cream over the pie. Garnish with lime zest for the final aromatic **High Note**.

data.title: Kimchi Jjigae (Kimchi Stew)
ingredients: 2 cups Kimchi, coarsely chopped (plus 2 tbsp kimchi juice)
8 oz Pork Belly or Shoulder, thinly sliced (or tofu for vegetarian)
4 oz Mushrooms, sliced (shiitake, oyster, or cremini)
2 tbsp Doenjang (Korean soybean paste, optional but recommended)

body:
## Chef's Note

Kimchi jjigae is Korean comfort food in its rawest form - kimchi is already fermented and pungent, so when you braise it with pork in stock, it becomes even more funky and complex. This is not a refined dish; it's what Korean mothers make on cold nights when they have leftover kimchi and want something warming and bold. The pork adds richness (or use tofu for vegetarian), and gochugaru (Korean chili flakes) amplifies the heat. Korean home cooks don't measure precisely - they taste and adjust. The final balance should be hot, salty, and deep-savory.

## Directions

1. **Prepare Ingredients:** Chop the kimchi into roughly 1-inch pieces, reserving 2 tbsp of the brine. Slice the pork belly thinly (it will cook fast). Slice the onion and mushrooms. Mince the garlic.

2. **Heat the Pan:** Place a medium saucepan over medium-high heat. Add 1 tbsp vegetable oil and let it get hot.

3. **Cook the Pork:** Add the sliced pork and let it sit for 1-2 minutes without stirring to develop color. Stir and cook another 1-2 minutes until the pork is mostly opaque. Don't fully cook it - it will finish cooking in the braise.

4. **Add Aromatics:** Add the minced garlic and cook for 30 seconds until fragrant. Add the sliced onion and mushrooms, cooking for 2 minutes until they begin to soften.

5. **Build the Flavor Base:** Add the gochugaru and gochujang, stirring quickly so they coat the vegetables and heat in the hot pan (about 30 seconds). This blooms the chili flavors. If using doenjang, add it now.

6. **Add Kimchi:** Add the chopped kimchi and stir everything together. Cook for 2 minutes so the kimchi heats through and releases its pungent aroma.

7. **Braise:** Add the stock and kimchi brine, stirring well. Bring to a gentle simmer over medium heat. Once simmering, reduce heat to low and simmer uncovered for 12-15 minutes so the flavors meld and the pork becomes tender. The liquid should reduce slightly and taste deeply savory and spicy.

8. **Taste and Season:** Taste carefully. Add fish sauce for more umami, sugar to balance heat and salt, or gochugaru if you want more spice. The balance should feel bold but balanced - no single flavor should overwhelm.

9. **Finish:** Drizzle with 1 tbsp sesame oil. Remove from heat.

10. **Serve:** Ladle into individual bowls over warm rice. Garnish with chopped green onions and sesame seeds. Serve with kimchi on the side and extra rice.

**Kimchi Quality:** Use kimchi that's at least a few days old - the older and funkier the better. Store-bought kimchi is fine; homemade is better.

**Pork Options:** Pork belly is traditional because it becomes tender and adds richness. But pork shoulder, beef, or tofu all work.

**Heat Level:** Gochugaru and gochujang can be intense. Start with the amounts listed and taste before adding more. You can always add heat; you can't take it out.

**Doenjang Note:** Doenjang (soybean paste) adds deep umami and is traditional but optional. If using, dissolve it in a bit of stock before adding to avoid lumps.

**Make-Ahead:** Kimchi jjigae tastes better the next day as flavors deepen. Store in the refrigerator for up to 4 days and reheat gently.

6. Add Kimchi: Add the chopped kimchi and stir everything together. Cook for 2 minutes so the kimchi heats through and releases its pungent aroma.
7. Braise: Add the stock and kimchi brine, stirring well. Bring to a gentle simmer over medium heat. Once simmering, reduce heat to low and simmer uncovered for 12-15 minutes so the flavors meld and the pork becomes tender. The liquid should reduce slightly and taste deeply savory and spicy.
8. Taste and Season: Taste carefully. Add fish sauce for more umami, sugar to balance heat and salt, or gochugaru if you want more spice. The balance should feel bold but balanced - no single flavor should overwhelm.
9. Finish: Drizzle with 1 tbsp sesame oil. Remove from heat.
10. Serve: Ladle into individual bowls over warm rice. Garnish with chopped green onions and sesame seeds. Serve with kimchi on the side and extra rice.

Kimchi Quality: Use kimchi that's at least a few days old - the older and funkier the better. Store-bought kimchi is fine; homemade is better.

Pork Options: Pork belly is traditional because it becomes tender and adds richness. But pork shoulder, beef, or tofu all work.

Heat Level: Gochugaru and gochujang can be intense. Start with the amounts listed and taste before adding more. You can always add heat; you can't take it out.

Doenjang Note: Doenjang (soybean paste) adds deep umami and is traditional but optional. If using, dissolve it in a bit of stock before adding to avoid lumps.

Make-Ahead: Kimchi jjigae tastes better the next day as flavors deepen. Store in the refrigerator for up to 4 days and reheat gently.
export.notes:
Chef's Note

Kimchi jjigae is Korean comfort food in its rawest form - kimchi is already fermented and pungent, so when you braise it with pork in stock, it becomes even more funky and complex. This is not a refined dish; it's what Korean mothers make on cold nights when they have leftover kimchi and want something warming and bold. The pork adds richness (or use tofu for vegetarian), and gochugaru (Korean chili flakes) amplifies the heat. Korean home cooks don't measure precisely - they taste and adjust. The final balance should be hot, salty, and deep-savory.

data.title: Gochujang-Glazed Oven Wings
ingredients: 1.35 kg (3 lb) chicken wing drumettes and flats, fully thawed, tips excluded
1 tbsp aluminum-free baking powder, not baking soda
2 tsp neutral oil, for lightly greasing the racks
data.description: Rack-roasted wings with a thin gochujang, honey and sesame glaze added just before serving.

learning.focus: Dry and roast the skin before applying a moist glaze
learning.outcome: Browned wings with tender meat and a light spicy-sweet coating, served before the glaze softens the skin further.
before: Allow 8–24 hours uncovered in the refrigerator after seasoning. Keep trays on a low shelf below ready-to-eat food and within the raw poultry storage window.
Use baking powder, not baking soda, and two racks if needed to keep pieces apart. A crowded pile will not roast like a spaced layer.

checkpoints.cue: The chilled skin looks dry rather than slick with surface moisture.
checkpoints.why: Refrigerator drying and baking powder help the skin brown and blister; they do not reproduce every feature of deep-frying.

checkpoints.cue: Skin is browned and rendered; several large pieces reach at least 165°F / 74°C, usually around 175°F / 79°C for a more tender wing.
checkpoints.why: Color alone cannot check the meat near the bone. The higher texture target is distinct from the minimum safe temperature.

checkpoints.cue: Glaze lightly coats the wings with little pooling in the bowl.
checkpoints.why: Adding all the sauce automatically can overwhelm the skin. A moist glaze progressively softens a crisp surface.

troubleshooting.cause: Wings were wet, crowded or shielded from circulating oven heat.
troubleshooting.fix: Continue roasting briefly if the meat tolerates it; use dry, spaced wings next time. Glazing early cannot fix pale skin.

troubleshooting.problem: Glaze tastes very salty or hot
troubleshooting.cause: Gochujang and soy sauce vary substantially by brand.
troubleshooting.fix: Use a lighter coating and serve reserved sauce separately. For a mild alternative, choose the lemon-pepper recipe instead of trying to remove heat from a finished gochujang glaze.

substitutions.alternative: 2 tbsp maple syrup
substitutions.effect: A different sweetness and aroma; the thinner syrup may need slightly longer simmering. Taste before adding extra sweetener.

learning.timing: Plan 9 hr 15 min with an eight-hour dry: 15 minutes preparation, eight hours refrigerated drying and up to one hour roasting/finishing. A 24-hour dry extends elapsed time by sixteen hours. Sauce preparation overlaps roasting.
learning.storage: Refrigerate in shallow containers within 2 hours (1 hour above 90°F / 32°C), at 40°F / 4°C or below. Use within 3–4 days; reheat leftovers to 165°F / 74°C. Reheat wings in a hot oven until 165°F / 74°C; watch the sugary glaze for scorching. Store unused glaze separately. The skin will not retain its original crispness after refrigeration.

body:
## Chef's Note

These oven wings pair a Korean gochujang glaze with rack roasting. Dry the skin thoroughly before cooking, then apply the sauce lightly at service. Honey gives sweetness, vinegar lifts the glaze and sesame oil finishes its aroma. This is an oven preparation with its own texture, not a promise of identical results to double-fried chicken.

## Directions

1. **Dry and season:** Pat fully thawed drumettes and flats dry. Lightly oil two oven-safe racks and set them over rimmed trays. Toss wings thoroughly with the baking powder and salt so there are no concentrated powder patches.
2. **Refrigerate to dry:** Arrange in a single spaced layer on the racks. Refrigerate uncovered for 8–24 hours at 40°F / 4°C or below, on a low shelf with the trays containing drips. Include this time within the usual 1–2-day refrigerated raw-poultry storage window.
3. **Roast and check:** During the last 15 minutes of refrigerated drying, heat the oven to 425°F / 220°C with racks in the upper and lower thirds. Roast about 25 minutes, then turn wings and swap tray positions. Roast another 20–30 minutes, checking until skin is browned and several large pieces reach at least 165°F / 74°C away from bone. Around 175°F / 79°C is a useful tenderness target for wings. Remove smaller finished pieces earlier if necessary.
4. **Make glaze:** During roasting, combine gochujang, honey, soy, vinegar, water, garlic and ginger in a small saucepan. Simmer gently about 3–4 minutes, stirring, until garlic smells mellow and the glaze flows from a spoon. Turn off heat and stir in sesame oil. Keep warm; do not reduce to a stiff paste.
5. **Coat at service:** Put cooked wings in a clean bowl and toss with about two-thirds of the glaze. Add more only if needed for a thin coating; reserve the rest in a separate serving bowl. Do not broil the honey-coated wings or coat them repeatedly for a long hold.
6. **Serve:** Finish with scallions, sesame seeds and optional measured gochugaru. Divide into four main portions with separately prepared rice and cucumbers, or offer eight smaller appetizer portions. The 1.35 kg weight includes bones, not that much edible meat.

## Offering both wing flavors

For a four-person main platter with this glaze and [lemon pepper butter](/mise/recipes/lemon-pepper-wings), roast one 1.35 kg batch using the shared wing preparation only once. Split the cooked wings evenly and make half of each recipe's sauce and garnishes. That provides two flavor choices within the same total wing quantity; making both full recipes doubles the food.

## Chef's Note

Seasoned mung bean sprouts are a Korean side dish served at almost every meal - tender, nutty, and finished with sesame oil and toasted sesame seeds. The bean sprouts cook just until tender but still have a slight crunch. Toast the sesame seeds before adding them so you get their full nutty flavor, not just a starchy taste.
## Directions

1.  **Thermal Prep:** Bring a large pot of water to a boil with 1 tsp salt. Prepare an ice-water bath.
2.  **Blanch:** Rinse sprouts in cold water. Add to boiling water and cook for 1-2 minutes until just translucent but still firm.
3.  **Shock:** Drain immediately and submerge in the ice water for 2 minutes to stop the cooking.
4.  **The Squeeze:** Squeeze the cold sprouts with your hands until **no more liquid drips out**. They should feel like a dense, dry mass.
5.  **Toss:** In a large bowl, whisk the scallion, garlic, salt, and sesame oil. Separate the sprouts and toss vigorously with the dressing and sesame seeds.
6.  **Serve:** Best served chilled or at room temperature.

data.title: Oi Muchim (Korean Cucumber Salad)
ingredients: 600 g English or Persian cucumbers, ends trimmed
1 tbsp gochugaru (Korean red chile flakes), or less to taste
data.description: Sliced cucumbers tossed with gochugaru, garlic, sesame, and a sharp-sweet dressing. A brief salt-and-drain step limits dilution.

learning.focus: Manage cucumber water before dressing
learning.outcome: Seasoned cucumber slices with a crisp bite and a coating of chile dressing, rather than a bowl of diluted liquid.
before: Use cucumber weight rather than count; English and Persian sizes vary greatly.
Start with less gochugaru for a mild dish. This is a freshly seasoned salad, not fermented or shelf-stable pickles.

checkpoints.cue: Water beads on the slices and collects below the colander.
checkpoints.why: Salt draws some water out before dressing. It limits dilution but does not stop cucumbers releasing water later.

checkpoints.cue: Slices are coated but still feel firm when bitten.
checkpoints.why: Thicker slices and gentle draining preserve more crunch than forcefully wringing very thin rounds.

troubleshooting.cause: Cucumbers were not drained well or the dressed salad sat for a long time.
troubleshooting.fix: Lift the cucumbers out with a slotted spoon. Next time blot after draining and toss closer to serving.

troubleshooting.cause: Gochugaru heat differs by brand and batch.
troubleshooting.fix: Add more plain sliced cucumber. Next time begin with a teaspoon of gochugaru and increase after tasting.

substitutions.alternative: Gluten-free tamari
substitutions.effect: Makes a gluten-free option when the other packaged ingredients are also gluten-free. Taste before adding more because salt levels vary.

learning.timing: 30 minutes includes 20 minutes salting; mix the dressing during that wait. No additional 10-minute marinade is necessary.
learning.storage: Best freshly dressed. Refrigerate within 2 hours (1 hour above 90°F / 32°C) at 40°F / 4°C or below. Use by the next day for texture; it will release more liquid and soften. This recipe is not a preservation method.

body:
## Chef's Note

Oi muchim is a seasoned cucumber side dish. This version uses gochugaru, garlic, a little sugar, and sesame, with rice vinegar for brightness. A short salting period reduces the water that would otherwise dilute the dressing. Keep the cucumbers refrigerated and serve soon after dressing.

## Directions

1. **Slice:** Wash cucumbers and cut into rounds about 1/4 inch thick. If an English cucumber is very wide, halve it lengthwise first and slice into half-moons.
2. **Salt and drain:** Toss with the measured salt in a colander over a bowl. Leave for 20 minutes, tossing once halfway through. Discard the drained liquid and gently blot the slices with a clean towel; do not wring them dry. Taste a slice: if unusually salty, rinse briefly, drain, and blot again.
3. **Mix dressing:** During the wait, combine gochugaru, vinegar, soy sauce, sugar, sesame oil, and garlic in a serving bowl. Stir until the sugar dissolves.
4. **Toss and serve:** Add drained cucumbers, scallions, and sesame seeds. Toss gently and serve promptly. If using as a noodle-salad topping, lift portions out with a slotted spoon so excess dressing does not flood the noodles.

body:
## Chef's Note

These Korean-Mexican fusion tacos were popularized by LA's Kogi BBQ truck in 2008, combining Korean gochujang-based sauce with traditional Mexican tortillas. The sauce whisks together gochujang, sesame oil, soy sauce, and sugar into a sweet-spicy glaze. Paper-thin cucumbers quick-pickled in vinegar for an hour provide a cool, tangy crunch that balances the rich sauce.

## Directions

1.  **The Sauce:** In a small bowl, whisk together the Gochujang, sugar, soy sauce, vinegar, and sesame oil until smooth. Set aside.
2.  **The Pickle:** In a separate bowl, toss cucumber slices with vinegar, sugar, chili, and salt. **Refrigerate for at least 1 hour** (but no more than 3) to maintain the "Snap."
3.  **The Sear:** Heat a large skillet over high heat. Add the cooked pork or chicken and 1/4 cup of the Kogi sauce. Toss vigorously for 3-4 minutes until the edges are crispy and the meat is lacquered.
4.  **Toast:** Warm the tortillas over an open flame or in a dry pan until charred in spots.
5.  **Assemble:** Place a generous scoop of the glazed meat into each tortilla.
6.  **Finish:** Top with a pile of the chilled cucumber pickles and extra scallions. Serve immediately.

body:
## Chef's Note

The secret to a great Keema is **Deep Browning**. You must sear the ground lamb until it develops a dark, savory crust before adding the aromatics. The peas provide a sweet "pop" that balances the richness of the lamb. We finish with a heavy hit of lemon juice and fresh cilantro to provide the **Acid Balance** that keeps this dish from feeling heavy.
For kids, serve the heat on the side or reduce/omit the spicy elements.

## Directions

1.  **Sear:** Heat a large skillet over high heat. Add the lamb and cook, breaking it up with a spoon, until deeply browned and slightly crispy.
2.  **Aromatics:** Add the diced onion to the lamb fat. Cook for 5 minutes until soft. Stir in the ginger and garlic and sauté for 30-45 seconds.
3.  **Bloom:** Add the cumin seeds, turmeric, chili, and tomato paste. Stir constantly for 1 minute until fragrant.
4.  **Simmer:** Add a splash of water (about 1/4 cup) to keep it saucy. Stir in the frozen peas. Cover and simmer for 5 minutes.
5.  **Finish:** Stir in the Garam Masala, lemon juice, and cilantro.
6.  **Serve:** Serve with warm Naan or over rice.

data.title: Lavender London Fog Cocktail
data.description: A chilled Earl Grey and gin cocktail with oat milk, vanilla and a restrained hint of lavender, shaken and served in a coupe.
data.source: User-provided recipe, adapted with oat milk at the user's suggestion

scaling.reason: Shake one cocktail at a time. The preparation batches below make tea for 2 cocktails and syrup for about 6; repeat the cocktail measures for each glass.

ingredients: 2 oz (60 mL) Earl Grey concentrate, thoroughly chilled (from the batch below)
1/2 oz (15 mL) plain barista-style oat milk, chilled and shaken in its carton; preferably unsweetened
1/2 oz (15 mL) lavender–vanilla syrup, chilled (from the batch below)
Solid ice cubes, enough to fill the shaker
--- Earl Grey concentrate — 120 mL, enough for 2 cocktails ---
4 g loose Earl Grey black tea
120 mL water at 95°C / 203°F, plus enough to restore the strained tea to 120 mL
--- Lavender–vanilla syrup — approximately 90–100 mL, about 6 cocktails ---

learning.focus: Control tea and lavender extraction before chilling and shaking a cocktail.
learning.outcome: A cold, lightly cloudy tea-beige drink with clear bergamot aroma, gentle vanilla sweetness and a subtle lavender finish.
before: Use culinary lavender and plain Earl Grey black tea, without additional lavender or vanilla flavoring.
Choose plain barista-style oat milk for more body than a low-fat oat drink; sweetness and foaming vary by brand. Shake the carton before measuring.
Prepare the tea and syrup ahead, and chill a 7 oz coupe. A 6 oz coupe may be tight after shaking adds water and bubbles.

checkpoints.cue: The strained tea smells distinctly of bergamot; the measured finished batch is 120 mL.
checkpoints.why: Topping up replaces water retained by the leaves and makes the two cocktail portions consistent.

checkpoints.cue: The sugar is completely dissolved and all lavender flowers are strained out after 3 minutes.
checkpoints.why: A timed, brief infusion limits the floral intensity; leftover flowers would continue steeping.

checkpoints.cue: The shaker is very cold, often frosted, and the strained drink has a fine layer of small bubbles.
checkpoints.why: Shaking mixes the oat milk with the tea while cooling and diluting the drink; a tall, lasting foam cap is not the goal.

troubleshooting.problem: The drink tastes perfumed or soapy.
troubleshooting.cause: Lavender strength varies, and too much or too long an infusion can dominate.
troubleshooting.fix: Remake the syrup with less lavender or a shorter infusion; do not mask it by adding more vanilla. Taste it in the cocktail before increasing lavender in a later batch.

troubleshooting.problem: The tea finish is harsh or drying.
troubleshooting.cause: The particular tea may extract too strongly at this concentration and steep time.
troubleshooting.fix: For the next batch, try a 3-minute steep at the same leaf weight and finished volume. Taste the chilled tea before mixing.

troubleshooting.problem: The drink is too thin or too sweet.
troubleshooting.cause: Oat milk has much less fat than heavy cream, and oat drinks differ in body and sweetness.
troubleshooting.fix: Try a barista-style oat milk if using a thin oat drink. If more body is wanted, test 3/4 oz (22.5 mL) oat milk in the next glass. If too sweet, reduce syrup to 1/4 oz (7.5 mL), which also reduces lavender and vanilla.

substitutions.alternative: 1/2 oz (15 mL) heavy cream
substitutions.effect: Restores the original, richer dairy version; the drink is no longer dairy-free and may look paler. This is a flavor and texture alternative, not an equivalent fat content.

learning.timing: Allow approximately 15 minutes to prepare the components and assemble the drink, plus about 1 hour of chilling; chill longer if needed. With cold tea and syrup ready, allow 5 minutes per cocktail. Tea and syrup can be prepared alongside one another.
learning.storage: Refrigerate tea and syrup separately in clean covered containers at 40°F / 4°C or below promptly after preparation. For this small-batch recipe, prepare them the day of serving or the day before. Follow the oat milk carton’s refrigeration and opened-use instructions. Shake the cocktail only when ready to serve; do not store it mixed.

body:
## Chef's Note

This chilled cocktail takes its cue from the Earl Grey, milk and vanilla flavors of a London Fog. Oat milk gives it a lighter body than the original cream version, while a small amount of lavender supports the bergamot. Keep the infusions brief and chill both preparations before shaking so the drink arrives cold, gently frothy and tea-forward.

## Directions

1. **Brew the concentrate:** Steep the 4 g Earl Grey tea in 120 mL water at **95°C / 203°F for 4 minutes**. Strain through a fine-mesh strainer, then add enough water to bring the strained tea back to **120 mL**. This makes two 60 mL cocktail portions.
2. **Make the syrup:** Stir the 60 g sugar into 60 g hot water until dissolved. Off the heat, add the culinary lavender and steep for **3 minutes**. Strain finely, then stir in the vanilla extract. Expect approximately **90–100 mL syrup**, enough for about six cocktails after straining losses.
3. **Chill:** Transfer the tea and syrup to separate clean containers and refrigerate until thoroughly cold, allowing about **1 hour**, or longer as needed. Chill a **7 oz coupe glass** before mixing.
4. **Measure one cocktail:** Shake the oat milk carton. Add **1 1/2 oz (45 mL) gin, 2 oz (60 mL) cold tea concentrate, 1/2 oz (15 mL) oat milk and 1/2 oz (15 mL) cold syrup** to the shaker. The remaining tea and syrup are for additional cocktails; do not add the whole batches.
5. **Shake and strain:** Fill the shaker with solid ice cubes and shake firmly for **10–12 seconds**, until the shaker is very cold and often frosted. Strain through both the cocktail strainer and a fine-mesh strainer into the chilled coupe. Look for a lightly cloudy tea-beige drink with fine bubbles on the surface; the amount of foam depends on the oat milk.
6. **Serve:** Serve immediately, **without ice or garnish**. Taste before increasing lavender in a future syrup batch; the bergamot should remain clear.

data.title: Lemon Basil Shrimp Risotto
ingredients: 1 1/2 lbs Large Shrimp (U10), peeled and deveined
5-6 cups Chicken or Vegetable Broth, heated

body:
## Chef's Note

Risotto originated in Northern Italy (Milan and the Veneto) where short-grain rice has been grown since the 15th century. The technique requires patience - adding hot broth one ladle at a time and stirring constantly releases the rice's starch (amylopectin), which creates the signature creamy texture without needing excessive butter or cream. This is called "mantecatura" in Italian. Arborio is the most common variety, though Carnaroli is preferred by Italian chefs for its firmer texture. Sear the shrimp first and add them back at the end so they don't overcook and become rubbery. The lemon cuts through the richness.

## Directions

1.  **The Crunch:** In a large wide skillet, melt butter over medium-high. Add shrimp in a single layer. Sear for 2 minutes per side until just opaque. Remove to a plate.
2.  **Foundation:** In the same pan, add onions and sauté for 2-3 minutes until translucent. Add garlic and sauté for 30-45 seconds.
3.  **Toast:** Add the Arborio rice. Stir for 2 minutes until the edges of the grains look translucent (The Toast Method).
4.  **Deglaze:** Pour in the wine. Stir until completely absorbed.
5.  **The Bind:** Add the hot broth one ladle at a time. Stir constantly. Wait until each ladle is fully absorbed before adding the next. This will take 18-22 minutes.
6.  **The Texture:** Once the rice is al dente, stir in the heavy cream, Parmesan, lemon juice, and zest.
7.  **Combine:** Fold the seared shrimp and fresh basil into the risotto. Toss for 1 minute until the shrimp are warmed through.
8.  **Serve:** Garnish with extra basil and a "High Note" crack of black pepper.

Sear the shrimp first and add them back at the end so they don't overcook and become rubbery. The lemon cuts through the richness.

steps.text: The Crunch: In a large wide skillet, melt butter over medium-high. Add shrimp in a single layer. Sear for 2 minutes per side until just opaque. Remove to a plate.
Foundation: In the same pan, add onions and sauté for 2-3 minutes until translucent. Add garlic and sauté for 30-45 seconds.
Toast: Add the Arborio rice. Stir for 2 minutes until the edges of the grains look translucent (The Toast Method).
Deglaze: Pour in the wine. Stir until completely absorbed.
The Bind: Add the hot broth one ladle at a time. Stir constantly. Wait until each ladle is fully absorbed before adding the next. This will take 18-22 minutes.
The Texture: Once the rice is al dente, stir in the heavy cream, Parmesan, lemon juice, and zest.
Combine: Fold the seared shrimp and fresh basil into the risotto. Toss for 1 minute until the shrimp are warmed through.
Serve: Garnish with extra basil and a "High Note" crack of black pepper.

data.title: Lemon Broccoli Tortellini
ingredients: 1 lb refrigerated or frozen cheese tortellini
1 1/2 lb fresh broccoli, cut into similar bite-sized florets, thick stems sliced thinner
4 cloves garlic, minced, divided equally between broccoli and sauce
1 large lemon, zested before juicing, juice divided between broccoli and finish
Salt and freshly ground black pepper, to taste
1/2 cup hot pasta cooking water, reserved before draining; use only as needed
data.source: Adapted from Two Peas & Their Pod, Lemon Broccoli Tortellini
data.description: Cheese tortellini with roasted broccoli, wilted spinach and a lemon-butter finish.

learning.focus: Coordinate a roasted vegetable with delicate filled pasta and a gentle cheese finish
learning.outcome: Tender tortellini with intact seams, browned broccoli and a light lemon-butter coating.
before: Use a rimmed half-sheet pan and spread broccoli without overlap, adding a second tray if necessary. A large deep skillet allows the spinach to wilt while tortellini cooks separately.

Read the tortellini package before starting: refrigerated and frozen products have different times and may specify a center temperature. Floating alone is not a universal doneness test. Choose vegetarian-rennet cheese and suitable filled pasta for a vegetarian version.

For larger batches use more roasting area and toss in separate vessels if needed. Scale the cooking-water reserve, but add by sauce consistency. Keep florets similar in size and do not multiply pasta time.

checkpoints.cue: Broccoli stems yield to a knife and edges have brown patches; garlic is golden, not black.
checkpoints.why: Charred tips do not establish stem tenderness, and small garlic pieces scorch quickly on exposed tray areas.

checkpoints.cue: Tortellini are cooked as their package directs and the seams remain intact.
checkpoints.why: Filled pasta can split with vigorous boiling or prolonged waiting in water.

checkpoints.cue: The pan no longer bubbles hard when cheese is folded in, and the sauce lightly coats the pasta.
checkpoints.why: Gentle handling and off-heat cheese addition limit tearing and clumping.

troubleshooting.cause: Small pieces sat exposed on a hot tray.
troubleshooting.fix: Tuck garlic among the broccoli rather than on bare metal and stir during roasting. Remove blackened bits; do not disguise their bitterness with more lemon.

troubleshooting.cause: They boiled aggressively or were tossed roughly.
troubleshooting.fix: Use a gentle boil and fold with a broad spoon; broken pieces cannot be sealed again.

troubleshooting.cause: All cooking water was poured in despite wet spinach or pasta.
troubleshooting.fix: Add it gradually. If still too loose, let it settle briefly while gently folding; do not boil filled pasta hard to reduce the sauce.

substitutions.alternative: The same package weight of frozen cheese tortellini
substitutions.effect: Cook from frozen if directed, with its own timing and filling endpoint; do not assume identical counts or serving volume.

substitutions.alternative: The same grated volume of vegetarian-rennet hard cheese
substitutions.effect: Keeps a savory finish; confirm the tortellini filling also suits the diet.

learning.timing: Allow about 45 minutes, with fifteen minutes preparation and oven heating, twenty to twenty-five minutes roasting and several minutes assembly. Heat pasta water during roasting, start the shallot/spinach base near the end, and time tortellini by its package so it finishes close to the broccoli. Very slow oven heating or thick stems extend the total.
learning.storage: Refrigerate promptly in shallow containers within 2 hours, or 1 hour above 90°F / 32°C, at 40°F / 4°C or below. Plan to use the next day for texture. Reheat the portion needed with a little water, stirring gently, to 165°F / 74°C throughout. The pasta softens and the cheese sauce may become less smooth; it is best freshly tossed.

body:
## Chef's Note

Roast broccoli for browned edges, then fold it through cheese tortellini and wilted spinach. Split the garlic between the tray and the pan, and save part of the lemon juice for the finish. Add cooking water gradually so the butter coats the pasta without leaving a thin puddle.

## Directions

1. **Prepare:** Heat the oven to **400°F / 205°C**. Cut broccoli into similar bite-sized florets and slice thick stems thinner. Mince shallot and garlic, zest then juice the lemon, and set a large pot of water on to boil.
2. **Roast broccoli:** Toss broccoli with olive oil, **half the garlic and half the lemon juice**, salt and pepper. Spread on a rimmed half-sheet pan in one layer, using a second tray if crowded. Keep garlic among the florets rather than scattered on bare metal. Roast **20–25 minutes**, turning once, until stems are tender and edges browned. Remove any pieces that finish early.
3. **Start the sauce:** Near the end of roasting, melt butter in a large deep skillet over medium-low. Soften shallot for about **3–5 minutes**. Add **the remaining garlic** and pepper flakes for **30–45 seconds**, then spinach. Turn gently for about **2 minutes** until wilted. Lower heat or turn it off while waiting for pasta.
4. **Cook tortellini:** Time this stage by the package so it finishes near the vegetables. Season the boiling water moderately, add tortellini and cook as directed, avoiding a violent boil. Meet any specified filling temperature. Reserve **the listed amount of cooking water** before draining.
5. **Combine gently:** Add drained tortellini and broccoli to the spinach skillet. Add zest and about **half the reserved water**. Fold over low heat just until hot, then remove from the burner. Add Parmesan gradually and **half of the remaining lemon juice**. Fold gently, adding further water only until lightly coated. Taste before adding the rest of the lemon juice, salt or pepper. Serve promptly.

Adapted from [Two Peas & Their Pod’s Lemon Broccoli Tortellini](https://www.twopeasandtheirpod.com/lemon-broccoli-tortellini/).

data.title: Lemon Chicken Orzo Soup
ingredients: 680 g boneless skinless chicken breast, cut into 3/4-inch pieces
1 1/2 cups (360 ml) additional chicken broth, only as needed to loosen
1/2 tsp fine salt, added gradually only if needed
3 tbsp fresh lemon juice, added gradually to taste
Water, only for the optional separate-orzo make-ahead method, per pasta package
data.description: Diced chicken and small pasta in a lightly thickened vegetable broth, finished with lemon zest, juice and parsley.

learning.focus: Control the starch from both flour and pasta
learning.outcome: Tender chicken and orzo in a lightly bodied broth that remains spoonable, with a fresh lemon aroma.
before: Cut carrots and celery small enough to soften before orzo overcooks. Keep chicken refrigerated until adding to the soup.
Orzo absorbs broth during cooking and storage. The additional broth is a measured adjustment supply, not an automatic full addition.

checkpoints.cue: Flour coats the softened vegetables before broth is added gradually.
checkpoints.why: Dispersing flour first and stirring in liquid limits lumps; its starch thickens when heated with water.

checkpoints.cue: Orzo is just tender and thick chicken pieces reach 165°F / 74°C.
checkpoints.why: The grain and chicken need separate checks even though they share a pot. Stirring protects the small pasta from sticking.

checkpoints.cue: The soup flows from a ladle before lemon is adjusted.
checkpoints.why: Evaporation and starch absorption change concentration. Set the consistency first, then judge salt and acid.

troubleshooting.cause: Orzo absorbed liquid during a long hold.
troubleshooting.fix: Add some of the extra broth gently. For future make-ahead batches, cook orzo separately and add it by portion.

troubleshooting.cause: Pieces were small or the noodle brand needed longer.
troubleshooting.fix: Lift cooked chicken out briefly, finish the orzo, then return chicken to warm through.

troubleshooting.cause: All lemon juice was added without tasting after reduction.
troubleshooting.fix: Dilute with a little unsalted broth. Next time stage the juice and use the zest for more aroma without automatically adding more acid.

substitutions.alternative: 680 g boneless skinless chicken thigh in 3/4-inch pieces
substitutions.effect: Richer and less lean. It may need longer; confirm 165°F while watching the pasta so it does not overcook.

learning.timing: About 45 minutes includes preparation, vegetable softening, heating the broth and a 10–12-minute pasta/chicken simmer. Larger vegetable pieces extend the schedule.
learning.storage: Refrigerate in shallow containers within 2 hours (1 hour above 90°F / 32°C), at 40°F / 4°C or below. Use within 3–4 days; reheat leftovers to 165°F / 74°C. For a planned batch, cook orzo separately and store it apart from soup. If already combined, expect thicker leftovers and loosen with broth during reheating.

body:
## Chef's Note

This stovetop soup gets a little body from flour and more starch from the orzo as it cooks. It should stay spoonable rather than becoming a pasta stew. Lemon zest gives aroma; juice adds acidity, so they can be adjusted separately. The smaller pasta and lightly thickened broth make this distinct from the slow-cooker chicken soup with separate fusilli.

## Directions

1. **Soften vegetables:** Heat butter and oil in a 5-quart pot over medium heat. Add onion, small carrot and celery pieces, and pepper. Cook about 7–9 minutes, stirring, until the vegetables soften; deep browning is not required.
2. **Disperse flour:** Add garlic and thyme and stir about 30 seconds. Sprinkle flour over the vegetables and stir for 1 minute. Add the initial 6 cups broth gradually, stirring to prevent flour clumps and loosen any brown residue.
3. **Heat and add chicken:** Bring to a steady simmer. Add diced chicken, stir to separate pieces, and return to a simmer. Keep the extra broth separate for later adjustment.
4. **Cook orzo and check:** Add orzo and simmer gently about 10–12 minutes, stirring across the bottom frequently. Check that pasta is just tender and several thick chicken pieces reach 165°F / 74°C. Extend if needed, lifting cooked chicken out briefly if the pasta needs significantly longer.
5. **Set consistency and season:** Add additional broth in small amounts if needed for a spoonable soup and return to a gentle simmer. Taste and add salt gradually only if needed. Turn off heat, add parsley, lemon zest and half the juice, then taste before adding the remainder.
6. **Serve:** Divide among six bowls and serve promptly. For making ahead, cook the orzo separately in boiling water according to its package and add it to each serving; keep it separate from stored soup.

body:
## Chef's Note

Italian cooks know the rule: bright greens stay bright only if cooked hot and fast. Broccolini (which is less sulfurous than broccoli) sautés in under 5 minutes over high heat with just garlic, oil, and lemon. The acid from the lemon cuts any bitterness and adds brightness that prevents the dish from feeling heavy. This is a classic preparation called 'garlicky greens' or sautéed spinach technique applied to broccolini - quick, elegant, and perfect for weeknight dinners.

## Directions

1. **Prep:** Zest the lemon and set zest aside. Cut the lemon into wedges for serving.
2. **Heat:** Heat olive oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat. Add thinly sliced garlic and red pepper flakes. Sauté for 30-45 seconds until fragrant but not browned.
3. **Add Broccolini:** Add the broccolini to the pan and toss constantly for 3-4 minutes until the stems are tender-crisp and some leaves are slightly browned. Season with salt and a pinch of black pepper.
4. **Brightness:** Squeeze half the lemon juice over the broccolini and toss once more. Taste and adjust seasoning.
5. **Finish:** Transfer to a serving dish. Garnish with lemon zest and serve immediately with lemon wedges on the side.

data.title: Lemon and Herb Instant Couscous
ingredients: 250 g plain instant couscous; not pearl couscous
420 ml low-sodium vegetable or chicken broth, adjusted to the chosen package instructions
2 tbsp fresh lemon juice, divided and partly added to taste
1/4 tsp fine salt, added only as needed
data.description: Fine instant couscous hydrated off heat and finished with lemon, olive oil, parsley and mint.

learning.focus: Match hydration to the instant product and add fresh flavors after fluffing
learning.outcome: Tender, loose small grains with lemon aroma and fresh herbs, without a hard center or wet clumps.
before: Choose plain instant couscous intended for off-heat hydration. Pearl couscous and traditional non-instant couscous need different cooking methods.
The 420 ml starting liquid is for 250 g plain instant couscous. Follow the actual package if it calls for a different amount or rest.

checkpoints.cue: The couscous stands tightly covered off the heat for the package’s hydration time.
checkpoints.why: Instant couscous has already been processed for quick hydration. Continuing to boil it can turn the small grains into a wet mass.

checkpoints.cue: There is no pool of liquid, and a tasted grain has no dry center.
checkpoints.why: Hydration is confirmed by texture, not simply by reaching a five-minute timer.

checkpoints.cue: A fork separates the grains before lemon and chopped herbs are folded through.
checkpoints.why: Gentle lifting keeps the grains loose; adding herbs after cooking preserves more of their fresh aroma.

troubleshooting.cause: It needed more liquid, the starting broth was not boiling, or the lid leaked.
troubleshooting.fix: Sprinkle over 1–2 tbsp boiling water, cover and wait another 3 minutes. Check again before adding more; do not drown it with a second full measure.

troubleshooting.cause: Too much liquid was used for the product or the grains were stirred roughly.
troubleshooting.fix: Spread gently in a broad dish to release steam. Do not keep mashing with a spoon; severely overhydrated grains cannot be made separate again.

substitutions.alternative: Use the same quantity of vegetable broth and omit feta
substitutions.effect: Makes a vegan version with suitable packaged ingredients. The oil, lemon and herbs still provide a complete finish.

substitutions.alternative: 2 tbsp additional parsley
substitutions.effect: Keeps a fresh herbal finish with less cooling mint aroma.

learning.timing: About twenty minutes includes herb chopping and zesting, heating broth, a typical five-minute covered hydration and finishing. Package instructions and extra hydration corrections can extend this.
learning.storage: Refrigerate in shallow containers within 2 hours (1 hour above 90°F / 32°C), at 40°F / 4°C or below. Use within 3–4 days; reheat leftovers to 165°F / 74°C. Best on the day for herb aroma. For making ahead, refrigerate the hydrated couscous separately from herbs and feta; reheat with a small splash of water to 165°F / 74°C, then finish the portion being served.
