body:
## Chef's Note

Shari is seasoned rice used for sushi; a bowl of plain short-grain rice has a different flavor. Add the vinegar seasoning while the cooked grains are hot and lift them gently with a paddle. Fan briefly to release steam, then use the rice soon rather than keeping it warm on the counter for hours.

## Directions

1. **Rinse and soak:** Rinse the rice several times, gently swishing and draining until the water is less cloudy. Drain well, transfer to a heavy 3-quart saucepan and add the measured cooking water. Wipe away visible grit from the kombu with a barely damp cloth and add it. Soak for 30 minutes.
2. **Heat and cook:** Bring toward a boil over medium heat with the lid slightly ajar. Remove the kombu when the water starts bubbling. Close the lid, reduce to low and simmer gently for 12–15 minutes.
3. **Rest and check:** Move off the heat and leave covered for 10 minutes. Check a grain for a tender center. If grains are still firm and water remains, cover and cook on low for 3–5 minutes, then rest off heat for 5 minutes and check again. If the pot is dry but the center is hard, use the measured-water correction in troubleshooting. Already mushy rice will not become firm through extra stirring or cooking.
4. **Mix the seasoning:** While the rice cooks, stir four fifths of the measured vinegar, the sugar and two thirds of the measured salt in a small bowl. Warm briefly if needed to dissolve, without boiling. Reserve the remaining vinegar and salt.

data.title: Mediterranean Chicken Bowls
ingredients: 1.5 lbs Chicken Thighs, boneless and skinless
2 cups Cooked Yellow Rice or Quinoa

body:
## Chef's Note

This modular grain bowl treats each component as an independent element. Marinating chicken thighs in oregano and lemon, then searing over high heat develops a charred, crispy crust characteristic of Greek souvlaki. Layering creamy hummus at the bowl's base prevents fresh cucumbers and tomatoes from becoming soggy. Pickled red onions provide bright acidity.

## Directions

1.  **Marinate:** In a large bowl, toss chicken thighs with olive oil, lemon juice, oregano, and garlic. **Let sit for at least 15 minutes** (ideally 2 hours).
2.  **The Sear:** Heat a large skillet or grill to medium-high. Cook chicken for 5-6 minutes per side until deeply charred and the internal temp is 165°F.
3.  **Rest:** Transfer to a board and let rest for 5 minutes. Slice into thin strips.
4.  **Assemble:** In four deep bowls, spread a generous base of hummus. Top with a scoop of warm rice or quinoa.
5.  **Layer:** Arrange the sliced chicken, cucumbers, and tomatoes in distinct "stacks" around the bowl.
6.  **Finish:** Top with crumbled feta and a massive pile of [Pickled Red Onions](/mise/recipes/pickled-red-onions). Serve with a lemon wedge for the final **High Note**.

data.title: Lemon-Oregano Chicken with Roasted Peppers
ingredients: 900 g boneless skinless chicken thighs, excess loose fat trimmed
3 tbsp olive oil, for the marinade
3/4 tsp fine salt, for the chicken
1/2 tsp ground black pepper, for the chicken
400 g bell peppers, cored and cut into 3/4-inch strips
200 g red onion, peeled and cut into 3/4-inch wedges
1 tbsp olive oil, for the vegetables
1/4 tsp fine salt, for the vegetables
1/4 tsp ground black pepper, for the vegetables
1 tbsp chopped parsley, optional finishing herb
data.description: Boneless thighs in a measured lemon, garlic and oregano marinade, with peppers and onions roasted on a separate tray.

learning.focus: Control marinade concentration and give chicken and vegetables room to roast
learning.outcome: Tender, cooked-through thighs with lemon-oregano flavor, plus soft peppers and onions with browned edges rather than a tray of pooled liquid.
before: Plan thirty minutes of refrigerated marinating; chop the vegetables and preheat during that interval. Do not marinate chicken on the counter.
Use two rimmed half-sheet pans: chicken on the lower rack, vegetables above. Separating them allows either to finish first and keeps the vegetables out of raw chicken juices.

checkpoints.cue: Opened-out thighs sit separately, with a thin coating rather than a deep puddle of marinade.
checkpoints.why: Excess liquid and crowded surfaces slow browning. The marinade flavors the exterior; a short soak does not carry herbs uniformly through the whole thigh.

checkpoints.cue: Every thigh reaches at least 165°F / 74°C at its thickest part; peppers bend easily and onion layers are tender.
checkpoints.why: Chicken doneness and vegetable texture need separate checks. A charred edge alone proves neither.

troubleshooting.cause: They were piled together or released more moisture than the oven could remove.
troubleshooting.fix: Spread them out and leave their tray in longer after removing cooked chicken. Do not keep roasting finished chicken just to brown the peppers.

troubleshooting.cause: Small garlic pieces or thin drips dried against the hot tray.
troubleshooting.fix: Do not scrape bitter blackened deposits over the meat. Reduce heat slightly if needed and keep cooking to the measured endpoint; next time avoid pouring excess marinade onto the pan.

substitutions.alternative: 1/3 cup bottled Greek-style vinaigrette in place of the entire marinade
substitutions.effect: Use a dressing you have tasted before raw chicken contact. Omit the listed marinade oil, lemon, garlic, oregano, salt and pepper; its flavor and salinity will differ by brand. The vegetable seasoning stays unchanged.

learning.timing: About eighty minutes includes initial preparation, a thirty-minute refrigerated marinade, 25–35 minutes roasting and a five-minute rest. Vegetable preparation and oven preheating overlap marinating. Four hours of marination is an optional longer plan, not included in this total.
learning.storage: Refrigerate cooked leftovers in shallow containers within 2 hours (1 hour above 90°F / 32°C), at 40°F / 4°C or below. Use within 3–4 days and reheat to 165°F / 74°C. Keep any cold serving sauce separate.

sources.title: Suzy Karadsheh — Greek sheet-pan chicken roasting reference
USDA FSIS — Poultry basting, brining and marinating
FoodSafety.gov — Safe minimum internal temperatures
FoodSafety.gov — Clean, separate, cook, chill
USDA FSIS — Leftovers and food safety

body:
## Chef's Note

A measured marinade lets you control lemon, oil and salt instead of assuming every bottled dressing has the same balance. Give the chicken a coating and a refrigerated rest, then roast it opened flat. A second tray lets the peppers and onions lose moisture and brown without forcing the chicken to wait for them.

## Directions

1. **Marinate cold:** Whisk marinade oil, lemon juice, garlic, oregano, chicken salt and chicken pepper. Toss with chicken, cover and refrigerate for 30 minutes, or up to 4 hours for a longer preparation window. Keep the chicken’s original storage/use-by limit in mind; marinating does not reset it.
2. **Prepare trays and vegetables:** During the marinade, heat the oven to 425°F / 220°C with racks in the upper and lower thirds. Toss peppers and onion with their separate oil, salt and pepper and spread on one rimmed half-sheet pan. Lift the thighs from the marinade, allow excess to drip off, open them flat and space them on a second pan. Discard the raw-contact marinade; do not use it as a serving sauce. Wash raw-meat utensils and hands.
3. **Roast and check separately:** Put chicken below the vegetable tray. Roast for about 25–35 minutes, turning the vegetable pieces and rotating each tray front to back after fifteen minutes. Start checking chicken at twenty-five minutes: insert a thermometer into the thickest part of every thigh and continue until each reaches at least 165°F / 74°C. Remove finished pieces to a clean board. Vegetables should be soft through the thick onion wedges with browned edges; let them continue separately if needed.
4. **Rest and portion:** Rest the cooked chicken for five minutes, then slice across the meat. Divide the full chicken and vegetable batches among four plates. Scatter the optional measured parsley over the vegetables. This recipe supplies the protein and roasted vegetables; bread, grains and sauces are additional components.

## Build the platter

The [Lemon-Oregano Chicken Pita Platter](/mise/meals/mediterranean-chicken-night) gives exact quantities and a preparation schedule for pita, tzatziki and fresh vegetables. The old recipe’s serving spread is preserved there so it is counted once. For a plate, choose a grain instead of adding it on top of a full bread portion.

## About variations

This method is written for boneless thighs with a measured center temperature. Bone-in pieces and breasts need different preparation and timing; do not assume adding ten minutes makes them equivalent. For a spice-led home shawarma adaptation, use the separate [Chicken Shawarma](/mise/recipes/chicken-shawarma) recipe rather than renaming this lemon-oregano roast after adding two spices.

About variations

This method is written for boneless thighs with a measured center temperature. Bone-in pieces and breasts need different preparation and timing; do not assume adding ten minutes makes them equivalent. For a spice-led home shawarma adaptation, use the separate Chicken Shawarma (https://jordansilton.com/mise/recipes/chicken-shawarma) recipe rather than renaming this lemon-oregano roast after adding two spices.

data.title: Mediterranean Grain Salad
ingredients: 1/2 tsp Kosher Salt (plus more to taste)
1 cup Kalamata Olives, pitted and halved

body:
## Chef's Note

This salad bridges lunch and dinner - hearty enough with farro's chewy texture to anchor a meal, but light enough for summer eating. Farro is the grain of ancient Rome and remains central to Mediterranean cooking because it has more fiber and protein than wheat, and a nutty flavor that holds up to bold olive oil and vinegar. Make it ahead without the herbs and feta; they stay bright when added just before serving or at the table.

## Directions

1. **Cook the Farro:** Rinse the farro under cold water. In a medium pot, bring broth and salt to a boil. Add farro, stir once, then reduce heat to low. Cover and simmer for 25-30 minutes until tender but still chewy (not mushy). Drain any excess liquid and spread on a sheet pan to cool to room temperature - this keeps the grains from clumping.

2. **Prepare the Vegetables:** While the farro cools, dice the cucumber, tomatoes, and bell pepper into roughly 1/2-inch pieces. Finely dice the red onion. Place all in a large bowl with the olives.

3. **Make the Dressing:** In a small jar or bowl, whisk together the olive oil, lemon juice, oregano, grated garlic, and black pepper. Taste and adjust acidity - it should be bright and tangy.

4. **Combine:** Add the cooled farro to the bowl with the vegetables. Pour the dressing over and toss well to coat every grain and vegetable.

5. **Finish:** Just before serving, fold in the crumbled feta, parsley, mint, and dill. Taste and adjust salt and lemon juice. Serve at room temperature or chilled.

6. **Make-Ahead:** This salad tastes even better the next day as flavors meld. Store covered in the refrigerator for up to 4 days. Add the feta and fresh herbs just before serving to prevent them from getting soggy.

data.title: Mediterranean Pinwheels
ingredients: 6 large Spinach or Sun-dried Tomato Tortillas
2 tbsp Oil (reserved from sun-dried tomato jar)
6 oz Sun-dried Tomatoes in oil, chopped
10 oz Frozen Spinach, thawed and squeezed bone-dry

body:
## Chef's Note

These quick appetizers or lunch components require proper technique to avoid falling apart. Blending cream cheese with flavored oil from sun-dried tomatoes creates a tacky, flavor-rich spread that binds the fillings to the tortilla. Squeeze spinach until bone-dry - wet spinach makes tortillas soggy and causes rolls to unravel.

## Directions

1.  **The Bind:** In a food processor, blend cream cheese, garlic, a few sun-dried tomatoes, and 2 tbsp of the tomato oil until completely smooth.
2.  **Prep:** Lay out the 6 tortillas. Spread a thick, even layer of the cream cheese mixture over each, leaving a 1/2-inch border at the top.
3.  **Layer:** Scatter the chopped spinach, remaining sun-dried tomatoes, Parmesan, and feta over the cream cheese. Place a single line of fresh basil leaves across the center of each tortilla.
4.  **The Roll:** Starting from the edge parallel to the basil, roll the tortilla **very tightly**, squeezing gently as you go to ensure the "Emulsion" binds the layers.
5.  **The Finish:** Wrap each log tightly in plastic wrap and **refrigerate for at least 30 minutes** (mandatory for clean slicing).
6.  **Cut:** Using a sharp serrated knife, slice into 1-inch pinwheels.

data.title: Mediterranean Salmon with Lemon-Herb Emulsion
ingredients: 4 skin-on salmon fillets, 6–8 oz each, of similar thickness
2 tbsp olive oil, for searing salmon
3 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil, for the dressing
1 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil, for the orzo
1 tsp smoked paprika, divided equally between salmon and chickpeas
1 cup canned chickpeas, measured after draining and rinsing, then thoroughly dried
Fresh parsley and mint, chopped, to taste
Salt and freshly ground black pepper, to taste
data.description: Crisp-skinned salmon over herbed orzo, chickpeas, tomatoes and feta, with a shaken lemon, olive oil and oregano dressing.

learning.focus: Coordinate crisp fish and chickpeas with a freshly shaken dressing
learning.outcome: Browned salmon skin and lightly crisp chickpeas over tender orzo, with a bright, fluid lemon dressing.
before: Measure the four separate oil allocations before starting: dressing, fish, chickpeas and orzo. This sauce is an olive-oil dressing, not a warm butter emulsion.

Use a rimmed tray for chickpeas, a saucepan for orzo and a broad skillet for fish. Four large salmon portions may require two skillets or two batches; reserve enough time for that before cooking the fish.

For scaled quantities, preserve fillet thickness and a single layer on the tray and in skillets. Add pans or complete batches rather than stacking. Check fish independently; doubled ingredients do not double cooking time.

checkpoints.cue: Chickpeas are dry at the surface, beginning to brown and lightly crisp outside.
checkpoints.why: Wet chickpeas steam first. Canned chickpeas can remain tender inside; they need not become hard throughout.

checkpoints.cue: The shaken dressing briefly looks cloudy and uniform, then may separate as it stands.
checkpoints.why: Agitation disperses oil into lemon juice, but this dressing is not permanently stabilized. Shake again at service.

checkpoints.cue: Skin is browned and releases with a gentle spatula nudge; the thickest centers reach 145°F / 63°C before removal.
checkpoints.why: A browned skin and a cooked center are different checks, especially with thick portions.

troubleshooting.cause: Wet skin, inadequate pan heating or trying to turn too early.
troubleshooting.fix: Give the skin another brief interval to brown, then ease a thin spatula underneath. Lower the heat if it is scorching; do not tear it loose by force.

troubleshooting.cause: Oil droplets naturally coalesce after shaking stops.
troubleshooting.fix: Shake or whisk again immediately before spooning it over the food. No butter or extra oil is needed to repair ordinary separation.

troubleshooting.cause: Pasta moisture hydrates their roasted exterior.
troubleshooting.fix: Scatter them on each plate at the last moment instead of mixing them into the wet pasta in advance.

substitutions.alternative: The same dry volume of another small pasta
substitutions.effect: Cook by its package directions and judge tenderness; the finished volume can differ.

substitutions.alternative: Skinless salmon of the same portion size
substitutions.effect: There will be no crisp skin. Start on the presentation side and turn gently, still checking the center temperature.

substitutions.alternative: Omit it
substitutions.effect: Makes the dressing sharper; add the lemon gradually to find the balance you like.

learning.timing: Allow about 55 minutes: 20 minutes preparation and oven heating, 25–35 minutes chickpea roasting with pasta and dressing prepared in parallel, then about 8–12 minutes for fish. Start fish near the end of roasting. Two fish batches add roughly 10–15 minutes; two skillets avoid that serial wait but require attention. Pasta follows its own package cooking time. Active work is about 35–40 minutes.
learning.storage: Refrigerate leftovers promptly in shallow containers within 2 hours, or 1 hour above 90°F / 32°C, at 40°F / 4°C or below. Plan to eat the next day for quality. Reheat the portion needed to 165°F / 74°C; the fish will become firmer. Do not leave the finished dish at room temperature for an extended meal. Store chickpeas separately from dressed orzo; their crispness fades. Reheat only the portion wanted and add a freshly shaken dressing if available.

sources.title: FoodSafety.gov — Fish cooking and leftover reheating temperatures
FoodSafety.gov — Separation, prompt cooling and refrigeration

body:
## Chef's Note

This lemon-herb emulsion is a shaken olive-oil dressing: it turns cloudy as oil disperses into lemon juice, then separates again as it stands. Shake just before serving. Add roasted chickpeas at the last moment so the moist orzo does not immediately soften their crisp edges.

## Directions

1. **Prepare:** Heat the oven to **400°F / 205°C**. Drain, rinse and thoroughly dry the chickpeas. Zest the lemon, then juice it. Halve tomatoes, chop herbs and measure the separate oil amounts. Pat salmon skin dry, remove pin bones and refrigerate while starting the sides.
2. **Roast chickpeas:** Toss chickpeas with **their allotted oil, half the smoked paprika**, salt and pepper. Spread in one layer on a rimmed tray. Roast about **25–35 minutes**, shaking at about 15 minutes, until lightly crisp and beginning to brown. Begin checking at 20 minutes; do not insist that the centers turn hard.
3. **Mix dressing and cook orzo:** Shake **the dressing oil**, garlic, honey, oregano and **half the lemon juice** in a closed jar. Taste, then add more of the remaining lemon juice, salt and pepper as needed. Meanwhile cook orzo in boiling salted water according to its package until tender with a little bite. Drain, then toss with **the orzo oil**, tomatoes, feta, parsley and mint. Cover briefly to keep warm while the fish cooks.
4. **Heat the skillet:** When chickpeas are about 10 minutes from ready, season salmon with lemon zest, **the remaining smoked paprika**, salt and pepper. Heat **the salmon oil** in a broad skillet over medium-high until shimmering, not smoking heavily. If portions cannot fit with space between them, use two skillets with the oil divided between them, or cook in batches, reserving a proportional share of the searing oil for each batch.
5. **Sear and finish:** Lay salmon skin-side down, away from you. Press gently with a spatula for the first few seconds to keep skin in contact. Cook about **4–6 minutes** until the skin browns and releases; reduce heat if spices darken rapidly. Turn carefully and cook about **2–6 minutes** more, depending on thickness. Check the thickest center from the side for **145°F / 63°C**. If the outside is done before the center, lower the heat and continue gently. Remove each portion when ready.
6. **Assemble:** Divide the herbed orzo among plates, scatter over roasted chickpeas and add salmon with its skin facing up. Shake the dressing again and spoon around the fish and over the orzo, keeping the skin exposed. Serve immediately. The pasta, legumes and tomatoes are already part of this dish; a separate grain is unnecessary.

Meanwhile cook orzo in boiling salted water according to its package until tender with a little bite. Drain, then toss with the orzo oil, tomatoes, feta, parsley and mint. Cover briefly to keep warm while the fish cooks.
4. Heat the skillet: When chickpeas are about 10 minutes from ready, season salmon with lemon zest, the remaining smoked paprika, salt and pepper. Heat the salmon oil in a broad skillet over medium-high until shimmering, not smoking heavily. If portions cannot fit with space between them, use two skillets with the oil divided between them, or cook in batches, reserving a proportional share of the searing oil for each batch.
5. Sear and finish: Lay salmon skin-side down, away from you. Press gently with a spatula for the first few seconds to keep skin in contact. Cook about 4–6 minutes until the skin browns and releases; reduce heat if spices darken rapidly. Turn carefully and cook about 2–6 minutes more, depending on thickness. Check the thickest center from the side for 145°F / 63°C. If the outside is done before the center, lower the heat and continue gently. Remove each portion when ready.
6. Assemble: Divide the herbed orzo among plates, scatter over roasted chickpeas and add salmon with its skin facing up. Shake the dressing again and spoon around the fish and over the orzo, keeping the skin exposed. Serve immediately. The pasta, legumes and tomatoes are already part of this dish; a separate grain is unnecessary.
export.notes:
Chef's Note

This lemon-herb emulsion is a shaken olive-oil dressing: it turns cloudy as oil disperses into lemon juice, then separates again as it stands. Shake just before serving. Add roasted chickpeas at the last moment so the moist orzo does not immediately soften their crisp edges.

data.title: Melon Daiquiri
ingredients: 6 cups Honeydew Melon, peeled, deseeded and cubed
1/2 cup Fresh Lime Juice (The Acid Balance)

body:
## Chef's Note

The daiquiri is a Cuban drink named after a beach near Santiago - born from American occupation and the sugar trade. A good daiquiri is balanced: rum, lime juice, and sugar in equal parts, with the lime juice providing the backbone. Using fresh melon brings fruit sweetness without needing extra sugar, which keeps the drink bright instead of cloying.

## Directions

1.  **Thermal Prep:** Freeze your melon cubes for 30 minutes prior to starting for the best texture.
2.  **Blend:** Combine the honeydew, light rum, lime juice, and melon liqueur in a high-powered blender.
3.  **Process:** Pulse on low, then increase to high until perfectly smooth. Add a handful of ice only if needed to reach a "thick-shake" consistency.
4.  **Skew:** Thread 3 cantaloupe cubes onto each sugar cane skewer.
5.  **Serve:** Pour into chilled coupes or martini glasses. Garnish with the skewers and serve immediately for the maximum "Bounce."

data.title: Arroz Rojo
ingredients: 1 cup plain tomato puree, or 1 cup freshly blended Roma tomatoes
1 cup chicken broth, plus hot water as needed if the rice remains firm
data.description: Long-grain rice toasted in oil, then simmered with tomato, onion, garlic and broth. A covered rest helps the grains settle before fluffing.

learning.focus: Toast drained rice, then control absorption and resting
learning.outcome: Tender tomato-colored grains that fluff apart without a hard center or soupy liquid.
before: Use regular long-grain white rice, not brown, instant or precooked rice. Choose a heavy pan with a snug lid.

Measure the blended tomato by volume; a fixed count of Roma tomatoes does not guarantee a cup. Use plain puree, not tomato paste or seasoned pasta sauce. Different tomato products still vary in concentration.
Drain rinsed rice thoroughly before adding it to warm oil. For a larger batch choose a pot with enough room for the rice to expand and toast evenly; do not multiply the cooking time.

checkpoints.cue: Rice is opaque, lightly golden and fragrant, with no dark burned grains.
checkpoints.why: Stirring distributes the oil and heat; residual rinse water must evaporate before the rice begins browning.

checkpoints.cue: A tasted grain is tender and there is no pool of liquid at the bottom.
checkpoints.why: Tomato solids, rice variety and lid evaporation affect hydration; liquid disappearance alone cannot establish tenderness.

checkpoints.cue: The pot remains covered off heat for the full 10 minutes.
checkpoints.why: The pause lets moisture settle through the rice before fluffing.

troubleshooting.problem: Rice is hard and the pan is dry
troubleshooting.cause: Evaporation or tomato concentration left too little available water.
troubleshooting.fix: Add a small splash of hot water, cover and continue gently. Check after a few minutes; repeat if needed, then give it the covered rest.

troubleshooting.cause: More liquid remained than the grains needed.
troubleshooting.fix: Uncover briefly over very low heat to let excess moisture escape, then remove from heat. Avoid repeated stirring; already broken, mushy grains cannot be made whole again.

troubleshooting.cause: Heat was too high for the thick tomato liquid or the pan dried out.
troubleshooting.fix: Move unburned rice to a clean pan without scraping the base. Finish gently with a little hot water if the grains are still firm.

substitutions.alternative: Fresh Roma tomatoes blended smooth and measured to the same volume
substitutions.effect: Fresh tomato varies in water and solids; check both grain tenderness and remaining liquid rather than assuming identical cooking behavior.

substitutions.alternative: Vegetable broth
substitutions.effect: Makes the base suitable for a meat-free meal when all ingredients meet that requirement; broth salt levels vary.

learning.timing: Plan about 45 minutes: roughly 10 minutes rinsing, draining and chopping; 3–5 minutes toasting, 1 minute aromatics, bringing liquid to a boil, 15–18 minutes simmering and 10 minutes covered resting. The 25-minute cook field excludes the separate rest. Additional tenderness corrections take longer.
learning.storage: Refrigerate promptly in shallow containers, within 2 hours of cooking (1 hour above 90°F / 32°C), at 40°F / 4°C or colder. Use within 3–4 days. Do not leave a covered pot on the counter to cool. Reheat only the portion needed to 165°F / 74°C throughout. Reheat with a small splash of water under a loose cover, stirring to heat evenly. Do not leave cooked rice cooling in a large covered pan.

FoodSafety.gov — Cooling and refrigeration

body:
## Chef's Note

Toasting brings a lightly nutty flavor to this tomato rice. It does not seal the grains against water: the rice still needs enough liquid and gentle cooking to soften. Measure the tomato, drain the rinsed rice well, and leave time for the covered rest before serving.

## Directions

1. **Rinse and drain:** Rinse the dry rice in several changes of cool water until less cloudy. Drain thoroughly in a fine-mesh strainer, shaking out excess water while you dice the onion and mince the garlic.
2. **Toast:** Warm the oil in a heavy saucepan over medium heat. Carefully add the drained rice; residual water can spatter. Stir constantly for about 3–5 minutes, until the grains look opaque and lightly golden and smell nutty. Lower the heat if individual grains darken quickly.
3. **Add aromatics:** Stir in the onion and garlic. Cook for about 1 minute, stirring, until fragrant without browning the garlic.
4. **Add liquid:** Carefully stir in the measured tomato puree, broth and salt. Bring to a gentle boil, stirring once to distribute the rice and release any grains stuck to the base.
5. **Simmer and check:** Place the cilantro sprig on top. Cover tightly and reduce to a low simmer. Cook about 15–18 minutes without repeatedly opening the lid. Taste a grain: it should have no hard center, and free liquid should be absorbed. If firm and dry, add a little hot water and continue covered; if firm with liquid remaining, continue gently without adding more.
6. **Rest:** Remove from heat once tender and leave covered for 10 minutes.
7. **Finish:** Remove the cilantro sprig. Fluff gently with a fork and divide into four side portions.

data.title: Skillet Esquites (Mexican Corn Salad)
ingredients: 4 cups (600 g) fresh sweet-corn kernels or thawed frozen corn, thoroughly drained
2 tbsp Mexican crema or sour cream
2 tbsp fresh lime juice, divided, plus more to taste
1/2 tsp pure ground ancho chile (not a salted seasoning blend)
Fine salt, to taste after adding the cotija
data.description: Sweet corn with browned edges, lime, chile, and cotija in a light creamy dressing. Learn to manage pan moisture before adding the delicate finishing ingredients.

learning.focus: Brown corn before dressing it
learning.outcome: Tender kernels with golden-brown patches, a light creamy coating, and enough lime to balance the corn’s sweetness.
before: Drain and blot thawed corn; water clinging to kernels slows browning.
Plan two batches in a 12-inch skillet. Have dressing ingredients ready before the corn finishes.

checkpoints.cue: Kernels sizzle steadily and show brown patches, with little pooled liquid.
checkpoints.why: Smaller batches give water room to evaporate. A steaming heap may soften before it browns.

checkpoints.cue: Corn is warm rather than furiously steaming when the dressing is added.
checkpoints.why: A brief pause limits overheating the dairy and helps fresh herbs keep their character.

troubleshooting.cause: The kernels were wet or the pan was crowded.
troubleshooting.fix: Cook in smaller batches and let visible water evaporate before stirring frequently. Do not chase black color after the corn has become soft.

troubleshooting.cause: Cotija and seasoning blends differ in salt content.
troubleshooting.fix: Use pure ground chile and add salt only after tasting. If already oversalted, fold in additional unsalted corn; more lime does not remove salt.

substitutions.alternative: Crumbled feta, same weight
substitutions.effect: Tangier and moister; taste before adjusting lime and salt.

substitutions.alternative: 4 tbsp plain Greek yogurt
substitutions.effect: Tarter, less rich, and more sensitive to heat; let corn cool further and start with less lime.

learning.timing: 30 minutes includes cutting or draining the corn and two pan batches. Very wet frozen corn can take longer.
learning.storage: Refrigerate within 2 hours (1 hour above 90°F / 32°C) at 40°F / 4°C or below. Best within 1–2 days for texture. For make-ahead, cool corn promptly and store dressing and herbs separately; combine near serving.

American Chemical Society — Chemistry of grilling
FoodSafety.gov — Clean, separate, cook, chill

body:
## Chef's Note

Esquites takes several forms, including brothy cups and fried preparations. This skillet salad uses sweet corn. Brown some surfaces for flavor, then finish with chile, lime, cheese, and a modest creamy dressing. Blackening every kernel would hide the corn's sweetness.

## Directions

1. **Prepare and mix the dressing:** Drain corn thoroughly and blot away surface water. Whisk mayonnaise, crema, 1 tbsp lime juice, ground ancho chile, and garlic in a large bowl. Set aside the remaining lime, cheese, scallions, cilantro, and optional jalapeño.
2. **Brown the first batch:** Heat 1 tbsp oil in a 12-inch skillet over medium-high until shimmering. Add half the corn and spread it out. Leave for about 2 minutes, then stir and continue cooking for 3–5 minutes, until tender with golden-brown patches. Reduce heat if it spits violently or scorches. Transfer to a wide plate.
3. **Repeat:** Add the remaining oil and corn. Cook the second batch in the same way, adjusting the heat as needed. If dark residue is burning, remove it carefully before adding the second batch.
4. **Dress while warm:** Let the corn stop steaming vigorously for 2–3 minutes. Add both batches to the dressing and toss. Fold in cotija, scallions, cilantro, and optional jalapeño.
5. **Balance and serve:** Taste, add the remaining lime by the teaspoon as needed, and add salt only if the cheese has not supplied enough. Divide into six side portions and serve warm or cool. Chill promptly if making ahead.

data.title: Yogurt-Marinated Chicken and Onion Kabobs
data.source: Adapted from Jennifer Segal's Middle Eastern-Style Grilled Chicken Kabobs, Once Upon a Chef
ingredients: 2 1/2 lbs (1130 g) boneless skinless chicken thighs, trimmed and cut into about thirty-six 1 1/2-inch pieces
250 g peeled red onion, cut into 1-inch squares and separated into single or thin paired layers
1 cup (240 g) plain whole-milk Greek yogurt
1/2 tsp crushed red pepper flakes, plus up to 1/2 tsp more for extra heat
1 tsp neutral oil, for grill grates (or 1 tbsp for the three-batch skillet option)
data.description: Skinless chicken and thin onion layers in a garlic, lemon and yogurt marinade, grilled with warm spices and a measured center-temperature check. Plan the overnight soak and grill capacity.

learning.focus: Match skewer geometry and heat to a yogurt-coated chicken center
learning.outcome: Juicy chicken with a thin browned spice coating, softened onion edges with a little bite, and no raw thick onion stacks or bitter black yogurt crust.
before: Use boneless skinless thighs and keep the pieces similar in size. Long flat pieces can be threaded through twice, but do not roll them into thick tight bundles. Separate onion chunks into one or two thin layers so they do not act like dense plugs between the meat.

Set out twelve 10–12-inch metal skewers, about two per diner. The default schedule cooks six at a time, preserving a cooler part of the grill for managing darkening marinade. Only cook all twelve together if the cooking zone holds them without touching and leaves the cooler zone clear. If even six do not fit with space, use smaller rounds and allow additional time. More skewers do not automatically fit a small grill or grill pan.

All yogurt in this recipe is raw-contact marinade. If you want a serving sauce, prepare a separate clean sauce as an additional component; do not spoon leftover marinade over the cooked kabobs. The yogurt marinade is not an included dip.

checkpoints.cue: Onion layers are thin, chicken pieces are loosely threaded, and only a thin film of marinade remains on each skewer.
checkpoints.why: Thick onion bundles and compressed chicken cook slowly; heavy pools of yogurt can stick or scorch before the center is ready.

checkpoints.cue: The coating develops golden to brown patches and releases with gentle help from a broad spatula, without blackening over sustained flames.
checkpoints.why: Turning too early can tear a wet coating away. Too much heat burns the garlic and dairy before it necessarily cooks the meat through.

checkpoints.cue: The largest chicken pieces on every skewer reach at least 165°F / 74°C, measured through the side away from the metal.
checkpoints.why: Charred edges and white-looking chicken are not reliable center-temperature tests, and a hot metal skewer can give a misleading reading.

troubleshooting.cause: Excess marinade, a cool or dirty grate, or turning before the first surface has set.
troubleshooting.fix: Use a clean lightly oiled grate and leave only a thin coating. Let the surface cook before turning; slide a broad metal spatula underneath to release it gently. Do not pull so hard that raw centers tear apart.

troubleshooting.problem: Onion is hard when chicken is done
troubleshooting.cause: Thick multi-layer chunks or a tightly packed skewer slowed the onion cooking.
troubleshooting.fix: Remove cooked chicken with clean utensils and finish the onion over gentler heat. Next time use the thin layers specified; a little onion bite is intended, but a raw dense center is not.

troubleshooting.problem: Marinade blackens while chicken is underdone
troubleshooting.cause: The direct zone is too hot or the pieces were too thickly folded.
troubleshooting.fix: Move to the cooler zone and finish with the lid closed between checks until 165°F / 74°C. Do not serve at a lower temperature to save the coating; severe burned flavor cannot be corrected with more lemon.

substitutions.alternative: 240 g plain low-fat Greek yogurt
substitutions.effect: Less rich and potentially thinner depending on the brand; let excess coating drain well. Plain regular yogurt is wetter, so it is not treated as an identical consistency.

substitutions.alternative: 250 g peeled yellow onion in the same thin layers
substitutions.effect: Less purple color and a slightly different onion flavor; retain the geometry and tenderness check.

substitutions.ingredient: Outdoor grill and 1 tsp grate oil
substitutions.alternative: A 12-inch heavy skillet and 1 tbsp neutral oil total, divided into three 1-tsp portions
substitutions.effect: Follow the chicken and onion marinade preparation, but omit grill setup and skewering. Drain excess coating as directed. Preheat the skillet over medium heat for about three minutes, then add the first teaspoon cooking oil. Cook unskewered chicken and onion in three roughly equal batches, about 375 g chicken plus a third of the onion per round. Use medium-high heat initially and reduce to medium once the coating colors. Turn periodically and check each thick center to 165°F / 74°C, allowing about twelve to fifteen minutes per round. Wipe out burned deposits between rounds, then add the next teaspoon oil. Allow roughly twenty to thirty extra minutes overall; a grill pan has less contact area and may need smaller batches. The first round has a longer hold and loses some surface texture. Serve each batch promptly, or transfer finished batches to a clean oven-safe dish in a low oven, checking food stays at or above 140°F / 60°C. A 200°F / 95°C oven is a starting setting, not proof of food temperature. Cover loosely if needed to limit drying; the coating softens during holding. Rest the final batch five minutes, then finish with parsley and lemon as in step 6.

learning.timing: The default nine hours fifteen minutes includes thirty-five minutes of prep split before and after an eight-hour refrigerated marinade, about thirty-five minutes for two grilling rounds and changing batches, and five minutes final rest. Refrigerate eight to twenty-four hours; a longer soak adds directly to elapsed time. Begin gas preheating during the last fifteen minutes of marinating, or allow about twenty-five to thirty minutes for charcoal. A sufficiently large grill can cook all twelve together in about fifteen to twenty minutes, reducing the overall schedule by around fifteen to twenty minutes. These are planning estimates; size, heat and the measured center temperature determine when the chicken is done.
learning.storage: Keep marinating chicken at 40°F / 4°C or below and cook within its original one-to-two-day refrigerated storage window; marinating does not restart it. Discard raw-contact marinade. Remove cooked meat and onion from skewers and refrigerate in shallow containers within two hours, or one hour above 90°F / 32°C. Use within three to four days and reheat to 165°F / 74°C, adding a small splash of water if needed to limit drying. Store any separately prepared sauce according to its own recipe. The marinade does not preserve the chicken for a week.

## Chef's Note

This home-style version is adapted from Jennifer Segal's Middle Eastern-inspired chicken kabobs, with garlic, lemon, yogurt and a restrained pinch of cinnamon. The yogurt is a marinade rather than a serving sauce. Thin onion layers and evenly cut chicken help the skewers finish together; a thin coating develops browned patches while excess marinade can stick and scorch.

## Directions

1. **Prepare and coat:** Cut the peeled onion into one-inch squares and separate into single or thin paired layers. Cut chicken into about thirty-six pieces roughly 1 1/2 inches across, keeping thickness similar. In a bowl large enough to hold everything, whisk yogurt, olive oil, lemon juice and zest, garlic, paprika, cumin, cinnamon, the desired red pepper flakes, salt and black pepper. Add chicken and onion and turn to coat evenly. Cover and refrigerate for eight to twenty-four hours.
2. **Prepare the grill:** Near the end of marinating, heat a gas grill with the lid closed, then keep a medium-high cooking zone and a low or unlit zone. For charcoal, allow coals to establish and arrange them on one side, leaving the other side cooler. Follow the grill's lighting instructions. Set out a clean serving platter and utensils; the raw-marinated tray is not the serving platter.
3. **Thread and drain:** Divide chicken among twelve 10–12-inch skewers, about three pieces each. Distribute onion in thin layers between the chicken and at both ends, keeping the whole food-bearing length over the cooking zone. Do not thicken the onion stacks to use it up; use an additional onion-only skewer if needed and count it in the grill capacity. All this onion has contacted raw chicken and must be cooked; it cannot become a raw garnish. Thread without tightly compressing or wrapping pieces into thick bundles. Let excess marinade drain back into its bowl so a thin film remains, then discard the residue. Keep six skewers refrigerated while the first six cook, unless the grill is large enough for the whole batch with a clear cooler zone. Lightly oil clean grates with the measured teaspoon neutral oil using a folded paper towel held in long tongs.
4. **Grill the first round:** Lay six skewers over the cooking zone without touching. Close the lid between turns and turn about every three minutes once the first surface releases, using a broad spatula to help if needed. Cook for about twelve to fifteen minutes, moving skewers to the cooler zone if the coating browns too quickly. Cook any extra onion skewer alongside until the layers soften and reach 165°F / 74°C because of their raw-chicken contact. Onion edges should soften with some browned spots; the chicken coating need not become uniformly crisp.
5. **Check and repeat:** Begin checking around twelve minutes. Probe the largest pieces on each skewer from the side, avoiding the hot metal, and continue until each reaches at least 165°F / 74°C. Check any unusually thick pieces separately. Transfer fully cooked skewers to the clean platter and cover loosely during the short second round. Cook the remaining six the same way, keeping the same thermometer endpoint. A tight cover softens the coating, and the first round will not retain the same surface texture as chicken served straight from the grill.
6. **Rest and finish:** Rest the final round for five minutes, then serve two skewers per person with the chopped parsley and lemon wedges. For six plates, add one-and-a-half four-side batches of Lemon and Herb Instant Couscous, starting with 375 g dry couscous, plus vegetables or salad. Alternatively, warm six pita breads and add a vegetable side. These are extra components and preparation time. The onion in each portion is a seasoning vegetable, about 40 g raw weight, not a full vegetable side.

data.title: Mini-Shell Pasta with Bacon and Peas
ingredients: 10 slices smoked bacon, cut crosswise into thin slivers
2 tbsp crème fraîche or heavy cream
1 lemon, juiced, added gradually to taste
2 tbsp fresh mint, finely chopped, divided between sauce and garnish
1 cup hot pasta cooking water, reserved before draining; use only as needed
Salt and freshly ground black pepper, to taste
data.source: Adapted from The New York Times, Mini-Shell Pasta with Creamy Smoked Bacon and Peas
data.description: Small pasta shells with smoked bacon, sweet peas, mint and a rich Parmesan finish, loosened with pasta water.

learning.focus: Cook peas completely and add a generous cheese finish away from direct heat
learning.outcome: Tender shells holding peas, smoky bacon pieces and a creamy Parmesan coating with fresh mint.
before: Read the bacon and pea package instructions. Bacon slice thickness changes both fat yield and cooking time; no fixed slice-to-weight conversion is assumed.

Use a large deep skillet, with the pasta pot available as a larger mixing vessel if needed. For more servings cook bacon in rounds, dividing the butter among them, and finish in separate batches if the pot is too full to toss.
Grate Parmesan finely before starting. The measured cheese is a generous part of this sauce; add it gradually and do not assume the pasta-water reserve must all go in.

checkpoints.cue: Bacon is cooked through and golden with crisp edges, without burnt butter solids.
checkpoints.why: Sliver thickness and water content determine rendering time; moderate heat gives fat time to emerge.

checkpoints.cue: Peas have completed their package cooking process and are hot throughout.
checkpoints.why: A brief stir in bacon fat is not a universal cooking method for frozen vegetables.

checkpoints.cue: The pan is off heat and cheese disperses gradually into a moist coating.
checkpoints.why: A large cheese addition can clump when it lands in a very hot dry pan.

troubleshooting.cause: The pan was too hot or cheese entered in one mound.
troubleshooting.fix: Move to a bowl or cooler pot and toss with a little warm water. Some clumps may remain; boiling harder will not reliably smooth them.

troubleshooting.cause: Heat was too high or slivers uneven.
troubleshooting.fix: Lower the heat and stir more often. Discard blackened pieces; butter and bacon should smell toasted, not acrid.

troubleshooting.cause: Bacon and the generous Parmesan dose were combined with heavily salted water.
troubleshooting.fix: Avoid extra salt until tasting. Use plain warm water instead of salty cooking water if more liquid is needed; lemon does not remove salt.

substitutions.alternative: The listed equal volume of heavy cream
substitutions.effect: Less tangy and slightly thinner; both remain only a small addition to the Parmesan-based finish.

substitutions.alternative: The same dry weight of another small pasta shape
substitutions.effect: Follow package timing; shapes without pockets will hold fewer peas inside.

learning.timing: Plan about 40 minutes including water heating and fifteen minutes cutting/grating in parallel. Bacon commonly needs ten to fifteen minutes; cook pasta and peas alongside it, then allow several minutes for combining and the cheese finish. Thick bacon or extra rounds take longer.
learning.storage: Refrigerate promptly in shallow containers within 2 hours, or 1 hour above 90°F / 32°C, at 40°F / 4°C or below. Plan to use the next day for texture. Reheat the portion needed with a little water, stirring, to 165°F / 74°C throughout. Pasta absorbs sauce and softens during storage; fresh herbs and cheese lose some of their original texture.

body:
## Chef's Note

Mini shells catch the peas while smoked bacon and a generous amount of Parmesan make a rich sauce. Cook the peas fully, then combine the hot ingredients and move away from direct heat before adding cheese. Keep some of the measured mint for serving so its aroma stays fresh.

## Directions

1. **Start water and prepare:** Bring pasta water to a boil. Cut bacon into thin slivers, finely grate Parmesan, chop mint and juice the lemon. Season the water moderately; bacon and cheese bring much of the salt.
2. **Cook bacon:** Melt butter in a large deep skillet over medium-low to medium. Add bacon and cook, stirring, about **10–15 minutes** or as its package directs, until cooked through and golden with crisp edges. Lower heat if butter darkens quickly. Keep the rendered fat for the sauce; do not add more oil.
3. **Cook pasta and peas:** Meanwhile cook pasta according to package directions until tender with a little bite. Cook peas fully according to their package in a separate saucepan or microwave-safe bowl and drain. Reserve **the listed pasta water** before draining pasta without rinsing.
4. **Combine:** Stir cooked peas, crème fraîche or cream and **half the mint** into the bacon pan over low heat. Add hot pasta and about **one-quarter of the reserved water**. Toss gently until hot and coated, using the pasta pot instead if the skillet is too full.
5. **Add cheese off heat:** Remove from the burner and wait until bubbling subsides. Fold in Parmesan a handful at a time, adding warm water in small amounts as needed for a creamy coating. Add **half the lemon juice**, taste, then add more of the remaining juice only as needed. The sauce should remain slightly loose for plating.
6. **Serve:** Add black pepper and taste before salt. Divide into the intended portions and scatter **the remaining measured mint** over the top. Serve promptly.

Adapted from [The New York Times’ Mini-Shell Pasta with Creamy Smoked Bacon and Peas](https://www.nytimes.com/2009/10/11/magazine/11food-rex002.html).

data.title: Mint Tzatziki with Honey
data.source: Adapted from Food & Wine’s Greek-Style Lamb Burgers with Yogurt-Cucumber Sauce
ingredients: 1 cup (240 g) plain full-fat Greek yogurt
100 g English cucumber, ends trimmed, finely diced
data.description: Thick Greek yogurt with crisp diced cucumber, fresh mint, olive oil, garlic and a little honey. Spoon it into lamb pitas or serve alongside grilled meat and vegetables.

learning.focus: Balance a mint yogurt sauce while keeping its cucumber texture
learning.outcome: Aim for a soft mound on the spoon, crisp cucumber pieces and a tangy finish.
before: Use thick plain Greek yogurt. Wash and dry the cucumber and mint before cutting; pat the diced cucumber with a clean towel to remove surface water.
Make this ready-to-eat sauce before handling raw meat. Keep its bowl, utensils and serving spoon separate from raw-meat equipment.

checkpoints.cue: The cucumber is cut into small, distinct pieces with no puddle on the board.
checkpoints.why: Fine dice supplies a light crunch. Drying the surface limits added free water, although cucumber can still release liquid while the sauce stands.

checkpoints.cue: The sauce holds a soft mound; yogurt tang and mint remain clear, with garlic and honey in the background.
checkpoints.why: Tasting the combined sauce lets you judge the salt against the yogurt, cucumber and honey instead of seasoning each ingredient separately.

troubleshooting.problem: Sauce is loose or develops a puddle
troubleshooting.cause: Thin yogurt or wet cucumber added excess free liquid.
troubleshooting.fix: Spoon off obvious liquid and stir gently. Next time use thick Greek yogurt and pat the dice dry; do not add more honey or oil to thicken it.

troubleshooting.cause: The clove was large or strongly flavored.
troubleshooting.fix: Stir in more plain Greek yogurt, then taste before adding any more salt. This increases the yield and softens the mint and honey too. Use a small clove next time; extra honey will sweeten the sauce without removing garlic.

substitutions.alternative: The same amount of low-fat Greek yogurt
substitutions.effect: Less creamy; choose a thick plain brand and keep the same oil amount. Unstrained ordinary yogurt may make a thinner sauce. Both contain milk.

substitutions.alternative: 100 g trimmed Persian cucumber
substitutions.effect: Keep the fine dice and surface-drying step. If using a cucumber with a coarse seed cavity, remove it before weighing the 100 g.

learning.timing: About 15 minutes to wash, dice, chop, mix and taste. Serve immediately or refrigerate while preparing the rest of the meal. Stir and taste again before serving if held.
learning.storage: Cover and refrigerate at 40°F / 4°C or below; use within 3–4 days of mixing, or sooner if an ingredient needs using sooner. Keep out of refrigeration no longer than 2 hours in total, or 1 hour above 90°F / 32°C. Use a clean serving spoon and stir before serving. Refrigeration does not restart the sauce's preparation date.

body:
## Chef's Note

Fine cucumber dice keeps a little crunch, while thick Greek yogurt and olive oil give the sauce a cool, spoonable texture. Fresh mint should stay clear, with garlic and a little honey in the background. The honey softens the tartness without making the sauce taste sweet.

## Directions

1. **Prepare the cucumber and herbs:** Wash and dry the cucumber and mint. Cut the cucumber into fine dice, about 3 mm across, then pat with a clean kitchen towel. Finely chop the mint and mince the small garlic clove.
2. **Mix:** Stir the yogurt, olive oil and honey together until evenly blended. Fold in the cucumber, mint, garlic and half the measured salt.
3. **Taste and serve:** Taste, then add the reserved salt only if needed. Serve now, or cover and refrigerate while preparing the meal; stir and taste again before serving. For four lamb pitas, start with 2–3 tablespoons in each and offer the rest alongside. The full batch makes approximately 1 1/2 cups, depending on the yogurt and cucumber.

## Another variation

For a dill-and-lemon sauce with drained grated cucumber, use [Dill Tzatziki](/mise/recipes/tzatziki-sauce). It has a smoother cucumber texture and a larger batch yield.

data.title: Miriam’s Melt-In-Your-Mouth Rosh Hashanah Brisket
ingredients: 2 large Spanish Onions, sliced into thick rounds

body:
## Chef's Note

Rosh Hashanah brisket is a Jewish holiday tradition that carries prayer and memory into the kitchen - the dish is as much about the ritual as the flavor. A long, low braise at 300°F for hours breaks down the connective tissue into gelatin, which is why it's so tender. The braising liquid becomes a gravy that coats each slice.

## Directions

1.  **Foundation:** Preheat oven to 400°F. Lay the onion rounds in a single layer at the bottom of a heavy baking dish or Dutch oven.
2.  **Rub:** In a small bowl, mix the paprika, garlic powder, salt, and chives. Rub the mixture aggressively into every surface of the brisket.
3.  **The High Sear:** Place the brisket on top of the onions. Roast uncovered for 1 hour. This builds the "bark" and browns the onions.
4.  **The Braise:** Remove from oven. Pour the balsamic vinegar and honey over the meat. Cover the dish **extremely tightly** with a heavy lid or double layer of foil.
5.  **Low & Slow:** Lower the oven temperature to 250°F. Return the brisket to the oven and cook for 4 more hours until fork-tender.
6.  **The Chill (Optional but Recommended):** Let the meat cool in its juices, then refrigerate overnight. This allows the fat to be easily removed and the meat to be sliced perfectly thin.
7.  **Serve:** Slice against the grain. Return to the sauce and reheat gently before serving.

data.title: Misir Wot (Ethiopian Red Lentil Stew)
ingredients: 1.5 cups Red Lentils, rinsed until water runs clear
3 tbsp Niter Kibbeh (Ethiopian spiced butter) or Extra-Virgin Olive Oil for vegan
2 large Red Onions, finely diced (about 3 cups total)
1 tsp Kosher Salt, plus more to taste
1 tbsp Fresh Lemon Juice, for finishing

body:
## Chef's Note

Misir wot gets its soul from two things: deeply caramelized onions and berbere spice. The onions must be cooked low and slow without any oil for the first 10 minutes -- this dry-sauteing technique is traditional and concentrates their sweetness before the niter kibbeh is added. Do not rush this step. Berbere is a complex Ethiopian spice blend (chili, fenugreek, coriander, cardamom, and more); it is available at most spice shops or online. There is no adequate substitute -- it defines the dish.

## Directions

1.  **Dry-Saute the Onions:** Place the diced red onions in a large, heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven over medium heat with no oil. Cook, stirring frequently, for 8-10 minutes. The onions will release their moisture and begin to dry out, soften, and concentrate in flavor. This traditional step is essential.

2.  **Add the Fat and Spices:** Add the niter kibbeh (or olive oil) to the softened onions. Cook for 3-4 minutes until the onions begin to turn golden. Add the garlic and ginger, stirring for 30-45 seconds. Stir in the berbere spice blend, tomato paste, cardamom, and fenugreek. Cook for 2 minutes, stirring constantly to prevent burning. The pot should be deeply red and intensely fragrant.

3.  **Cook the Lentils:** Add the rinsed red lentils, 3 cups water, and salt. Stir well to combine. Bring to a boil, then reduce to a gentle simmer. Cover and cook for 25-30 minutes, stirring every 5-7 minutes to prevent sticking, until the lentils have completely broken down into a thick, porridge-like stew.

4.  **Adjust the Consistency:** The wot should be thick and scoopable, not soupy. If it thickens too much, add water a few tablespoons at a time. If it is too thin, simmer uncovered for a few more minutes.

5.  **Finish:** Stir in the lemon juice. Taste and adjust salt and berbere to your heat preference.

6.  **Serve:** Traditionally served on injera (Ethiopian sourdough flatbread) for scooping. Alternatively, serve over steamed basmati rice. The wot should be vibrant red, thick, and deeply spiced.

data.title: Miso-Glazed Roasted Cauliflower
ingredients: Sesame Seeds and Scallions for garnish

body:
## Chef's Note

Miso is umami condensed - it transforms mild cauliflower into something deeply savory and addictive. The glaze contains the holy trifecta: miso (salt and depth), mirin (sweetness and shine), and sesame oil (richness). Roasting at high heat caramelizes the glaze onto the florets. This is how Japanese home cooks make vegetables disappear from the plate. The key is not overcrowding the pan; each piece needs direct contact with heat to caramelize.

For a non-vegan variation, replace the mirin with 1 1/2 tbsp honey plus 1/2 tbsp soy sauce, in addition to the separately listed soy sauce. Use mirin for the vegan version.

## Directions

1. **Make Glaze:** In a small bowl, whisk together miso, mirin, soy sauce, sesame oil, rice vinegar, and fresh ginger. Taste - it should taste aggressively salty and umami-rich (the cauliflower will mellow it).
2. **Prep Oven:** Preheat to 425°F. Line a large baking sheet with parchment paper.
3. **Toss:** Pat cauliflower florets dry (moisture prevents caramelization). Place in a large bowl. Pour the miso glaze over and toss with your hands until every floret is coated.
4. **Spread:** Arrange florets in a single layer on the baking sheet, cut-side down. Do not crowd.
5. **Roast:** Bake for 25-30 minutes until the cauliflower is tender inside and the glaze is caramelized and slightly charred on the edges. Shake the pan halfway through.
6. **Finish:** Remove from oven. Garnish generously with sesame seeds and thinly sliced scallions. Serve hot.

data.title: Miso-Mashed Potatoes
data.description: Yukon Gold potatoes gently mashed with white miso, butter, warm milk and a little garlic, finished with optional scallions.
ingredients: 900 g peeled and trimmed Yukon Gold potatoes, cut into even 1-inch pieces
2 L cold water, or enough to cover the potatoes by about 1 inch
8 g salt, for the cooking water
4 tbsp (57 g) unsalted butter, cut into small pieces
2 tbsp (36 g) plain white rice miso, without added dashi; choose certified gluten-free miso if needed
1/2 cup (120 ml) whole milk, plus up to 1/4 cup (60 ml) more if needed
1/8 tsp fine salt, optional after tasting
2 tbsp thinly sliced washed scallion greens, optional garnish

learning.focus: Disperse salty miso in warm dairy and fold it into fully tender potatoes
learning.outcome: A creamy mash that forms a soft mound, with evenly distributed miso, no hard potato centers and no gluey stretch.
before: Potato weight is after peeling; buy about 1.05 kg to allow for trimming. This is four generous starch portions, or six smaller portions alongside another starch. Do not add it to a rice-based plate without reconsidering the rice portion.

Miso supplies substantial salt and varies by brand. Use plain white rice miso, not instant soup mix or a paste containing fish-based dashi. Confirm the label for gluten-free cooking; color alone does not establish ingredients or allergen suitability. Soy and dairy remain in this recipe.

A ricer gives a finer texture; a hand masher leaves small soft pieces. Avoid a blender or food processor. Have the dairy warm before the cooked potatoes are ready so they can be mashed and served hot.

checkpoints.cue: A knife passes easily through several pieces and a cooled sample has no firm or chalky center.
checkpoints.why: Fully cooked pieces mash with less force; extra mixing cannot substitute for enough cooking.

checkpoints.cue: The miso is dispersed with no large salty clumps and the butter is melted; the mixture is warm without boiling.
checkpoints.why: Dispersing the seasoning first gives even flavor without prolonged stirring of the potatoes.

checkpoints.cue: The drained potato surfaces lose their wet sheen without browning or forming a crust.
checkpoints.why: Remove clinging cooking water, not all moisture. The mash still needs liquid for a creamy texture.

checkpoints.cue: The mash drops softly from the spatula rather than stretching, and the miso flavor is even throughout.
checkpoints.why: Gentle folding limits mechanical damage and starch release; warm dairy keeps the mixture hot and easy to combine.

troubleshooting.cause: Some pieces were too large or were drained before their centers softened.
troubleshooting.fix: Cook to the tenderness cue before draining. After dairy is added, gentle covered heating may soften small lumps, but beating harder risks sticky potatoes.

troubleshooting.problem: The mash is stiff but not sticky
troubleshooting.cause: This potato batch needs more milk, or it cooled while waiting.
troubleshooting.fix: Warm the listed additional milk and fold it in one tablespoon at a time until the mash forms a soft mound. Stop before it becomes loose and pourable.

troubleshooting.cause: The miso was unusually salty or finishing salt was added before tasting.
troubleshooting.fix: Do not add the optional salt. If already too salty, additional plain cooked potato can dilute it; extra butter or a squeeze of citrus cannot remove salt.

troubleshooting.cause: Excess mixing disrupted too much cooked potato tissue.
troubleshooting.fix: Stop working it. More milk can loosen consistency but will not restore the original texture. Use gentler hand tools next time.

substitutions.alternative: The same starting volume of half-and-half or heavy cream
substitutions.effect: Produces a richer mash. Cream supplies less water than milk; use the extra liquid only as the texture needs it rather than assuming identical absorption.

substitutions.alternative: Red miso, starting with 1 tbsp and adding more only after tasting
substitutions.effect: Gives a stronger fermented flavor and darker color. Salt levels vary; this is a flavor adjustment, not an equal-strength replacement or a gluten-free assurance.

substitutions.alternative: The same peeled weight of russet potatoes
substitutions.effect: Gives a fluffier, more floury mash that may use more of the milk reserve; check tenderness before draining.

learning.timing: Allow roughly 50–60 minutes: about 15 minutes peeling and cutting, 10–15 minutes heating the pot, 18–22 minutes simmering, and 5–8 minutes draining, drying and mashing. Warm the miso dairy during the simmer and prepare the optional scallions then. A slow burner or larger batch extends the time; twenty minutes boiling is not the full recipe time.
learning.storage: Refrigerate in shallow containers within two hours, or one hour above 90°F / 32°C, at 40°F / 4°C or below. Use within three to four days and reheat covered to 165°F / 74°C throughout, folding in a little milk as needed. Store the optional scallions separately and add after reheating. For a short service hold, cover a heatproof bowl over gently simmering water and keep the mash at or above 140°F / 60°C, measured with a thermometer; limit this to about thirty minutes for texture.

body:
## Chef's Note

White miso gives a familiar butter-and-milk mash a savory fermented seasoning. This Japanese-inspired variation uses miso as both flavor and seasoning, so taste before adding finishing salt. Whisk the miso into warm dairy first, then fold gently into fully tender potatoes; warmth helps keep dinner hot, while limited mixing protects the texture.

## Directions

1. **Cut and cover:** Peel and trim the potatoes to the listed net weight, then cut into even one-inch pieces. Rinse briefly, put in a 5-quart pot and cover with about two liters cold water, adding enough to sit an inch above the potatoes. Add the eight grams of cooking-water salt.
2. **Simmer to tenderness:** Bring to a boil, then reduce to a steady simmer. Cook about 18–22 minutes after the water begins simmering, until several tested pieces yield easily to a knife and a cooled bite is completely soft in the center. Keep cooking if needed; larger pieces take longer.
3. **Warm the miso dairy during cooking:** In a small saucepan over low heat, whisk the initial half-cup milk with the miso and garlic powder until the miso has no large clumps. Add the butter and warm gently until melted. Do not boil or reduce the mixture. Wash and slice the optional scallions while the potatoes finish.
4. **Drain and briefly dry:** Drain well in a colander. Return potatoes to the pot over low heat for one to two minutes, shaking gently, until surface water evaporates and the pieces look matte. Remove from heat before they stick or brown.
5. **Mash and fold:** Pass the hot potatoes through a ricer or mash gently by hand. Fold in the warm miso dairy in two additions with a spatula, stopping as soon as it is incorporated. If stiff, warm and add the reserved milk one tablespoon at a time until the mash forms a soft mound. Do not beat it smooth in a blender.
6. **Taste and serve:** Taste before adding the optional one-eighth teaspoon of salt; the miso may supply all the finishing seasoning needed. Scatter with the optional scallions and divide into four generous side portions, or six smaller portions on a plate with another starch. Pair with a simply seasoned roast and a crisp or lemony vegetable.

data.title: Miso Salmon with Bok Choy
data.source: Jordan Silton
data.description: Citrus-miso salmon with garlic, scallions and oyster-seasoned bok choy over jasmine rice.
ingredients: 540 ml water, for rice, plus water for rinsing
900 g skinless, boneless salmon, divided into four similar fillets
1/4 tsp freshly ground black pepper, divided
1 tsp neutral oil, for the foil
600 g trimmed baby bok choy, washed and dried
4 tsp neutral oil, for the skillet, divided
2 tbsp water, for the bok choy, divided

learning.focus: Coordinate a briefly marinated fish with greens cooked in manageable batches
learning.outcome: Salmon with a browned citrus-miso surface and a flaking center, plus juicy bok choy stems and tender green leaves.
before: Choose four fillets about 1 inch thick. The salmon amount is net of skin and pin bones; buy trimmed portions or allow extra purchase weight.
Baby bok choy varies greatly in size. Weigh 600 g after trimming, split small heads lengthwise and quarter thick ones; wash between the stalks and drain well.
Reserve the finishing marinade in a clean bowl before the rest touches fish. The generous marinade is mostly drained away; it is not all baked onto the fillets or poured over the rice.
Use two burners, a skillet lid and a broiler-safe metal pan lined with foil. Finish the bok choy before switching to broil so the fish has your full attention.

checkpoints.cue: Two tablespoons of the mixed marinade sit in a separate clean bowl before fish is added to the remainder.
checkpoints.why: This gives a clean finishing glaze without reusing raw-contact marinade.

checkpoints.cue: The fish carries a thin coating, with no deep marinade puddle or clumps of garlic on the pan.
checkpoints.why: Excess liquid prevents surface browning, while exposed miso and minced aromatics can scorch.

checkpoints.cue: Bok choy stems have light brown patches and yield to a knife with a little bite; leaves are tender.
checkpoints.why: Two batches leave room for contact with the pan; a short covered finish cooks the thicker stems.

checkpoints.cue: Glaze is bubbling and browned, and each fillet reaches 145°F / 63°C at its thickest center.
checkpoints.why: A dark surface can appear before the fish is cooked through.

troubleshooting.problem: The fish glaze scorches before the center is ready
troubleshooting.cause: The broiler is too close, the fish is thicker than specified or the coating is piled on.
troubleshooting.fix: Stop broiling, move to the middle rack and finish at 400°F, shielding browned areas loosely with foil. Burnt garlic or miso will remain bitter.

troubleshooting.cause: Water remained between stalks or the pan was crowded or cool.
troubleshooting.fix: Uncover and let water evaporate before adding the oyster sauce. Use the two stated batches and dry the washed vegetable well next time.

substitutions.alternative: The same trimmed weight of full-size bok choy
substitutions.effect: Slice stems into 1/2-inch pieces and keep leaves separate; cook stems first, adding leaves near the end. Timing changes with stem thickness.

substitutions.alternative: Mushroom-based vegetarian stir-fry sauce
substitutions.effect: Removes the oyster ingredient but changes flavor and may change saltiness; the dish still contains fish. Check labels if avoiding wheat.

substitutions.alternative: Prepared plain rice
substitutions.effect: Use about 4 cups cooked rice for the original four servings. The complete short-grain rice recipe takes about 65 minutes from dry; its soak cannot be fitted into this jasmine schedule without extending dinner.

learning.timing: About 55 minutes includes rice preparation, a 15-minute refrigerated marinade, oven heating, two bok choy batches and a watched broiler finish. Start rice and heat the oven first; prepare greens while fish marinates. The fish roasts while greens cook, but pause the skillet before broiling. Allow longer for thick fillets, a slower oven or rice requiring a different package method.
learning.storage: Refrigerate salmon, bok choy and rice in separate shallow containers within 2 hours, or 1 hour above 90°F / 32°C, at 40°F / 4°C or below. Use within 3–4 days, counting rice from its original cooking date. Reheat cooked components to 165°F / 74°C; warm salmon gently, rice covered with a sprinkle of water and greens briefly in a pan. The greens soften after storage. Discard the raw-contact marinade after draining the fish; the cooking directions do not turn it into a serving sauce.

body:
## Chef's Note

Jordan Silton's miso salmon pairs a honey-miso marinade with lemon, rice vinegar, garlic and scallions. Oyster-seasoned bok choy and jasmine rice complete the plate. Drain the fish well before roasting and watch closely during the brief broiler finish.

## Directions

1. **Start rice and heat the oven:** Heat the oven to 400°F / 205°C with a rack in the middle and another positioned for the later broil. Rinse the jasmine rice and drain well. Put it in a heavy 2-quart saucepan with 540 ml water, bring to a boil, cover and reduce to low. Simmer about 15 minutes until water is absorbed, then move off the heat and rest covered for 10 minutes. Fluff before serving. This is a starting method for regular jasmine white rice; follow the package if its ratio differs.
2. **Mix and divide the marinade:** While the rice cooks, whisk miso, honey, soy sauce, mirin, lemon juice, rice vinegar, half the minced garlic, half the scallions and half the pepper. Reserve 2 tbsp in a clean bowl for finishing. Check fish for pin bones and pat dry; place it in a shallow dish with the remaining marinade, turn to coat, cover and refrigerate for 15 minutes. Do not leave this acidic marinade on overnight.
3. **Prepare the vegetables and pans:** During the marinade, split small bok choy heads lengthwise; quarter larger heads so thick stem sections are about 1 inch across. Wash between the stalks, drain and dry thoroughly, then divide into two equal batches. Divide the remaining garlic, scallions and pepper between those batches. Line a metal half-sheet pan with foil and spread its teaspoon of oil where the fish will sit.
4. **Roast the salmon:** Lift fish from the marinade, letting excess drip off. Gently scrape off thick clumps, leaving a thin coating. Arrange on the prepared pan with space between portions and discard the raw-contact marinade. Roast about 12–16 minutes, until the fish is nearly cooked; check its center toward the end. If it reaches 145°F / 63°C before the final broil, it is already cooked and needs at most a very brief coloring step.
5. **Cook bok choy in two batches:** While fish roasts, heat a 12-inch skillet over medium-high heat with 2 tsp neutral oil. Add half the bok choy cut-side down and cook 2–3 minutes until lightly browned. Turn, add half the reserved vegetable garlic and scallions, and stir 30 seconds until fragrant. Add 1 tbsp water, cover and steam 1–2 minutes until stems are crisp-tender. Uncover, evaporate any pooled water, then toss with 1 tbsp oyster sauce, 1/2 tsp sesame oil and half the remaining pepper. Transfer to a serving dish and loosely cover. Repeat with the second batch and the remaining vegetable ingredients. Turn off the skillet before broiling; if the fish is waiting for its finish, set its pan briefly on a heatproof surface.
6. **Glaze and briefly broil:** Spread the clean reserved 2 tbsp marinade over the four fillets, using a clean utensil. Switch to high broil and place the fish surface 7–9 inches below the element. Watch continuously for 1–3 minutes, until the coating bubbles and browns. Check each fillet sideways in its thickest center and cook to 145°F / 63°C. If color arrives first, finish gently in the oven as described above. Let the fish stand briefly while fluffing and serving the rice.
7. **Serve the complete dinner:** Divide all the rice and bok choy among four bowls or plates and add one fillet to each. The original batch supplies about 225 g raw salmon and 150 g trimmed bok choy per diner, with roughly a cup of cooked rice. A small cucumber salad is an optional cool contrast, rather than a second required vegetable batch.

1. Start rice and heat the oven: Heat the oven to 400°F / 205°C with a rack in the middle and another positioned for the later broil. Rinse the jasmine rice and drain well. Put it in a heavy 2-quart saucepan with 540 ml water, bring to a boil, cover and reduce to low. Simmer about 15 minutes until water is absorbed, then move off the heat and rest covered for 10 minutes. Fluff before serving. This is a starting method for regular jasmine white rice; follow the package if its ratio differs.
2. Mix and divide the marinade: While the rice cooks, whisk miso, honey, soy sauce, mirin, lemon juice, rice vinegar, half the minced garlic, half the scallions and half the pepper. Reserve 2 tbsp in a clean bowl for finishing. Check fish for pin bones and pat dry; place it in a shallow dish with the remaining marinade, turn to coat, cover and refrigerate for 15 minutes. Do not leave this acidic marinade on overnight.
3. Prepare the vegetables and pans: During the marinade, split small bok choy heads lengthwise; quarter larger heads so thick stem sections are about 1 inch across. Wash between the stalks, drain and dry thoroughly, then divide into two equal batches. Divide the remaining garlic, scallions and pepper between those batches. Line a metal half-sheet pan with foil and spread its teaspoon of oil where the fish will sit.
4. Roast the salmon: Lift fish from the marinade, letting excess drip off. Gently scrape off thick clumps, leaving a thin coating. Arrange on the prepared pan with space between portions and discard the raw-contact marinade. Roast about 12–16 minutes, until the fish is nearly cooked; check its center toward the end. If it reaches 145°F / 63°C before the final broil, it is already cooked and needs at most a very brief coloring step.
5. Cook bok choy in two batches: While fish roasts, heat a 12-inch skillet over medium-high heat with 2 tsp neutral oil. Add half the bok choy cut-side down and cook 2–3 minutes until lightly browned. Turn, add half the reserved vegetable garlic and scallions, and stir 30 seconds until fragrant. Add 1 tbsp water, cover and steam 1–2 minutes until stems are crisp-tender. Uncover, evaporate any pooled water, then toss with 1 tbsp oyster sauce, 1/2 tsp sesame oil and half the remaining pepper. Transfer to a serving dish and loosely cover. Repeat with the second batch and the remaining vegetable ingredients. Turn off the skillet before broiling; if the fish is waiting for its finish, set its pan briefly on a heatproof surface.
6. Glaze and briefly broil: Spread the clean reserved 2 tbsp marinade over the four fillets, using a clean utensil. Switch to high broil and place the fish surface 7–9 inches below the element. Watch continuously for 1–3 minutes, until the coating bubbles and browns. Check each fillet sideways in its thickest center and cook to 145°F / 63°C. If color arrives first, finish gently in the oven as described above. Let the fish stand briefly while fluffing and serving the rice.
7. Serve the complete dinner: Divide all the rice and bok choy among four bowls or plates and add one fillet to each. data.title: Miso Soup
ingredients: 4 cups prepared dashi, homemade or made with instant dashi granules according to package instructions
4 oz Silken Tofu, cut into small cubes

body:
## Chef's Note

Miso soup is a miracle of **Emulsion and Timing**. The most common mistake is boiling the miso - high heat kills the delicate probiotics and ruins the aroma. Always whisk the miso with a little warm broth separately and add it only _after_ the pot has been removed from the heat. The foundation is **Dashi**: if you don't have time to make it from scratch, use instant dashi granules for that essential oceanic umami.

## Directions

1.  **Dashi:** Bring the four cups of prepared dashi to a gentle simmer over medium heat, then reduce heat to low.
2.  **Seaweed & Tofu:** Add the wakame and tofu cubes. Simmer gently for 2 minutes until the seaweed is rehydrated.
3.  **The Miso:** Place the miso paste in a small bowl. Ladle in about 1/2 cup of the hot broth. Whisk until the miso is completely smooth and liquid.
4.  **Finish:** **Turn off the heat.** Stir the miso liquid back into the pot.
5.  **Serve:** Add the green onions and serve immediately in small bowls.

data.title: Candy-Coated Chocolate Cookies
ingredients: 1 tsp Baking Soda + 1 tsp Sea Salt

body:
## Chef's Note

Folding only 3/4 of the candies into the dough, then pressing the remaining candies into the tops of the dough balls after scooping ensures vibrant colors stay visible on the finished cookies instead of bleeding into the batter during baking. Using a high ratio of brown sugar to white sugar creates chewy cookies that contrast the crisp candy shell.

## Directions

1.  **Cream:** In a large bowl, beat the shortening (or butter) with both sugars until light and fluffy (2 mins). Add eggs and vanilla; beat until emulsified.
2.  **Dry Mix:** Whisk together flour, baking soda, and salt. Gradually add to the wet mix until **just combined**.
3.  **Inclusions:** Fold in 1 cup of the candies.
4.  **Shape:** Preheat oven to 350°F. Drop teaspoon-sized balls of dough onto ungreased sheets.
5.  **Press:** Press 3-4 of the remaining candies into the top of each ball.
6.  **Bake:** Bake for 9-11 minutes until the edges are just golden. Do not over-bake; they will set on the pan.
7.  **Cool:** Let rest on the pan for 5 minutes to ensure proper texture.
