data.title: Chocolate Sandwich Cookie Cheesecake
data.source: Adapted from Kraft Recipes, now at Snackworks
data.description: A dense chocolate cheesecake with a thin chocolate-cookie base, chocolate-creme cookie pieces through the filling and more cookies baked on top.

scaling.reason: This batch fits one 9-inch springform pan. A different pan diameter or filling depth needs its own baking and cooling schedule.

ingredients: 32 regular-size chocolate sandwich cookies with chocolate-flavored creme, about 14–15 g each, divided; keep the creme filling
32 oz (907 g) full-fat block cream cheese, softened as directed
8 oz (227 g) semisweet baking chocolate, chopped
1 tsp neutral oil, for greasing the pan

learning.focus: Make a smooth cheesecake batter with little added air and bake to a set center
learning.outcome: A cold, clean-cut slice with a dense chocolate filling, distinct cookie pieces and a thin crumb base.
before: Use a 9-inch springform pan at least 3 inches deep, with a secure base and clasp. This recipe bakes directly in the oven. Set the pan on a rimmed sheet to catch any fat that escapes the seam, and clear refrigerator space for the pan.

Choose full-fat block cream cheese, not whipped cheese or a soft tub spread. Cube it and soften, covered, for about 45–60 minutes in a cool kitchen, until a spatula can press it smooth. Take the eggs out for only the final 20–30 minutes. Keep total pre-bake counter time under 2 hours, or 1 hour above 90°F / 32°C.

The cookies have chocolate-flavored creme between chocolate wafers. Their size matters: buy 32 cookies weighing about 450–480 g in total. Mini, thin and heavily overfilled cookies change the crumb and filling balance.
The cheesecake contains milk and egg; cookies usually add wheat and soy, and chocolate may contain milk or soy. Check packaged ingredients for additional allergens.

checkpoints.cue: The cheese mixture is smooth before the eggs go in, with no white lumps on the spatula.
checkpoints.why: Soft cheese blends more readily. Trying to remove lumps after adding eggs can beat unnecessary air into the batter.

checkpoints.cue: The batter is uniformly chocolate-colored, with no egg streaks or foamy cap.
checkpoints.why: Low-speed mixing combines the eggs while limiting air that can expand during baking and leave cracks as the cake settles.

checkpoints.cue: The outer filling is set, the central few inches tremble together rather than slosh, and the center reaches at least 160°F / 71°C.
checkpoints.why: Appearance describes the texture, while the measured center temperature checks the egg-containing filling. Waiting for a completely rigid hot center can overbake the edges.

checkpoints.cue: The chilled cake is cold through the center and a cut slice holds its shape.
checkpoints.why: The filling firms as it cools. A warm cheesecake can look set on top while remaining too soft to slice neatly.

troubleshooting.problem: Small white cheese lumps remain before adding eggs
troubleshooting.cause: The cheese was too cold or the bowl was not scraped thoroughly.
troubleshooting.fix: Stop and let the bowl stand briefly within the stated counter-time limit, then press and mix the cheese smooth, scraping the bottom. Do this before adding eggs; high-speed beating afterward can add excess air.

troubleshooting.cause: Excess air, overbaking or filling stuck to the pan as it contracted.
troubleshooting.fix: Finish chilling and slice gently; a crack does not need repair. Next time mix slowly after adding eggs, check the center near the end of baking and loosen the edge while the cake is still warm.

troubleshooting.problem: The base crumbles when a slice is lifted
troubleshooting.cause: The thin cookie layer was unevenly pressed or the cake was cut before fully chilled.
troubleshooting.fix: Chill thoroughly and lift each slice with a broad server, collecting loose crumbs alongside. Keep the cookie creme and crush the crust portion finely next time; do not move cookies from the filling into the base midway through assembly.

troubleshooting.problem: The center is still fluid at the first check
troubleshooting.cause: The batter began colder, the pan is deeper or the oven runs cool.
troubleshooting.fix: Continue baking in 5-minute intervals until the center reaches 160°F / 71°C and moves as a soft set mass. A dark cookie topping does not establish the filling's doneness.

substitutions.alternative: The same total weight of similarly sized chocolate sandwich cookies with vanilla creme
substitutions.effect: Gives a cookies-and-cream contrast instead of chocolate throughout. Keep the twelve-cookie crust and twenty-cookie inclusion allocation when the cookies have the stated size; do not substitute thin wafers without their filling.

substitutions.alternative: The same 227 g weight of bittersweet baking chocolate around 60–70% cacao
substitutions.effect: Makes the filling darker and less sweet. Keep the sugar and cream cheese amounts; unsweetened chocolate is not an equivalent swap.

learning.timing: Allow about 10 hours from refrigerated cheese to serving: 45–60 minutes softening, about 45 minutes for setup, melting, mixing and the crust stage, 50–70 minutes for the filled cake, about 1 hour on a rack and at least 6 hours refrigerated. The crust's 10-minute bake overlaps other preparation; total oven time is about 60–80 minutes. A colder batter or a cake that has not chilled through needs longer. Making it the day before gives the most flexible serving schedule.
learning.storage: Refrigerate the cake within 2 hours of leaving the oven, or within 1 hour above 90°F / 32°C; do not wait for the center to become cold on the counter. Leave space around the pan for air circulation. Keep covered at 40°F / 4°C or below and use within 3–4 days of baking. Serve chilled and return unused slices promptly. Discard slices left out for more than 2 hours, or 1 hour above 90°F / 32°C.

body:
## Chef's Note

Melted semisweet chocolate gives this cheesecake its dense chocolate filling, with chocolate-creme cookies in the base, middle and top. Smooth the softened cream cheese before adding the eggs, then mix slowly. Chill the cake thoroughly before cutting so the filling supports the cookie pieces.

## Directions

1. **Prepare the pan and cookies:** Once the cheese is softened as described above, heat the oven to 325°F / 163°C with a rack in the middle. Grease the bottom and sides of the springform pan with the measured oil. Finely crush twelve whole cookies, creme included. Quarter the other twenty cookies and keep all their crumbs. Measure a level 1 1/2 cups of these pieces and crumbs without packing for the filling; set all the remaining pieces aside for the top.
2. **Bake the crust and melt the chocolate:** Press the fine crumbs evenly and firmly across the bottom of the pan, with no bare patches. Set the pan on a rimmed baking sheet and bake for 10 minutes. Cool on a rack while mixing the filling. Put the chopped chocolate in a dry microwave-safe bowl and heat at half power in 20–30-second bursts, stirring between each, until just melted. Let it become lukewarm but still fluid; avoid getting water in it.
3. **Smooth the cheese:** Beat the softened cream cheese, sugar and vanilla at low to medium-low speed until smooth, about 2–3 minutes, stopping to scrape the bottom and sides of the bowl. Mix in the lukewarm chocolate until the color is even. Scrape again; avoid whipping the mixture fluffy.
4. **Add eggs and cookies:** Add the eggs one at a time on low speed, mixing only until each disappears. Scrape the bowl and fold in the measured 1 1/2 cups of cookie pieces with a spatula. Do not taste the raw batter. Spread gently over the cooled crust and scatter all the remaining quartered cookies and crumbs over the top.
5. **Bake to a set center:** Bake on the rimmed sheet for about 50–70 minutes, checking at 50 minutes. The edges should be set and the central few inches should tremble together when the pan is nudged, without a liquid wave. Check the filling in the center with an instant-read thermometer, avoiding cookie pieces and the pan base; it must reach at least 160°F / 71°C. Continue in 5-minute intervals if needed, then remove to a rack.
6. **Cool and chill:** After about 10 minutes, carefully run a thin knife between the cake and the pan wall without opening the clasp. Cool on the rack for about 1 hour total, then refrigerate in the pan, loosely covered and with space around it. Refrigerate within 2 hours of leaving the oven, or within 1 hour if the kitchen is above 90°F / 32°C. Once cold, cover well. Chill for at least 6 hours, preferably overnight, until cold and firm through the center.
7. **Unmold and slice:** Release the clasp and lift off the ring; leave the cake on its base for support. Cut into sixteen slices with a sharp knife, wiping it clean between cuts. Serve chilled, with coffee or unsweetened tea if desired.

6. Cool and chill: After about 10 minutes, carefully run a thin knife between the cake and the pan wall without opening the clasp. Cool on the rack for about 1 hour total, then refrigerate in the pan, loosely covered and with space around it. Refrigerate within 2 hours of leaving the oven, or within 1 hour if the kitchen is above 90°F / 32°C. Once cold, cover well. Chill for at least 6 hours, preferably overnight, until cold and firm through the center.
7. Unmold and slice: Release the clasp and lift off the ring; leave the cake on its base for support. Cut into sixteen slices with a sharp knife, wiping it clean between cuts. Serve chilled, with coffee or unsweetened tea if desired.

data.title: Overnight Oats
ingredients: 1/2 cup Old-Fashioned Rolled Oats (not instant, not steel-cut)
Toppings: fresh fruit, nut butter, granola, toasted coconut, or nuts

body:
## Chef's Note

Overnight oats are essentially Bircher muesli, invented by Swiss physician Maximilian Bircher-Benner around 1900. The principle is simple: oats hydrate overnight in liquid, softening into a creamy, pudding-like texture without any heat. Greek yogurt adds protein and tanginess, while chia seeds absorb liquid and create body. The ratio that consistently works is 1:1 oats to liquid plus a quarter-cup of yogurt. Old-fashioned rolled oats are essential -- instant oats turn to mush and steel-cut oats stay crunchy. This is a base recipe; the variations are endless.

## Directions

1.  **Combine:** In a jar or airtight container, stir together oats, milk, yogurt, chia seeds, maple syrup, vanilla, and salt. Make sure the chia seeds are distributed throughout -- they clump if left on the surface.
2.  **Refrigerate:** Seal the container and refrigerate for at least 4 hours, or overnight (up to 5 days).
3.  **Adjust:** In the morning, stir the oats. If they are too thick, add a splash of milk and stir to loosen. If too thin, add a spoonful of oats and let sit for 10 minutes.
4.  **Top and Serve:** Add your toppings of choice. Serve cold straight from the jar, or microwave for 1-2 minutes if you prefer warm oats.

### Variation Ideas

- **PB&J:** Stir in 1 tbsp peanut butter and top with smashed raspberries.
- **Banana Nut:** Add half a mashed banana to the base mixture and top with walnuts and a drizzle of honey.
- **Berry:** Top with mixed berries and a sprinkle of granola.
- **Carrot Cake:** Stir in 1/4 cup shredded carrot, a handful of raisins, and a pinch of cinnamon. Top with walnuts and a drizzle of maple syrup.
- **Tropical:** Use coconut milk and top with mango, toasted coconut, and macadamia nuts.

data.title: Pad See Ew
ingredients: 750 g boneless skinless chicken thighs, sliced about 1/4 inch thick
1 tbsp regular soy sauce, for the chicken
1 tsp neutral oil, for the chicken
1000 g fresh wide rice noodles (sen yai); see dried-noodle substitution
500 g Chinese broccoli (gai lan), trimmed; thick stems sliced 1/4 inch thick and leaves cut into 2-inch pieces
4 tbsp neutral oil, for cooking, divided
2 tbsp water, for steaming the broccoli, plus small splashes if needed
2 tbsp Thai sweet dark soy sauce
1 tbsp unseasoned rice vinegar, optional, divided among plates to taste
data.description: Soy-seasoned wide rice noodles with chicken, Chinese broccoli, and egg, finished in five small batches for a home stove.

learning.focus: Give tender rice noodles space and brief contact with the pan
learning.outcome: Broad, intact noodles with a savory-sweet soy coating and some toasted patches, tender chicken, set egg, and Chinese broccoli with a bite.
before: Set out five portions of noodles, sauce and cooked ingredients before the final stir-frying. Five servings do not belong in one home skillet at once.
Use Thai sweet dark soy as specified. Chinese dark soy and Indonesian kecap manis differ in salt and sweetness; they are not identical replacements.

checkpoints.cue: Thick chicken slices reach 165°F / 74°C before removal.
checkpoints.why: The quick final noodle finish should rewarm cooked meat, not compensate for partly cooked chicken.

checkpoints.cue: Broccoli stems are tender with a little resistance, leaves are wilted, and eggs have no wet raw streaks.
checkpoints.why: Preparing these components separately prevents hard stems or raw egg from forcing extra noodle cooking.

checkpoints.cue: A single portion is evenly coated, with a few toasted spots and no burnt sauce smell.
checkpoints.why: Small batches lose moisture faster. Gentle lifting preserves the rice-noodle structure once it softens.

troubleshooting.cause: Heat was too high for the sugar concentration or the pan was dry.
troubleshooting.fix: Lower heat and add a small splash of water. Wipe out blackened residue before the next batch; aim for occasional toasted patches, not a black crust.

troubleshooting.cause: They were cold and stiff, overhydrated, or tossed roughly.
troubleshooting.fix: Warm stiff fresh noodles briefly according to the package before separating. Fold with a broad spatula and cook one portion at a time.

troubleshooting.cause: Sweet soy brands vary or an especially sweet substitute was used.
troubleshooting.fix: Use the optional vinegar sparingly at the table; next time reduce the added sugar or sweet soy after testing one portion. More vinegar does not remove sugar.

substitutions.alternative: 375 g dried extra-wide rice noodles
substitutions.effect: Provides five practical portions with a different texture and variable hydrated yield. Follow package stir-fry preparation until just tender through the center, rinse if directed and drain well; divide into five before frying.

substitutions.alternative: 500 g broccolini, thick stems thinly sliced
substitutions.effect: Less leafy and generally less bitter. Check stems for tenderness before adding to noodles.

learning.timing: About 65 minutes allows preparation, two chicken batches, separate vegetables and eggs, and five final batches of roughly 3–4 minutes. Dried-noodle soaking may add time. Serve portions as they finish.
learning.storage: Refrigerate in shallow containers within 2 hours (1 hour above 90°F / 32°C), at 40°F / 4°C or below. Use within 3–4 days; reheat leftovers to 165°F / 74°C. Fresh noodle texture deteriorates after chilling; use leftovers the next day for best quality and reheat with a small splash of water.

body:
## Chef's Note

Soy-seasoned rice noodles, Chinese broccoli, chicken and egg make five portions of pad see ew. Cook the vegetables and eggs first, then finish each portion separately so the noodles have room to brown. Offer a little vinegar at the table so each diner can adjust the sweetness and acidity.

## Directions

1. **Prepare chicken and noodles:** Toss chicken with marinade soy, cornstarch, and its teaspoon of oil; refrigerate during preparation. Gently separate flexible fresh noodles and divide into five 200 g portions. If cold and stiff, warm briefly according to their package before separating. Use the substitution instructions for dried noodles.
2. **Organize sauce and vegetables:** Mix oyster sauce, sauce soy, Thai sweet dark soy, sugar, sauce water, and white pepper until uniform. Cut broccoli, keeping stems and leaves separate. Chop garlic and beat the eggs.
3. **Cook chicken in two batches:** Heat 1 1/2 tsp cooking oil in a large skillet or wok over medium-high heat. Spread half the chicken in one layer. Leave 1–2 minutes, then turn and stir-fry until several thick slices reach 165°F / 74°C, about 4–6 minutes total. Transfer to a clean bowl. Repeat with another 1 1/2 tsp oil and the rest of the chicken.
4. **Cook vegetables and eggs:** Reduce heat to medium. Add 2 tsp oil and stir garlic for about 30 seconds until fragrant. Add broccoli stems and the steaming water; cover for about 2–3 minutes, until stems are almost tender. Uncover, add leaves and stir-fry 1–2 minutes until wilted and water has evaporated. Transfer to a bowl. Add 1 tsp oil, then beaten eggs; stir gently until fully set with no wet streaks, about 1–2 minutes. Transfer out. Divide chicken, broccoli, egg, and well-stirred sauce into five portions.
5. **Finish one serving:** Heat about one-fifth of the remaining 2 tbsp oil in the skillet over medium-high heat. Add one noodle portion and one sauce portion. Lift and fold gently to coat, then spread and leave about 15–20 seconds. Turn and repeat once or twice for a few toasted patches, reducing heat if sauce starts to burn. Add one portion each of chicken, broccoli and egg with their share of any cooking juices. Fold until hot throughout, about 3–4 minutes total for this final batch. Add a small splash of water only if the noodles need loosening.
6. **Taste, plate, and repeat:** Taste the first portion and adjust the remaining sauce if necessary. Plate promptly and repeat step 5 four more times. Offer the measured vinegar at the table in small amounts. Serve plates as they finish, with an optional cool cucumber side; the main already contains its noodles, protein and vegetables.

body:
## Chef's Note

In the 1930s, Thai Prime Minister Plaek Phibunsongkhram launched a cultural campaign to create a unified national identity, which included promoting a 'national dish.' Pad Thai was born from this movement - a street food that used local ingredients and represented Thai cuisine to the world. The name literally means 'Thai-style stir-fried noodles,' and by the 1960s it had become Thailand's most recognizable dish internationally, despite being less than a century old. Real tamarind paste (sold in blocks, not concentrate) gives it the distinctive tangy-funky flavor that separates authentic Pad Thai from overly-sweet takeout versions.
For kids, serve the heat on the side or reduce/omit the spicy elements.

## Directions

1.  **The Soak:** Place dry noodles in a large bowl of cool water. Soak for 40 minutes until flexible but still firm. Drain.
2.  **The Crunch:** Heat 1 tbsp oil in a wok. Fry peanuts until golden; remove. Fry tofu matchsticks until golden and firm; remove.
3.  **Aromatics:** Heat 1 tbsp oil. Sauté garlic, shallots, and dried chili for 30 seconds until fragrant. Add the drained noodles and the tamarind mixture (sugar, fish sauce).
4.  **Toss:** Stir-fry over high heat. If the noodles feel too firm, add 1 tbsp of water at a time until they are chewy and translucent.
5.  **The Egg:** Push noodles to the side. Scramble the egg until set, then fold into the noodles.
6.  **Combine:** Add the shrimp and cooked tofu. Toss for 2 minutes until shrimp are pink and just opaque.
7.  **Finish:** Fold in the bean sprouts and chives. Toss for 15 seconds.
8.  **Serve:** Mound on a plate. Top with crushed peanuts, extra sprouts, and a lime wedge.

export.notes:
Chef's Note

In the 1930s, Thai Prime Minister Plaek Phibunsongkhram launched a cultural campaign to create a unified national identity, which included promoting a 'national dish.' Pad Thai was born from this movement - a street food that used local ingredients and represented Thai cuisine to the world. The name literally means 'Thai-style stir-fried noodles,' and by the 1960s it had become Thailand's most recognizable dish internationally, despite being less than a century old. Real tamarind paste (sold in blocks, not concentrate) gives it the distinctive tangy-funky flavor that separates authentic Pad Thai from overly-sweet takeout versions.
For kids, serve the heat on the side or reduce/omit the spicy elements.

data.title: Pad Woon Sen
ingredients: 6.3 oz Dried Mung Bean Glass Noodles

body:
## Chef's Note

Pad woon sen is a Thai glass noodle stir-fry that's lighter than pad thai. Mung bean glass noodles should be soaked in hot (not boiling) water for exactly 10 minutes to reach their optimal translucent texture. Sautéing cabbage and peppers over high heat until they develop charred edges before adding noodles creates smoky depth.

## Directions

1.  **Noodles:** Soak mung bean noodles in hot water for 10 minutes. Drain and rinse in cold water.
2.  **The Sauce:** In a small bowl, whisk together oyster sauce, fish sauce, soy sauce, and sugar.
3.  **The Egg:** In a wok, heat a splash of oil. Scramble the eggs with a pinch of salt until just set. Remove and roughly chop.
4.  **The Crunch:** Heat oil until smoking. Sauté cabbage and peppers for 3-4 minutes until charred at the edges but still firm. Transfer to the egg plate.
5.  **Aromatics:** Add fresh oil. Sauté onions and carrots for 2 minutes until soft. Add garlic and sauté for 45 seconds.
6.  **Bind:** Add the drained noodles and the sauce. Toss vigorously over medium-high for 3 minutes until the noodles are glossy and have absorbed the liquid.
7.  **Finish:** Return the eggs and charred veg to the wok. Stir in the Thai chile and scallions for the mandatory **High Note**.
8.  **Serve:** Serve hot or at room temperature for the Kitchen Standard fuel profile.

data.title: Pan Fried Noodles with Shrimp
ingredients: 1 lb Large Shrimp, peeled and deveined
8 oz Fresh Hong Kong-style Egg Noodles
4 oz Yu Choy or Bok Choy

body:
## Chef's Note

Pan-fried noodles (gon chow min) are a Cantonese restaurant specialty. The technique: boil noodles briefly, then pan-fry them into a crispy "bird's nest" cake - crunchy on the outside, soft inside. Treating shrimp with baking soda (then rinsing thoroughly) gives them a firm, snappy texture. The clear, golden gravy poured over the top softens the center noodles while leaving edges crispy. A dramatic presentation dish.

## Directions

1.  **The Crunch:** Toss shrimp with baking soda. Let sit for 5 minutes, then **rinse thoroughly** and pat dry.
2.  **The Noodles:** Boil noodles for 1 minute (al dente). Drain and rinse with cold water. Shake dry.
3.  **The Cake:** Heat 2 tbsp oil in a large non-stick pan. Spread noodles in an even layer. Fry undisturbed for 5 minutes until the bottom is a golden-brown disc. Flip (in sections if needed) and crisp the other side. Transfer to a platter.
4.  **The Veg:** Blanch the greens in boiling water for 30 seconds. Arrange around the noodles.
5.  **The Sear:** In a hot wok or skillet, sear the shrimp for 1 minute per side. Add ginger and garlic for 30 seconds. Splash in the Shaoxing wine.
6.  **The Gravy:** Pour in the sauce mixture (stock, oyster sauce, soy, pepper). Bring to a boil. Stir in the cornstarch slurry and cook until thickened and clear.
7.  **Serve:** Pour the hot shrimp gravy directly over the center of the crispy noodle cake. Serve immediately.

data.title: Panang Curry with Chicken
ingredients: 450 g boneless skinless chicken thighs, sliced about 1/2 inch thick
300 ml full-fat unsweetened coconut milk, divided
3 tbsp panang curry paste, or less for a particularly strong paste
1 tbsp neutral oil, only if needed when frying the paste
2 tbsp unsalted roasted peanuts, finely ground
150 g red bell pepper, thinly sliced
4 makrut lime leaves, central ribs removed and leaves sliced into very fine threads
2 tsp palm sugar or brown sugar, added gradually to taste
1 tbsp fish sauce, added gradually only as needed
2 tbsp water, used only if needed to loosen the sauce
data.description: Thin chicken slices and red pepper in a small amount of rich coconut curry sauce, thickened with ground peanuts and scented with makrut lime leaves.

learning.focus: Build a concentrated sauce before finishing the chicken
learning.outcome: Tender chicken slices with a thick, spoonable coconut-peanut coating and clear makrut-lime-leaf aroma.
before: This recipe contains peanuts. Check the curry paste too; removing a garnish or choosing sunflower seeds does not automatically make a packaged paste suitable for someone avoiding nuts.
Use panang paste and full-fat coconut milk. This recipe measures 300 ml milk rather than assuming that every can size belongs in the pan. Refrigerate unused milk promptly.

checkpoints.cue: Paste is fragrant and thickened without blackened residue.
checkpoints.why: Coconut products do not all separate visibly. Fragrance and controlled heat matter more than forcing every can to crack.

checkpoints.cue: Sauce leaves a brief trail when a spatula crosses the pan.
checkpoints.why: Reducing excess water before the chicken finishes makes a clinging panang sauce without prolonged meat cooking.

checkpoints.cue: Chicken centers reach 165°F / 74°C and the sauce remains spoonable.
checkpoints.why: The sauce should coat the meat, but reducing it to a dry paste can concentrate seasoning and overcook chicken.

troubleshooting.problem: Sauce is thin after chicken cooks
troubleshooting.cause: The pan was narrow or the sauce needed more reduction before adding meat.
troubleshooting.fix: Lift cooked chicken out, simmer the sauce briefly until thicker, then return chicken. Do not simmer the meat indefinitely to correct sauce consistency.

troubleshooting.cause: Peanuts were chopped coarsely instead of finely ground.
troubleshooting.fix: A little fine nut texture is normal. Next time grind the nuts to a fine meal; large crunchy pieces are a topping, not the same thickener.

troubleshooting.problem: Curry is too sweet or salty
troubleshooting.cause: The paste already contained seasoning or the full additions went in before tasting.
troubleshooting.fix: Loosen with a little water if over-reduced. Next time stage sugar and fish sauce; brands vary too much for an automatic full addition.

substitutions.alternative: 2 tbsp finely ground unsalted toasted sunflower seeds
substitutions.effect: Gives a different flavor with some similar body. Verify paste and all other ingredients separately; this substitution alone does not establish a nut-free dish.

substitutions.ingredient: Packaged paste, fish sauce and coconut milk
substitutions.alternative: Versions labeled gluten-free
substitutions.effect: Check every package rather than assuming all panang products have the same ingredients.

learning.timing: About 40 minutes includes preparation, developing/reducing the sauce and gently cooking the chicken. Plain rice is prepared separately.
learning.storage: Refrigerate in shallow containers within 2 hours (1 hour above 90°F / 32°C), at 40°F / 4°C or below. Use within 3–4 days; reheat leftovers to 165°F / 74°C. The peanut sauce thickens when cold; loosen gently with a little water when reheating.

body:
## Chef's Note

Ground peanuts give this panang curry body, while makrut lime leaves provide its distinctive aroma. Red pepper adds sweetness and color. Grind the peanuts finely so they blend into the thick sauce; panko is not a substitute for their flavor or texture. Serve with rice prepared separately.

## Directions

1. **Prepare:** Grind roasted peanuts to a fine meal. Remove the stiff central ribs from lime leaves, stack the leaves and slice into very fine threads. Slice pepper before handling chicken, then slice chicken and clean the work area. Measure the coconut milk and reserve 180 ml, leaving 120 ml for the paste.
2. **Cook the paste:** Simmer the 120 ml coconut milk in a wide skillet over medium heat about 3–5 minutes until thickened, stirring. Add panang paste and stir for about 2 minutes until fragrant. If no oil releases and paste is sticking, add the measured neutral oil. Do not continue cooking a dry paste simply to force visible splitting.
3. **Thicken the sauce:** Add the reserved coconut milk, finely ground peanuts, half the lime-leaf threads and half the sugar. Simmer gently about 3–5 minutes, stirring, until the sauce thickens enough to leave a brief spatula trail across the pan.
4. **Cook chicken and pepper:** Add chicken and pepper, separating the slices in the sauce. Simmer gently about 6–10 minutes, stirring, until several thick chicken slices reach 165°F / 74°C and the pepper is tender with a little bite. Use the measured water in small splashes only if the sauce becomes too dry before chicken cooks.
5. **Balance and finish:** Taste the fully cooked curry. Start with about 1 tsp fish sauce and add more only if needed; add remaining sugar only if wanted. Fold in the remaining fine lime-leaf threads and warm for about 30 seconds. Serve four modest main portions with separately prepared [plain rice](/mise/recipes/steamed-white-rice).

## Chef's Note

A crisp lives or dies by its topping - here, the secret is cooking the butter to brown butter stage (dark milk solids, nutty aroma) before mixing with the dry ingredients, so every crumb tastes like toasted nuts. The blueberry filling is tightened with cornstarch and lemon juice, preventing a soupy cobbler while keeping the fruit's bright acidity front and center.
## Directions

1.  **The Fruit:** In a saucepan, combine blueberries, 1/4 cup water, and lemon juice. Whisk sugar and cornstarch together and stir into the fruit. Cook over medium for 4 minutes until the juices thicken. Pour into a greased 9-inch square dish.
2.  **The Crumble:** In a small pan, melt butter over medium-high. Continue heating for 5 minutes, stirring often, until the milk solids turn dark brown and smell like toasted nuts. Remove from heat immediately.
3.  **The Mix:** In a large bowl, whisk flour, brown sugar, and salt. Drizzle the brown butter over the mix. Stir with a fork until large, crispy clumps form.
4.  **Bake:** Sprinkle the crumble generously over the fruit. Bake at 350°F for 30 minutes until the fruit is bubbling and the topping is a deep mahogany.
5.  **Serve:** Let cool for 10 minutes to allow the syrup to set. Serve warm with a scoop of [Vanilla Ice Cream](/mise/recipes/old-fashioned-vanilla-ice-cream).

data.title: Parmigiano Reggiano Cheesecake
ingredients: 40 oz (5 packs) Cream Cheese, room temperature

body:
## Chef's Note

Savory cheesecake with Parmigiano-Reggiano is a Northern Italian tradition that blurs the line between cheese course and dessert - the aged cheese brings nutty, crystalline depth against the graham cracker crust. The water bath is non-negotiable: it creates gentle, even heat that prevents the edges from overcooking while the center sets. Pull it when the center still jiggles - residual heat finishes the job.

## Directions

1.  **The Crust:** Pulse the cheese, crackers, and seeds in a food processor. Mix with butter and press into a 10-inch springform pan. Bake at 350°F for 15 minutes. Cool.
2.  **The Filling:** Cream the cream cheese and sugar until silky. Add the sour cream, vanilla, and grated Parmigiano.
3.  **Eggs:** Add eggs **one at a time**, mixing on low speed to avoid aerating the batter (bubbles cause cracks!).
4.  **The Seal:** Wrap the bottom of the pan in heavy-duty foil. Place in a large roasting pan.
5.  **The Bath:** Pour the batter into the crust. Pour hot water into the roasting pan until it reaches halfway up the side of the springform pan.
6.  **Bake:** Bake at 325°F for 85-90 minutes until the edges are set but the center still has a slight jiggle.
7.  **The Chill:** Turn off the oven, crack the door, and let it sit for 1 hour. Then refrigerate for at least 6 hours.

data.title: Pasta with Abruzzi-Style Lamb Sauce
ingredients: 3/4 lb Boneless Lamb (Leg or Shoulder), finely diced or ground
1 (28 oz) can Whole Peeled Tomatoes, crushed by hand

body:
## Chef's Note

This ragù comes from Abruzzo, the mountainous region in central Italy where sheep farming has been a way of life for centuries. Abruzzese cuisine is rustic and hearty, designed to sustain shepherds in the mountains. Traditional lamb ragù starts with pancetta to render fat and add smokiness, then builds with white wine (not red) and rosemary, which grows wild in the Apennine mountains. Hand-crushing the tomatoes gives a chunkier, more rustic texture than smooth tomato sauce. Pecorino Romano (sheep's milk cheese) is the traditional finishing cheese in this region - it's sharper and saltier than Parmigiano-Reggiano. Dice the lamb yourself rather than buying pre-ground for better texture.

## Directions

1.  **Render:** Heat olive oil in a large skillet. Add the onion and pancetta. Cook until the pancetta fat has melted and the onions are gold (8 mins).
2.  **Sear:** Add the diced lamb and rosemary. Season with salt and pepper. Brown the meat aggressively until it develops a crust.
3.  **Deglaze:** Pour in the white wine. Scrape the bottom of the pan to release the fond. Simmer until the wine has evaporated by 75%.
4.  **Simmer:** Add the crushed tomatoes and their juices. Reduce heat to low and simmer gently for 30-40 minutes until the sauce is thick and the fat starts to separate.
5.  **Boil:** Cook pasta in salted water until al dente.
6.  **Combine:** Toss the hot pasta directly into the lamb sauce. Add the Pecorino and toss to coat.
7.  **Serve:** Serve with extra cheese and a crack of black pepper.

data.title: Pasta with Sausage, Basil & Mustard
ingredients: 1 1/2 lb raw hot Italian pork sausage, casings removed
Red pepper flakes, a pinch or to taste
Parmesan, for grating at the table
Salt and freshly ground black pepper, to taste
1 cup hot pasta cooking water, reserved before draining; use only as needed
data.source: Adapted from Nigel Slater, Food & Wine
data.description: Hot Italian sausage in a creamy whole-grain mustard sauce with a generous handful of fresh basil.

learning.focus: Brown sausage and control reduction before adding cream and herbs
learning.outcome: Cooked sausage crumbles and tender pasta coated in a creamy, mustard-speckled sauce with fragrant basil.
before: Use raw pork sausage for this version. Remove casings and break the meat into small crumbles. Poultry sausage needs a different temperature endpoint, described below.

Use a broad deep skillet with enough room for the sausage and the listed pasta after cooking; transfer the finish to the pasta pot if crowded. Brown larger batches in rounds with oil divided between them, and reduce sauce by consistency rather than multiplying minutes.
Have the cream and mustard measured before draining pasta. Basil goes in at the end. This is a rich cream-and-sausage dish, so a simple salad can accompany it without another full starch.

checkpoints.cue: Sausage crumbles have browned patches and representative thicker pieces reach 160°F / 71°C.
checkpoints.why: Color and a fixed five-minute sear do not establish that raw ground pork is cooked.

checkpoints.cue: Wine has visibly reduced by roughly half before cream enters.
checkpoints.why: This concentrates the pan flavor without requiring prolonged reduction of the cream sauce.

checkpoints.cue: Sauce coats the pasta and basil is still fragrant rather than dark and cooked down.
checkpoints.why: Basil needs the final toss, while excess simmering thickens sauce and dulls its aroma.

troubleshooting.cause: Cream reduced too long or pasta absorbed moisture while waiting.
troubleshooting.fix: Toss in warm reserved water a little at a time. Stop heating once the coating is right.

troubleshooting.problem: Sausage looks gray with little browning
troubleshooting.cause: It was crowded and released moisture faster than it evaporated.
troubleshooting.fix: Let excess moisture evaporate or brown in rounds next time. Do not scorch the pan while trying to make every crumble crisp.

troubleshooting.cause: Sausage and mustard vary in strength.
troubleshooting.fix: Add mustard gradually and taste before extra salt or Parmesan. More basil does not remove excess salt; adjust the initial seasoning next time.

substitutions.alternative: The same weight of raw Italian-style poultry sausage
substitutions.effect: Cook representative thicker crumbles to 165°F / 74°C. It may release less fat and brown differently; do not reuse the pork endpoint.

substitutions.alternative: The same volume of unsalted stock
substitutions.effect: Removes wine and makes a milder sauce. The wine version is not guaranteed alcohol-free by a short reduction.

substitutions.alternative: Mild Italian sausage and omit extra flakes
substitutions.effect: Keeps the cream, mustard and basil identity with less heat.

learning.timing: Allow about 40 minutes including water heating and ten minutes preparation. Sausage often needs eight to twelve minutes, wine about five, cream two to three and the final toss a minute or two. Pasta cooks in parallel. Extra sausage rounds or a small burner add time.
learning.storage: Refrigerate promptly in shallow containers within 2 hours, or 1 hour above 90°F / 32°C, at 40°F / 4°C or below. Plan to use the next day for texture. Reheat the portion needed with a little water, stirring, to 165°F / 74°C throughout. Pasta absorbs sauce and softens during storage; fresh herbs and cheese lose some of their original texture.

body:
## Chef's Note

Whole-grain mustard and fresh basil give this cream sauce its character. Brown the sausage before reducing the wine, then simmer the cream only long enough to coat the pasta. Fold basil in off heat and taste before adding more salt or cheese.

## Directions

1. **Start water and prepare:** Bring pasta water to a boil. Remove sausage casings, measure sauce ingredients and slice basil. Season water moderately, then time pasta by its package so it finishes near the sauce.
2. **Brown and cook sausage:** Heat olive oil in a broad deep skillet over medium-high. Add sausage and break into small crumbles. Cook about **8–12 minutes**, stirring, until browned in places and representative thicker pieces reach **160°F / 71°C**. Brown in rounds if necessary, sharing the oil between them, then return all cooked meat to the pan.
3. **Reduce wine:** Add wine and scrape up browned bits. Simmer about **5 minutes**, or until the liquid is reduced roughly by half; pan width changes the time.
4. **Make the sauce:** Lower heat, stir in cream, **about two-thirds of the mustard** and the pepper flakes. Simmer gently about **2–3 minutes**, until lightly thickened. Taste and add the remaining mustard if wanted. Meanwhile cook pasta until tender with a little bite and reserve **the listed water amount** before draining.
5. **Toss and serve:** Add pasta to the sauce and fold over low heat just until coated, adding warm pasta water in small amounts if too thick. Remove from heat and fold in basil. Taste before adding salt or pepper. Divide into the intended portions and offer Parmesan for grating at the table.

Adapted from [Nigel Slater’s recipe at Food & Wine](https://www.foodandwine.com/pasta-with-sausage-basil-and-mustard-6415687).

export.name: Pasta with Sausage, Basil & Mustard
export.ingredients:
1 lb dry penne or rigatoni
1 1/2 lb raw hot Italian pork sausage, casings removed
3/4 cup dry white wine
3/4 cup heavy cream
3 tbsp whole-grain Dijon mustard
1 cup fresh basil, thinly sliced
1 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil
Red pepper flakes, a pinch or to taste
Parmesan, for grating at the table
Salt and freshly ground black pepper, to taste
1 cup hot pasta cooking water, reserved before draining; use only as needed
export.directions:
1. Start water and prepare: Bring pasta water to a boil. Remove sausage casings, measure sauce ingredients and slice basil. Season water moderately, then time pasta by its package so it finishes near the sauce.
2. Brown and cook sausage: Heat olive oil in a broad deep skillet over medium-high. Add sausage and break into small crumbles. Cook about 8–12 minutes, stirring, until browned in places and representative thicker pieces reach 160°F / 71°C. Brown in rounds if necessary, sharing the oil between them, then return all cooked meat to the pan.
3. Reduce wine: Add wine and scrape up browned bits. Simmer about 5 minutes, or until the liquid is reduced roughly by half; pan width changes the time.
4. Make the sauce: Lower heat, stir in cream, about two-thirds of the mustard and the pepper flakes. Simmer gently about 2–3 minutes, until lightly thickened. data.title: Patatas Bravas
ingredients: 2 lbs Yukon Gold Potatoes, peeled and cut into 1.5-inch irregular chunks
2 tsp Smoked Paprika (pimenton de la Vera, hot or sweet)
1/2 tsp Cayenne Pepper, or to taste
1/3 cup Mayonnaise (use vegan mayonnaise for the vegan option; for alioli)

body:
## Chef's Note

The double-cook method is what separates bar-standard patatas bravas from unforgettable ones. Parboiling the potatoes first roughens the edges and gelatinizes the starch, creating a shatteringly crisp exterior when they hit the hot oil. Make the bravas sauce in advance -- it benefits from resting as the smokiness from the pimenton rounds out. Cut the potatoes into irregular chunks, not uniform cubes; the jagged edges crisp up better.

## Directions

1.  **Make the Bravas Sauce:** Heat 2 tbsp olive oil in a medium saucepan over medium heat. Add the diced onion and cook for 5-6 minutes until softened. Add the garlic and cook 30 seconds. Stir in the smoked paprika, sweet paprika, and cayenne. Cook for 30 seconds until fragrant. Add the crushed tomatoes, sugar, and salt. Simmer for 15-20 minutes until thickened. Stir in the sherry vinegar. For a smooth sauce, blend with an immersion blender or pass through a sieve. Set aside.

2.  **Make the Alioli:** Whisk together the mayonnaise, grated garlic, and lemon juice. Season with a pinch of salt. Refrigerate until serving.

3.  **Parboil the Potatoes:** Place the potato chunks in a large pot of generously salted cold water. Bring to a boil and cook for 8-10 minutes until the edges are tender but the centers still have some resistance. Drain well and spread on a sheet pan to steam dry for 10 minutes. This step is crucial for crispiness.

4.  **Fry the Potatoes:** Heat 4 cups of oil in a large heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven to 375F. Working in batches to avoid crowding, fry the potatoes for 5-7 minutes, turning occasionally, until deeply golden and crispy. Transfer to a wire rack set over a sheet pan. Season immediately with flaky sea salt.

5.  **Serve:** Pile the hot potatoes on a warm serving platter. Drizzle generously with the bravas sauce and dot with the alioli. Serve immediately with toothpicks or small forks -- this is tapas, after all.

data.title: Patate al Forno
ingredients: 2 lbs Yukon Gold Potatoes, cut into 1-inch chunks

body:
## Chef's Note

Patate al forno are classic Italian oven-roasted potatoes - a Sunday staple in Roman homes. The secret to crispy edges is drying the potatoes thoroughly after cutting; any moisture will cause them to steam instead of crisp. Roasting at 450°F gets you golden, crunchy exteriors while keeping the insides creamy. Fresh rosemary is traditional and adds a wonderful aromatic note.

## Directions

1.  **Prep:** Preheat oven to 450°F (mandatory for snap). Line a large rimmed baking sheet with parchment paper.
2.  **Dry:** Cube the potatoes. Place them in a bowl and pat **bone-dry** with multiple paper towels.
3.  **Toss:** Add the olive oil, salt, garlic powder, and rosemary. Toss vigorously until every chunk is heavily coated.
4.  **Spread:** Spread the potatoes in a **single layer** on the pan. If they are crowded, they will steam instead of crisp.
5.  **Roast:** Bake for 35-40 minutes. Flip with a metal spatula halfway through. They are done when they are deep mahogany gold and "pop" when bitten.
6.  **Serve:** Sprinkle with a final pinch of sea salt and serve immediately.

data.title: Peach Pie Biscuit Bombs
ingredients: 1 cup Fresh Peaches, sliced into 1-inch pieces

body:
## Chef's Note

These are a shortcut's triumph - using refrigerated biscuits legitimately, not apologetically. The filling is a lesson in flavor layering: warm peaches, creamy melted brie (unexpected richness), brown butter (nutty depth), and brown sugar with cinnamon (familiar sweetness). Brush with brown butter twice - once before baking and again after - for a flaky exterior and luxurious finish.
## Directions

1.  **Prep:** Preheat oven to 375°F. Line a baking sheet with parchment.
2.  **Split:** Pull each raw biscuit in half horizontally.
3.  **Layer:** Place 3 peach slices and 1 tsp of Brie in the center of the bottom half. Sprinkle with brown sugar and cinnamon. Drizzle with a drop of honey.
4.  **Seal:** Place the top half back on. Pinch the edges firmly and roll gently in your palms to form a uniform "ball." Arrange 2 inches apart on the pan.
5.  **The Sizzle:** In a small pan, melt 3 tbsp butter until it crackles and turns nutty brown. Brush each "bomb" generously with the brown butter.
6.  **Bake:** Bake for 12-15 minutes until the tops are deep golden brown and the biscuit has a flaky "Bounce."
7.  **Serve:** Brush once more with the remaining brown butter. Serve warm while the Brie is molten.

data.title: Peach Pie Pancakes
ingredients: 1/2 cup Plain Greek Yogurt for richness

body:
## Chef's Note

The secret to peach pie pancakes that aren't heavy is using Greek yogurt as the primary binder, creating a dense, custardy texture that mimics pie filling without excessive oil. Making small, 2-tablespoon "silver dollar" pancakes ensures the diced peaches are distributed evenly and the pancake cooks through before the fruit releases too much moisture. The cinnamon provides essential aromatic warmth.

## Directions

1.  **Dry Mix:** In a medium bowl, whisk together flour, baking powder, cinnamon, and salt.
2.  **The Emulsion:** In a separate bowl, whisk yogurt, milk, vanilla, and melted butter until perfectly smooth.
3.  **Combine:** Gradually add the dry mix to the wet in 4 parts. Stir with a spatula until **just incorporated**. Small lumps are mandatory for a light texture.
4.  **Fold:** Gently fold in the diced peaches.
5.  **Prep:** Heat a non-stick skillet over **low-medium** heat (crucial for whole wheat). Lightly grease with oil spray.
6.  **Pour:** Drop 2-tbsp portions onto the skillet. Cook for 2-3 minutes until bubbles form and the edges look set.
7.  **Flip:** Flip gently and cook for 1-2 more minutes until golden brown.
8.  **Serve:** Serve with warm maple syrup and a few extra fresh peach slices.

data.description: Tender golden beets, ripe tomatoes and peaches with a lemon-honey shallot dressing, goat cheese, mint and thyme.

learning.focus: Cook and cool beets before combining with delicate summer fruit
learning.outcome: Beet slices tender through the center, distinct peach and tomato slices, and fresh herbs over a light dressing.
before: Start with raw beets for the full method. Their cooking and cooling are part of the total time; do not layer hot beets with peaches, herbs and cheese.

Use a small roasting dish deep enough to contain water and be covered tightly. Keep beets in a single layer when scaling, use additional dishes if needed and keep the same water depth. Larger roots take longer regardless of serving count.
Wash tomatoes, peaches and herbs, and dry them before cutting. Choose peaches that are ripe but firm enough to hold slices. Peeling peaches is optional if their skins are tender.

checkpoints.cue: A thin knife slides easily into the center of each beet.
checkpoints.why: Covered beets in water need tenderness, not a golden-brown surface, as their endpoint.

checkpoints.cue: Peeled beet slices are no longer warm before assembly.
checkpoints.why: Warm beets soften fresh fruit and wilt herbs; cooling is an actual recipe stage.

checkpoints.cue: The dressing coats slices without hiding the separate fruit and beet textures.
checkpoints.why: Gentle layering protects ripe tomatoes and peaches from being crushed.

troubleshooting.problem: Beets are still firm after an hour
troubleshooting.cause: They were larger or the oven and covered dish heated more slowly.
troubleshooting.fix: Check that water remains in the dish, cover again and continue in short intervals until a knife enters the center easily. Do not rely on color.

troubleshooting.cause: Very ripe tomatoes and peaches released water or the salad waited after dressing.
troubleshooting.fix: Serve promptly and spoon only enough juices over each portion to coat. Slice fruit closer to service next time.

substitutions.alternative: Plain fully cooked, peeled beets of comparable size, chilled and drained
substitutions.effect: Skip baking and cooling and allow about 25 minutes for assembly. Pickled beets change acidity, and red beets will stain other ingredients.

substitutions.alternative: The same weight of crumbled feta
substitutions.effect: Firmer and usually saltier; taste before adding extra salt to the platter.

learning.timing: Plan about 2 hours from raw beets, including oven heating, roughly 50–75 minutes covered baking, cooling and slicing. Prepare dressing and fruit during the cooling stage. Very large beets take longer. With already cooked, chilled beets, assembly takes about 25 minutes.
learning.storage: Refrigerate cooked beets promptly in shallow containers if preparing ahead, within 2 hours or 1 hour above 90°F / 32°C, and keep at 40°F / 4°C or below. Use within 3–4 days. Keep fresh fruit, herbs, cheese and dressing separate until assembly. Refrigerate assembled leftovers promptly and use by the next day for quality; peaches and tomatoes release juice.

body:
## Chef's Note

Bake the beets until a knife reaches the center easily, then cool them before layering with the peaches and tomatoes. The covered cooking keeps the beets moist; browning is not the goal. Mint, thyme and goat cheese go on at the end. Adapted from [MyRecipes’ Peach Salad with Tomatoes and Beets](https://www.myrecipes.com/recipe/peach-salad-tomatoes-beets).

## Directions

1. **Bake beets:** Heat the oven to 425°F / 220°C. Put scrubbed beets in a small roasting dish with about 1 inch of water. Cover tightly and bake until a thin knife slides easily to the center, checking after about 50 minutes and continuing as needed, often 60–75 minutes. Keep some water in the dish; carefully add hot water if it is drying out.

2. **Cool and slice:** Remove the cover carefully, keeping away from the escaping steam, and lift beets from the water. Cool until comfortable to handle, rub off skins, trim roots and cut into 1/4-inch slices. Spread slices on a plate and let them cool fully before assembling; allow roughly 20–30 minutes total cooling, longer if needed.

3. **Prepare dressing and fruit:** While beets cool, whisk oil, half the measured lemon juice, honey and shallot together. Season to taste. Slice tomatoes into 1/4-inch rounds. Pit and slice peaches and toss gently with the remaining half of the lemon juice.

4. **Assemble:** Layer cool beet and tomato slices on a wide platter and season lightly with salt and pepper. Arrange peach slices over them and spoon over the shallot dressing without stirring the fragile layers.

5. **Finish:** Scatter with goat cheese, mint and thyme. Serve promptly so the herbs remain fresh and the fruit holds its shape.

data.title: Peanut Noodles
ingredients: 1 lb Noodles (spaghetti, angel hair, or wheat noodles)
1/4 tsp Red Pepper Flakes (adjust to taste)
1/4 to 1/2 cup Warm Water (to achieve sauce consistency)

body:
## Chef's Note

Peanut noodles are Chinese-American comfort food born from the post-WWII boom when peanut butter became accessible in Chinese restaurants. What started as a Chinatown fusion dish is now everywhere - and for good reason. It's simultaneously cold (for summer), warm (for any season), endlessly customizable, and tastes just as good the next day. The sauce comes together in one bowl and clings to whatever noodles you use. Balance is key: the peanut butter needs enough acid (vinegar) and salt (soy) to not taste heavy.

## Directions

1. **Make the Sauce:** In a small bowl, whisk together peanut butter, soy sauce, rice vinegar, sesame oil, honey, minced garlic, ginger, and red pepper flakes. The mixture will be thick. Whisk in warm water a little at a time until you reach the consistency you want - think thickened pasta sauce that clings to noodles, not a soup. Taste and adjust for salt, heat, and acid.

2. **Cook the Noodles:** Bring a large pot of salted water to a boil. Add noodles and cook according to package directions until al dente. Drain well - don't rinse (the starch helps the sauce cling). If making this ahead, toss drained noodles with 1 tsp sesame oil to prevent sticking.

3. **Combine:** In a large bowl, add warm or room-temperature noodles. Pour peanut sauce over the noodles and toss until every strand is coated. If the sauce seems too thick, add a few splashes of warm water.

4. **Finish:** Sprinkle with sliced green onions, fresh cilantro, sesame seeds, and roasted peanuts if using. Serve with lime wedges on the side.

5. **To Serve Cold:** Let the dressed noodles cool to room temperature (or chill for up to 4 hours). The sauce will continue to coat as it cools. If it tightens, add a splash of warm water before serving.

**Warm or Cold:** Eat immediately while warm, or chill and serve cold the next day. Both are completely valid.

**Customization:** Top with shredded carrots, cucumber, steamed edamame, or blanched broccoli. This is a base - build on it.

ingredients: 5 cups baby spinach, washed if needed and dried
1 large ripe but firm Bosc pear, cored and thinly sliced

data.source: Adapted from Chowhound, Pear and Spinach Salad
data.description: Baby spinach and crisp pear with softened raw onion and a sharp honey-Dijon dressing.

learning.focus: Balance a strong dressing against delicate leaves and sweet fruit
learning.outcome: Dry spinach lightly coated with mustard dressing, crisp pear slices and onion with a milder bite.
before: Wash spinach unless labeled ready to eat and dry thoroughly. Measure the listed leaves rather than assuming every bag contains the same amount.
Use a ripe pear that still feels firm enough to slice. Core it and cut near serving time to limit browning. Prepare the dressing and greens while onion soaks.
The dressing quantity is larger than the initial coating allowance. Reserve what the leaves do not need rather than soaking the salad; use a roomy bowl or separate batches when scaling.

checkpoints.cue: Drained onion is dry before joining the leaves.
checkpoints.why: Soaking water carried into the bowl dilutes dressing and encourages pooling.

checkpoints.cue: Spinach is lightly glossy, with little dressing on the bowl bottom.
checkpoints.why: This mustard-forward dressing is strong; more dressing is not automatically better.

checkpoints.cue: Pear slices hold their shape and leaves remain springy at serving.
checkpoints.why: Gentle tossing and immediate service protect delicate spinach.

troubleshooting.cause: The full strong dressing was poured onto the leaves or the pear was underripe.
troubleshooting.fix: Start with less dressing and taste a bite with pear. Reserve unused dressing; adding more to the bowl cannot correct excessive sharpness.

troubleshooting.cause: It was dressed too early or was wet.
troubleshooting.fix: Lift from pooled dressing and serve promptly. Keep leaves dry and dressing separate until the last moment next time.

substitutions.alternative: A similarly sized firm-ripe Anjou pear
substitutions.effect: Texture and sweetness differ; slice thinly and taste with the dressing before adding more.

substitutions.alternative: Omit it
substitutions.effect: Removes the pungent bite and the soaking step; do not replace the omitted volume with extra dressing.

learning.timing: About 20 minutes with a ten-minute onion soak overlapped with washing/drying greens and whisking dressing, then slicing pear and tossing. Starting with wet unwashed spinach can add drying time.
learning.storage: Keep greens, onion and dressing separately refrigerated at 40°F / 4°C or below until assembling; slice pear near serving. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours, or 1 hour above 90°F / 32°C. Use dressed salad by the next day for quality; pear may brown and leaves wilt. Reserve unused dressing in the refrigerator and use within three days as a quality limit, stirring again before use.

## Chef's Note

A strong honey-Dijon dressing needs only a light hand on baby spinach. Soak the onion while preparing everything else, dry it well and slice the pear just before tossing. Taste a bite with fruit before adding more dressing. Adapted from [Chowhound’s Pear and Spinach Salad](https://www.chowhound.com/recipes/pear-and-spinach-salad-27663).

## Directions

1. **Soak onion:** Put thinly sliced onion in ice water for 10 minutes. Meanwhile wash and dry spinach if needed and prepare the dressing. Drain onion and pat thoroughly dry.

2. **Whisk dressing:** Combine Dijon, vinegar, the measured dressing water, olive oil and honey. Whisk until smooth. Add salt and pepper to taste; the mustard already contains salt.

3. **Assemble:** Core and thinly slice pear. Put spinach, pear and dry onion in a wide bowl. Start with about one-third of the mixed dressing and lift gently to coat. Taste a leaf with pear, then add more dressing only as needed; reserve any excess.

4. **Serve:** Adjust black pepper if desired and divide among side plates. Serve immediately while spinach retains its texture.

data.title: Peking Duck
ingredients: 3 tbsp Sweet Bean Sauce (Tian Mian Jiang)

body:
## Chef's Note

Peking duck from Beijing is famous for its crackling-crisp skin. The secret: pour boiling water over the raw duck to tighten the skin, brush with maltose syrup, then air-dry uncovered in the fridge for 24-48 hours. This separates the skin from the fat layer so it bakes into a glass-like, shatteringly crisp texture. Roast on a wire rack for even air circulation. Serve the skin and meat separately with thin pancakes, scallions, cucumber, and sweet bean sauce.

## Directions

1.  **Prep:** Pat duck **bone-dry**. Rub 2 tbsp salt over the skin and cavity. Let rest for 1 hour.
2.  **The Blanch:** Pour 6 cups of boiling water slowly over the entire duck skin (both sides). You will see the skin tighten instantly.
3.  **The Lacquer:** Whisk maltose, boiling water, and vinegar. Brush a heavy layer over the duck. Let dry for 1 hour, then brush a second layer.
4.  **The Dehydrate:** Place duck on a wire rack over a tray. **Refrigerate uncovered for 24-48 hours** until the skin feels like parchment paper.
5.  **Thermal Prep:** Bring duck to room temp. Stuff the cavity with aromatics and apples. Seal the opening with skewers.
6.  **Bake:** Preheat convection oven to 390°F (or 425°F conventional). Roast for 15 minutes.

data.title: Whole-Berry Cranberry Sauce
ingredients: 340 g fresh or frozen cranberries, divided
1 strip orange peel, about 2 by 1 inches, without white pith
data.description: A spoonable cranberry sauce with some tender berry pieces, a light orange fragrance and an optional fuller orange variation.

learning.focus: Cook fruit to a tender texture and judge sauce consistency after cooling
learning.outcome: A tart-sweet spoonable sauce with tender berries and no hard raw fruit, stiff candy-like syrup or watery ring.
before: This makes roughly two cups, about twelve 2–3-tablespoon condiment portions. It is not twelve bowls of dessert. Make it the day before a holiday meal so chilling does not compete with the roast schedule.
Frozen berries can go in without thawing and may take a few extra minutes to return to a simmer. Sort fresh berries and discard damaged fruit.
This is refrigerator sauce, not a canning or shelf-storage formula. Its sugar amount is a flavor and texture choice, not a preservation claim.

checkpoints.cue: Most of the first berries have split and the liquid lightly coats a spoon, but it still flows freely when hot.
checkpoints.why: Cranberry solids and natural pectin contribute body as the sauce cooks and cools. Cooking hot sauce until it looks like cold jam can overconcentrate it.

checkpoints.cue: The later berries are tender when pressed with a spoon, even if some retain their shape.
checkpoints.why: Adding raw berries after turning off the heat leaves hard, sharply tart fruit. A short final simmer preserves more texture while cooking it through.

checkpoints.cue: A cooled spoonful tastes tart-sweet and the chilled sauce is spoonable rather than runny.
checkpoints.why: Temperature changes perceived consistency; a cooled sample is more useful than judging boiling syrup alone.

troubleshooting.problem: Sauce is too stiff after chilling
troubleshooting.cause: Too much water evaporated during cooking.
troubleshooting.fix: Stir in water a teaspoon at a time until spoonable. If needed, warm gently first, then chill again promptly.

troubleshooting.problem: Sauce is thinner than desired after chilling
troubleshooting.cause: It retained more water or the berries broke down less than expected.
troubleshooting.fix: Return to a gentle simmer for a few minutes, stirring, then cool a small sample to reassess. This recipe aims for a spoonable sauce, not a firm molded gel.

troubleshooting.cause: The peel carried thick white pith or remained in the sauce too long.
troubleshooting.fix: Remove it. Bitterness already extracted cannot be strained away; use a thinner pith-free strip next time.

substitutions.ingredient: 180 ml water and one strip orange peel
substitutions.alternative: 120 ml water plus 60 ml fresh orange juice and 1 tsp finely grated orange zest
substitutions.effect: Gives a stronger cranberry-orange sauce. Use the juice with the water and stir the zest in after cooking; omit the peel strip. This replaces the former separate orange-sauce recipe.

substitutions.alternative: 100 g sugar
substitutions.effect: A noticeably tarter and potentially looser sauce. Keep refrigerated under the same short storage guidance; this is not an equivalent gel or a canning variation.

learning.timing: Allow about three hours including preparation, roughly twenty minutes on the stove and about two and a half hours cooling and chilling in a shallow container. Serve chilled when set to a spoonable consistency; a deeper vessel or warm refrigerator load can take longer. Making it a day ahead is simpler than fitting the chill into final meal preparation.
learning.storage: Transfer to a shallow heatproof container and refrigerate promptly, within two hours or one hour above 90°F / 32°C; do not wait for a deep hot pan to become completely cold on the counter. Keep at 40°F / 4°C or below and use within three to four days, or freeze in small portions. Use clean utensils. Store this sauce in the refrigerator or freezer, not in the pantry.

body:
## Chef's Note

Whole-berry cranberry sauce brings tart fruit to a rich holiday plate. This version cooks part of the fruit first, then adds the rest briefly so some tender pieces remain. Orange peel adds aroma rather than replacing the cranberries' acidity. Expect a spoonable sauce after chilling, not the firm shape of canned cranberry jelly.

## Directions

1. **Sort and divide:** Rinse and drain fresh cranberries, discarding spoiled berries. Set aside 85 g of the total for the later addition; the other 255 g go in first. Keep frozen berries frozen until each addition. Prepare a thin orange-peel strip with no thick white pith.
2. **Dissolve the sugar:** In a 2-quart saucepan, combine water, sugar, orange peel and salt. Heat over medium heat, stirring until the sugar dissolves and the liquid begins to simmer.
3. **Cook the first berries:** Add the 255 g cranberries, return to a gentle boil and reduce heat to a steady simmer. Cook about eight to ten minutes, stirring occasionally, until most berries have split. Keep clear of hot splashes; do not crush every berry smooth.
4. **Tenderize the remaining berries:** Add the reserved 85 g and simmer another three to five minutes, or until those berries are tender when pressed with a spoon. Some may retain their shape. The hot sauce should still flow; it will thicken as it cools. Remove the orange-peel strip.
5. **Cool and chill:** Put a small spoonful on a cool plate to assess flavor and body once cool enough to taste. Transfer the main batch to a shallow heatproof container and refrigerate promptly, loosely covered while cooling and covered fully once cold. Allow about two and a half hours to chill, or refrigerate overnight. Stir gently before serving two to three tablespoons per person.

## Cranberry-orange variation

Replace the 180 ml water with **120 ml water and 60 ml orange juice**. Omit the peel strip, then stir **one teaspoon finely grated orange zest** into the finished sauce after taking it off heat. Keep the same fruit and sugar quantities. This retains the citrus-forward option in one recipe; two tablespoons of zest are unnecessary for this batch.

## A tarter variation

Use **100 g sugar** instead of 150 g if the meal needs a sharper condiment. Expect a different sweetness and possibly looser body, and judge a chilled spoonful. Do not assume removing sugar leaves identical texture or turns this into a shelf-stable preserve.

data.title: Cream Cheese Mashed Potatoes
ingredients: 1360 g peeled Yukon Gold potatoes, cut into even 1-inch pieces
3 L cold water, or enough to cover potatoes by about 1 inch
12 g salt, for the cooking water
75 g unsalted butter, cut into small pieces
115 g cream cheese, cut into small pieces
3/4 cup (180 ml) half-and-half, plus up to 1/4 cup (60 ml) more if needed
1/2 tsp fine salt, for finishing, divided
data.description: Yukon Gold potatoes mashed gently with warm butter, half-and-half and cream cheese, with enough liquid for a soft mound rather than a sticky paste.

learning.focus: Fully tenderize potatoes, then limit the work needed to mash them
learning.outcome: A warm, creamy mash that falls softly from a spoon, without hard lumps, free liquid or an elastic, gluey texture.
before: Potato weight is peeled and trimmed; buy roughly 1.6 kg to allow for peel and trimming. Expect about six cups, or eight roughly three-quarter-cup side portions.

A ricer gives a finer texture; a hand masher leaves some small pieces. Neither requires beating to a fixed sixty-second rule. Avoid a blender or food processor, which can make the mash sticky very quickly.

checkpoints.cue: A knife passes through several potato pieces without resistance and a tasted center is fully soft.
checkpoints.why: Firm pieces become lumps; extra mixing cannot substitute for enough cooking.

checkpoints.cue: Drained potato surfaces look matte after a short return to the warm pot, without a brown crust.
checkpoints.why: Removing clinging cooking water avoids a diluted mash. Potatoes still need moisture; the goal is not to dry out every part of them.

checkpoints.cue: Dairy folds in with little stirring, and the mash holds a soft mound rather than stretching like glue.
checkpoints.why: Excess mechanical work disrupts more cooked potato tissue and releases starch, increasing stickiness. Warm additions keep the mixture hot and easy to combine.

troubleshooting.cause: Some chunks were larger or insufficiently cooked.
troubleshooting.fix: Check tenderness before draining. If already mixed, do not keep beating; further gentle covered heating may soften small pieces, but a perfectly smooth result is no longer assured.

troubleshooting.problem: Mash is stiff but not gluey
troubleshooting.cause: The potatoes absorbed less liquid or the mash cooled during preparation.
troubleshooting.fix: Fold in a little of the listed additional warm half-and-half, one tablespoon at a time, and keep warm gently.

troubleshooting.cause: Too much mixing or blending released excessive starch.
troubleshooting.fix: Stop working it. More milk or beating will not restore the original texture; serve as it is or use in another cooked dish rather than claiming a cure.

substitutions.alternative: The same volume of whole milk
substitutions.effect: A less rich finish; add gradually because the needed amount depends on the potatoes.

substitutions.alternative: 1360 g peeled russet potatoes
substitutions.effect: A fluffier, more floury mash that may need more of the listed liquid. Check tenderness rather than using an identical timer.

learning.timing: About fifty-five minutes includes peeling and cutting, heating the large pot, approximately eighteen to twenty-two minutes simmering and draining, drying and mashing. Warm dairy during the potato cooking time. Larger batches take longer to heat and need an appropriately sized pot.
learning.storage: Refrigerate in shallow containers within two hours, or one hour above 90°F / 32°C, at 40°F / 4°C or below. Use within three to four days and reheat to 165°F / 74°C throughout, adding a little milk as needed. For short service holding, keep covered above 140°F / 60°C over a gentle water bath and check with a thermometer; do not assume an unmeasured slow-cooker warm setting is adequate.

body:
## Chef's Note

Cream cheese gives these American-style mashed potatoes a rich, mildly tangy finish. Yukon Golds suit a creamy mash; use a ricer for a fine texture or accept small pieces from a hand masher. Cook the potatoes completely before mashing, then fold in the warm dairy only as much as needed. There is no universally correct number of seconds on an electric mixer.

## Directions

1. **Cut and cover:** Peel and trim enough potatoes to weigh 1360 g, then cut into even one-inch pieces. Briefly rinse, put in a large pot and add about three liters cold water to cover by an inch. Add the twelve grams of cooking-water salt.
2. **Simmer until fully tender:** Bring to a boil, reduce to a steady simmer and cook about eighteen to twenty-two minutes. Test several pieces with a knife and taste a cooled piece; the centers should be fully soft, not just puncturable. While they cook, warm butter, cream cheese and the initial 180 ml half-and-half together over low heat, stirring until the butter melts and the cream cheese softens. Do not boil the dairy.
3. **Drain and dry briefly:** Drain thoroughly. Return the potatoes to the pot over low heat for one to two minutes, shaking or turning gently until the surfaces lose their wet sheen. Remove from heat before they brown or stick.
4. **Mash gently:** Pass hot potatoes through a ricer or use a hand masher until the large pieces are gone. Fold in the warm dairy mixture in two additions with a spatula. Stop when combined. If too stiff, warm and add the optional extra half-and-half a tablespoon at a time until it holds a soft mound.
5. **Taste and serve:** Fold in pepper and half the finishing salt, then taste; add the rest only if needed. The cooking-water salt was largely drained away, while cream cheese contributes its own seasoning. Serve about three-quarters of a cup per person alongside the main.

## A short hold

For up to about thirty minutes, keep the hot mash covered in a heatproof bowl over gently simmering water, with the bowl above the water. Check that the mash stays above 140°F / 60°C. Fold once if needed and adjust with a spoonful of warm milk; avoid repeated stirring or direct burner heat that scorches the base. Longer storage needs cooling and reheating as described above.

export.name: Cream Cheese Mashed Potatoes
export.ingredients:
1360 g peeled Yukon Gold potatoes, cut into even 1-inch pieces
3 L cold water, or enough to cover potatoes by about 1 inch
12 g salt, for the cooking water
75 g unsalted butter, cut into small pieces
115 g cream cheese, cut into small pieces
3/4 cup (180 ml) half-and-half, plus up to 1/4 cup (60 ml) more if needed
1/2 tsp fine salt, for finishing, divided
1/2 tsp coarsely ground black pepper
export.directions:
1. Cut and cover: Peel and trim enough potatoes to weigh 1360 g, then cut into even one-inch pieces. Briefly rinse, put in a large pot and add about three liters cold water to cover by an inch. Add the twelve grams of cooking-water salt.
2. Simmer until fully tender: Bring to a boil, reduce to a steady simmer and cook about eighteen to twenty-two minutes. Test several pieces with a knife and taste a cooled piece; the centers should be fully soft, not just puncturable. While they cook, warm butter, cream cheese and the initial 180 ml half-and-half together over low heat, stirring until the butter melts and the cream cheese softens. Do not boil the dairy.
3. Drain and dry briefly: Drain thoroughly. Return the potatoes to the pot over low heat for one to two minutes, shaking or turning gently until the surfaces lose their wet sheen. Remove from heat before they brown or stick.
4. Mash gently: Pass hot potatoes through a ricer or use a hand masher until the large pieces are gone. Fold in the warm dairy mixture in two additions with a spatula. Stop when combined. If too stiff, warm and add the optional extra half-and-half a tablespoon at a time until it holds a soft mound.

export.notes:
Chef's Note

Cream cheese gives these American-style mashed potatoes a rich, mildly tangy finish. Yukon Golds suit a creamy mash; use a ricer for a fine texture or accept small pieces from a hand masher. Cook the potatoes completely before mashing, then fold in the warm dairy only as much as needed. There is no universally correct number of seconds on an electric mixer.

A short hold

For up to about thirty minutes, keep the hot mash covered in a heatproof bowl over gently simmering water, with the bowl above the water. Check that the mash stays above 140°F / 60°C. Fold once if needed and adjust with a spoonful of warm milk; avoid repeated stirring or direct burner heat that scorches the base. Longer storage needs cooling and reheating as described above.

data.title: Peruvian-Style Beef Empanadas
data.description: Mild beef-and-onion empanadas with cumin, sweet paprika and a little tomato paste, baked in store-bought discs and served with lime.
data.source: Adapted from a family recipe discussion

ingredients.name: 5-inch empanada disc labeled for baking
ingredients.preparation: one 12-count package at the original yield; thawed as directed on the package

steps.title: Brown the beef

Break it into small crumbles and cook another 4–6 minutes, stirring, until cooked through to 160°F / 71°C. Spoon off pooled fat, leaving a thin film in the pan. Transfer the cooked beef to a clean bowl.

steps.title: Soften the vegetables
steps.text: Lower the heat to medium and add {{ingredients}} to the same skillet. Cook for 6–8 minutes, stirring, until fully softened and the onion is translucent with lightly golden edges. Lower the heat if the browned bits start to blacken.

steps.title: Bloom the spices
steps.text: Lower the heat to medium-low. Stir in {{ingredients}} for about 30 seconds, just until fragrant; do not let the garlic or paprika scorch.

steps.title: Cook the tomato paste
steps.text: Stir in {{ingredients}} for about 1 minute, until it darkens slightly and coats the vegetables.

steps.title: Finish the filling
steps.text: Return the beef and add {{ingredients}}, using the lower end of the broth range first. Scrape up the browned bits and stir over medium heat for 1–2 minutes. Add the remaining broth only if the filling seems dry. Stop when moist crumbles cling together lightly and a spatula drawn across the pan leaves no puddle.

steps.title: Taste and cool
steps.text: Taste the fully cooked filling and add {{ingredients}} only if needed. learning.focus: Manage moisture before enclosing a filling in pastry
learning.outcome: Golden pastry with a sealed edge and a savory, moist beef filling that does not leak liquid into the base.
before: Use one package of 12 approximately 5-inch discs specifically labeled for baking. Frying-only discs are not a reliable substitute. Package thawing and baking instructions take precedence.
Measure the onion after finely chopping it; half a cup avoids relying on an inconsistent onion size. Use sweet, not hot, paprika.
Keep the filling cool and the pastry pliable but cool. Have room in the refrigerator for a shallow cooling dish and, if necessary, the assembled tray.

checkpoints.cue: Beef has browned patches and reaches 160°F / 71°C before cooling.
checkpoints.why: Contact with the hot pan develops flavor; brown color alone does not establish that ground beef has reached a safe temperature.

checkpoints.cue: The filling is moist, with no free liquid collecting behind the spatula.
checkpoints.why: Excess liquid soaks the pastry and can escape through the seam; cooking it bone-dry sacrifices juiciness.

checkpoints.cue: The disc folds over the filling without stretching, leaving a clean sealing border.
checkpoints.why: The stated portion is a starting point. Disc thickness and flexibility determine the actual capacity.

checkpoints.cue: The underside is golden and the center reaches 165°F / 74°C.
checkpoints.why: Top color alone can hide an underbaked bottom or a center that has not reheated fully.

troubleshooting.problem: The seam opens or filling leaks
troubleshooting.cause: Too much filling, wet or greasy edges, or pastry that became too warm.
troubleshooting.fix: Before baking, remove a little filling, clean and reseal the border, then chill if soft. A split baked empanada cannot be resealed; serve it open once fully cooked.

troubleshooting.problem: The filling is greasy or watery
troubleshooting.cause: Pooled beef fat or broth was left in the pan.
troubleshooting.fix: Spoon off free fat and cook briefly uncovered until no liquid pools, then cool again before filling. Do not add broth automatically if the mixture is already moist.

troubleshooting.problem: The pastry is pale or tough
troubleshooting.cause: The discs are intended only for frying, the oven is not fully heated, or the package requires a different bake.
troubleshooting.fix: Check the package and use its baking directions. An egg wash improves color but cannot make frying-only dough behave like baking pastry.

substitutions.alternative: Red bell pepper in the same measured amount
substitutions.effect: Keeps the filling mild; the red pepper may taste a little sweeter. Dice finely and soften completely.

substitutions.alternative: Water in the same small amount
substitutions.effect: Loosens the browned bits without extra salt; the filling will be slightly less beefy.

substitutions.alternative: Omit the egg and wash water
substitutions.effect: The crust will be more matte and possibly paler. Check the disc ingredients separately if avoiding eggs.

learning.timing: Allow about 1 hour 50 minutes from thawed discs: 10 minutes chopping, about 20 minutes cooking the filling, 20–30 minutes chilling, 15 minutes filling and sealing, 20–25 minutes baking, and 10 minutes resting. About 40–45 minutes is hands-on. Preheat during cooling. Package-directed thawing, extra chilling for soft pastry, and additional baking batches add time. Making the filling a day ahead leaves about 45–50 minutes for assembly, baking, and resting.
learning.storage: Refrigerate cooked filling promptly in a shallow container; cover once chilled. Keep filling or baked empanadas at 40°F / 4°C or below and use within 3–4 days of cooking the filling. Do not restart that clock after baking. Refrigerate within 2 hours, or 1 hour above 90°F / 32°C. For a crisp reheated crust, use a 350°F / 175°C oven until the center reaches 165°F / 74°C; cover loosely if browning too quickly. Cool and freeze baked empanadas for up to 3 months for quality, then thaw in the refrigerator before reheating.
