ingredients: 2 tbsp yellow bell pepper, finely diced
additional fine salt, to taste, only if needed
12 5-inch empanada discs labeled for baking, one 12-count package at the original yield; thawed as directed on the package
1 tsp water for egg wash, optional

body:
## Chef's Note

Empanadas take many forms across Latin America, including Peru's baked savory pastries. This mild family adaptation uses beef, onion and warming spices, without hard-boiled eggs, olives or raisins. Cool the filling before folding so the pastry stays easy to handle and bakes with a crisp base.

## Directions

1. **Prepare:** Thaw the discs according to their package before starting; keep covered and refrigerated until needed. Finely chop the vegetables so they fit comfortably inside the pastry. Set out a shallow heatproof dish for cooling the filling and line a large rimmed baking sheet with parchment.
2. **Brown the beef:** Set out olive oil and 85/15 ground beef. Heat the oil in a 10- to 12-inch skillet over medium-high heat until shimmering. Add the beef in a thin layer and leave it undisturbed for about 2 minutes, until browned underneath. Break it into small crumbles and cook another 4–6 minutes, stirring, until cooked through to 160°F / 71°C. Spoon off pooled fat, leaving a thin film in the pan. Transfer the cooked beef to a clean bowl.
3. **Soften the vegetables:** Lower the heat to medium and add yellow onion and yellow bell pepper to the same skillet. Cook for 6–8 minutes, stirring, until fully softened and the onion is translucent with lightly golden edges. Lower the heat if the browned bits start to blacken.
4. **Bloom the spices:** Lower the heat to medium-low. Stir in garlic clove, ground cumin, sweet paprika, dried oregano, and ground turmeric for about 30 seconds, just until fragrant; do not let the garlic or paprika scorch.
5. **Cook the tomato paste:** Stir in tomato paste for about 1 minute, until it darkens slightly and coats the vegetables.
6. **Finish the filling:** Return the beef and add unsalted beef broth, fine salt, and ground black pepper, using the lower end of the broth range first. Scrape up the browned bits and stir over medium heat for 1–2 minutes. Add the remaining broth only if the filling seems dry. Stop when moist crumbles cling together lightly and a spatula drawn across the pan leaves no puddle.
7. **Taste and cool:** Taste the fully cooked filling and add additional fine salt only if needed. Spread it in a thin layer in the shallow dish and refrigerate promptly for about 20–30 minutes, or until cool throughout; stir once to release trapped warmth. Do not wait for a deep bowl to cool on the counter. While it chills, heat the oven to 400°F / 200°C conventional, or the temperature specified by the disc package, with a rack in the middle.
8. **Portion the filling:** Work with 5-inch empanada discs labeled for baking, keeping unused discs covered and cool. Start with 1 1/2 tablespoons of cooled filling per disc, then add a little more up to about 2 tablespoons only if it closes easily. Leave a clean 1/2-inch border. Share the filling across the batch; do not stretch the pastry or force in surplus filling. Refrigerate any extra filling separately.
9. **Seal:** Lightly moisten the clean border with water for sealing. Fold each disc over the filling, gently press out trapped air, then press and crimp firmly with a fork. Set on the lined sheet with about 1 inch between empanadas. If the pastry becomes soft or sticky, refrigerate the assembled tray for 10 minutes before baking.
10. **Glaze if desired:** For the optional glaze, beat large egg (if using) and water for egg wash (if using) together and brush a thin layer over the tops. Omit both for an unglazed finish. Discard leftover wash. Cut one small slit in the top of each empanada to vent steam.
11. **Bake:** Bake for about 20–25 minutes, rotating the tray halfway through, until the pastry is golden on top and underneath and the filling reaches 165°F / 74°C. Follow the disc package if it specifies a different temperature or time; begin checking at its earliest stated time. Use a second sheet if needed rather than crowding; larger batches need additional trays and time, not a higher oven temperature.
12. **Rest and serve:** Rest on a wire rack for 10 minutes before eating; the filling can be very hot. Serve with lime and powdered sugar (if using), squeezing the lime onto each bite and adding only a light dusting of sugar if using. Allow 2–3 empanadas per person with a crisp green salad, or serve individually as a snack.

11. Bake: Bake for about 20–25 minutes, rotating the tray halfway through, until the pastry is golden on top and underneath and the filling reaches 165°F / 74°C. Follow the disc package if it specifies a different temperature or time; begin checking at its earliest stated time. Use a second sheet if needed rather than crowding; larger batches need additional trays and time, not a higher oven temperature.

data.title: Philly Tuna Roll
ingredients: 230 g trimmed boneless, skinless yellowfin tuna, weighed after removing tough connective tissue; see raw-service sourcing note
115 g full-fat block cream cheese, cold
100 g English cucumber, weighed after removing the watery seed core
4 full sheets unseasoned roasted nori, about 19 x 20 cm each; trim as directed
120 ml water, for dampening hands and the knife
1 tsp unseasoned rice vinegar, for the hand-dipping water
data.description: Tuna, cold cream-cheese strips and crisp cucumber rolled with nori outside. Measured fillings and a larger wrapper keep the creamy center contained.

learning.focus: Arrange firm strips into a compact filling line
learning.outcome: A closed roll with a distinct cream-cheese center, crunchy cucumber and clean slices rather than a flattened cheese smear.
before: Use block cream cheese, not whipped spread. Cut it cold and return the portions to the refrigerator while setting up the rice and mat.
Use trimmed 19 x 15 cm nori rectangles for this filling amount. Sushi nori sheets and small seasoned snack seaweed are different products. Read the raw-fish sourcing note before buying tuna.

checkpoints.cue: Cream cheese holds firm strip shapes and cucumber surfaces are dry.
checkpoints.why: Soft cheese smears under rolling pressure and wet cucumber loosens the filling.

checkpoints.cue: The wrapper reaches around the filling without force and closes along the bare edge.
checkpoints.why: Even filling distribution and enough nori control closure better than extra squeezing.

troubleshooting.problem: Cream cheese smears or squeezes from the ends
troubleshooting.cause: It warmed during preparation or the roll was compressed too firmly.
troubleshooting.fix: Refrigerate the unrolled portions until firm. Press just enough to make the next roll cohesive; shape loose pieces into a small bowl portion instead of repeatedly squeezing an already damaged roll.

troubleshooting.cause: Filling is heaped in the center or the wrapper is undersized.
troubleshooting.fix: Open before sealing and distribute strips evenly end to end. Remove a little filling if needed and serve that small portion separately; do not overload another roll to use it up. Check nori size and weighed portions.

substitutions.alternative: The same weight of reduced-fat block cream cheese
substitutions.effect: Less rich and sometimes softer; keep cold. Whipped tub spread is harder to form into stable strips. Both versions contain milk.

substitutions.alternative: The same trimmed weight of Persian cucumber
substitutions.effect: Keep the skin if tender and pat the strips dry; remove any coarse watery core before weighing.

learning.timing: About 120 minutes from dry rice includes the shari's 80-minute preparation, ingredient cutting during its waits and four rolls assembled/cut afterward. Allow about 45 minutes with freshly prepared, barely warm rice. First-time rolling, rice reheating/cooling or a slower rice-cooker cycle may need longer. Thaw frozen tuna in the refrigerator beforehand, often overnight.
learning.storage: Plan raw rolls for same-day service within any earlier supplier limit. Keep tuna and cheese at 40°F / 4°C or below and take out one roll's portions at a time. Do not plan assembled raw rolls as next-day lunches. Count prep and service time together; discard perishables left unrefrigerated over 2 hours, or 1 hour above 90°F / 32°C. Store unused clean rice separately according to its recipe; chilling will change its texture.

body:
## Chef's Note

This tuna-and-cream-cheese variation keeps its Philly name and its nori-outside wrapping. Cold cheese strips provide a defined creamy center beside cucumber; they should not be spread across the rice. Sesame goes onto the rice before rolling so it stays with the roll instead of falling off dry nori.

## Before buying raw tuna

Tell the supplier it will be eaten raw and confirm species, handling and applicable parasite controls. “Sushi-grade” alone does not establish suitability. Yellowfin has a specific FDA parasite-freezing exemption, but other raw-seafood hazards remain. Do not rely on domestic freezing, vinegar or appearance to establish raw safety. Thaw frozen tuna in the refrigerator as directed, removing vacuum packaging before refrigerator thawing.

FDA advises children, pregnant people, older adults and people with weakened immune systems to avoid raw seafood. Choose a fully cooked preparation for those diners. This roll contains fish, milk and sesame.

## Directions

1. **Prepare rice and the station:** Follow [Sushi Rice (Shari)](/mise/recipes/master-sushi-rice), weigh 320 g for this recipe and refrigerate surplus rice promptly. Let the rolling portion become barely warm during final preparation. Wrap a clean mat in food-safe plastic film. Mix the hand-dipping water and vinegar; it reduces sticking and is not a sanitizer. Do not dip a raw-filling-coated hand or blade into this clean water. Wash hands and clean the blade before returning to it, use a separate damp cloth for wiping the cutting blade, and replace the water if contaminated.
2. **Prepare cheese and cucumber:** During the rice process, cut cold cream cheese into strips about 6 mm thick. Wash the cucumber, remove its watery core and weigh 100 g, then cut into slender matchsticks and pat dry. Divide cheese into four equal portions of about 29 g and cucumber into four 25 g portions. Refrigerate, keeping the cheese firm.
3. **Prepare fish near rolling:** With separate clean equipment, remove tough visible connective tissue, weigh the listed usable amount of tuna and cut across the muscle grain where visible into strips about 6–10 mm thick. Shorter strips can be laid end to end. Divide into four equal portions of about 58 g and refrigerate. Clean the work area and hands before handling the rolling equipment.
4. **Portion rice and nori:** Divide the rice into four 80 g portions. Trim the first nori sheet to about 19 x 15 cm, saving its dry offcut airtight for another use. Keep the other sheets untrimmed until the first closure check. Place one rectangle shiny side down with the 19 cm edge nearest you. Lightly dampen fingers, shake off excess water and spread one rice portion evenly, leaving a 1 cm bare strip at the far edge. Scatter one quarter of the sesame seeds onto the rice.
5. **Fill and roll:** Take out one portion each of tuna, cheese and cucumber. Using clean utensils, arrange them in an even horizontal line about 4 cm from the near edge; keep their ends aligned and avoid a mound in the middle. Lift the mat's near edge and tuck nori and rice over the filling. Pull the mat out of the way while rolling forward so it stays outside. Close on the bare edge, barely moistening it if needed, and press gently through the mat. Check the first roll's closure, then trim the remaining sheets to match and proceed with the other three; no rice ridge is needed.
6. **Cut and serve:** Place seam-side down briefly while preparing the knife. Wipe and lightly dampen a sharp blade. Cut each roll in half, then halve each section twice, producing eight pieces per roll; wipe and dampen the blade as needed between cuts. Serve promptly as 32 pieces, about two main portions or four appetizer portions. Keep unused raw fish and cheese portions refrigerated during the work.

data.title: Pho Bo (Beef Pho)
ingredients: 3 lbs Beef Marrow Bones, cut into 3-inch pieces
2 large Yellow Onions, unpeeled and halved
3 tbsp Fish Sauce, plus more to taste
1 lb Dried Rice Noodles (banh pho, medium width)
1/2 lb Eye of Round, sliced paper-thin against the grain
Hoisin Sauce and Sriracha, for serving

body:
## Chef's Note

The soul of great pho bo lives in the charred aromatics and the long, patient simmer. Blackening the onions and ginger under the broiler builds a smoky sweetness that no shortcut can replicate. The most common mistake is boiling the broth too hard, which turns it cloudy and greasy. Keep it at a bare simmer -- you want lazy bubbles, not a rolling boil. Parboiling the bones first and rinsing them clean is the single most important step for a clear, golden broth.

## Directions

1.  **Parboil the Bones:** Place the marrow bones and brisket in a large stockpot. Cover with cold water and bring to a vigorous boil for 10 minutes. Drain, rinse the bones and meat under cold water, and scrub the pot clean. This removes impurities and is essential for a clear broth.

2.  **Char the Aromatics:** While the bones parboil, place the halved onions and ginger cut-side down on a sheet pan. Broil on high for 12-15 minutes until deeply blackened and softened. The char is critical for flavor.

3.  **Toast the Spices:** In a dry skillet over medium heat, toast the star anise, cinnamon stick, cloves, coriander seeds, and cardamom pod for 2-3 minutes until fragrant. Place them in a spice sachet or cheesecloth bundle.

4.  **Build the Broth:** Return the cleaned bones and brisket to the scrubbed pot. Add 6 quarts cold water, charred aromatics, and spice bundle. Bring to a boil, then immediately reduce to the gentlest possible simmer. Skim any foam that rises during the first 30 minutes.

5.  **Remove the Brisket:** After 1.5-2 hours, check the brisket with a chopstick. When it slides through with little resistance, transfer the brisket to an ice bath for 10 minutes (this firms the meat for slicing), then refrigerate. Continue simmering the bones for 2 more hours.

6.  **Season the Broth:** After a total of 4 hours, strain the broth through a fine-mesh strainer lined with cheesecloth. Discard solids. Stir in the fish sauce, sugar, and salt. Taste and adjust -- the broth should be deeply savory with a hint of sweetness.

7.  **Prepare the Noodles:** Soak the rice noodles in warm water for 20-25 minutes until pliable. Just before serving, cook in rapidly boiling water for 30-60 seconds until tender. Drain immediately.

8.  **Prepare the Meats:** Slice the chilled brisket across the grain into thin pieces and reheat it in simmering broth to 165°F / 74°C throughout. For the fully cooked eye of round, cook the slices in simmering broth before assembly, checking representative pieces with a suitable thin-tip thermometer for at least 145°F / 63°C, then allow a 3-minute rest before serving. Color change or brief contact with hot broth alone does not establish doneness; if the thin slices cannot be reliably measured, do not assume this endpoint has been verified.

9.  **Assemble:** Divide noodles among deep bowls. Top with the reheated brisket and cooked, rested eye of round. Ladle hot broth over the meat and noodles. Serve immediately with a platter of bean sprouts, Thai basil, cilantro, lime wedges, jalapenos, hoisin, and sriracha.

Toast the Spices: In a dry skillet over medium heat, toast the star anise, cinnamon stick, cloves, coriander seeds, and cardamom pod for 2-3 minutes until fragrant. Place them in a spice sachet or cheesecloth bundle.

Build the Broth: Return the cleaned bones and brisket to the scrubbed pot. Add 6 quarts cold water, charred aromatics, and spice bundle. Bring to a boil, then immediately reduce to the gentlest possible simmer. Skim any foam that rises during the first 30 minutes.

Remove the Brisket: After 1.5-2 hours, check the brisket with a chopstick. When it slides through with little resistance, transfer the brisket to an ice bath for 10 minutes (this firms the meat for slicing), then refrigerate. Continue simmering the bones for 2 more hours.

Season the Broth: After a total of 4 hours, strain the broth through a fine-mesh strainer lined with cheesecloth. Discard solids. Stir in the fish sauce, sugar, and salt. Taste and adjust -- the broth should be deeply savory with a hint of sweetness.
Prepare the Noodles: Soak the rice noodles in warm water for 20-25 minutes until pliable. Just before serving, cook in rapidly boiling water for 30-60 seconds until tender. Drain immediately.

Prepare the Meats: Slice the chilled brisket across the grain into thin pieces and reheat it in simmering broth to 165°F / 74°C throughout. For the fully cooked eye of round, cook the slices in simmering broth before assembly, checking representative pieces with a suitable thin-tip thermometer for at least 145°F / 63°C, then allow a 3-minute rest before serving. Color change or brief contact with hot broth alone does not establish doneness; if the thin slices cannot be reliably measured, do not assume this endpoint has been verified.

Assemble: Divide noodles among deep bowls. Top with the reheated brisket and cooked, rested eye of round. Ladle hot broth over the meat and noodles. Serve immediately with a platter of bean sprouts, Thai basil, cilantro, lime wedges, jalapenos, hoisin, and sriracha.

Chef's Note

The soul of great pho bo lives in the charred aromatics and the long, patient simmer. Blackening the onions and ginger under the broiler builds a smoky sweetness that no shortcut can replicate. The most common mistake is boiling the broth too hard, which turns it cloudy and greasy. Keep it at a bare simmer -- you want lazy bubbles, not a rolling boil. Parboiling the bones first and rinsing them clean is the single most important step for a clear, golden broth.

data.title: Quick Refrigerator-Pickled Red Onions
ingredients: 200 g red onion, peeled and very thinly sliced into half-moons
1/2 cup (120 ml) apple cider or distilled white vinegar, labeled 5% acidity
1 tsp (6 g) fine or pickling salt
data.description: Thin red onion in a measured vinegar brine: a refrigerated condiment with crisp texture and a mellowing raw bite.

learning.focus: Keep the vinegar-to-water ratio defined and distinguish quick pickles from shelf-stable preserves
learning.outcome: Thin, crisp onion slices with a clear vinegar tang and less raw bite; color becomes more evenly pink as they stand refrigerated.
before: Use a clean heatproof pint jar or similar covered container. Check that the vinegar says 5% acidity; do not use an unknown-strength homemade vinegar.
The stated yield is drained onion, not the jar volume including brine. Forty-five minutes gives a first-use pickle; flavor is more developed the next day.

checkpoints.cue: Salt and sugar are dissolved in the hot vinegar-water mixture.
checkpoints.why: A uniform brine distributes seasoning. Sugar balances taste; this recipe is not relying on sugar to preserve onions at room temperature.

checkpoints.cue: The sliced onion sits below the liquid with space at the top of the jar.
checkpoints.why: Thin slices pack closely and soften a little in hot brine. Adding plain water to cover would dilute the defined acidity.

troubleshooting.problem: Liquid does not cover the onions
troubleshooting.cause: The container is too wide or the slices are loosely packed.
troubleshooting.fix: Press gently with a clean spoon or move to a narrower heatproof container. If needed, make another measured batch of the same brine; never top up with plain water.

troubleshooting.cause: Thick slices or a short refrigerated rest left a strong raw bite.
troubleshooting.fix: Give it more refrigerated time and use a small drained portion. Slice thinner next time; pink color alone does not mean the flavor is fully developed.

substitutions.alternative: The same volume of distilled white vinegar labeled 5% acidity
substitutions.effect: A cleaner, sharper vinegar flavor; keep the measured water quantity unchanged.

learning.timing: Ten minutes preparation, about five minutes heating and thirty minutes cooling/chilling before the first taste. Refrigerate promptly after filling; allow a day for fuller flavor. Do not count a ten-minute preparation time as fully developed pickles.
learning.storage: Keep covered at 40°F / 4°C or below, use clean utensils and use within two weeks. Keep these pickles refrigerated; do not can them or store them in the pantry. Discard moldy or otherwise spoiled contents; do not skim and reuse the brine for a new batch.

body:
## Chef's Note

Thin slicing makes a quick pickle practical: the brine reaches a greater share of each slice in a short time. The result is a tart refrigerated condiment, not a fermented onion or a shelf-stable preserve. Drain the portion you use so its vinegar accents a taco without soaking the bread.

## Directions

1. **Slice and pack:** Peel and rinse the onion, trim its ends and slice about 1/16–1/8 inch thick. Pack into a clean heatproof pint jar, leaving roughly 1/2 inch at the top.
2. **Heat the brine:** Put the measured vinegar, water, sugar and salt in a small saucepan. Bring to a simmer, stirring until dissolved, then remove from heat.
3. **Cover the onion:** Pour hot brine over the onion and gently press it down with a clean spoon. Leave about 1/2 inch headspace. Use a narrower container or additional same-ratio brine if coverage is inadequate; do not add plain water.
4. **Refrigerate and develop:** Cover with a clean lid and refrigerate promptly on a heatproof pad, with space around the jar. After about thirty minutes, taste a drained slice once cool enough. It will still have some raw bite; longer refrigerated time, ideally until the next day, makes the flavor more even.
5. **Use:** Lift out only the needed portion with a clean fork and drain. The full batch yields approximately 1 1/2 cups drained onions; use a tablespoon or two as a condiment, leaving the rest submerged and refrigerated.

data.title: Pizza Beans
ingredients: 2 cans (15 oz each) Giant White Beans (Butter or Gigante), rinsed

body:
## Chef's Note

This Tex-Mex inspired skillet dish swaps pizza dough for protein-rich white beans, creating a comfort food that's lighter but equally satisfying. Cooking kale just until wilted preserves a slight bite that contrasts with the creamy beans and melted cheese. Giant butter beans or gigante beans work best for their substantial, meaty texture.

## Directions

1.  **Prep:** Preheat oven to 450°F.
2.  **Base:** Heat oil in an oven-safe heavy skillet (cast iron is best). Sauté the onion until soft (8 mins). Add the garlic and cook for 1 minute.
3.  **Greens:** Add the kale to the pan and stir until it just turns bright green and collapses.
4.  **Simmer:** Stir in the tomatoes, beans, and oregano. Season with salt and pepper. Let it simmer for 5 minutes to marry the flavors.
5.  **Assemble:** Top with mozzarella and Parmesan.
6.  **Bake:** Transfer the skillet to the oven. Bake for 15-20 minutes until the cheese is bubbling and has golden brown spots.
7.  **Serve:** Let rest for 5 minutes. Scoop into bowls and serve with crusty bread.

data.title: Pizza
ingredients: 600 g prepared, risen pizza dough, at stretching temperature; divide into two equal balls
flour, for dusting the work surface and peel, as needed
olive oil, for lightly oiling the pans, if using the pan route, optional
120 g fresh pineapple, cut into small pieces and blotted dry
40 g baby spinach, washed if needed and dried thoroughly
data.description: Two generously topped 12-inch pizzas with pepperoni, pineapple, spinach and whole-milk mozzarella, starting with prepared dough.

scaling.reason: Written for two 12-inch pizzas, baked one at a time. Keep the dough portions and topping shares together; make another full batch for more pizzas.

data.source: Family recipe

ingredients.preparation: at stretching temperature; divide into two equal balls

ingredients.name: flour
ingredients.allowance: for dusting the work surface and peel, as needed

ingredients.name: olive oil
ingredients.allowance: for lightly oiling the pans, if using the pan route

steps.title: Choose the baking route
steps.text: Start with fully risen dough that is relaxed enough to stretch. Follow its recipe or package for thawing, proofing and warming before this schedule. Heat the oven to 500°F with a middle rack. For the pan route, keep two metal pans with enough flat area for 12-inch pizzas at room temperature; check that they are rated for 500°F. For the stone route, put a suitably rated stone in the cold oven and heat it for 1 hour; have a peel that fits the pizza ready. Neither route uses parchment.

steps.title: Divide the toppings
steps.text: Make two equal sets of toppings before shaping. Each pizza gets 1/2 cup sauce, 6 oz mozzarella, 30 g pepperoni, 60 g pineapple and 20 g spinach. Cut pineapple into approximately 1/4-inch pieces and blot away surface liquid. Keep the second set of perishable toppings refrigerated until needed.

steps.title: Shape on a cool surface
steps.text: Have {{ingredients}} ready. Divide the dough into two 300 g balls. Cover one while stretching the other to a 12-inch round with a slightly thicker rim. If it springs back, cover and rest 10 minutes. Transfer the bare round to a lightly oiled room-temperature pan, or to a lightly floured peel for the stone route. On a peel, check that it slides freely before topping.

steps.title: Top one pizza
steps.text: Use one half each of {{ingredients}} on the first pizza. Spread its sauce leaving a 3/4-inch border, then distribute the cheese, pepperoni and pineapple evenly. Reserve the spinach. If using a peel, check that the pizza still moves freely and launch promptly; do not leave a dressed pizza waiting on the peel.

steps.title: Bake and wilt the spinach
steps.text: Reserve one half of {{ingredients}} for this pizza and the other half for the second. Put the pan on the oven rack, or slide the pizza directly from the peel onto the stone. Start checking after 10 minutes; allow roughly 12–15 minutes total. When the rim is nearly browned and the cheese is bubbling, pull the pizza out safely with its pan or peel, scatter on its spinach portion and return it for the final 1–2 minutes. The spinach should wilt and the underside should be browned, with a set center that supports a slice. Check underneath with a spatula or peel; a dark rim alone does not establish doneness. Extend the bake if needed.

steps.title: Serve and repeat
steps.text: Move the first pizza to a rack for 2 minutes, then slice and serve. Keep the oven on; let a stone recover for about 5 minutes between pizzas. Shape and top the second pizza on its own room-temperature pan or prepared peel, using the remaining topping portions, and repeat the bake. Never assemble dough directly on a hot pan or reach over a hot stone.

learning.focus: Control topping moisture and bottom heat
learning.outcome: A browned, supporting base beneath melted cheese, juicy pineapple, pepperoni and lightly wilted spinach.
before: The clock starts with prepared dough already risen and ready to stretch. Cold or frozen dough needs its own additional preparation.
Use two pans so the second pizza can be assembled on a cool surface. A stone is optional and requires a peel and an hour of preheating.

checkpoints.cue: The dough stretches without tearing and, on a peel, slides before topping.
checkpoints.why: Rest reduces spring-back; a stuck, fully dressed pizza is difficult to transfer safely.

checkpoints.cue: The bottom is browned and the center is set, not just the rim.
checkpoints.why: Wet toppings can leave the center soft even when exposed edges have browned.

troubleshooting.cause: Wet toppings, a cool baking surface or insufficient baking.
troubleshooting.fix: Continue baking and check underneath. Next time blot the pineapple thoroughly and allow the oven or stone to reach its full preheat.

troubleshooting.cause: The dough is cold or needs to relax after handling.
troubleshooting.fix: Cover and rest for another 10 minutes before stretching; allow more warming time if it still feels cold.

substitutions.alternative: Omit it for a meat-free version
substitutions.effect: The pizza loses its peppery, salty accent. For a vegetarian result also check that the dough, sauce and cheese are suitable.

learning.timing: Allow about 60–70 minutes for the pan route: oven heating overlaps 20 minutes of preparation, followed by two separate 12–15-minute bakes and handling. With a stone, allow about 1 hour 40 minutes including its full hour preheat and recovery. These are planning estimates with ready-to-stretch dough; dough preparation and extra rests add time. Serve the pizzas in rounds.
learning.storage: Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours, or 1 hour above 90°F / 32°C, in shallow covered containers at 40°F / 4°C or below. Use within 3–4 days or freeze; reheat to 165°F / 74°C throughout.

body:
## Chef's Note

Pepperoni, pineapple and spinach bring salty, sweet and fresh contrasts to a generous cheese pizza. Keep the toppings dry and check the underside before serving: a browned rim can hide a soft center. This batch makes two 12-inch pizzas for four portions, served as each pizza comes out of the oven.

## Directions

1. **Choose the baking route:** Start with fully risen dough that is relaxed enough to stretch. Follow its recipe or package for thawing, proofing and warming before this schedule. Heat the oven to 500°F with a middle rack. For the pan route, keep two metal pans with enough flat area for 12-inch pizzas at room temperature; check that they are rated for 500°F. For the stone route, put a suitably rated stone in the cold oven and heat it for 1 hour; have a peel that fits the pizza ready. Neither route uses parchment.
2. **Divide the toppings:** Make two equal sets of toppings before shaping. Each pizza gets 1/2 cup sauce, 6 oz mozzarella, 30 g pepperoni, 60 g pineapple and 20 g spinach. Cut pineapple into approximately 1/4-inch pieces and blot away surface liquid. Keep the second set of perishable toppings refrigerated until needed.
3. **Shape on a cool surface:** Have prepared, risen pizza dough, flour, and olive oil (if using) ready. Divide the dough into two 300 g balls. Cover one while stretching the other to a 12-inch round with a slightly thicker rim. If it springs back, cover and rest 10 minutes. Transfer the bare round to a lightly oiled room-temperature pan, or to a lightly floured peel for the stone route. On a peel, check that it slides freely before topping.
4. **Top one pizza:** Use one half each of thick pizza sauce, whole-milk low-moisture mozzarella, ready-to-eat pepperoni slices, and fresh pineapple on the first pizza. Spread its sauce leaving a 3/4-inch border, then distribute the cheese, pepperoni and pineapple evenly. Reserve the spinach. If using a peel, check that the pizza still moves freely and launch promptly; do not leave a dressed pizza waiting on the peel.
5. **Bake and wilt the spinach:** Reserve one half of baby spinach for this pizza and the other half for the second. Put the pan on the oven rack, or slide the pizza directly from the peel onto the stone. Start checking after 10 minutes; allow roughly 12–15 minutes total. When the rim is nearly browned and the cheese is bubbling, pull the pizza out safely with its pan or peel, scatter on its spinach portion and return it for the final 1–2 minutes. The spinach should wilt and the underside should be browned, with a set center that supports a slice. Check underneath with a spatula or peel; a dark rim alone does not establish doneness. Extend the bake if needed.
6. **Serve and repeat:** Move the first pizza to a rack for 2 minutes, then slice and serve. Keep the oven on; let a stone recover for about 5 minutes between pizzas. Shape and top the second pizza on its own room-temperature pan or prepared peel, using the remaining topping portions, and repeat the bake. Never assemble dough directly on a hot pan or reach over a hot stone.

## Timing and leftovers

With ready-to-stretch dough, allow about 60–70 minutes for the pan route or 1 hour 40 minutes for the stone route. Oven heating overlaps topping preparation; two pizzas still need two baking rounds. Cold or frozen dough needs its own preparation before this schedule.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours, or 1 hour above 90°F / 32°C, at 40°F / 4°C or below. Use within 3–4 days or freeze; reheat to 165°F / 74°C throughout.

parsed.directionsText:
1. Choose the baking route: Start with fully risen dough that is relaxed enough to stretch. Follow its recipe or package for thawing, proofing and warming before this schedule. Heat the oven to 500°F with a middle rack. For the pan route, keep two metal pans with enough flat area for 12-inch pizzas at room temperature; check that they are rated for 500°F. For the stone route, put a suitably rated stone in the cold oven and heat it for 1 hour; have a peel that fits the pizza ready. Neither route uses parchment.
2. Divide the toppings: Make two equal sets of toppings before shaping. Each pizza gets 1/2 cup sauce, 6 oz mozzarella, 30 g pepperoni, 60 g pineapple and 20 g spinach. Cut pineapple into approximately 1/4-inch pieces and blot away surface liquid. Keep the second set of perishable toppings refrigerated until needed.
3. Shape on a cool surface: Have prepared, risen pizza dough, flour, and olive oil (if using) ready. Divide the dough into two 300 g balls. Cover one while stretching the other to a 12-inch round with a slightly thicker rim. If it springs back, cover and rest 10 minutes. Transfer the bare round to a lightly oiled room-temperature pan, or to a lightly floured peel for the stone route. On a peel, check that it slides freely before topping.
4. Top one pizza: Use one half each of thick pizza sauce, whole-milk low-moisture mozzarella, ready-to-eat pepperoni slices, and fresh pineapple on the first pizza. Spread its sauce leaving a 3/4-inch border, then distribute the cheese, pepperoni and pineapple evenly. Reserve the spinach. If using a peel, check that the pizza still moves freely and launch promptly; do not leave a dressed pizza waiting on the peel.
5. Bake and wilt the spinach: Reserve one half of baby spinach for this pizza and the other half for the second. Put the pan on the oven rack, or slide the pizza directly from the peel onto the stone. Start checking after 10 minutes; allow roughly 12–15 minutes total. When the rim is nearly browned and the cheese is bubbling, pull the pizza out safely with its pan or peel, scatter on its spinach portion and return it for the final 1–2 minutes. The spinach should wilt and the underside should be browned, with a set center that supports a slice. Check underneath with a spatula or peel; a dark rim alone does not establish doneness. Extend the bake if needed.
6. Serve and repeat: Move the first pizza to a rack for 2 minutes, then slice and serve. Keep the oven on; let a stone recover for about 5 minutes between pizzas. Shape and top the second pizza on its own room-temperature pan or prepared peel, using the remaining topping portions, and repeat the bake. Never assemble dough directly on a hot pan or reach over a hot stone.

body:
## Chef's Note

Homemade play-dough is a rainy-day project that's actually food science at work - a cooked dough that stays pliable for months. The cream of tartar is the key: it acts as a preservative and keeps the dough soft, so it won't crack or harden in an airtight container. The oil and salt also help preserve texture.
## Directions

1.  **Combine:** In a medium non-stick saucepan, whisk together the flour, salt, and cream of tartar.
2.  **Emulsify:** Add the water, oil, and food coloring. Whisk until no lumps remain.
3.  **The Cook:** Place over medium heat. Stir constantly with a wooden spoon for 3-5 minutes.
4.  **The Pull:** The mixture will look like a liquid, then suddenly clump together. Continue stirring until the dough pulls away from the sides of the pan and forms a single, non-sticky ball.
5.  **Knead:** Remove from heat and place on a clean surface. Once cool enough to touch, knead for 1 minute until perfectly smooth.
6.  **Store:** Store in an airtight container for up to 6 months to maintain the "Bounce."

data.title: Poke Bowl Bar
ingredients: 680 g total prepared raw seafood: yellowfin tuna, salmon or shucked scallop adductor muscles; choose one or split the total between two, following the sourcing note
4 cups prepared [Sushi Rice (Shari)](/mise/recipes/master-sushi-rice), or the same total of plain cooked rice and shari
1/8 tsp fine salt, for the avocado, only if needed
1/2 recipe [Oi Muchim (Korean Cucumber Salad)](/mise/recipes/korean-pickled-cucumbers), prepared and lifted from excess dressing
150 g frozen unsalted shelled edamame, cooked according to the package and chilled
1 sheet nori, cut into thin strips
2 tbsp chopped cilantro or microgreens, optional
1 tsp furikake, optional; check the label
1 tbsp extra soy sauce, optional for the table
2 tbsp prepared spicy mayonnaise, optional; check the label
data.description: A measured four-bowl bar with a choice of seafood, rice, fresh vegetables, cucumber salad and garnishes. Keep the seafood cold and finish each bowl as it is eaten.

learning.focus: Build a small cold-food bar without multiplying every component
learning.outcome: Four balanced bowls with the selected seafood kept cold, one total rice allowance and toppings that stay distinct until each diner assembles a bowl.
before: Choose one seafood or divide the total between two. Do not buy the full stated amount of each choice. Confirm raw-service sourcing before shopping; wild salmon, tuna and scallop products do not have identical parasite controls.
Make rice and chill cooked edamame before cutting seafood. Use small fish bowls nested in ice, separate spoons, and refrigerator space for refills; keep meltwater outside the food bowls.

checkpoints.cue: Each seafood bowl is cold and lightly coated, with excess dressing kept out of communal toppings.
checkpoints.why: Separate bowls preserve choice and prevent raw-seafood contact from spreading across the bar.

checkpoints.cue: Each bowl receives roughly one quarter of the total rice and seafood before optional garnishes.
checkpoints.why: Choosing two types divides the allocation; it does not double the meal.

troubleshooting.problem: The bar has far too much fish or rice
troubleshooting.cause: Each alternative was purchased or cooked as a full additional batch.
troubleshooting.fix: Set aside properly chilled unused portions before service. Next time divide the listed total among choices; do not replenish a serving bowl by pouring fresh seafood onto an older portion.

troubleshooting.problem: The assembled bowl is salty or wet
troubleshooting.cause: Fish dressing, cucumber dressing, soy and furikake accumulated.
troubleshooting.fix: Leave pooled dressing behind, skip extra soy and furikake, and keep garnishes separate so diners can taste before adding more.

substitutions.alternative: The same cooked volume of plain short-grain white rice
substitutions.effect: Less sweet and acidic. Use four cups total across both kinds, not four cups of each. Plain rice also needs safe holding and refrigeration.

substitutions.alternative: The same amount of chile crisp
substitutions.effect: Adds oil and texture; inspect the label for allergens. Soy and sesame are already present; scallops add molluscan shellfish, while mayonnaise may add egg and furikake may add fish or other allergens.

learning.timing: About 95 minutes includes one fresh shari preparation, cucumber salting, package-directed edamame cooking/chilling, vegetable preparation and setting out the bar. Much of the vegetable work overlaps the rice. Allow about 40–50 minutes when rice, cucumber salad and cooked edamame are already refrigerated, including reheating rice to 165°F / 74°C and briefly cooling the serving portion. Making a second rice type from scratch needs another pot or cooker and may extend the schedule. Frozen seafood thawing is extra, often overnight.
learning.storage: Keep seafood at 40°F / 4°C or below until serving and replenish small portions from the refrigerator. Track total time out of temperature control; discard perishables after 2 hours, or 1 hour above 90°F / 32°C. Plan raw seafood for same-day service and respect earlier supplier limits. Do not save assembled raw bowls; store untouched rice and vegetables separately under their own component limits. Do not save raw-contact dressing as a general sauce.

body:
## Chef's Note

Poke is seasoned cut seafood from Hawaii; this multi-topping bar is a contemporary bowl format. Choosing two seafoods or rice types changes the variety, not the total portion needed. Cucumber salad, soy and furikake each add seasoning, so offer them separately and start lightly.

## Raw seafood sourcing

Tell the supplier the seafood will be served raw and ask for its species, cold-chain handling and applicable parasite-control information. “Sushi-grade” and “sashimi-grade” labels alone do not establish suitability. For wild salmon, require documented supplier parasite-destruction freezing; fresh wild-caught fish is not automatically preferable for raw service. For farmed salmon, obtain supplier documentation of either parasite-destruction freezing or qualifying raising and feeding conditions; a farmed label alone is insufficient. Yellowfin tuna and scallop products consisting only of the shucked adductor muscle have specific parasite-freezing exemptions, not a general guarantee of raw safety. Do not use a household freezer as an assumed substitute for a documented commercial process.

Freezing does not remove every seafood hazard, and this dressing is not a safety treatment. FDA advises children, pregnant people, older adults and people with weakened immune systems to avoid raw seafood; choose a fully cooked meal for those diners. Follow supplier refrigerator-thawing instructions and remove vacuum packaging before refrigerator thawing.

## Directions

1. **Prepare the rice and cucumber salad:** Make [Sushi Rice (Shari)](/mise/recipes/master-sushi-rice) and measure four cooked cups for the bar, refrigerating any extra promptly. For two rice types, use two cups shari and two cups safely prepared [Plain Short-Grain White Rice](/mise/recipes/steamed-white-rice). During the rice process, make a half batch of [Oi Muchim](/mise/recipes/korean-pickled-cucumbers), starting with 300 g cucumber, then lift the finished half batch from excess dressing for the four bowls.
2. **Prepare edamame and vegetables during rice soaking/cooking:** Cook shelled edamame early in the rice process according to its package, drain and chill promptly in a shallow container. Wash and cut the fresh cucumber, carrot, cabbage, scallions and optional jalapeno and herbs with clean equipment. Slice avocado last and coat with 1 tsp lime juice, adding the measured optional salt only after tasting. Refrigerate vegetables until needed and keep nori dry.
3. **Mix the dressing:** Whisk soy sauce, toasted sesame oil, rice vinegar, ginger and the remaining 1 tsp lime juice. Taste before any seafood touches it. Leave out sriracha for a mild dressing or add it now; for one mild and one spicy seafood bowl, divide the clean dressing in proportion to the seafood weights and add sriracha only to the spicy portion.
4. **Cut and dress seafood while rice cools:** During the final rice cooling period, with separate clean equipment, cut cold tuna or salmon into 1/2-inch cubes, or slice scallop muscles about 1/4 inch thick. Divide the dressing among the chosen seafoods in proportion to their weights and refrigerate for about 5–10 minutes. Keep each type in its own bowl with its own spoon. This short wait seasons the seafood; it does not cook it or establish safety.
5. **Set out and assemble:** Nest small seafood bowls in ice, with meltwater unable to enter them. Check the seafood with a clean food thermometer to confirm 40°F / 4°C or below; clean the probe between seafoods and return portions to the refrigerator if the ice setup cannot keep them cold. Set out the rice barely warm and the prepared vegetables cold, with separate spoons and garnishes alongside. For four bowls, allow about one cup total rice and one quarter of the total seafood per person; a diner choosing two seafoods splits that portion. Lift seafood and cucumber salad from pooled dressing. Add avocado, edamame and fresh vegetables, then sesame, scallion and dry nori. Offer the measured optional garnishes and sauces sparingly. Assemble only when ready to eat and refrigerate unused rice promptly.

## Scaling the bar

Scale the total fish and rice allocation across the choices, then divide dressing in proportion to the fish. Larger rice batches need a suitable pot or separate batches, and more fish needs additional refrigerated space and ice capacity. Allow extra preparation time; keep reserve seafood refrigerated.

Chef's Note

Poke is seasoned cut seafood from Hawaii; this multi-topping bar is a contemporary bowl format. Choosing two seafoods or rice types changes the variety, not the total portion needed. Cucumber salad, soy and furikake each add seasoning, so offer them separately and start lightly.

Raw seafood sourcing

Tell the supplier the seafood will be served raw and ask for its species, cold-chain handling and applicable parasite-control information. “Sushi-grade” and “sashimi-grade” labels alone do not establish suitability. For wild salmon, require documented supplier parasite-destruction freezing; fresh wild-caught fish is not automatically preferable for raw service. For farmed salmon, obtain supplier documentation of either parasite-destruction freezing or qualifying raising and feeding conditions; a farmed label alone is insufficient. Yellowfin tuna and scallop products consisting only of the shucked adductor muscle have specific parasite-freezing exemptions, not a general guarantee of raw safety. Do not use a household freezer as an assumed substitute for a documented commercial process.

Freezing does not remove every seafood hazard, and this dressing is not a safety treatment. FDA advises children, pregnant people, older adults and people with weakened immune systems to avoid raw seafood; choose a fully cooked meal for those diners. Follow supplier refrigerator-thawing instructions and remove vacuum packaging before refrigerator thawing.

Scaling the bar

Scale the total fish and rice allocation across the choices, then divide dressing in proportion to the fish. Larger rice batches need a suitable pot or separate batches, and more fish needs additional refrigerated space and ice capacity. Allow extra preparation time; keep reserve seafood refrigerated.

data.title: Pressure-Cooker Bolognese
ingredients: 1 lb Pork or Veal Shoulder, chopped small
1 lb Mild or Spicy Italian Sausage, bulk
1 cup Dry Red Wine (The Finishing Touch)
1 can (28 oz) San Marzano Tomatoes, hand-crushed

body:
## Chef's Note

Ragù alla Bolognese originated in Bologna in the late 18th century as a slow-cooked meat sauce. The official recipe registered with the Bologna Chamber of Commerce in 1982 specifies a soffritto base (onion, celery, carrot), ground beef, pancetta, tomato paste, wine, and milk or cream - simmered for hours until thick and meaty. This pressure cooker version shortcuts the time while maintaining depth by developing a dark fond (browned bits) when searing the meat, then deglazing with red wine to extract those flavors. Use San Marzano tomatoes if possible - they're less acidic and sweeter than regular canned tomatoes. The balsamic vinegar at the end is not traditional but adds complexity.

## Directions

1.  **The Sear:** Set pressure cooker to "Sauté" (High). Brown the pork pieces in olive oil (5 mins); remove. Brown the crumbled sausage; remove.
2.  **The Base:** Add onion, carrots, and celery. Sauté for 5 minutes until soft. Add garlic and bay leaf; cook for 30-45 seconds.
3.  **The Bloom:** Stir in the tomato paste. Cook for 2 minutes until it turns a deep brick-red.
4.  **Deglaze:** Pour in the wine. Scrape the bottom of the pot vigorously to release the fond. Simmer for 2 minutes.
5.  **Pressure:** Return the meat to the pot. Add the crushed tomatoes. Secure the lid. Set to **High Pressure for 45 minutes**.
6.  **Reduce:** Perform a "Natural Release." Open the lid and set back to "Sauté." Simmer for 15-20 minutes until the sauce is thick and meaty.
7.  **Finish:** Stir in the fresh basil and balsamic vinegar. Taste and adjust with salt and pepper.
8.  **Serve:** Serve over [Fresh Egg Pasta](/mise/recipes/fresh-egg-pasta) with plenty of Parmesan.

data.title: Prohibition-Style Gin Lemon Fizz
ingredients: 3 oz Fresh Lemon Juice (The Acid Balance)
12 oz unsweetened sparkling water with lemon juice (to top)

body:
## Chef's Note

This cocktail showcases complex aromatic layering. The combination of herbal gin, rich cognac, and a hint of smoky mezcal creates a flavor profile that balances depth with brightness. Unsweetened sparkling water with lemon juice instead of standard soda water provides real fruit acidity that bridges the agave and botanicals. The orange bitters are added twice (in the shaker and on the surface) to ensure the aroma precedes the flavor.

## Directions

1.  **Thermal Prep:** Chill 3 highball glasses in the freezer.
2.  **The Base:** In a cocktail shaker filled with large ice cubes, combine gin, mezcal, cognac, lemon juice, agave, and 4 dashes of the orange bitters.
3.  **Aeration:** Shake vigorously for 15 seconds until the shaker is frosted and the mixture is perfectly cold.
4.  **Strain:** Double strain the mixture into the chilled highball glasses filled with fresh ice.
5.  **Effervescence:** Top each glass with 4 oz of unsweetened sparkling water with lemon juice. Stir once, very gently, to preserve the bubbles.
6.  **The Finishing Touch:** Add 1 final dash of orange bitters to the surface of each drink. Garnish with a lemon peel twist (expressed over the rim).

data.title: Puffy Muffin Chicken Salad
ingredients: 1/4 cup Red Onion, finely minced (the crunch)
1 tbsp Fresh Lemon Juice (The Acid Balance)

body:
## Chef's Note

Chicken salad with puffed muffins is a comfort food combo - creamy, chicken-based filling inside a tender, slightly sweet muffin. The muffin base matters: too dense and it overwhelms the filling; too light and it falls apart. Use a standard muffin recipe, then fill and bake so the muffin bakes around the filling rather than being stuffed afterward.

## Directions

1.  **Poach:** Bring a pot of salted water to a gentle boil. Add chicken tenders and cook for 8-10 minutes until just cooked through. Drain and let cool for 5 minutes.
2.  **The Pull:** While still warm, use two forks (or your hands) to pull the chicken into bite-sized shreds. Place in a large bowl.
3.  **The Mix:** In a small bowl, whisk together mayonnaise, lemon juice, salt, and pepper until perfectly smooth.
4.  **Combine:** Add the celery, grapes, and minced red onion to the chicken. Pour the dressing over the top.
5.  **Fold:** Toss gently until every piece of chicken is coated in the creamy emulsion.
6.  **Set:** Refrigerate for **at least 30 minutes** before serving. This allows the flavors to bloom and the texture to firm up.

scaling.reason: This method uses one 4–5 lb bone-in shoulder in a 6-quart slow cooker. Prepare separate batches for more servings; doubling the whole cut can exceed the cooker’s capacity and changes the heating time.

data.description: Bone-in pork shoulder slow-cooked with a smoky-sweet rub, onion, garlic, apple cider vinegar and Worcestershire, then pulled and moistened with its defatted cooking juices.

learning.focus: Use a slow cooker’s covered moisture and a pull-apart texture check for pork shoulder
learning.outcome: Moist, fork-pullable pork in distinct shreds or rough pieces, seasoned with the smoky rub and just enough defatted cooking juice to hold it together.
before: Use a 6-quart slow cooker only if the 4–5 pound bone-in shoulder fits below the lid without forcing it and the cooker instructions allow this size of whole cut. Cook one shoulder per cooker; a larger or doubled whole cut needs separate equipment and its own timing check.
Use hickory smoked salt for the rub. Its saltiness and smoke level are part of the rub; another smoked salt may season the pork differently.

Start with a fully thawed shoulder. The optional overnight seasoning is additional refrigerator time, not part of the 11-hour-30-minute same-day plan. Keep the raw pork covered or contained in the refrigerator at 40°F / 4°C or colder.

checkpoints.cue: The rub is evenly mixed before it touches the pork, with no pockets of brown sugar or smoked salt.
checkpoints.why: Mixing first distributes the sweet, smoky and savory seasonings across the shoulder instead of concentrating one component on a few bites.

checkpoints.cue: A thermometer in the thickest pork away from the bone reaches at least 145°F / 63°C, and a fork turns and separates the meat easily.
checkpoints.why: The temperature is the minimum safety check; the pull-apart texture is the separate endpoint for this cut. Either cue alone does not replace the other.

checkpoints.cue: The pork looks moist and seasoned after tossing, without standing in a pool of liquid.
checkpoints.why: Decanting the juices makes the amount returned deliberate. Too much liquid washes out the texture rather than restoring moisture.

troubleshooting.problem: Pork reaches the minimum temperature but will not pull apart
troubleshooting.cause: The shoulder needs more covered cooking for its connective tissue to soften, or the cooker runs cool.
troubleshooting.fix: Cover and continue on LOW, checking the fork texture in 30-minute intervals. Do not treat 10–11 hours as a universal finish time.

troubleshooting.problem: Pork is wet and bland after it is returned to the cooker
troubleshooting.cause: Too much cooking liquid was returned at once.
troubleshooting.fix: Lift out the pork with tongs and leave the excess liquid behind. Toss in a little defatted juice at a time.

troubleshooting.problem: The slow-cooker lid will not close over the shoulder
troubleshooting.cause: The cut is too large or too tall for the cooker.
troubleshooting.fix: Use a larger slow cooker or cook the shoulder in a separate batch. Do not cook with an ajar lid, which changes the heat and moisture conditions.

substitutions.alternative: A gluten-free Worcestershire sauce
substitutions.effect: Preserves the savory, tangy pot base for a gluten-free table when the product label also confirms it. Flavor and saltiness can vary, so taste the finished pork before adding any more seasoning.

learning.timing: Allow about 11 hours 30 minutes on the same day: roughly 15 minutes to mix and apply the rub, assemble the cooker and start cooking; 10–11 hours on LOW; then up to 15 minutes to rest, pull, decant, skim and moisten the pork. Finish by temperature and fork texture. Optional overnight seasoning is separate refrigerator time. The cutting, decanting and final toss happen after the slow cook and do not run in parallel.
learning.storage: Portion the pork with a little cooking juice into shallow containers and refrigerate within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the air is above 90°F / 32°C, at 40°F / 4°C or colder. Use cooked meat within 3–4 days, or freeze portions within that window for later use. Reheat a portion on the stovetop, in the oven or in the microwave until it reaches 165°F / 74°C throughout; do not use the slow cooker to reheat refrigerator-cold leftovers.

body:
## Chef's Note

This pulled pork uses a bone-in Boston butt, hickory-smoked salt, smoky-sweet rub
and a simple vinegar–Worcestershire pot base. The
clock gets the shoulder close, but the finished meat should meet both a safe
temperature and the fork-pullable texture that makes it ready to shred. Decant
the cooking liquid before returning any of it so the meat stays moist rather
than soupy.

## Directions

1. **Mix and apply the rub:** Start with a fully thawed pork shoulder. Mix the brown sugar, hickory smoked salt, smoked paprika, garlic powder, onion powder, cumin and pepper. Rub it over every surface of the pork. For an optional overnight seasoning, put the pork in a covered container and refrigerate at 40°F / 4°C or colder; this time is not included in the recipe total.
2. **Build the pot base:** Scatter the onion and garlic across the bottom of a 6-quart slow cooker. Pour in the apple cider vinegar and Worcestershire sauce.
3. **Load the shoulder:** Set the rubbed shoulder, fat cap up, on the aromatics. The lid must close fully. Do not add extra liquid; the pork releases juices as it cooks.
4. **Cook until safe and pullable:** Cover and cook on LOW for about 10–11 hours. Check the thickest pork away from the bone with an instant-read thermometer; it must reach at least 145°F / 63°C. It is ready to pull only when a fork turns and separates the meat easily and the bone slides out cleanly. If it is safe but still firm, cover and continue in 30-minute intervals until tender.
5. **Pull the pork:** Transfer the shoulder to a cutting board and rest for at least 3 minutes before pulling. Remove the bone and discard large pieces of fat or gristle. Pull or chop the pork into rough pieces.
6. **Decant, skim and moisten:** Pour the cooking liquid into a heatproof jug and skim off excess fat. Return the pork to the slow cooker. Add the defatted liquid a little at a time, tossing after each addition, until the meat is moist and flavorful rather than submerged.
7. **Serve or store promptly:** Serve with cornbread and coleslaw, or use the pork in tacos, bowls or sandwiches. For later meals, portion and chill it promptly using the storage guidance.

body:
## Chef's Note

These breakfast cookies are ideal for busy mornings when you need portable nutrition. The secret to their incredible texture is using both rolled and quick-cooking oats, creating a cookie that's dense and chewy without crumbling. Coconut oil and honey serve as the primary binders and natural sweeteners. These cookies are intentionally designed not to spread; you must flatten them by hand before baking to achieve the desired shape.

## Directions

1.  **The Emulsion:** In a small bowl, whisk the melted coconut oil and honey until smooth. In a separate large bowl, whisk the eggs and pumpkin puree. Combine the two mixtures.
2.  **The Dry Mix:** In a massive bowl, toss together both types of oats, flaxseed, cranberries, pumpkin seeds, and spices.
3.  **Combine:** Pour the pumpkin emulsion over the dry ingredients. Stir vigorously until a thick, sticky dough forms.
4.  **Shape:** Preheat oven to 350°F. Line a baking sheet with parchment. Scoop 1/4-cup portions of dough and **press down firmly** with your palm to create a 3/4-inch thick disk.
5.  **Bake:** Bake for 15-20 minutes until the edges are golden brown and the center feels firm.
6.  **The Finish:** Let cool completely on the pan. This is mandatory for the flax and coconut oil to set the "Bounce."

body:
## Chef's Note

Soft pumpkin cookies surround a creamy cheesecake filling, with cinnamon-ginger sugar on the outside. Chilling makes the dough easier to wrap, while freezing firms the sweetened cream cheese enough to handle. Divide both mixtures into 12 equal portions so every cookie has the same dough-to-filling ratio.

## Directions

1. **Mix the dry ingredients:** Whisk the dough's all-purpose flour, baking soda, ground cinnamon, ground ginger, ground nutmeg, and fine salt together.
2. **Cream the butter and sugars:** With a stand or hand mixer, beat the dough's unsalted butter, light brown sugar, and granulated sugar until lighter, about 1 minute.
3. **Finish the dough:** Measure the plain pumpkin puree before gently blotting or squeezing away excess moisture with a clean paper towel, then mix it into the butter mixture. Mix in the prepared dry ingredients on low speed only until combined, scraping the bowl as needed.
4. **Chill the dough:** Divide the dough into 12 equal portions on a parchment-lined tray. Refrigerate for about 1 hour, until firm enough to flatten and fill.
5. **Firm the filling:** While the dough chills, beat the filling's full-fat block cream cheese, granulated sugar, and vanilla extract until smooth. Divide into 12 equal dollops on a parchment-lined plate. Freeze for at least 45 minutes, until easy to pick up; they need not become rock-hard.
6. **Prepare to fill:** Heat the oven to 350°F while the dough and filling finish chilling. Line two large baking sheets with parchment. Stir the coating's granulated sugar, ground cinnamon, and ground ginger together in a small bowl.
7. **Wrap and coat:** Flatten each chilled dough portion, place one filling portion in the middle, and wrap the dough around it, pinching the seams closed. If the dough sticks to warm hands, flatten it between two pieces of parchment. Rechill the dough or filling if either becomes too soft to handle. Roll the stuffed portions in the cinnamon-ginger sugar, space them 3 inches apart on the sheets, and flatten slightly. Keep any portions waiting to bake refrigerated.
8. **Bake:** Bake for 16–19 minutes per batch, until the outside and edges have set; do not wait for deep browning. The centers will still feel soft. Allow extra time if your oven requires baking one sheet at a time.
9. **Cool and refrigerate:** Let the cookies firm on the tray for 10 minutes, then transfer to a rack. After this brief initial cooling, refrigerate the cream-cheese-filled cookies in a single layer to finish cooling; cover once cold. Get them into the refrigerator within 2 hours of baking, or 1 hour if the room is above 90°F. Serve chilled.

## Timing and storage

Allow about 2 hours for mixing, overlapping dough and filling chills, shaping, one oven batch, and initial cooling. Extra oven batches, rechilling during assembly, and cooling completely for cold service take longer.

The filled, baked cookies need refrigeration even though the dough contains no egg. Store covered at 40°F or below and use within 3–4 days, or freeze for longer storage and thaw in the refrigerator. Keep the cream-cheese filling and assembled unbaked cookies chilled whenever you pause; the dough's one-hour handling chill is not a room-temperature storage allowance. Limit the baked cookies' combined cooling and serving time out of refrigeration to 2 hours, or 1 hour above 90°F.

export.total_time: About 2 hours (estimated; includes chilling and initial cooling)
export.notes:
Chef's Note

Soft pumpkin cookies surround a creamy cheesecake filling, with cinnamon-ginger sugar on the outside. Chilling makes the dough easier to wrap, while freezing firms the sweetened cream cheese enough to handle. Divide both mixtures into 12 equal portions so every cookie has the same dough-to-filling ratio.

Timing and storage

Allow about 2 hours for mixing, overlapping dough and filling chills, shaping, one oven batch, and initial cooling. Extra oven batches, rechilling during assembly, and cooling completely for cold service take longer.

data.title: Aromatic Purple Rice

scaling.reason: The first cooking stage needs the stated water depth, and the complete batch is sized for this pot. Make another batch for more portions.

ingredients: 1/2 cup whole-grain aromatic purple rice, with a stated stovetop cooking time around 45 minutes; not glutinous black rice or a quick-cooking blend
1 1/8 cups (270 ml) water, for starting the purple rice
1 1/2 cups Japanese-style medium-grain white rice, not brown or parboiled
1 1/8 cups (270 ml) water, for soaking and cooking the white rice
3/4 cup (180 ml) unsalted chicken stock, for soaking and cooking the white rice
1/4 tsp fine salt, plus up to 1/4 tsp more after tasting
1 tsp coconut oil or unsalted butter, optional
1/2 cup (120 ml) hot water, reserved only for correcting evaporation or firm grains
data.description: Tender white rice and nutty purple grains cook together in a lightly seasoned broth after the whole grain gets a head start.

learning.focus: Give whole-grain rice a head start, then finish the blend in its colored cooking liquid
learning.outcome: Lightly cohesive purple-tinted rice, with tender white grains and a gentle chew from the whole purple grains. Neither grain has a hard center.
before: Use standard 240 ml measuring cups. Choose whole-grain aromatic purple rice whose package calls for about 45 minutes on the stove; faster-cooking glutinous black rice needs a different head start.
A tightly lidded 2-quart pot with a 6–7-inch base suits the small first stage and leaves room for the complete batch. Keep the simmer very gentle so the purple grain does not dry out.
The starting liquid totals 720 ml: 270 ml with the purple rice and 450 ml with the white rice. Keep all of it. The separate 120 ml hot-water reserve is extra, used only if needed.

checkpoints.cue: A purple grain is swollen with a softened outside and a firmer center, not hard throughout.
checkpoints.why: Partial cooking gives the whole grain time to hydrate before adding the faster-cooking white rice.

checkpoints.cue: Both grains are gently simmering in the same purple-tinted liquid after the pot reheats.
checkpoints.why: The white grains absorb that liquid as they cook, carrying its color and stock seasoning into the blend.

checkpoints.cue: Both sampled grains are tender inside and there is no pool of water at the bottom.
checkpoints.why: A dry pot or a purple color alone does not show that both grain centers have finished cooking.

troubleshooting.problem: The purple stage dries before the grain is partly tender
troubleshooting.cause: The simmer was too strong or the lid allowed too much steam to escape.
troubleshooting.fix: Lower the heat and add 2 tbsp from the hot-water reserve. Re-cover and check after five minutes. This is extra correction water; do not discard purple liquid or add a second white-rice water allowance later.

troubleshooting.problem: Grains are still firm and the combined pot is dry
troubleshooting.cause: More water evaporated than expected or this grain needs additional hydration.
troubleshooting.fix: Add 2 tbsp from the remaining reserve, cover and cook gently another five minutes, then taste both grains. Use no more than the listed 120 ml reserve across the whole recipe. If white rice is already soft, further cooking will soften it more; a longer purple head start is the better adjustment for the next batch.

troubleshooting.problem: Both grains are tender but rice is wet
troubleshooting.cause: The rice or pot retained more water than needed.
troubleshooting.fix: Uncover briefly over very low heat to release surface moisture, then turn off the heat. Avoid vigorous stirring, which breaks the soft white grains.

substitutions.alternative: The same volume of water or unsalted vegetable stock
substitutions.effect: Gives a vegetarian version; use coconut oil or omit the optional fat for a vegan version. Choose gluten-free stock or water for the gluten-free version.

learning.timing: Allow about 80 minutes, including rinsing, heating, a 25–30-minute purple-rice head start, reheating after the white rice is added, a 15–20-minute combined simmer and a ten-minute rest. The white rice's 20-minute soak overlaps the purple stage. Active work is about 15–20 minutes; additional hydration can extend the total.
learning.storage: Divide into shallow containers and refrigerate within 2 hours, or 1 hour above 90°F / 32°C. Keep at 40°F / 4°C or below for 3–4 days. Reheat to 165°F / 74°C, covered with a little water to soften the refrigerated grains. Do not leave the full pot cooling slowly on the counter.

body:
## Chef's Note

White rice softens the chewy texture and nutty flavor of whole-grain purple rice. Give the purple grain a head start, then let both finish in the same colored cooking liquid. The white grains take on a purple tint while a little chicken stock rounds out the flavor.

## Directions

1. **Rinse separately:** Rinse the purple rice briefly in cool water and drain. Rinse the white rice in several changes of water until much of the loose starch has washed away, then drain well. Purple pigment may continue to tint its rinsing water; it need not run colorless.
2. **Start the purple rice:** Put purple rice and its 270 ml water in the saucepan. Bring to a boil, cover tightly and reduce heat to a very gentle simmer. Set a timer for 20 minutes and continue with the white rice while it cooks.
3. **Soak the white rice:** Combine drained white rice with its 270 ml water, 180 ml chicken stock and the initial 1/4 tsp salt in a bowl. Soak for 20 minutes in this measured liquid. Keep all the liquid for the cooking pot; do not drain it afterward.
4. **Check the head start:** At 20 minutes, check that the purple rice is still moist and taste a grain. Continue gently until the grains are swollen with softened outsides but firmer centers, usually 25–30 minutes total. If still hard throughout, give them another five minutes before adding the white rice. If the pot is drying, add 2 tbsp from the separate hot-water reserve and lower the heat. Re-cover between checks. Retain all the purple cooking liquid.
5. **Combine and reheat:** Add the white rice with all its soaking liquid to the purple rice and stir once to distribute the grains. Bring back to a gentle boil, allowing about five minutes for the pot to reheat. Cover, reduce heat to low and simmer gently for 15–20 minutes, starting that timer only once the combined pot is simmering.
6. **Check both grains and rest:** Taste a white grain and a purple grain. Both should be tender inside, with the purple grain retaining a slight chew, and the cooking liquid should be absorbed. Use the measured correction reserve if the pot is dry and grains are firm. Once ready, turn off heat and rest covered for 10 minutes.
7. **Fluff and season:** Fold gently with a rice paddle or fork, incorporating the optional coconut oil or butter. Taste and add some or all of the reserved salt if wanted. The batch makes approximately 5–6 cups; divide into seven small side portions, roughly 3/4 cup each depending on final yield.

body:
## Chef's Note

Folding chunks of bittersweet, white, and milk chocolate into unsweetened chocolate batter, then drizzling melted versions on top before swirling creates varying textures in every square - some pockets stay fudgy, others develop crisp edges. A full pound of unsweetened chocolate as the base provides bitter depth that balances the sugar and eggs, preventing these dense, rich brownies from tasting overly sweet.

## Directions

1.  **The Melt:** Preheat oven to 300°F. In a large saucepan, melt the butter and unsweetened chocolate over low heat until glossy. Let cool for 10 minutes.
2.  **The Emulsion:** In a massive bowl, whisk sugar, eggs, vanilla, and salt until thick and pale. Stir in the melted chocolate.
3.  **Incorporate:** Gradually fold in the flour until **just combined**. Fold in 5 oz each of the chopped bittersweet, white, and milk chocolates.
4.  **Assemble:** Spread the batter into two greased 9x13-inch pans.
5.  **The Swirl:** Melt the remaining chopped chocolates in separate microwave-safe bowls. Drizzle the three chocolates over the batter and use a knife to create a marbled "High Note" pattern.
6.  **Bake:** Bake for 35-40 minutes until the tops are mirror-shiny and the edges are firm.
7.  **The Finish:** Cool **completely** in the pans before slicing into squares. This is mandatory for the structural integrity.

data.title: Queso Fundido with Chorizo
ingredients: 2 Poblano Peppers, roasted, peeled, and diced

body:
## Chef's Note

Queso fundido is Mexico's answer to fondue - molten cheese with smoky chorizo, meant to be scooped with warm tortillas. The key is using Oaxaca cheese, which melts into long, stretchy strands without breaking. Roasting the poblanos first adds a layer of charred sweetness that elevates this beyond typical bar queso. Serve it straight from the oven in the cast iron - it stays molten for about 10 minutes before it starts to set. Make a half-batch without chorizo for vegetarians.

## Directions

1. **The Char:** Roast poblanos directly over a gas flame or under the broiler, turning until blackened all over (about 8 minutes). Place in a bowl, cover with plastic wrap for 5 minutes. Peel off skins, remove seeds, and dice.

2. **The Render:** Preheat oven to 400°F. In a 10-inch cast iron skillet, cook chorizo over medium-high heat, breaking into small pieces, until crispy and fat has rendered (5-6 minutes). Transfer chorizo to a plate, leaving fat in pan.

3. **The Soften:** Add onion and garlic to the chorizo fat. Sauté until softened (3 minutes). Add diced poblanos and stir to combine.

4. **The Melt:** Remove skillet from heat. Scatter both cheeses evenly over the vegetables. Top with the crispy chorizo.

5. **The Bubble:** Bake for **8-10 minutes** until cheese is completely melted and bubbling at the edges.

6. **The Finish:** Remove from oven. Top with fresh cilantro and pickled jalapeños if using.

Skip the chorizo. Sauté the onion and garlic in 1 tbsp olive oil. Add 1 tsp smoked paprika and 1/2 tsp cumin for smoky depth.

data.title: Caprese Pasta
ingredients: 8 oz fresh mozzarella, drained and cut into pieces about 1/2 inch across
6 ripe Roma tomatoes, cored, seeded and chopped
1 tbsp fresh lemon juice, added to taste
Salt and freshly ground black pepper, to taste
1/2 cup hot pasta cooking water, reserved before draining; use only as needed
data.source: Adapted from Sara Welch, Dinner at the Zoo
data.description: Angel hair with warm tomatoes, garlic, basil and soft pieces of fresh mozzarella.

learning.focus: Warm tomatoes and soften fresh mozzarella without melting it into a sticky mass
learning.outcome: Distinct juicy tomato pieces and soft mozzarella among lightly coated, tender angel hair.
before: Drain mozzarella well and cut into small similar pieces. Large halved bocconcini vary in size and can stay cold in the center while pasta overcooks.
Prepare tomatoes, garlic and cheese before dropping angel hair into boiling water; it cooks quickly and should not wait while the sauce starts.
Use a large skillet or serving bowl with room to lift the strands gently. For bigger batches use more than one vessel rather than vigorous tossing that crushes tomatoes and tangles noodles.

checkpoints.cue: Garlic smells fragrant without brown edges and tomatoes are warm but retain their shape.
checkpoints.why: This is a brief warm tomato coating, not a long-reduced sauce.

checkpoints.cue: Angel hair is tender with a little bite at its package-directed time.
checkpoints.why: An exact two-minute rule does not suit every product, and there is no further boiling stage.

checkpoints.cue: Pasta is hot but no longer steaming fiercely before mozzarella is folded in.
checkpoints.why: A brief cooling pause helps cheese stay in soft pieces instead of melting into strings and clumps.

troubleshooting.cause: It was stirred into very hot pasta or heated on the burner.
troubleshooting.fix: Stop heating and handle gently. Fully melted cheese will not become neat cubes again; next time let pasta cool briefly before adding it.

troubleshooting.cause: Tomatoes were especially juicy or mozzarella was not drained.
troubleshooting.fix: Lift pasta out of pooled liquid and use little or no reserved water. Drain cheese and remove tomato seeds/loose gel before cooking next time.

troubleshooting.problem: Angel hair sticks into a mass
troubleshooting.cause: It drained and waited before sauce was ready.
troubleshooting.fix: Toss gently with a small splash of warm cooking water. Prepare the tomato coating first on the next batch.

substitutions.alternative: The same dry weight of spaghetti
substitutions.effect: Takes longer to boil; use its package timing and keep the tomato coating off heat until needed.

substitutions.alternative: Fresh mozzarella made with vegetarian rennet
substitutions.effect: Supports the vegetarian option. Low-moisture pizza mozzarella melts differently and will not give the same soft fresh-cheese pieces.

learning.timing: Allow about 35 minutes including twenty minutes preparing the tomatoes and cheese while water heats, a brief tomato sauté, package-dependent pasta cooking and a short cooling pause before mozzarella. A fifteen-minute meal assumes much of the cutting and water heating is already done.
learning.storage: Refrigerate promptly in shallow containers within 2 hours, or 1 hour above 90°F / 32°C, at 40°F / 4°C or below. Plan to use the next day for texture. Reheat the portion needed with a little water, stirring, to 165°F / 74°C throughout. Pasta absorbs sauce and softens during storage; fresh herbs and cheese lose some of their original texture.

body:
## Chef's Note

Warm the tomatoes just enough to release some juice, then toss with the pasta away from the burner. Let the mixture lose its fiercest heat before adding mozzarella. The aim is soft pieces of fresh cheese, not a melted cheese sauce.

## Directions

1. **Prepare before boiling pasta:** Bring a large pot of water to a boil. Core, seed and chop tomatoes, mince garlic, drain and cut mozzarella, and chop basil. Season water with salt.
2. **Warm tomatoes:** Heat olive oil in a large skillet over medium-low to medium. Stir in garlic and Italian seasoning for **30–60 seconds**, until fragrant without browning. Add tomatoes and a little salt; cook about **2–3 minutes** until warm but still distinct. Remove from heat.
3. **Cook angel hair:** Add pasta to the boiling water and stir gently. Cook according to its package until tender with a little bite, tasting near the end. Reserve **the listed cooking water** before draining without rinsing.
4. **Combine and cool briefly:** Add pasta to the tomato mixture away from heat, transferring to a serving bowl if the skillet is crowded or retains strong heat. Add **half the lemon juice** and lift gently to coat, using a small splash of cooking water only if dry. Let stand about **1–2 minutes**, until no longer steaming fiercely.
5. **Fold and serve:** Fold in mozzarella and basil gently. Taste, then add the remaining lemon juice, salt and pepper only as needed. Serve promptly while the cheese is softened but still in distinct pieces; do not return to the burner to force melting.

Adapted from [Sara Welch’s Caprese Pasta at Dinner at the Zoo](https://www.dinneratthezoo.com/caprese-pasta/).
