data.title: Shaved Brussels Sprout Salad
ingredients: 3 tbsp Apple Cider Vinegar (The Acid Balance)

body:
## Chef's Note

Shaving Brussels sprouts paper-thin transforms them from dense and bitter to light and crisp - a technique that became popular in modern Italian-American restaurants during the 2000s. Tossing the shaved sprouts with vinegar dressing 15 minutes before serving softens them slightly while maintaining their crunch. Pecorino Romano adds the sharp, salty note that balances the sweet apple and tangy dressing.

## Directions

1.  **The Dressing:** In a large bowl, whisk together vinegar, honey, oil, salt, and pepper until thick and emulsified.
2.  **The Crunch:** Core the apple and cut into fine matchsticks. Immediately toss with 1 tbsp of the dressing to prevent browning.
3.  **Shave:** Use a mandoline or a very sharp chef's knife to shave the Brussels sprouts as thinly as possible. Discard the tough woody stems.
4.  **Bind:** Add the shaved sprouts to the dressing. Toss vigorously with your hands until every strand is coated. Let stand at room temperature for **at least 15 minutes**.
5.  **Finish:** Add the apples and the Pecorino. Toss gently to combine.
6.  **Serve:** Season with an extra crack of black pepper and serve chilled.

data.title: Shaved Fennel Citrus Salad
ingredients: 2 large fennel bulbs, stalks removed, tender fronds reserved
2 large navel or Cara Cara oranges
1 tbsp reserved citrus juice, collected while preparing the oranges or grapefruit
1/4 tsp kosher salt, added gradually to taste
2 tbsp shaved Parmesan; choose vegetarian-rennet cheese for a vegetarian version, or omit for vegan
1/4 cup pitted Castelvetrano olives, halved, optional
Cold water and ice, only if crisping the shaved fennel
data.description: Paper-thin fennel and juicy citrus with a light honey-lemon dressing, optional olives and shaved Parmesan.

learning.focus: Prepare crisp shaved vegetables and citrus without watering down their dressing
learning.outcome: Tender-crisp fennel ribbons and intact citrus segments with a light coating of dressing.
before: A sharp knife works if you can slice the fennel thinly; a mandoline is convenient, not essential. Use its hand guard and stop before the remaining piece gets too small to hold safely.
Wash produce before cutting. Reserve fronds from the same bulbs, not an additional bunch. Work over a bowl when segmenting citrus so the juice for the dressing is captured.

Two large bulbs make generous sides; bulb size varies. For larger batches allow additional shaving and segmenting time, use broad platters and dress in batches near service. Ingredient arithmetic does not shorten knife work.

checkpoints.cue: A fennel ribbon bends easily and can be bitten through without a woody center.
checkpoints.why: Thin slicing makes raw fennel easier to eat; thick core pieces need trimming rather than extra dressing.

checkpoints.cue: Segments are free of white pith and membrane, with their juice collected separately.
checkpoints.why: Pith adds bitterness, while uncontrolled juice on the platter dilutes the dressing.

checkpoints.cue: The fennel is lightly glossy with no deep pool of dressing beneath it.
checkpoints.why: Drying after an ice bath and dressing gradually keep the salad crisp and the citrus intact.

troubleshooting.cause: Slices are thick or include the dense core.
troubleshooting.fix: Trim out woody pieces and slice thinner. Dressing cannot make thick raw wedges instantly tender.

troubleshooting.cause: Fennel was not dried after soaking or citrus released excess juice.
troubleshooting.fix: Lift onto a clean platter with a slotted spoon and offer extra dressing separately. Next time dry thoroughly and dress just before serving.

troubleshooting.cause: Olives and cheese already provided enough salt.
troubleshooting.fix: Stop adding the measured salt and extra cheese. Taste a complete bite before seasoning the rest; more lemon does not remove salt.

substitutions.alternative: Omit it
substitutions.effect: Makes a sweeter, less bitter salad without changing the required oranges.

substitutions.alternative: Omit Parmesan and use the listed agave option
substitutions.effect: Makes the salad vegan; olives can supply a briny accent if desired.

learning.timing: Allow about 30 minutes for trimming and shaving two bulbs, segmenting citrus and assembling. A five-to-ten-minute optional fennel ice bath can overlap citrus preparation. Knife experience and bulb size affect preparation time; no cooking is required.
learning.storage: For same-day preparation, refrigerate washed shaved fennel, drained citrus and dressing separately at 40°F / 4°C or below; dry fennel before assembly. Dress near service. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours, or 1 hour above 90°F / 32°C, and use the next day for texture. Citrus dressing is not a preservation treatment.

sources.title: FoodSafety.gov — Clean, separate, cook, chill

body:
## Chef's Note

Thin fennel ribbons bring anise flavor and crunch, while citrus adds juice and sweetness. A short ice bath can refresh the shaved fennel, but dry it well afterward. Add dressing gradually and taste with the olives and cheese before using all the salt.

## Directions

1. **Shave fennel:** Wash the bulbs and fronds. Trim stalks and damaged outer layers, halve the bulbs lengthwise and cut out the hard core. Shave thinly with a sharp knife or a guarded mandoline. If the ribbons need crisping, immerse in ice water for **5–10 minutes** while preparing the citrus; drain and spin or pat thoroughly dry.
2. **Segment citrus:** Cut the tops and bottoms off the oranges and optional grapefruit. Set on a flat cut end and slice away peel and white pith. Over a bowl, cut between membranes to release segments. Squeeze the remaining membranes to collect juice, and measure the listed amount for the dressing. Reserve any excess juice for another use, rather than pouring it all over the salad.
3. **Whisk dressing:** Whisk olive oil, lemon juice, **the measured reserved citrus juice**, honey or agave, pepper and **half the salt**. Taste with a fennel ribbon. The dressing should be bright but not harsh; the cheese and optional olives will add more salt.
4. **Assemble and taste:** Spread dried fennel on a broad platter and arrange citrus segments over it. Add optional olives. Drizzle about **half the dressing**, turn gently and taste a complete bite with a little Parmesan if using. Add more dressing and the remaining salt only as needed. Offer unused dressing separately. Finish with the Parmesan and reserved tender fronds and serve promptly.

data.title: Roasted Chicken, Broccoli and Cheddar Bake
ingredients: 680 g (1 1/2 lb) boneless skinless chicken thighs, cut into 1 1/2-inch pieces
450 g broccoli florets, cut into even 1 1/2-inch pieces, washed and dried
data.description: Chicken and broccoli roasted separately, then combined with a smooth broth-based Cheddar sauce and measured panko topping.

learning.focus: Cook the components to their own endpoints before the short sauced bake
learning.outcome: Tender chicken, broccoli with some roasted flavor and a smooth Cheddar coating under a crisp breadcrumb top.
before: Use separate trays so the broccoli can come out before the chicken if needed. A crowded mixed tray makes independent doneness harder to control.
The final sauce softens roasted surfaces. The crisp element at serving is the breadcrumb topping, not a guarantee of crunchy broccoli underneath.

checkpoints.cue: Broccoli is just tender with browned tips; thick chicken pieces reach 165°F / 74°C.
checkpoints.why: Vegetable texture and poultry temperature are different endpoints, even when they share an oven.

checkpoints.cue: The broth mixture coats a spoon before cheese is added off the heat.
checkpoints.why: Flour starch thickens the aqueous base. Gentle cheese melting limits graininess; boiling after cheese goes in can destabilize the sauce.

checkpoints.cue: The center is hot, the sauce bubbles at the edges and panko is golden.
checkpoints.why: A browned top alone cannot verify the temperature of a deeper casserole.

troubleshooting.problem: Cheese sauce looks oily or grainy
troubleshooting.cause: Cheese was stirred into a fiercely boiling base or held over high heat.
troubleshooting.fix: Remove from heat and whisk in a tablespoon of warm broth. A badly split sauce may not fully recover; next time thicken the broth first and melt cheese gently.

troubleshooting.cause: It was roasted until fully soft, then baked too long in sauce.
troubleshooting.fix: Remove it from the first roast as soon as barely tender and keep the final bake brief. Larger even florets are more forgiving than tiny fragments.

substitutions.alternative: 115 g mild Cheddar
substitutions.effect: Usually gives a milder, smoother sauce. Very aged, dry cheese can melt less evenly; grate finely and add gradually.

substitutions.alternative: 680 g chicken breast, cut into 1 1/2-inch pieces
substitutions.effect: Begin temperature checks earlier and remove at 165°F / 74°C. Breast is less forgiving of the second heating, so avoid extra browning time.

learning.timing: About seventy minutes includes preheating and preparation, 15–25 minutes component roasting, sauce making during the roast, assembly, a 10–15-minute final bake and a five-minute stand.
learning.storage: Refrigerate in shallow containers within 2 hours (1 hour above 90°F / 32°C), at 40°F / 4°C or below. Use within 3–4 days; reheat leftovers to 165°F / 74°C. Store in shallow portions rather than leaving a deep dish to cool on the counter. Reheat covered to 165°F / 74°C; the breadcrumb topping will soften.

## Chef's Note

Roasting before adding sauce gives broccoli and chicken some browned flavor. The broth-based roux then thickens the liquid around the cheese, so the finished bake is creamy without relying on condensed soup. This is a casserole with a roasting stage; it needs two trays, a saucepan and a baking dish.

## Directions

1. **Prepare the trays and topping:** Heat oven to 425°F / 220°C with racks in the upper and lower thirds. Toss chicken on one tray with 1 tbsp oil and half the salt and pepper. Toss dry broccoli on the other tray with the remaining tablespoon oil and salt/pepper. Spread both out. Mix panko with its separate tablespoon oil.
2. **Roast independently:** Roast both trays, swapping rack positions once. Start checking broccoli at 15 minutes and chicken at 18 minutes. Remove broccoli when barely tender with browned tips, usually 15–20 minutes. Chicken may need 18–25 minutes; check thick pieces reach 165°F / 74°C. Remove each tray when ready rather than waiting for them to match.
3. **Make sauce during roasting:** Melt butter in a saucepan over medium-low. Whisk in flour and cook 1–2 minutes without darkening. Add broth gradually, whisking smooth after each addition. Bring to a gentle simmer and cook 3–4 minutes, stirring, until thickened enough to coat a spoon. Remove from heat, wait for bubbling to subside and stir in Cheddar a handful at a time, then garlic powder.
4. **Assemble:** Put roasted chicken and broccoli in a 3-quart baking dish. Pour over the sauce and fold gently to coat. Scatter the oiled panko evenly over the top. Use a dish deep enough to contain the sauce without packing the food tightly.
5. **Bake and serve:** Return to the 425°F oven for about 10–15 minutes, until panko is golden, edges bubble and the center reaches 165°F / 74°C. If the topping colors early, shield it loosely with foil. Let stand about 5 minutes before portioning into four servings; handle the hot dish carefully.

data.title: Sheet Pan Chicken Fajitas
data.source: Adapted from Natalie Mortimer at The Modern Proper

scaling.reason: This six-portion batch uses two rimmed half-sheet pans. More filling needs additional pans and oven rounds; a smaller batch still needs room around the chicken and its own doneness checks.

ingredients: 2 lb (907 g) boneless skinless chicken breast, trimmed
1 red bell pepper, stemmed, seeded and sliced
1 yellow bell pepper, stemmed, seeded and sliced
1 green bell pepper, stemmed, seeded and sliced
1 tbsp olive oil, for coating the filling
1 tsp olive oil, for the two pans
1 1/2 tsp ground ancho chile, without salt or other seasonings
Ripe avocado, sliced, optional, for serving
Salsa or hot sauce, optional, for serving
data.description: Lime-seasoned chicken breast, three colors of peppers and red onion roasted on two pans, with warm tortillas and fresh cilantro. A brief optional broil adds browned edges.

learning.focus: Match strip thickness and pan loading to an even roast
learning.outcome: Chicken is cooked through but still moist, peppers are tender with some browned edges, and the warm tortillas bend easily around the filling.
before: Use two rimmed metal half-sheet pans and an oven that can hold them on upper- and lower-third racks with air space. Foil is optional; parchment must not go under the broiler. If only one pan fits, cook two separate rounds, keeping the second raw portion refrigerated.

Mix the eight listed seasonings as the complete seasoning for this batch; do not add a taco-seasoning packet as well. Use ground ancho chile without added salt, not hot cayenne. The blend already includes salt.

Prepare peppers, onion and ready-to-eat toppings before cutting chicken. Do not wash raw chicken. Use separate clean utensils for cooked food and wash hands and the cutting surface after raw preparation. Vegetables tossed with raw chicken must cook with it.

checkpoints.cue: Chicken strips lie flat without overlapping; vegetables are spread loosely around them.
checkpoints.why: Crowding traps moisture and makes the mixture steam; some pan juice is still normal.

checkpoints.cue: Several thick chicken strips on each pan reach 165°F / 74°C and peppers bend readily.
checkpoints.why: Strip thickness and oven hot spots affect timing; surface color cannot establish doneness.

checkpoints.cue: Vegetable edges brown in spots before the spices blacken.
checkpoints.why: A broiler heats the surface quickly and can scorch the coating while the chicken dries out.

troubleshooting.problem: Chicken is done before the vegetables are tender
troubleshooting.cause: Chicken strips were thinner or vegetables thicker than intended.
troubleshooting.fix: Move cooked chicken to a clean bowl and cover. Continue roasting the vegetables until tender, then combine. Next time cut consistently; do not keep cooking done breast meat just to darken the peppers.

troubleshooting.cause: Vegetables release water, especially if packed tightly or wet when seasoned.
troubleshooting.fix: Once the chicken is safely cooked, lift the filling out with a slotted spoon. For more color, remove the chicken, spoon off the pool and briefly broil the vegetables. Some overlap and juice are normal; this method does not produce dry skillet-seared vegetables.

troubleshooting.cause: The pan is too close to the element or stayed under it too long.
troubleshooting.fix: Stop broiling immediately. Move unburned food away from scorched residue; bitter burnt seasoning cannot be reversed.

substitutions.alternative: The same number of 6-inch corn tortillas
substitutions.effect: Changes the flavor and makes a gluten-free version when the tortillas and all seasonings are gluten-free. Warm according to the package; corn tortillas can split when cold.

substitutions.alternative: The same number of similar-sized bell peppers in other colors
substitutions.effect: Green peppers taste more grassy and red or yellow peppers sweeter. Keep the same cut and avoid crowding the pans; very large peppers may need more pan space.

substitutions.alternative: Prepared guacamole served in its place
substitutions.effect: Adds onion, tomato, lime and spice as well as avocado. The complete dinner specifies its amount and preparation time; it does not require both avocado toppings.

learning.timing: Allow about 55–60 minutes for preheating, cutting, seasoning, two-pan roasting, optional broiling and warming twelve tortillas. Active work is about 30–40 minutes. Begin checking the chicken after 15 minutes; the two-pan roast may need 20–25 minutes. A one-pan oven requires separate rounds and about 20–30 extra minutes. There is no required ten-minute marinade wait.
learning.storage: Refrigerate filling in shallow containers within 2 hours, or 1 hour above 90°F / 32°C, at 40°F / 4°C or below. Use within 3–4 days; reheat to 165°F / 74°C. Keep tortillas and cold toppings separate. Slice avocado near service; it loses fresh texture and color during storage.

body:
## Chef's Note

These Tex-Mex chicken fajitas use the oven for the peppers, onion and chicken together. Two pans leave room for the filling to roast, though the vegetables will still release some juice. Add half the lime before cooking and the rest afterward; broiling is optional, and the skinless chicken does not need a crisp crust.

## Directions

1. **Heat the oven and prepare toppings:** Heat the oven to 375°F / 190°C with racks in the upper and lower thirds. Lightly coat the two rimmed pans, or their foil liners, with the separate teaspoon of oil, dividing it equally. Chop cilantro and set out the tortillas; keep the avocado whole until near service.
2. **Cut and season:** Slice peppers into 1/4-inch-wide strips and onion into 1/4-inch slices, separating the layers. Pat chicken dry and cut across the grain into strips about 1/2 inch thick and 2–3 inches long; split very thick breast sections horizontally first. Mix all eight seasonings in the large bowl with the filling's tablespoon of oil and half the lime juice. Add chicken, peppers and onion and toss thoroughly. Roast as soon as the oven is ready, or cover and refrigerate briefly while it finishes heating.
3. **Load both pans:** Divide the filling evenly between the pans, keeping chicken strips separate and flat. Spread the vegetables around them in a loose layer rather than a heap. Each pan holds about half the chicken, peppers and onion. Wash the raw-food bowl, utensils and preparation surface before they touch cooked food or toppings.
4. **Roast and check:** Roast for about 20–25 minutes, turning the filling and exchanging the upper and lower pans after about 10 minutes. Begin checking chicken at 15 minutes. Insert a thin-tip thermometer sideways into the thickest part of several substantial strips on each pan; every checked strip must reach 165°F / 74°C. Continue cooking any unfinished pan and recheck. The peppers should be tender but still hold their shape. Transfer done chicken to a clean covered bowl if the vegetables need longer.
5. **Optional browning:** Once the chicken is safely cooked, remove it to the clean bowl if not already there. Leave the vegetables spread on their pans, spooning off a large pool of juice if necessary. Broil one pan at a time about 6–8 inches from the element for roughly 1–3 minutes, watching continuously for browned edges. Keep the other pan and chicken out of the broiler. Skip this step if the vegetables already have enough color. Recombine the hot filling and add the remaining lime juice.
6. **Warm tortillas:** While the finished filling is covered for this brief step, microwave the tortillas in stacks of four between lightly damp paper towels for about 30–45 seconds per stack, adding short bursts until hot and flexible. Follow the package if it gives a different method. Wrap the warm stack in a clean towel. For a skillet, warm one or two tortillas at a time in a dry pan over medium-high, about 10–30 seconds per side; allow several extra minutes for all twelve.
7. **Serve:** Slice the optional avocado. Divide the filling among twelve tortillas and add the cilantro and avocado, serving two fajitas per person. Offer any remaining filling alongside; do not overfill a tortilla until it tears. Offer salsa or hot sauce if desired. Rice, beans and guacamole have their own preparation times in the complete dinner plan.

Insert a thin-tip thermometer sideways into the thickest part of several substantial strips on each pan; every checked strip must reach 165°F / 74°C. Continue cooking any unfinished pan and recheck. The peppers should be tender but still hold their shape. Transfer done chicken to a clean covered bowl if the vegetables need longer.
5. Optional browning: Once the chicken is safely cooked, remove it to the clean bowl if not already there. Leave the vegetables spread on their pans, spooning off a large pool of juice if necessary. Broil one pan at a time about 6–8 inches from the element for roughly 1–3 minutes, watching continuously for browned edges. Keep the other pan and chicken out of the broiler. Skip this step if the vegetables already have enough color. Recombine the hot filling and add the remaining lime juice.
6. Warm tortillas: While the finished filling is covered for this brief step, microwave the tortillas in stacks of four between lightly damp paper towels for about 30–45 seconds per stack, adding short bursts until hot and flexible. Follow the package if it gives a different method. Wrap the warm stack in a clean towel. For a skillet, warm one or two tortillas at a time in a dry pan over medium-high, about 10–30 seconds per side; allow several extra minutes for all twelve.
7. Serve: Slice the optional avocado. Divide the filling among twelve tortillas and add the cilantro and avocado, serving two fajitas per person. Offer any remaining filling alongside; do not overfill a tortilla until it tears. Offer salsa or hot sauce if desired. Rice, beans and guacamole have their own preparation times in the complete dinner plan.

data.description: Even chicken breasts roasted with red onion and tomatoes, with a restrained honey-balsamic finish and softened feta.

learning.focus: Separate the chicken endpoint from tomato reduction and cheese browning
learning.outcome: Cooked-through chicken that remains moist, softened feta, some burst tomatoes for sauce and some less-collapsed tomatoes for contrast.
before: Even thick breast portions to about 3/4 inch so they finish in a similar window. Use a rimmed half-sheet pan with room between pieces.
Make the finishing mixture in a clean bowl and use separate utensils so it never contacts raw chicken. Feta and mustard already contribute salt.

checkpoints.cue: Tomatoes are beginning to collapse, but the chicken still has open space around it.
checkpoints.why: Some tomato juice is desirable here as sauce. Piling vegetables over the meat creates more steaming and uneven cooking.

checkpoints.cue: Each chicken center reaches 165°F / 74°C before removal.
checkpoints.why: A guaranteed rise from 160°F during resting depends on conditions that this home recipe does not control. Measure the endpoint instead of predicting it.

troubleshooting.problem: Sauce is watery when chicken is done
troubleshooting.cause: Tomatoes released abundant liquid before it could evaporate.
troubleshooting.fix: Remove cooked chicken and let the vegetables and sauce roast for a few more minutes. Do not dry the breasts out to reduce tomato juice.

troubleshooting.cause: Sweet drips are scorching on an exposed part of the pan.
troubleshooting.fix: Spoon liquid from the juicy tomato area over darkening spots and lower oven heat if needed. Discard bitter burned deposits; keep checking the chicken endpoint.

substitutions.alternative: 150 g drained brined white cheese
substitutions.effect: Saltiness, firmness and melting differ. Taste with the sauce; do not promise the same cheese crust.

learning.timing: About fifty-five minutes includes twenty minutes of preparation and oven heating, 25–30 minutes roasting and a five-minute rest. Extra vegetable reduction or thicker chicken adds time. A grain or bread is an additional component.
learning.storage: Refrigerate in shallow containers within 2 hours (1 hour above 90°F / 32°C), at 40°F / 4°C or below. Use within 3–4 days and reheat to 165°F / 74°C. Reheat with the tomato juices; feta and tomatoes become softer.

body:
## Chef's Note

Two additions of tomatoes create a useful texture contrast, but the later tomatoes will be softer than raw ones, not crispy. Feta softens and may color at its edges; a wet tomato tray is not a reliable way to make a crisp cheese crust. Finish each component by its own cue instead of holding cooked chicken in the oven until the picture looks right.

## Directions

1. **Prepare:** Heat the oven to 425°F / 220°C. Cut and weigh the vegetables, drain feta, and even the four chicken portions to about 3/4 inch thick. In a clean bowl, whisk balsamic vinegar, honey, Dijon, oregano, garlic powder and 1 tbsp of the oil. Reserve this mixture away from raw meat.
2. **Arrange:** Use the remaining 1 tbsp oil to coat the chicken, onion and 400 g of the tomatoes on a rimmed half-sheet pan. Season chicken with its measured salt and pepper. Spread everything with gaps, keeping vegetables beside rather than piled over the meat. Wash hands and raw-meat utensils.
3. **First roast, then finish:** Roast for twelve minutes. Add the remaining 200 g tomatoes and the four feta slabs in the spaces. Spoon the reserved clean balsamic mixture across chicken, vegetables and cheese. Do not use a raw-contact marinade as a late drizzle.
4. **Measure:** Return to the oven for roughly 13–18 minutes. Start checking the thickest center of every chicken piece from the side after about twenty minutes total roasting, and remove pieces individually once they reach 165°F / 74°C. Continue as needed. Tomatoes should be juicy with some collapsed and some still holding shape, and onion should be tender. If those need longer, leave them in after removing the chicken.
5. **Rest and serve:** Rest cooked chicken five minutes, then divide it with the vegetables, feta and tomato pan juices among four plates. Scatter the two tablespoons basil. Pair with a starch or a simple green salad as needed; an additional whipped-feta dip duplicates the cheese component.

data.title: Sheet Pan Italian Sausage Dinner
ingredients: 1.5 lbs Italian Sausage Links (sweet or hot, your preference)

body:
## Chef's Note

This is the ultimate Tuesday night dinner: everything roasts on one pan, the broccoli steams while you wait, and store-bought rolls round it out. The key is getting the potatoes in the oven first - they need a head start to get crispy while the sausages just need to cook through and brown. Use good Italian sausage from the butcher counter (sweet for kids, hot for adults, or one of each). Halving the potatoes gives you more cut surface to crisp up. Piercing the sausages releases fat that bastes the potatoes.

## Directions

1. **Prep:** Preheat oven to 425°F. Line a large sheet pan with parchment.

2. **Season Potatoes:** Toss halved potatoes with olive oil, garlic powder, Italian seasoning, salt, and pepper. Spread in a single layer on the sheet pan.

3. **Start Potatoes:** Roast potatoes alone for 15 minutes to get a head start on crisping.

4. **Add Sausage:** Remove pan, push potatoes to one side. Add sausage links, piercing each a few times with a fork. Return to oven.

5. **Roast Together:** Roast for 20 more minutes, flipping sausages halfway, until sausages are browned and cooked through (160°F internal) and potatoes are golden and crispy.

6. **Steam Broccoli:** While everything roasts, steam broccoli (about 5 minutes in a steamer basket or microwave).

7. **Serve:** Slice sausages on the bias. Serve with crispy potatoes, steamed broccoli, warm rolls, and mustard on the side.

## Notes

- **Sweet Italian Sausage:** Mild, fennel-forward, kid-friendly
- **Hot Italian Sausage:** Spicy kick, adult-preferred
- **Chicken Sausage:** Use raw chicken sausage only with a measured 165°F center endpoint; fully cooked products follow their package reheating instructions.
- For extra crispy potatoes, boil them first, smash with a fork, then roast at high heat

data.title: Sheet Pan Pesto Chicken Bowls
ingredients: 1 lb Fresh Broccoli, cut into florets

body:
## Chef's Note

Sheet pan meal prep bowls became hugely popular in the 2010s for their simplicity and make-ahead convenience. The trick is staged roasting: cook the chicken and mushrooms first to develop color, then add the quicker-cooking vegetables like broccoli and zucchini for the final 10 minutes. Tossing the chicken in pesto before roasting creates a flavorful coating that keeps the lean breast meat moist. Refrigerate promptly in shallow containers at 40°F or below and use within 3–4 days; freeze portions intended for later in the week.

## Directions

1.  **Prep:** Preheat oven to 400°F. Line a massive sheet pan with parchment.
2.  **The Pesto:** In a small bowl, whisk pesto, Parmesan, garlic, salt, and pepper.
3.  **Stage 1:** Toss the diced chicken and mushrooms with 1 tbsp oil and 2 tbsp of the pesto mixture. Spread on the pan. Bake for 10 minutes.
4.  **Stage 2:** Remove pan. Add the broccoli, zucchini, and cherry tomatoes. Toss with another 2 tbsp of pesto.
5.  **Bake:** Roast for 10 more minutes until the chicken is cooked through (165°F) and the broccoli is tender-crisp.
6.  **Store:** Divide among 4 bowls. Serve over pasta or rice. Use refrigerated portions within 3–4 days and reheat to 165°F. Freeze later portions; the vegetables may soften after reheating.

data.title: Sheet Pan Pineapple Shrimp Tacos
ingredients: 2 tbsp Lime Juice, for the shrimp
1 tsp Kosher Salt, for the shrimp, plus more to taste for the slaw
Corn Tortillas, as needed to serve the filling
Sliced Avocado, to taste, for serving
Sour Cream, to taste, for serving

body:
## Chef's Note

These Mexican-inspired shrimp tacos roast on a divided sheet pan where shrimp, pineapple, and onions cook in separate zones, allowing the pineapple's sugars to caramelize without making the shrimp soggy. A cold cabbage-cilantro slaw dressed at the last moment provides crisp contrast to the sweet, sticky shrimp. Lime juice adds brightness.
For kids, serve the heat on the side or reduce/omit the spicy elements.

## Directions

1.  **Marinate:** In a large bowl, whisk 1 tbsp oil, the 2 tbsp shrimp lime juice, garlic, the shrimp salt, and all spices. Add shrimp and **marinate in the refrigerator for 15 minutes**.
2.  **The Pan:** Preheat oven to 425°F. On a large sheet pan, toss onions with 1 tbsp oil and the water in one zone, toss pineapple with 1 tbsp oil in the second, and spread the marinated shrimp in the third.
3.  **Roast:** Bake for about 12-15 minutes, checking the thickest shrimp for firm, pearly, opaque flesh. Remove the shrimp as they finish; if the pineapple and onions need more browning, return those sections to the oven briefly.
4.  **The Slaw:** While the pan roasts, toss cabbage and cilantro with the remaining 1 tbsp oil, the juice of the slaw lime, and salt to taste. Refrigerate until serving.
5.  **Assemble:** Warm tortillas. Divide the slaw, shrimp, roasted onion and pineapple among the tortillas; the taco count depends on tortilla and shrimp size.
6.  **Finish:** Top with avocado and sour cream for the final aromatic **High Note**.

parsed.chefNote:

data.title: Shoyu Tuna Poke Bowl
ingredients: 450 g boneless, skinless yellowfin tuna suitable for intended raw service; see sourcing note
4 cups freshly cooked [Plain Short-Grain White Rice](/mise/recipes/steamed-white-rice)
300 g English cucumber, ends trimmed and thinly sliced
150 g frozen unsalted shelled edamame, cooked according to the package and chilled
2 tbsp prepared sriracha mayonnaise, optional; check the label
data.description: Cold tuna in a mild soy, sesame and ginger dressing over lightly seasoned rice, with cucumber, edamame and avocado. Raw fish requires informed sourcing and handling.

learning.focus: Finish cold tuna and seasoned rice just before serving
learning.outcome: Distinct tuna cubes, tender rice and crisp cucumber, with a light coating of shoyu dressing instead of a bowl flooded with sauce.
before: Read the raw-fish sourcing note before buying. Keep the tuna refrigerated while making rice and toppings; thaw frozen fish in the refrigerator as directed, removing vacuum packaging before refrigerator thawing.
Prepare ready-to-eat vegetables before cutting fish. Clean and sanitize the work area after raw-fish preparation and use separate serving utensils.

checkpoints.cue: Rice grains are intact and the seasoning is evenly distributed.
checkpoints.why: Gentle folding mixes seasoning while limiting broken, pasty grains.

checkpoints.cue: Cold tuna cubes retain clean edges and have a thin coating of dressing.
checkpoints.why: A short refrigerated seasoning period is a texture choice, not a cooking or safety treatment.

troubleshooting.cause: Already seasoned sushi rice received the inline seasoning again.
troubleshooting.fix: Fold in plain cooked rice to dilute if available. Next time use plain rice for the default or omit all rice seasoning for the prepared-shari option.

troubleshooting.problem: Fish releases liquid or tastes salty
troubleshooting.cause: A longer hold or the soy brand changed the texture or salt balance.
troubleshooting.fix: Lift the fish with a slotted spoon and omit extra bowl dressing. Do not try to rescue fish with uncertain handling by rinsing or adding vinegar.

substitutions.alternative: 4 cups already prepared Sushi Rice (Shari)
substitutions.effect: Omit only the three seasoning ingredients under Rice: its 2 tbsp vinegar, 1 tbsp sugar and 1/2 tsp salt. Keep the tuna-dressing ingredients. The linked shari has a stronger seasoning profile and a larger full-batch yield.

substitutions.alternative: The same amount of gluten-free tamari
substitutions.effect: A gluten-free option only if all packaged toppings are also suitable; salt levels differ. Fish, soy and sesame remain; mayonnaise may contain egg.

learning.timing: About 85 minutes when making plain rice from dry, including its 65-minute process, rice seasoning/cooling and final assembly. Prepare vegetables and edamame during the rice soak/cook; cut and dress fish during final rice cooling. Allow about 35–45 minutes with refrigerated rice and cooked edamame, including reheating rice to 165°F / 74°C and briefly cooling the serving portion. Frozen fish needs additional refrigerator thawing time, often overnight.
learning.storage: Plan to prepare and eat the raw tuna the same day, following any earlier supplier use limit. Keep it at 40°F / 4°C or below until assembly; do not save assembled raw-fish bowls for meal prep. Refrigerate extra rice and cooked edamame separately within 2 hours, or 1 hour above 90°F / 32°C, and follow their component storage instructions. Sauce that touched raw fish is not a clean table sauce.

body:
## Chef's Note

Poke is seasoned cut seafood from Hawaii; rice and a full set of bowl toppings are a serving format, not its definition. This mild shoyu bowl uses a little sugar and fresh cucumber, keeping chile mayonnaise optional. The dressing seasons the fish but does not make raw fish safe.

## Before buying raw fish

Tell the supplier you intend to eat the tuna raw and ask about its species, handling and applicable parasite controls. “Sushi-grade” or “sashimi-grade” wording alone does not establish those controls. Yellowfin tuna is among the FDA Food Code's specific tuna exemptions from parasite-destruction freezing; that exemption is not a guarantee against other hazards. Do not assume domestic freezing or the vinegar in this recipe makes fish suitable for raw service.

Raw seafood carries risk even with careful sourcing. FDA advises children, pregnant people, older adults and people with weakened immune systems to avoid it. For those diners, choose a fully cooked seafood meal. Keep the raw version a deliberate choice, not a universally child-friendly dinner.

## Directions

1. **Prepare the rice and edamame:** Follow [Plain Short-Grain White Rice](/mise/recipes/steamed-white-rice); its batch starting with 300 g dry rice should provide approximately the four cooked cups needed here, with any extra reserved separately. During soaking/cooking, prepare shelled edamame according to its package, drain and chill promptly in a shallow container. Thaw-only directions apply only to a product explicitly ready to eat.
2. **Season the rice:** Dissolve the rice vinegar, tablespoon of sugar and fine salt together, warming gently if necessary. Measure four cups hot plain rice and fold in this mixture. Spread gently in a wide bowl and let steam escape until the rice is barely warm, about 10 minutes. This brief cooling is part of final preparation, not an extended room-temperature hold.
3. **Prepare the toppings and sauce during the rice process:** While rice soaks or cooks, slice cucumber and scallion using clean equipment. Dice avocado near assembly, before switching to fish. Whisk the soy sauce, sesame oil, teaspoon of vinegar, ginger, half teaspoon sugar and scallion in a separate bowl. Taste the clean dressing before it touches fish.
4. **Cut and dress the tuna while rice cools:** During the final rice cooling period, on separate clean equipment, cut the cold tuna into 1/2-inch cubes. Fold into the dressing and refrigerate for about 5–10 minutes while setting out the bowls. Exact minute limits are not a safety control, and texture varies with the fish and dressing.
5. **Assemble and eat promptly:** Divide rice, tuna, cucumber, chilled shelled edamame and avocado among three bowls. Lift the fish from its dressing, adding only a little of its coating to each bowl; keep it away from communal toppings. Scatter sesame seeds and offer the measured optional mayonnaise separately. Add fish to rice only when each diner is ready to eat.

## Prepared sushi-rice option

Use four cups of [Sushi Rice (Shari)](/mise/recipes/master-sushi-rice) instead of the plain rice and all three rice-seasoning ingredients. Measure the cooked amount; a full shari recipe makes extra. Do not make both rice preparations.

data.title: Shrimp & Avocado Summer Rolls
ingredients: 18 medium raw shrimp, fully thawed, peeled, tails removed and deveined
6 round rice paper wrappers, 8–8.5 inches across, plus spares for tears
1 Hass avocado, peeled, pitted and thinly sliced
1 Fresno chile, seeded and minced, or Thai bird chile to taste
Salt, to taste, for cooking water and dipping sauce
Asian chile-garlic sauce, optional, for serving
data.description: Shrimp, creamy avocado and three fresh herbs wrapped in rice paper, with a sweet chile-lime dipping sauce. Drain the filling well and let each damp wrapper soften on the work surface before rolling.

learning.focus: Control filling moisture and wrapper hydration before rolling
learning.outcome: Pliable, intact rolls with distinct shrimp, avocado and herbs, without a soggy filling.
before: Thaw frozen shrimp in the refrigerator before starting. Wash and dry herbs, and keep raw shrimp separate from ready-to-eat fillings and clean assembly utensils.
Read the noodle and wrapper package instructions. Rice vermicelli thickness and rice-paper composition vary; do not assume one soaking time fits every product.
Use the stated large round wrappers. Divide the fillings into as many portions as wrappers before rolling, and keep spare wrappers for tears. Larger batches increase assembly time.

checkpoints.cue: Shrimp flesh is firm, pearly and opaque through the thickest part.
checkpoints.why: Size and starting temperature change cooking time; a two-minute timer alone does not establish doneness.

checkpoints.cue: The wrapper is pliable and slightly tacky on the board, not collapsing in the water.
checkpoints.why: A wetted sheet continues softening after it leaves the water. Over-soaking makes it harder to handle.

checkpoints.cue: The filling forms a compact strip with clear margins for the side folds.
checkpoints.why: Keeping filling away from the edges lets the wrapper close without stretching it to breaking point.

troubleshooting.problem: Rice paper tears or clings to itself
troubleshooting.cause: The sheet was soaked too long, overfilled or pulled too hard.
troubleshooting.fix: Move the filling to a fresh briefly wetted wrapper. Let it soften before folding, then roll snugly without stretching. If filling does not fit, use a spare wrapper for the excess.

troubleshooting.cause: Noodles, herbs or shrimp retained surface water.
troubleshooting.fix: Drain and blot the remaining fillings before making more rolls. Keep completed rolls separate so wet wrappers do not stick together.

troubleshooting.cause: They sat in a dense pile after draining.
troubleshooting.fix: Loosen briefly under cool water and drain thoroughly again. They should be tender and separate, not dried hard.

substitutions.alternative: A little Thai bird chile, added to taste
substitutions.effect: Usually much hotter; start with a small amount rather than assuming a whole pepper is equivalent.

substitutions.alternative: The same count of fully cooked, peeled medium shrimp
substitutions.effect: Skip cooking, keep chilled, pat dry and halve lengthwise. Texture and seasoning depend on the prepared product.

learning.timing: Allow about 45 minutes, including noodle preparation, heating water, cooking and cooling shrimp, preparing sauce and fillings, and rolling six wrappers. Make the sauce while noodles cool. First-time rolling or additional wrappers can take longer. Frozen shrimp must be thawed beforehand.
learning.storage: Serve freshly rolled for the most supple wrappers. If service is delayed, keep rolls separate in a covered container at 40°F / 4°C or below; refrigeration can firm the wrappers. Refrigerate promptly and use the same day for quality. Keep cumulative time out of refrigeration under 2 hours, or 1 hour above 90°F / 32°C.

body:
## Chef's Note

Creamy avocado, shrimp, mint, cilantro and chives fill these fresh rice-paper rolls. Their dipping sauce is sweet with lime, chile and garlic. Let the noodles and shrimp cool and drain before assembly, then wet one wrapper at a time; it should finish softening on the board rather than turn limp in the water.

## Directions

1. **Prepare the noodles:** Cook or soak the rice vermicelli according to its package instructions until tender without a hard center. Drain, rinse under cool running water and drain thoroughly. Snip very long strands into manageable lengths; do not try to dry the noodles until hard.
2. **Cook and cool the shrimp:** Bring a saucepan of water to a boil and season lightly with salt. Add the thawed shrimp and reduce to a gentle simmer. Start checking after about 2 minutes; continue until firm, pearly and opaque throughout, checking 145°F / 63°C in the thickest part with a suitable thin probe. Transfer to a clean ice-water bath just until cold, then drain and pat dry. Halve lengthwise using clean utensils.
3. **Make the sauce:** Stir the sugar into the measured warm water until dissolved. Add lime juice, minced chile and garlic. Season with a small pinch of salt to taste. Serve the optional chile-garlic sauce separately.
4. **Portion the fillings:** Slice the avocado and prepare the herbs. Divide all noodles, avocado, cilantro, mint, chives and shrimp equally among the wrappers. Each roll gets six shrimp halves at any batch size. Keep fillings chilled if you pause before assembly.
5. **Wet a wrapper:** Fill a wide shallow dish with water at the temperature recommended on the wrapper package. Briefly wet both sides of one sheet, then lay it flat on a clean smooth work surface. Let it become pliable and slightly tacky before folding; do not leave it soaking until limp.
6. **Fill and roll:** Arrange one portion of noodles, avocado and herbs in a compact strip across the lower third, leaving space at the sides. Arrange its shrimp halves curved side down near the filling. Fold the bottom over, fold in both sides and roll snugly without stretching. Repeat with all fillings; use a spare wrapper if one tears or the filling will not fit comfortably.
7. **Serve:** Keep rolls separate so they do not stick, and serve with the dipping sauce. The stated batch makes six substantial side rolls; for four diners, cut them in half and share three halves per person.

data.title: Shrimp and Corn Chowder
ingredients: 2 lbs Medium Shrimp, peeled and deveined
2 tbsp Fresh Lime Juice (The Acid Balance)

body:
## Chef's Note

The key to chowder without heavy flour is grating an unripe green plantain directly into the stock. This introduces a natural starch that thickens the soup into a velvety consistency as it simmers. We add the marinated shrimp at the very end and cook for exactly 2 minutes to ensure they stay tender and succulent. The lime juice cuts through the creamy corn.

## Directions

1.  **Marinate:** Toss shrimp with garlic, scallions, lime juice, and salt. Refrigerate for 1 hour.
2.  **Corn Milk:** In a food processor, puree half the corn with the milk. Strain through a coarse sieve, pressing to extract all the liquid.
3.  **The Base:** In a large pot, heat the oil. Sauté onion, pepper, and cumin for 5 minutes. Stir in the tomatoes.
4.  **Simmer:** Add the corn milk, stock, grated plantain, and remaining whole corn kernels. Bring to a boil, then simmer for 20 minutes until thick and aromatic.
5.  **Refine:** For the Kitchen Standard texture, ladle 2 cups of the soup into a blender and pulse until smooth, then return to the pot.
6.  **The Crunch:** Add the shrimp and its marinade. Cook for 2-3 minutes until just opaque.
7.  **Serve:** Stir in cilantro and cayenne. Serve in warmed bowls.

data.title: Shrimp and Grits
data.source: Adapted from Bobby Flay’s Shrimp and Grits at Food Network
ingredients: 1 cup dry regular stone-ground grits, with package instructions matching the ratio and simmer time below
4 cups (950 ml) water, for the grits, with package-specific adjustment if needed
1 cup (240 ml) additional hot water, for loosening the grits as needed
1/2 tsp fine salt, for the grits, divided and partly added to taste
2 cups (225 g) sharp cheddar, freshly grated
1 lb (450 g) raw peeled, deveined, tail-off shrimp, weighed after thawing and draining; about 31–40 shrimp in this net quantity
1/2 tsp freshly ground black pepper, divided
1 cup (100 g) thinly sliced scallions, white and green parts separated
1/4 cup (60 ml) water, for the shrimp pan
4 tsp fresh lemon juice, divided and partly added to taste
data.description: Tender shrimp, crisp bacon and scallion-lemon pan juices over rich cheddar grits. The grits package determines the cooking schedule; cook the shrimp only when the base is ready.

learning.focus: Finish the slow starch before the fast-cooking shrimp
learning.outcome: Grits that spread softly across a bowl without gritty centers, springy cooked shrimp, crisp bacon and a light lemon-scallion coating rather than a pool of bacon grease.
before: The sixty-minute plan requires stone-ground grits with package instructions for a four-to-one liquid-to-grits volume ratio and a twenty-to-twenty-five-minute simmer. Stone-ground does not guarantee one cooking time: coarser grits can need about ninety minutes unsoaked. Check the package before planning the meal.
The grits should yield roughly four to five cups after adding cheese, depending on evaporation and extra water; divide them among four bowls.

Shrimp weight is after thawing, draining, peeling and removing tails. A peeled 31–40-count-per-pound product gives roughly eight to ten shrimp per person. If peeling a shell-on product, buy extra and use the net prepared weight; its package count may give a different number per serving. Peeling adds preparation time, and frozen shrimp need thawing before the listed schedule begins.

Have all aromatics measured before shrimp cooking starts. A 12-inch skillet cooks the shrimp in two roughly 225 g rounds, so each piece lies flat rather than steaming in a pile. The bacon supplies the cooking fat: about one tablespoon of rendered fat, plus the thin film left in the pan.

checkpoints.cue: A cooled spoonful has tender corn particles with no hard center, and the mixture moves slowly when the pot is tilted.
checkpoints.why: Thickness alone does not mean the grits have hydrated. Water can evaporate while the centers remain firm, so taste before adding cheese.

checkpoints.cue: Bacon is browned and crisp, and the pan contains a measured tablespoon of fat rather than all the drippings.
checkpoints.why: The quantity of rendered fat varies by bacon. Controlling it keeps the shrimp topping from becoming greasy before it reaches already rich grits.

checkpoints.cue: Shrimp flesh is firm, pearly and opaque through the thickest part, with the largest pieces reaching 145°F / 63°C.
checkpoints.why: Surface pinkness alone can appear before the center is cooked. Stop by the center cue and temperature; continued frying makes shrimp tough rather than usefully crisp.

checkpoints.cue: The pan juices lightly coat the shrimp, and lemon brightens a bite with grits without tasting sharply sour.
checkpoints.why: A little water lifts the browned bacon residue; lemon is added at the finish and tasted alongside the salty cheese and bacon.

troubleshooting.problem: Grits are thick but still gritty
troubleshooting.cause: The product needs more cooking, or the pan lost water before the grains softened.
troubleshooting.fix: Add some of the listed hot water in small amounts and continue gently simmering, stirring and tasting. Do not add cheese yet or assume extra blending will replace hydration.

troubleshooting.problem: Grits are stiff after adding cheese
troubleshooting.cause: Cheese thickens the mixture and the starch firms as it cools.
troubleshooting.fix: Fold in hot water a tablespoon or two at a time until the grits spread softly. Keep gently warm; do not boil hard to force melted cheese back into a smooth texture.

troubleshooting.cause: They cooked too long, or were kept simmering while the grits and vegetables caught up.
troubleshooting.fix: Serve promptly with the pan juices. More cooking or extra butter cannot restore the original texture; next time finish the base first and remove cooked shrimp while building the brief pan sauce.

troubleshooting.problem: Topping tastes too salty or greasy
troubleshooting.cause: All bacon fat was retained, or extra salt was added before tasting with bacon and cheddar.
troubleshooting.fix: Measure the retained fat and leave shrimp unsalted initially. Taste the complete bite before finishing salt. An already oversalted topping needs more unsalted food to dilute it; lemon does not remove salt.

substitutions.alternative: 1 cup plain quick grits
substitutions.effect: A finer texture and a shorter starch stage. Use the actual package's water and cooking instructions. Some quick grits use four cups water and about five to seven minutes cooking for this quantity; check the package rather than assuming. Cook bacon and prepare everything before starting these faster grits. Allow about forty to forty-five minutes for the full main; instant packets are a different product and may contain additional salt.

substitutions.alternative: 1 cup coarser stone-ground grits with a longer package method
substitutions.effect: Follow that mill's unsoaked cooking method and liquid directions, then add the listed butter and cheese once the grains are tender. Very coarse unsoaked grits can extend this main to about two hours, with a different corn texture. The listed sixty-minute schedule does not apply.

substitutions.alternative: Omit the bacon and use 1 tbsp olive oil for cooking the shrimp and aromatics
substitutions.effect: Less smoke, crunch and salt, making a different but still useful shrimp-and-cheddar bowl. Taste the finished topping with grits before adding any additional salt.

learning.timing: Allow about sixty minutes with grits requiring the stated twenty-to-twenty-five-minute simmer and thawed, peeled shrimp: roughly twenty minutes for measuring, chopping, grating and heating the grits water, then a twenty-to-twenty-five-minute simmer and about fifteen minutes for finishing the grits, the shrimp and the pan finish. Cook bacon during the grits simmer. Finish the grits before cooking shrimp; a brief covered hold of about ten minutes is included in that sequence, not an extra mandatory rest for the seafood. Different grits, peeling or thawing add time.
learning.storage: Keep raw shrimp refrigerated at 40°F / 4°C or below and use within two days of purchase, or freeze. Thaw frozen shrimp overnight in the refrigerator, or in a sealed bag in cold water when preparing them to cook promptly. Refrigerate cooked grits, shrimp and bacon separately in shallow containers within two hours, or one hour above 90°F / 32°C. Use within three to four days. Reheat cooked leftovers to 165°F / 74°C, loosening grits with a little water and heating shrimp briefly at the end; their texture will be firmer. For a short service hold, keep grits covered above 140°F / 60°C with occasional stirring, and adjust with the listed hot water. Cook shrimp near serving rather than holding them in a simmering pan.

sources.title: Bobby Flay / Food Network — Shrimp and Grits
Palmetto Farms — Product-specific grits ratio and cooking method
Anson Mills — Coarse-grits hydration and much longer cooking schedule
Quaker — Quick grits product preparation
FDA — Raw seafood storage, thawing and shrimp cooking endpoints
FoodSafety.gov — Temperature control, holding and prompt cooling
FoodSafety.gov — Safe internal temperatures for cooked leftovers
FoodSafety.gov — Three-to-four-day leftover guidance

body:
## Chef's Note

This Southern bowl combines cheddar grits, bacon and shrimp with scallions and lemon. The bacon provides crunch while the shrimp should stay tender. Stone-ground grits vary substantially by mill and particle size, so finish their hydration before starting the quick shrimp stage.

## Directions

1. **Prepare before cooking:** Check that the grits package matches the stated liquid ratio and simmer time. Heat the four cups grits water in a 3-quart heavy saucepan while grating cheddar, dicing bacon and preparing scallions, garlic, parsley and lemon. Heat the additional cup of water in a kettle or microwave and keep covered for adjusting the grits; rewarm if needed. Keep white and green scallion parts separate. Pat thawed peeled shrimp dry and keep refrigerated. Set aside half the black pepper for grits and half for shrimp.
2. **Cook the grits:** Bring the water to a boil, whisk in grits and half the measured salt, then reduce to a gentle low simmer and cover. Stir thoroughly across the bottom every few minutes to prevent sticking. For grits with the stated package method, begin tasting at twenty minutes and allow about twenty to twenty-five; continue longer if the centers are still firm. If it gets thick before tender, add hot water from the listed additional cup in small amounts. The grains should feel tender in a cooled spoonful, not merely absorb all the water.
3. **Cook bacon and finish the base:** While grits simmer, cook diced bacon in the 12-inch skillet over medium heat for about eight to ten minutes, stirring until browned and crisp. Transfer bacon to a plate; carefully measure one tablespoon of rendered fat into a small heatproof cup and pour off the excess, leaving a thin film in the skillet. Discard or separately save the excess fat. Once grits are tender, take them off heat and fold in butter, cheddar and their half of the pepper. Taste before adding the remaining grits salt. Loosen with a little listed hot water if needed so the grits spread softly rather than stand in a firm mound. Cover and keep gently warm while cooking shrimp.
4. **Cook the first shrimp batch:** Heat the skillet with half the reserved tablespoon bacon fat over medium-high heat; keep the other half aside. Add half the shrimp in one layer and cook about one to two minutes per side. Check the thickest centers as described in the next step, then transfer cooked shrimp to a clean plate. They will return only briefly for coating, not simmer through the sauce preparation.
5. **Cook the second batch and check:** Add the remaining reserved fat and shrimp. Cook and turn as before, until the flesh is firm, pearly and opaque through the center. Check several of the largest shrimp with a thin-tip thermometer inserted into the thickest part for 145°F / 63°C; continue any larger or still-translucent pieces until done. Typical cooking is about three to four minutes per batch, but thickness determines it. Transfer this batch to the clean plate.
6. **Make a brief pan coating:** Reduce heat to medium-low. Add scallion whites to the fat film and stir for about one minute, then add garlic for about thirty seconds without browning it. If the pan looks dry, use a teaspoon from the measured pan water while the scallions soften. Add the rest of the separate quarter-cup pan water and scrape up brown, not black, residue; simmer for thirty to sixty seconds. Turn off heat and stir in three teaspoons lemon juice, most of the scallion greens, parsley and the shrimp's half of the pepper. Return shrimp and any juices just long enough to coat. Taste a shrimp with a little grit and add the remaining teaspoon lemon only if needed. Do not salt the topping automatically; bacon and cheese already contribute seasoning.
7. **Serve promptly:** Divide grits among four bowls, top with shrimp and the light pan juices, then scatter over crisp bacon and the reserved scallion greens. Distribute shrimp evenly, roughly eight to ten per bowl for the stated size. Serve a vegetable alongside; the grits provide the starch for the plate.

data.title: Shrimp & Mango Tacos
ingredients: 1 lb Small Shrimp, peeled and deveined
2 tsp Cumin Seeds, toasted and ground

body:
## Chef's Note

These Mexican-inspired tacos balance sweet mango with savory cumin-spiced shrimp. Briefly sautéing the mango with shrimp allows the fruit's sugars to release and create a tropical glaze when combined with lime juice. Fresh serrano chilies add bright heat that cuts through the sweet mango without overpowering.

## Directions

1.  **The Sear:** Heat oil in a heavy skillet or wok over medium-high. Add shrimp and salt. Sauté for 1-2 minutes until they begin to turn pink, adding the garlic for the last 30-45 seconds.
2.  **The Pulse:** Add the ground cumin and Serrano chilies. Stir-fry for 1 minute until the spices are fragrant and the chilies are bright.
3.  **The Glaze:** Stir in the chopped mango and cilantro. Cook for exactly 1 minute - just until the mango starts to soften at the edges.
4.  **Finish:** Remove from heat. Stir in the lime juice. Taste and adjust with extra salt.
5.  **Thermal Prep:** Wrap tortillas in a damp towel and microwave for 45 seconds (or char over an open flame).
6.  **Assemble:** Place 2 tortillas on each plate. Mound the shrimp-mango mixture into the center.
7.  **Serve:** Serve immediately with a side of [Mexican Red Rice](/mise/recipes/mexican-red-rice).

data.title: Shrimp and Snow Pea Noodles
ingredients: 8 oz raw shrimp, peeled and deveined, tails removed
8 oz fresh snow peas, strings removed, sliced diagonally
Kosher salt and black pepper, to taste
Water, for noodle preparation and a small splash if needed in the pan
data.source: Adapted from Delish, Shrimp & Snow Pea Stir-Fry
data.description: Rice noodles with shrimp and crisp snow peas in a sweet chili, soy, ginger and garlic coating.

learning.focus: Coordinate rice-noodle hydration with a brief shrimp stir-fry
learning.outcome: Flexible tender noodles that separate when lifted, with opaque shrimp and snow peas retaining a little bite.
before: Start with raw, fully thawed shrimp. Thaw overnight in the refrigerator, or in a sealed bag in cold water and cook promptly. Keep cold until preparation; dry well and keep raw-seafood utensils separate from cooked food. Peeling, deveining and thawing are additional time if buying unprepared shrimp.

Choose rice linguine suitable for stir-frying and follow its package preparation. Some products need about 25 minutes in hot water; follow your package. Have the noodles nearly tender before they enter the pan; a dry toss cannot reliably soften a hard center.
Use a 12-inch skillet or roomy wok. For larger quantities cook complete batches; eight ounces of dry noodles expand substantially and need room to turn without tearing.

checkpoints.cue: A noodle bends readily and is nearly tender without a hard center.
checkpoints.why: Package preparation is more reliable than imposing one soak duration on every rice noodle.

checkpoints.cue: Shrimp centers are firm, pearly and opaque before moving to a clean plate.
checkpoints.why: Browning sweet sauce does not establish the seafood endpoint.

checkpoints.cue: Noodles lift in separate glossy strands and are tender to the bite.
checkpoints.why: Gentle turning and a small water correction prevent dry sticking and tearing.

troubleshooting.problem: Noodles are hard in the pan
troubleshooting.cause: They were underhydrated or thicker than the original product.
troubleshooting.fix: Add a small splash of water, cover briefly and check tenderness before returning shrimp. Next time follow the noodle package rather than only the soak clock.

troubleshooting.cause: Excess wet marinade or too much heat scorched the sugar.
troubleshooting.fix: Remove shrimp and discard blackened pan residue before continuing. Use moderate to medium-high heat and drain excess marinade next time.

substitutions.alternative: The same weight of trimmed sugar snap peas, halved lengthwise
substitutions.effect: They are thicker and sweeter; cook until a cut piece is tender with a little bite rather than following the snow-pea timer.

learning.timing: Plan about 45 minutes, including heating water, roughly 25 minutes noodle preparation, a 15-minute refrigerated shrimp marinade overlapped with that preparation, and about 10–15 minutes at the stove. A different noodle package can change this time. About 25–30 minutes is hands-on.

sources.title: FDA — Selecting and serving seafood safely
FoodSafety.gov — Cold food storage chart
FoodSafety.gov — Safe minimum cooking temperatures
Delish — Original shrimp and snow pea noodles

learning.storage: Refrigerate in shallow containers within 2 hours, or 1 hour above 90°F / 32°C, at 40°F / 4°C or below. Use within 3–4 days. Reheat gently to 165°F / 74°C throughout; shrimp become firmer with reheating, so fresh service gives the best texture.

body:
## Chef's Note

Start the rice noodles before preparing the vegetables and shrimp. Hydrate them according to their package, then finish in the pan with the sweet chili coating. Lift cooked shrimp out while the noodles finish so the two ingredients do not have to share one cooking time. Adapted from [Delish’s Shrimp & Snow Pea Stir-Fry](https://www.delish.com/cooking/recipe-ideas/a35131589/shrimp-and-snow-pea-stir-fry-recipe/).

## Directions

1. **Prepare noodles:** Follow the package instructions for stir-fried rice linguine. For a product calling for a hot-water soak, use a heatproof bowl and expect roughly 25 minutes; separate clumps gently with a fork. Drain when nearly tender, rinsing only if directed, and drain thoroughly.

2. **Marinate and prepare:** While noodles hydrate, pat shrimp dry and season lightly with salt and pepper. Toss with one-fifth of the sweet chili sauce and refrigerate for 15 minutes. Trim and slice peas, grate ginger and mince garlic. Mix the remaining four-fifths of the sweet chili sauce with the measured soy sauce in a clean bowl.

3. **Cook shrimp:** Heat half the oil over medium-high. Lift shrimp from the marinade, letting excess drip away; discard the raw-contact marinade. Cook in a single layer about 1–2 minutes per side, as needed, until firm, pearly and opaque through the center; a fine-tip thermometer inserted into a thick shrimp should read 145°F / 63°C. Transfer to a clean plate. Lower heat if the sweet coating darkens rapidly.

4. **Cook vegetables:** Add remaining oil, snow peas and ginger. Stir-fry about 2 minutes until the peas brighten and retain a little bite. Add garlic and stir for about 30 seconds without letting it burn.

5. **Finish noodles:** Add drained noodles and the clean chili-soy mixture. Lift and turn gently for about 2–4 minutes until hot and tender; use a small splash of water if they stick or need further softening. Avoid vigorous stirring that tears the strands.

6. **Combine:** Return shrimp and plate juices only long enough to warm through, about 30 seconds. Taste before adding any further salt and pepper. Divide noodles and the actual shrimp count evenly among bowls and serve immediately.

data.title: Shrimp & Sweet Potato Noodle Stir-Fry
ingredients: 1 lb large shrimp, peeled and deveined
4 green onions, whites and greens separated, sliced
Gochugaru or red pepper flakes (optional, for heat)
2 tbsp high-smoke-point oil (avocado or grapeseed), divided

body:
## Chef's Note

This dish lives at the intersection of Korean japchae technique and Chinese wok fundamentals. Sweet potato noodles (dangmyeon) have a uniquely springy, glass-like chew that no other noodle replicates - but they turn into a gummy mass if you don't toss them in sesame oil immediately after draining. The cornstarch "velvet" on the shrimp isn't optional: it creates a thin barrier that keeps them succulent under high heat and gives the sauce something to grip. Bloom the garlic and ginger in oil with a pinch of gochugaru before the vegetables - it infuses the fat with a rounded heat that permeates the entire dish. For kids, serve the heat on the side or reduce/omit the spicy elements.

## Directions

1. **Velvet the Shrimp:** Pat the shrimp dry with paper towels. Toss cleaned shrimp with 1 tbsp soy sauce and 1 tbsp cornstarch in a bowl. Mix until evenly coated - the cornstarch creates a thin protective barrier that keeps shrimp succulent under high heat. Let sit for 10 minutes while you prep everything else.

2. **Cook the Noodles:** Boil sweet potato noodles for 6-7 minutes until just al dente - they should still have bite. Drain immediately, toss with 1 tsp toasted sesame oil to prevent sticking, and set aside. Don't skip the sesame oil - dangmyeon bonds to itself within seconds.

3. **Whisk the Sauce:** Combine 3 tbsp soy sauce, lime juice, honey, 1 tsp sesame oil, and fish sauce in a small bowl. Whisk until honey dissolves. Set near the stove.

4. **Sear the Shrimp:** Heat wok or heavy skillet over high heat (400-450°F) until smoking. Add 1 tbsp oil, swirl to coat. Sear shrimp in a single layer - about 1 minute per side until pink with charred spots but not fully curled. They'll finish in the sauce. Remove to a plate.

5. **Bloom the Aromatics:** Add remaining 1 tbsp oil to the hot wok. Toss in garlic, ginger, white parts of green onions, and a pinch of gochugaru if using. Stir for 30 seconds until fragrant - the oil should turn slightly red from the gochugaru. Don't let the garlic burn.

6. **High-Heat Vegetables:** Add julienned carrots first (they take longest) - toss for 2 minutes over high heat. Add snow peas and toss another 1-2 minutes. You want a snap when you bite a snow pea, not a limp string.

7. **The Marriage:** Add the noodles and seared shrimp back to the wok. Pour the sauce over everything. Use tongs to lift and toss constantly over high heat for 1-2 minutes. The residual cornstarch from the shrimp and the starch in the noodles will cause the sauce to thicken into a glossy glaze almost instantly.

8. **Finish:** Kill the heat. Fold in the green parts of the green onions, a final squeeze of lime, and a heavy sprinkle of toasted sesame seeds. Serve immediately - stir-fries don't wait.

data.title: Shrimp Fettuccine Alfredo
ingredients: 1 lb Jumbo Shrimp, peeled and deveined

body:
## Chef's Note

Italian-American fettuccine Alfredo with shrimp traces back to Alfredo di Lelio's 1908 Rome original - just butter and Parmigiano-Reggiano, no cream. Americans added cream for richness and stability, then added shrimp because this is what we do. The key is a quick high-heat sear on the shrimp (2 minutes per side until pink with light char) - overcooking turns them rubbery. If making the [Real Alfredo Sauce](/mise/recipes/real-alfredo-sauce) from scratch, use the same skillet you seared the shrimp in - those browned bits dissolve into the butter and become free flavor.

## Directions

1.  **Pasta:** Bring a large pot of heavily salted water to a boil. Cook fettuccine according to package directions. **Reserve 1/2 cup of pasta water before draining.**
2.  **Shrimp:** While pasta boils, toss shrimp with garlic powder, salt, and pepper.
3.  **Sear:** Heat oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat. Sear shrimp for 2 minutes per side until pink and opaque. Remove to a plate.
4.  **Sauce:**
    - If using **[Real Alfredo Sauce](/mise/recipes/real-alfredo-sauce)**: Prepare it in the same skillet used for the shrimp (scrape up those browned bits!).
    - If using **Jarred Sauce**: Pour into the skillet and heat until bubbling.
5.  **Combine:** Toss the hot pasta and the seared shrimp into the sauce. If it's too thick, add a splash of the reserved pasta water to loosen it up.
6.  **Garnish:** Top with fresh parsley and serve immediately.

data.title: Shrimp Linguine with Fresh Tomato, White Wine & Basil
ingredients: 1 lb raw large shrimp, weighed after peeling and deveining, shells reserved
1 tsp kosher salt, for seasoning shrimp
1 tsp olive oil, for shell stock
1 tbsp olive oil, for cooking shrimp
Kosher salt and black pepper, to taste
1 lemon, finely zest the whole fruit and juice half
Extra-virgin olive oil, optional, for finishing
2 cups reserved pasta cooking water, use only as needed
1 clove garlic, grated, for the optional topping
1 tbsp olive oil, for the optional topping
data.description: Fresh spinach linguine with shrimp, grated Roma tomatoes, white wine and basil, finished with butter and an optional crisp breadcrumb topping.

learning.focus: Build a shell stock and finish fresh pasta without overcooking shrimp
learning.outcome: Tender fresh linguine in a tomato-butter coating, with opaque shrimp, wilted spinach and fresh basil aroma.
before: Start with raw, fully thawed shrimp. Thaw overnight in the refrigerator, or in a sealed bag in cold water and cook promptly. Keep cold until preparation; dry well and keep raw-seafood utensils separate from cooked food. Thawing is additional time; the schedule below includes peeling and deveining.

Buy enough large shell-on shrimp to supply the listed pound of peeled, deveined meat, reserving their shells for stock. The required purchase weight varies; no fixed shell-on conversion is assumed. If buying already peeled shrimp, use the stock substitution below.

Use a small saucepan for stock, a pasta pot and a deep 12-inch sauté pan of about 4-quart capacity. A larger batch needs separate pans or complete batches; shell-stock reduction and fresh-pasta timing do not multiply with servings.

Prepare the sauce before dropping fresh linguine into boiling water. Fresh noodle thickness varies, so the package and a tasted strand govern timing. Grate tomatoes over a bowl to retain their juices.

checkpoints.cue: The strained stock is measured after simmering and reduced to half the starting water volume.
checkpoints.why: Evaporation differs by pan; a measured final volume controls the liquid added to tomato sauce.

checkpoints.cue: Shrimp centers are firm, pearly and opaque before removal.
checkpoints.why: A forty-five-second sear and a curl shape do not establish the center endpoint.

checkpoints.cue: The tomato sauce is lightly thickened but still flows from a spoon.
checkpoints.why: Tomato size and water content vary; reduce the sauce before the delicate fresh noodles enter.

checkpoints.cue: Cold butter melts into the pasta coating off heat without an oil pool.
checkpoints.why: Excessive heat or too little water can separate the finishing fat.

troubleshooting.cause: They stayed hot while the sauce reduced or pasta finished.
troubleshooting.fix: Lift cooked shrimp out and return only to warm and coat. Additional sauce cannot reverse overcooking.

troubleshooting.cause: Too much water evaporated or the butter finish was overheated.
troubleshooting.fix: Take off heat and toss gently with a small splash of warm reserved pasta water. Add more only if needed; do not pour the whole allowance in automatically.

substitutions.ingredient: Reserved shrimp shells and their stock
substitutions.alternative: Unsalted seafood stock, using half the listed starting water volume as the finished stock amount
substitutions.effect: Replaces the reduced shell stock, not the full starting water quantity; flavor depends on the stock. Omit the shell-stock oil and use all measured wine in the tomato sauce.

substitutions.alternative: The same weight of another fresh linguine
substitutions.effect: Changes spinach flavor/color; follow its package cooking time. An equal weight of dried pasta is not a like-for-like yield substitution.

learning.timing: Allow about 75 minutes for one cook, including peeling, tomato grating, stock simmer and reduction, optional topping and fresh-pasta finish. The 15–30-minute refrigerated shrimp seasoning overlaps stock preparation. Have the stock ready before building the tomato sauce; fresh pasta enters only at the end.

sources.title: FDA — Selecting and serving seafood safely
FoodSafety.gov — Cold food storage chart
FoodSafety.gov — Safe minimum cooking temperatures
Serious Eats — Small baking-soda shrimp dry brine

learning.storage: Refrigerate in shallow containers within 2 hours, or 1 hour above 90°F / 32°C, at 40°F / 4°C or below. Use within 3–4 days. Reheat gently to 165°F / 74°C throughout; shrimp become firmer with reheating, so fresh service gives the best texture.

body:
## Chef's Note

A quick shell stock gives the tomato sauce a seafood base, while butter rounds out the grated tomatoes and wine. Get the sauce ready before cooking the fresh linguine, then use pasta water sparingly and finish off heat. The optional garlic breadcrumbs add a crisp contrast.

## Directions

1. **Peel and season:** Peel and devein shrimp, reserving shells. Toss peeled meat with the measured shrimp salt and optional baking soda. Refrigerate for 15–30 minutes while preparing the stock and vegetables. Wash raw-contact tools and pat shrimp dry just before cooking.

2. **Make shell stock:** Heat the oil labeled for stock in a small saucepan over medium heat. Stir shells for about 2–3 minutes until pink and aromatic. Add a small splash taken from the measured wine and all the stock water. Bring to a gentle simmer and cook about 15 minutes. Strain through a fine-mesh strainer, pressing shells, then discard shells. Measure the liquid and reduce to half the starting water volume if necessary; add a little water if reduced below that target.

3. **Prepare optional topping:** If using it, warm the topping oil in the skillet over medium-low. Toast panko, stirring, until beginning to turn golden, about 2–3 minutes. Add the grated topping garlic and a little salt and stir about 30–60 seconds more until fragrant and golden. Transfer to a bowl. Meanwhile have tomatoes grated, shallots and garlic prepared and pasta water heating.

4. **Cook shrimp:** Add the oil labeled for shrimp to the skillet over medium-high. Cook shrimp in a single layer about 1–2 minutes per side or as needed until firm, pearly and opaque through the center; a fine-tip thermometer inserted into a thick shrimp should read 145°F / 63°C. Use batches if crowded, sharing the oil. Transfer to a clean plate.

5. **Soften aromatics:** Lower heat to medium. Add shallot oil and one-fifth of the butter. Cook shallots about 4–5 minutes until softened, then add sliced garlic and crushed red pepper and stir about 30–45 seconds until fragrant without darkening.

6. **Build tomato sauce:** Add all remaining measured wine and simmer about 2–4 minutes until reduced by roughly half. Add grated tomatoes with their juices and the measured finished stock. Simmer gently about 10–15 minutes until lightly thickened and flowing. Taste before adding salt and pepper.

7. **Cook pasta:** When sauce is ready, stir in baby spinach until wilted. Cook fresh linguine in salted boiling water according to its package, checking early and stopping just short of fully tender. Reserve the listed pasta water before draining. Do not assume every fresh noodle cooks in two minutes.

8. **Finish off heat:** Add pasta to sauce and turn gently, using a small splash of reserved water if needed. When the pasta is tender, remove from heat and add remaining four-fifths of the butter in small pieces, tossing until the coating is smooth. Fold in cooked shrimp and their juices only to warm through.

9. **Season and serve:** Add lemon zest, juice from half the lemon gradually to taste and most of the measured basil. Taste before adding further salt or pepper. Divide into bowls and finish with the remaining basil, optional olive-oil drizzle and optional breadcrumbs. Serve immediately.

Prepare optional topping: If using it, warm the topping oil in the skillet over medium-low. Toast panko, stirring, until beginning to turn golden, about 2–3 minutes. Add the grated topping garlic and a little salt and stir about 30–60 seconds more until fragrant and golden. Transfer to a bowl. Meanwhile have tomatoes grated, shallots and garlic prepared and pasta water heating.

Cook shrimp: Add the oil labeled for shrimp to the skillet over medium-high. Cook shrimp in a single layer about 1–2 minutes per side or as needed until firm, pearly and opaque through the center; a fine-tip thermometer inserted into a thick shrimp should read 145°F / 63°C. Use batches if crowded, sharing the oil. Transfer to a clean plate.

Soften aromatics: Lower heat to medium. Add shallot oil and one-fifth of the butter. Cook shallots about 4–5 minutes until softened, then add sliced garlic and crushed red pepper and stir about 30–45 seconds until fragrant without darkening.

Build tomato sauce: Add all remaining measured wine and simmer about 2–4 minutes until reduced by roughly half. Add grated tomatoes with their juices and the measured finished stock. Simmer gently about 10–15 minutes until lightly thickened and flowing. Taste before adding salt and pepper.

Cook pasta: When sauce is ready, stir in baby spinach until wilted. Cook fresh linguine in salted boiling water according to its package, checking early and stopping just short of fully tender. Reserve the listed pasta water before draining. Do not assume every fresh noodle cooks in two minutes.

Finish off heat: Add pasta to sauce and turn gently, using a small splash of reserved water if needed. When the pasta is tender, remove from heat and add remaining four-fifths of the butter in small pieces, tossing until the coating is smooth. Fold in cooked shrimp and their juices only to warm through.

Season and serve: Add lemon zest, juice from half the lemon gradually to taste and most of the measured basil. Taste before adding further salt or pepper. Divide into bowls and finish with the remaining basil, optional olive-oil drizzle and optional breadcrumbs. Serve immediately.
